FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR --solver-config-dir folder Where a run takes its solver option files (highs.opt, gurobi.opt, ...) from. Wins over the search of a run without it: solver_config/ next to the input database, in the workspace of a GUI project database, in the Spine Toolbox project folder, in the current folder. The run copies the files it used to <work folder>/solve_data/solver_config/. See Where the option files come from. FLEXTOOL_BENDERS_WORKERS --benders-workers positive integer Threads for the region solves of a Benders solve. Unset or 0: the number of regions, at most the number of cores minus one.

docs.title: Process and GUI settings
docs.text: Variable Set to What it does FLEXTOOL_NO_ENV_CHECK 1 Skip FlexTool's start-up checks of the native libraries: the processor check at import flextool (which offers to install the compatible polars build on a processor without AVX2) and the GUI's start-up probe. With the checks skipped, polars may crash on such a processor. FLEXTOOL_NO_UPDATE_CHECK 1 The GUI does not look for a newer FlexTool at start. FLEXTOOL_DPI DPI value, e.g. 144 GUI screen resolution, when the automatic detection is wrong. FLEXTOOL_SLICE systemd slice name Linux: GUI-started runs go into this systemd slice (needs systemd-run). MALLOC_ARENA_MAX integer Linux: cap on glibc's malloc arenas. The FlexTool engine (what flextool-run runs) sets 4, which keeps memory from fragmenting over long runs, unless you set a value. FLEXTOOL_RUN_LOG_MAX_BYTES bytes (default 4194304, 4 MiB; at most 268435456, 256 MiB) Size limit of the run log _run.log in each run's output_parquet/<run>/ folder. A longer log keeps its first 64 KiB and its last this many bytes, with a line that says how many bytes were left out between them. A larger value is taken as 256 MiB. The GUI's log window shows at most 2 MiB of a log: its start and its end, with a line that says how much is left out. FLEXTOOL_MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT seconds, a positive number (default 600, 10 minutes) Windows: how long a migration of an input database (--migrate, flextool-migrate-database, ...) waits for another migration of the same database to finish before it stops with a message naming the lock file <database>.migrate.lock. Not read on Linux or macOS, where the wait has no limit. See Terminal workflow. POLARS_PREFER_PKG 64 / 32 / compat polars' own: which polars build loads first. On a processor with AVX2, import flextool sets the fast build when the compatible build is installed too; a value you set is kept. POLARS_FORCE_PKG 64 / 32 / compat polars' own: load only this build. Also skips FlexTool's processor check. POLARS_MAX_THREADS integer polars' own: size of polars' thread pool. FlexTool uses it in place of its limit of 8, but never above the run's --threads / FLEXTOOL_THREADS. Set it before FlexTool starts; the run header prints the count polars uses.

docs.title: AI assistant
docs.text:
The assistant has no variables of its own: its choices are flags of flextool-assistant and its settings. It reads only the key of the AI service you chose, from that service's variable. A key in the variable wins over a key stored in the system keyring or in the key file, and the chat says where its key came from.

Variable Set to What it does OPENAI_API_KEY key The key of OpenAI for the assistant chat. It wins over a key stored in the system keyring or the key file. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY key The key of Anthropic for the assistant chat. It wins over a key stored in the system keyring or the key file. MISTRAL_API_KEY key The key of Mistral for the assistant chat. It wins over a key stored in the system keyring or the key file. OPENROUTER_API_KEY key The key of OpenRouter for the assistant chat. It wins over a key stored in the system keyring or the key file. GEMINI_API_KEY key The key of Google Gemini for the assistant chat. It wins over a key stored in the system keyring or the key file. OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH tokens, e.g. 16384 Ollama's own: the context length Ollama loads models with. The assistant needs at least 12288 (a smaller context sends no question); set it where the Ollama server starts and restart Ollama. PYTHON_KEYRING_BACKEND backend class keyring's own: which keyring backend stores the keys. FlexTool does not use a backend that stores keys unencrypted.

The provider libraries the assistant uses read more variables of their own: OPENAI_BASE_URL, OPENAI_ORG_ID, OPENAI_PROJECT_ID, OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS, OPENAI_LOG, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS and ANTHROPIC_LOG. FlexTool ignores them: it gives each library the address and the key itself and sends only the request headers it needs, so these variables change nothing. Proxy variables (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, ...) and the system proxy settings apply only to services on the internet, never to a model on this computer or your local network; the chat names the proxy it uses.

FlexTool also reads developer variables (diagnostics, profiling, Benders experiments, test switches). They are described in the developer guide, are not meant for production runs and can change between releases.

docs.title: Excel as input/output
docs.text:
FlexTool stores its data in Spine SQLite databases. The default editor is the Spine database editor, but the same data can also be round-tripped through a single Excel (.xlsx) workbook. The modelling content is identical regardless of which editor you use — only the editing UX changes. The same workbook can be exported, edited, and re-imported any number of times.

Excel is a stand-in for any compatible spreadsheet

Everywhere this page says "Excel", LibreOffice Calc works the same way. FlexTool reads and writes the OpenXML .xlsx format directly via openpyxl; no Microsoft Office installation is required at any step.

docs.title: When to choose Excel over the database editor
docs.text:
• You like to keep your scenario data in spreadsheets.
  • You want a single, self-contained file for review and for sharing.
  • You are doing bulk edits — copy/paste, fill-down, find-and-replace — that are awkward in the relational editor (although you can copy paste from spreadsheet to the Spine DB editor)
  • You need to hand the file to a collaborator who does not have Spine Toolbox installed.

If none of these apply, stay in the Spine database editor: edits are type-checked and committed directly to the DB, with no export/import step.

docs.title: The export, edit, import loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DB[(Spine SQLiteinput DB)]
    DB -->|export| PICK{Parameter-grouppicker}
    PICK -->|template.xlsx| EDIT[Edit in Excelor LibreOffice]
    EDIT -->|import| DB2[(Spine SQLiteinput DB)]
    DB2 --> RUN[Run scenarios]

Exporting produces a workbook whose every sheet carries the metadata needed to read it back later (the v2 self-describing format). Edit the file in any spreadsheet, then import it into a fresh or existing Spine DB. Sheets that were dropped during export — for example because their parameter group was unchecked — simply remain absent from the workbook and are not touched on import.

docs.title: From the FlexTool GUI
docs.text:
In the Add input source dialog, choose Add empty FlexTool input Excel. The GUI initialises a temporary template DB from the master JSON template, reads its parameter groups, and opens the group picker:

  • The picker is DB-driven — the checkbox list is built from the input DB's actual schema, so it always matches the parameters the running FlexTool version knows about.
  • The required groups for a functioning model — timeline, model, solve_basics, basics — are pinned to the top, highlighted, and pre-checked. A hover tooltip explains why they are recommended.
  • Bulk buttons let you switch between Select all, Required only, and Clear all.
  • Colours follow the active ttk theme, so the picker stays readable in both light and dark modes.

Smaller is usually better

Unchecking groups you don't intend to edit produces a slimmer workbook with fewer sheets to navigate. You can always re-export with more groups later — the underlying DB is unchanged.

After clicking OK, the workbook is saved into your project's input_sources directory.

docs.title: From the terminal
docs.text:
The same export is available without the GUI:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite \
    input_template.xlsx

Useful flags:

Flag Effect --groups timeline,model,solve_basics,basics Restrict to the listed parameter groups (same semantics as the GUI picker). Sheets that lose all their columns are dropped, unless listed in always_include_with_groups in export_settings.yaml. --include-advanced Include advanced sheets (solve sequences, periods available, stochastic data) even when empty. --old-format Emit the legacy v1 layout instead of v2 self-describing — only needed for tooling pinned to the older format.

A realistic minimal-template export:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite \
    starter.xlsx \
    --groups timeline,model,solve_basics,basics

docs.title: Editing in Excel or LibreOffice
docs.text:
The exported workbook uses the v2 self-describing format. Each sheet embeds its own header describing what it contains:

  • A definition row labels each column (alternative, entity: node, parameter: ..., index: ..., etc.).
  • A definition column labels metadata rows (description, data type, parameter, ...).
  • Their intersection — the crossing point — is auto-discovered by the reader, so adding rows or columns above the data block is safe as long as the header keywords stay intact.

A few practical notes:

  • Sheets whose parameter group was not selected at export time are simply absent. Re-export later if you decide to start editing them.
  • When any parameter on a sheet carries a database default, a default-value row is rendered above the data. Map- and Array- typed defaults are stringified for display; you should not normally need to edit this row.
  • A navigate sheet acts as an index/table of contents and the schema version is recorded there as well. The importer skips navigate and version on read.
  • Tab colours mirror the navigate groups configured in export_settings.yaml, which makes related sheets easy to spot.

Locale and scientific notation

LibreOffice and Excel can disagree on number locale (comma vs. dot) and on whether very large or very small numbers are rendered in scientific notation. If you exchange files across both tools, lock the spreadsheet locale to one convention (typically English/US) and the column format to plain Number for data columns.

docs.title: From the FlexTool GUI
docs.text: Add the edited .xlsx as an input source via the Add input source dialog. The GUI treats a workbook the same way it treats a Spine DB input — when a scenario runs, FlexTool reads the workbook and feeds the merged data to the engine. If you prefer a persistent DB, use the Convert action to materialise the workbook into a Spine SQLite file once, then keep editing the DB directly.

docs.title: From the terminal
docs.text:
For v2 (self-describing) workbooks — the canonical format going forward:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input \
    edited.xlsx \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite

This import first deletes the data of the target database (entities, alternatives, scenarios and parameter values) and then writes the workbook's data. To add a workbook's data to a database instead, give --no-purge: see How to replace a dataset and keep the old one as an alternative.

For v1 specification-driven workbooks — kept for backwards compatibility:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_tabular_input \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite \
    --tabular-file-path edited.xlsx

v2 is the canonical format

New code paths and the GUI's Add empty FlexTool input Excel action always produce v2 workbooks. The v1 reader stays available for files produced before the self-describing layout was introduced, and a separate reader handles legacy .xlsm files from very old FlexTool releases — but no new features are being added to either of them.

docs.title: Round-trip and version control
docs.text: On a well-formed DB, export followed by re-import is idempotent at the modelling-content level: only the edits you actually make should show up as a meaningful diff. That makes Excel a reasonable medium for PR-based review of model data — reviewers can open the workbook, flip through the sheets, and compare two checked-in versions side by side.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Very large time-series sheets (tens of thousands of rows) render slowly in both Excel and LibreOffice. Consider editing them as CSV or keeping them in the database when bulk data is involved.
  • The --groups flag drops sheets whose columns are all filtered out; if you need a structural sheet to stay around even when empty, add it to always_include_with_groups in export_settings.yaml.
  • Multi-dimensional parameters (2d_map, 3d_map, 4d_map) are laid out with extra index columns; reshape these with care, and re-export if you want a clean baseline.
  • Excel and LibreOffice may disagree on number locale and scientific notation — see the warning above.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Spine database editor — the default alternative editor.
  • FlexTool GUI — where the Excel-related actions live.
  • Terminal / CLI — for scripted export and import.
  • Choosing an interface — high-level comparison.

docs.title: FlexTool GUI
docs.text:
The FlexTool GUI is a standalone Tkinter application and the primary way to use FlexTool. It manages projects, input sources, scenario execution, and output generation in a single window. Start it from the FlexTool installation directory with:

python -m flextool.gui

See Install with FlexTool GUI for installation, and Architecture for what the GUI does under the hood. Spine Toolbox is the workflow-oriented alternative interface, and Excel / LibreOffice is the parallel spreadsheet editor for the same input sources. For headless / CI use see the Terminal CLI.

docs.title: Workflow at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    P[Projectload / create]
    I[Input sources.sqlite or .xlsx]
    A[Available scenariosfiltered by checked sources]
    Q[Execution queue]
    X[Executed scenariosparquet on disk]
    O[Outputs tablepngs / Excel / CSV / comparison]
    R[Result viewerto browse directly]

    P --> I --> A
    A -- Add checked --> Q
    Q -- Execute --> X
    X --> O
    X --> R

    I -. Edit .-> E[Spine DB editoror Excel / LibreOffice]
    Q -. Auto-genafter each run .-> O

Editing an input source jumps out to the Spine database editor or a spreadsheet application. The Auto-gen column on the Outputs table controls which derived artefacts are produced automatically after each successful execution.

docs.title: Top bar: Project
docs.text:
Each project lives in projects/<name>/ and owns its own input sources, execution history, and settings.yaml. The Project drop-down switches between projects; Project menu opens a popup with:

  • Manage projects… — create / rename / delete projects, and Export… / Import… a project package (see Sharing a project).
  • UI font size — radio choices (9, 10, 11, 12, 14 pt) plus Custom… to enter any integer between 6 and 32. The chosen size is applied live to every named Tk font (body / menu / heading / tooltip / fixed) and persisted to projects/projects.yaml. See Display and fonts.
  • Reset window layout — clears saved window sizes and sash positions for the result viewer and execution window. Any open viewer or execution window is closed; their defaults apply the next time they open.

F2 or double-click on the drop-down renames the current project. The most recently used project is reopened on the next launch.

docs.title: Input sources
docs.text:
The Input sources panel lists every .sqlite and .xlsx file in the project's input_sources/ directory plus any registered external references. Each input source contributes one or more scenarios.

Action Effect Add Add a new .xlsx or .sqlite source. Imports are migrated to the current FlexTool DB version automatically. Edit SQLite opens in the Spine database editor; Excel opens in the OS default spreadsheet app. Double-click does the same. Convert Convert an .xlsx input source to a SQLite database. Delete Remove the selected source from the project. External references unlink the reference; the file on disk is untouched. Refresh Rescan input_sources/ on disk.

The checkbox column decides whether the source's scenarios appear in Available scenarios. The # column is the source's persistent number — it is assigned the first time the source is seen and stored in settings.yaml (input_source_numbers). When a source is deleted its number is freed only when no executed-scenario folder on disk still references it; the next new source picks the lowest free number, so a deleted slot is reused once its outputs are also cleaned up. Hovering over a row with an error, empty, "editing" or frozen status shows a Toplevel tooltip explaining the status; external references show their POSIX path relative to the project root and a reminder that Delete only removes the reference.

Right-click a row for the same actions as the buttons. Column headers sort the list; the active sort direction is shown by a small arrow.

docs.title: Migration and frozen databases
docs.text:
When the list is refreshed, a .sqlite source older than this FlexTool (or at the current version but with an older SpineDB schema, e.g. after a spinedb_api update) is migrated to the current version: a source in input_sources/ without asking (a safety copy is kept until the migration has finished), an external reference after asking whether to migrate it in place or copy it into the project first. Checking the version reads the file read-only, so nothing in the file changes before you agree. Adding scenarios to the execution list, or opening Calibrate investments, checks their sources again and migrates any that changed since the last refresh; FlexTool does not run a database that is not at the current version.

A released model can be frozen so that it is never migrated in place without asking: right-click a .sqlite source → Freeze database… and give a label, e.g. Reference case 1.0 (at most 170 characters). Only a database at the current version can be frozen. A frozen source shows ❄ in the status column; the tooltip shows the label, the version and the date it was frozen. Unfreeze database removes the marker. The same can be done in a terminal with flextool-freeze (see Freeze a released database).

When a frozen source is older than this FlexTool (or has an older SpineDB schema), the refresh asks what to do with it. A frozen source newer than this FlexTool is left as it is; running it asks you to update FlexTool.

  • Migrate a copy (default): the copy, input_sources/<name>_v<version>.sqlite, is migrated and added as a new input source. It has its own source number, so its results go to new result folders. The copy is not frozen; it records the label, the old version and the SHA-256 of the frozen file it was made from. The frozen file stays unchanged and is not asked about again while the copy is there.
  • Migrate in place: after a second confirm, the frozen file itself is migrated. Its frozen marker is kept with the new version.
  • Cancel: the source is not migrated. Until the project is reopened (or FlexTool restarted) it shows ❄✗ (frozen, older version), its scenarios are not listed and it is not asked about again; right-click → Migrate frozen database… asks again.

Editing a frozen database in the database editor is not prevented; a frozen database is protected from migration only.

Excel input is described in Excel interface; the Spine database editor is described in Spine database.

docs.title: Add empty FlexTool input Excel
docs.text:
When you choose Add → empty Excel, the parameter-group picker dialog opens. Every parameter group from the FlexTool template is listed as a checkbox row. Required groups (currently timeline, model, solve_basics, basics) are highlighted at the top of the list with a yellow tint and a hover tooltip explaining that they are required for a functioning model, but can still be unchecked when assembling a model from several input sources. Bulk-action buttons select all, select required only, or clear all. The highlight colour adapts to the active dark / light theme.

See Excel interface for the resulting file structure.

docs.title: Convert a FlexTool 2.0 model
docs.text: Add → Convert from FlexTool 2.0 input file asks for the FlexTool 2 input data file (one of the master workbook's InputData/*.xlsm), then whether to import its sensitivities too; if yes, pick the FlexTool 2 master workbook (the one with the Sensitivity definitions sheet). The sensitivities become alternatives and scenarios on top of base. Converting an .xlsx FlexTool 2 file in the input sources list asks the same question. The conversion runs as one job in the Execution window: it imports the data and the sensitivities, migrates the database to the current version and ends with an import report that lists, by topic, every FlexTool 2 input that was not carried over or works differently in FlexTool 4, with the entities that use it and what to do. The database is written in the project's intermediate folder and moved into input_sources only when the conversion has succeeded; the new input source and its scenarios are then ticked. See Import old FlexTool v2 files for what the report lists and how must-run (fix / min / max generation) and storage start / finish are translated.

docs.title: Available scenarios [V]
docs.text:
Lists every scenario found in the checked input sources. The header text [V] is the keyboard shortcut: press V to focus the list.

Key Action V Focus the Available scenarios list A Select all rows Space Check / uncheck the selected rows Alt-A Add checked scenarios to the execution queue F9 Same as Alt-A Click column header Sort by that column Right-click Check selected / Add selected to execution jobs

The Add checked scenarios to the execution list button queues every checked row. Scenarios already pending or running are skipped.

docs.title: Executed scenarios [X]
docs.text:
A row appears here as soon as a scenario produces a parquet result tree under output_parquet/<scenario>_<src#>/. Parquet is the canonical result format — every other output is derived from it.

Key Action X Focus the Executed scenarios list E Check / uncheck all rows Space Check / uncheck the selected rows Right-click Check selected / View results / Delete irrevocably Click the View column Open the scenario's plot directory

Rows whose # (source number) no longer matches any current input source are shown greyed (foreground #888888) and tagged orphan. The row stays so the outputs are visible and can be deleted explicitly with Delete selected results irrevocably.

docs.title: Outputs (unified table)
docs.text:
The Outputs table replaces the older Auto-generate checkbox group and Output actions button column with a single bordered widget. Each row covers one derived artefact:

Column Meaning Output Display name (Scenario pngs, Scenario Excels, Scenario csvs, Comparison pngs, Comparison Excel). Auto-gen Checkbox: produce this output automatically after every successful scenario run. Persisted to settings.yaml. Status Clickable cell. Blank = not run, ✓ = produced, ⊘ = last attempt failed, animated spinner = currently running. Clicking the cell (re-)generates the output for the checked executed scenarios. Action Show opens the output folder in the system file manager; for Comparison Excel the label is Open because the target is a single file.

Parquet is always written for an executed scenario, regardless of any Auto-gen tick. Auto-gen only controls the derived artefacts; png / Excel / CSV outputs can always be (re-)generated later by clicking the Status cell of the relevant row.

docs.title: Side menu
docs.text:
The narrow column to the left of the Outputs table holds five user-tunable controls. It is split into a top group and a bottom group by a flexible spacer:

  • Save memory — checkbox that passes --save-memory to scenario runs. After the LP is built, polar-high's polars / numpy LP source is dropped, the LP is written to a temp MPS file, and HiGHS solves it in a separate subprocess (via cmd_solve_mps) so the solver's working set lives outside the FlexTool address space. Trades ~+90 s I/O per sub-solve for ~5–10 GB lower peak RSS. Also disables warm-LP reuse across cascade iterations (every sub-solve cold-rebuilds).
  • Debug — checkbox that passes --debug --csv-dump to scenario runs. --debug turns on verbose engine logging; --csv-dump writes the cascade's processed inputs to disk after the last sub-solve for inspection.
  • OS theme / Dark / Light — theme radio buttons. Takes effect on the next launch and is persisted to projects/projects.yaml.
  • Png settings — opens the plot configuration dialog (see Png settings).
  • Execution jobs — opens the Execution jobs window.
  • Results viewer — opens the Result viewer. When the viewer is already open the button relabels to Update view scenarios.

docs.title: Png settings
docs.text:
The Png settings dialog has separate sections for scenario and scenario-comparison plots:

  • Start timestep — first timestep to include in the plot range.
  • Duration — number of timesteps to plot (0 = until the end of the data).
  • Plot config file — YAML config defining what plots to render and how. The shipped default is the bundled flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml.
  • Active configs — checkbox list of named configurations from the chosen file. Only checked configs are rendered.
  • Dispatch plots (comparison section only) — toggle whether dispatch time-series plots are included in comparisons. In a multi-period scenario the periods follow one another along the time axis (the period names below the time steps), with a gap where a period does not continue the previous one; Start timestep and Duration count the time steps across the periods, so the default window shows only the start of the first period of a long run. The companion Edit dispatch plots… button opens a YAML editor for the dispatch config.
  • Just one file per plot — render only the first file of a plot that is split into several files (a quick overview).
  • Write plotted data (CSV) — also write the data drawn in each plot as a CSV file next to its image, with the same name (see Plotted data as CSV). A write_plot_data: true in the project's plot_settings.yaml turns this on whatever the checkbox says; the checkbox then shows as checked and greyed out, with "on in plot_settings.yaml" next to it.

The dialog is purely a configuration step; rendering happens via the Status cell of the relevant Outputs row (or automatically through Auto-gen).

docs.title: Execution jobs
docs.text: The Execution jobs window is a separate Toplevel dedicated to queue management. It coexists with the main window — actions in the main window keep working while the jobs window is open.

docs.title: Resource controls
docs.text:
The top row of the window holds five spinboxes; each is a per-project setting persisted to settings.yaml. Their defaults are deliberately conservative — one job at a time, one thread per run, auto-budget — so the GUI never starves the host machine by default:

Control Default Meaning Max. parallel executions 1 Number of scenario subprocesses that may run concurrently. Threads per run 1 Threads of each run: FlexTool's data processing and the solver. Passed to each subprocess as --threads; runs executed in parallel each use this many. Memory budget/job (GB, 0=auto) 0.0 (auto) Soft target. Jobs are allowed to exceed it when memory is available. Only enforced when free RAM drops below the reserve and swap growth reaches the allowance — the watchdog then kills whichever running job is most over its budget. In auto mode, every successful run records its measured peak × 1.5 as the budget for the next run, persisted under scenario_resource_history. First-run fallback is (system memory − reserve) ÷ max parallel jobs. Min free RAM (GB) 0.5 Floor for system free memory. The watchdog acts only when this floor is breached and the swap allowance is exhausted. Allow swap (GB) 0.0 How much swap growth to tolerate, measured since FlexTool started (pre-existing swap is ignored). 0 means kill as soon as free RAM dips below the reserve.

Together these settings let FlexTool absorb oversized-scenario pressure without taking the host system down.

docs.title: Memory enforcement
docs.text: On all platforms the in-process MemoryWatchdog (5-second poll) is the sole memory enforcer. It tracks per-job peak RSS and kills the most-over-budget running job only when free RAM falls below Min free RAM and swap growth reaches Allow swap. A killed-for-memory job shows a "⚠" suffix on its Peak GB cell. On Linux every job is launched via a transient systemd-run --user --scope; the FLEXTOOL_SLICE environment variable can place the scope in a user-defined cgroup slice (e.g. heavy.slice) for scheduling isolation. No MemoryHigh / MemoryMax property is set — they would stall or abort large polars collect_all calls. Windows and macOS launch the subprocess directly.

docs.title: Jobs table and progress pane
docs.text:
The horizontal split has the Jobs tree on the left and a per-job log on the right; the sash position is persisted globally. The jobs tree has columns Status icon, source #, Scenario, Peak GB, and Timestamp. Failed and killed rows are tagged failed and rendered bright red (#ff3333).

A status label at the bottom of the window shows running/max threads | used/total GB. When pending jobs are being held back the label appends | Thread limited (max workers reached) or | Memory limited (admission blocked by the reserve) and the label text turns theme-aware red — #c62828 on the light theme, #ff6b6b on dark / OS-theme. The colour clears as soon as there are no pending jobs or the limit is no longer active.

docs.title: Per-job actions
docs.text:
• ▲ / ▼ (or PgUp / PgDn) — reorder pending jobs.
  • Kill selected — terminate selected running or pending jobs.
  • Remove selected — drop finished or killed rows from the list.
  • Pause executions / Continue executions — pause the scheduler so already-running jobs finish but no new ones start.
  • Kill all — terminate everything that is running or pending.

The log pane appends lines as the selected job produces stdout and auto-scrolls only when the user is already at (or near) the bottom; scrolling up to read older output suppresses the auto-scroll.

docs.title: Result viewer
docs.text:
The Result viewer is its own window. It reads scenarios directly from parquet, so navigation is live and is not constrained by the Png settings (start timestep, duration, etc.); the Png settings only affect pre-rendered PNG output.

Key Action S Focus the Scenarios list P Focus the Plots list V Switch to single-scenario view X Switch to comparison view ↑ / ↓ Navigate scenarios / plots ← / → Previous / next variant in the current plot PgUp / PgDn Previous / next variant (alias) Ctrl-A Select all comparison rows Alt-↑ / Alt-↓ Reorder comparison rows Tab Cycle focus between the three panes

Click the Results viewer button in the side menu, or View results in the right-click menu of an executed scenario, to open it. Closing the main window also closes the viewer.

Two behaviour notes worth knowing:

  • Style scoping. The plot tree's selection highlight is mapped on a dedicated PlotTree.Treeview ttk style, so opening the viewer no longer overwrites the main window's global Treeview selection colours. The main window's blue selection survives a viewer open / close cycle.
  • Off-UI-thread figure builds. Plan-path figure construction (build_figure_from_plan) runs on a background executor. Most plots are essentially instant, but bar plots with hundreds of items per file can take tens of seconds; running them off the Tk main thread keeps the GUI responsive during the render and avoids the "freeze" the user would otherwise see.

docs.title: Display and fonts
docs.text:
All text-rendering widgets share six named Tk fonts that are configured at startup from GlobalSettings.font_size_pt (body / menu / text — default 10 pt) and GlobalSettings.code_font_size_pt (TkFixedFont used by logs; 0 = auto = body + 2). Headings are body + 2 pt bold; tooltips are body − 1. Sizes are POINTS, so Tk's scaling factor DPI-scales them automatically.

Changing the size via Project menu → UI font size calls setup_fonts and recomputes the Treeview row height live — every widget that uses the named fonts updates without restart. The new size is persisted to projects/projects.yaml.

Per-monitor DPI. When the main window is moved between monitors with different scaling factors, the <Configure> handler reads winfo fpixels 1i and, if the effective DPI has changed by more than 10 %, re-applies the configured font sizes so points render at the new DPI. Already-placed widgets keep their pixel positions until the user resizes or re-opens the window; this is intentionally a partial fix — it beats leaving text frozen-tiny or frozen-huge until restart. If auto-detection picks the wrong monitor, setting FLEXTOOL_DPI at startup forces a value.

docs.title: Sharing a project
docs.text:
A project can be sent to another computer as one file, <Name>_<YYYYMMDD>.flextool.zip. In Manage projects… select the project and click Export…:

  • Always in the package (greyed): the input sources, settings.yaml without the settings of this machine (execution limits, parallel executions, learned memory budgets), plot_settings.yaml, and the solver option files (*.opt) of the workspace's solver_config folder.
  • Copy external input files into the package (on by default): input files that the project reads from outside its folder are copied into input_sources/ of the package. They keep their source numbers, so a shipped result base_2 and a re-run of the same scenario on the other computer pair up.
  • Result runs: tick the runs to include, or use None / All. The size of each run is shown, and the total is the uncompressed size (parquet files barely compress). A run whose input file changed after the run is marked input changed after the run in amber: its results do not match the input being shipped. The package lists such runs. A run that is still being written — by this window, Spine Toolbox or the terminal, as its run record says — is marked running in red and cannot be exported until it ends. The viewer's shared y-axis ranges (output_parquet/_axis_bounds.json) go with the package cut to the ticked runs, so the names and ranges of the other runs stay home.
  • Run records: each result run has a run record (_run_status.json) and a run log (_run.log) that show this computer's folder paths, user name and host name. Remove this computer's folder paths, user name and host name from the run records, and leave the run logs out is on by default: the project folder becomes <project>, the home folder ~, other folders <path>/, and the host and user <host> / <user>; the verdict, times and solver stay. Untick it to ship the records and logs as they are.
  • Plots, CSV and Excel outputs, results.sqlite and the scratch folders (work/, converted/, intermediate/) are not packaged. The plots and the CSV and Excel outputs are made again from the results on the other computer; results.sqlite is written only when a scenario runs, or with flextool-write-outputs --write-methods spinedb from the terminal.

A .sqlite input that a program may be writing to (it has a -journal or -wal file next to it) is copied through SQLite, so the package holds a consistent database; otherwise it is copied byte for byte and keeps its SHA-256. A file that changes while it is being copied stops the export, and an input open in Excel is noted. File names that Windows cannot hold (CON, NUL, COM1…, the characters < > : " | ? *, a trailing dot or space, two names that differ only in case) stop the export with the names to change, because a package must unpack on Windows, macOS and Linux. When the package file exists already, Export asks before replacing it. The solver .opt files and the plot settings travel as they are: if they hold a folder path of this computer, the receiver has to change it.

Export is refused while the project has running or pending jobs. Frozen databases go into the package as they are and stay frozen. A manifest.json in the package records the FlexTool, polar-high, HiGHS, polars and spinedb_api versions, the data version and frozen marker of each input database, and the SHA-256, size and modification time of every file.

To import, click Import… in Manage projects… and pick the package. The dialog shows the project name, when and with which FlexTool it was made, the data version of each database and the result runs, without unpacking anything. The name is filled in from the package; when a project of that name exists (compared without case), the first free <Name>_2, <Name>_3… is suggested, and Import stays disabled while the name is taken. Warnings are shown in amber: a package made with a newer FlexTool (results and inputs may use features this version lacks), and databases that are migrated when the project opens (FlexTool asks first for a frozen one, as for any frozen database). A database newer than this FlexTool cannot be opened, and Import is disabled until FlexTool is updated. An input that was outside the project folder and not copied in is named: its scenarios cannot be run again until the receiver adds that file. Every checksum, every name and the free disk space are checked before anything is written; files keep their modification times, so the results are not reported as made from a changed input (a FAT32 disk keeps times only to 2 s, so there a result can show as made from a changed input). On success the new project opens; an import that was stopped leaves a hidden .<name>.partial folder, which is not listed as a project and is removed by the next import of that name.

The shipped solver options are unpacked to imported_solver_config/ in the project; the workspace's own .opt files are never changed. The import message says whether they differ from the workspace's, with the lines that differ. To run with the shipped options, copy imported_solver_config/*.opt to the workspace's solver_config folder, or start FlexTool with FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR set to the project's imported_solver_config folder. The same can be done from the terminal with flextool-project (see Sharing a project).

docs.title: Where things live on disk
docs.text:
• projects/projects.yaml — global settings (theme, font sizes, last project, jobs-window sash).
  • projects/<project>/settings.yaml — project settings: Auto-gen flags, Debug / Save-memory checkboxes, per-project execution_limits and max_workers, input_source_numbers, bare_output_owners, scenario_resource_history, viewer state.
  • projects/<project>/input_sources/ — .xlsx and .sqlite input files.
  • solver_config/ in the FlexTool workspace (the folder FlexTool is started from) — the solver option files (highs.opt…) that every run and calibration started from the GUI uses (the GUI passes the folder to each run as --solver-config-dir, so it does not matter where a project's input database is); $FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR, set before the GUI starts, points runs at another folder. Each run copies the files it used to projects/<project>/work/<run>/solve_data/solver_config/. An imported project keeps the options it was shipped with in projects/<project>/imported_solver_config/.
  • output_parquet/<scenario>_<src#>/ — canonical results, always written. New writes always carry the _<src#> suffix so the folder name itself records which source produced it. Pre-existing bare-name folders from older projects are still readable via bare_output_owners; the GUI flags rows whose source no longer exists as orphan.
  • output_plots/<scenario>_<src#>/ — PNGs from scenario plots.
  • output_excel/<scenario>_<src#>.xlsx — Excel export of one scenario.
  • output_csv/<scenario>_<src#>/ — CSV export of one scenario.
  • output_plot_comparisons/ — comparison plots and Excel workbook.
  • output_parquet_comparison/ — parquet feeding the comparison plots and viewer.

docs.text:

docs.title: Install FlexTool with the FlexTool GUI
docs.text:
This page describes how to install IRENA FlexTool using the built-in FlexTool GUI. This is the simplest installation path — it does not require Spine Toolbox (though you can optionally add it).

For the Spine Toolbox installation path, see Install with Spine Toolbox.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.11 (see requires-python in pyproject.toml for up-to-date requirements)
  • 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, Linux or macOS. Windows 7 and 8.1 cannot run FlexTool 4 (its libraries need Windows 10). If a library reports "DLL load failed" on Windows, install the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable (x64, https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe).
  • Processor (Intel/AMD): at least SSE4.2 and POPCNT (x86-64-v2: Intel Core i3/i5/i7 from 2009 on, AMD FX or Ryzen; Core 2 and Phenom II are not supported). AVX2 (most processors from 2013 on) runs the fastest build. Without AVX2 (for example Celeron/Pentium laptops up to about 2021, Intel Core before 2013, AMD FX), FlexTool uses the compatible build of the polars data library (about 10-30% slower): add the compat extra (pip install "flextool[compat]"). Without it, FlexTool says why it needs the compatible build and gives the pip command: in a terminal it asks before running it, the GUI asks at startup (in its terminal, or in a small yes/no dialog when started from a shortcut) before it loads polars and closes if you decline, a Spine Toolbox tool stops with the message, and flextool-update installs it. Run python -m flextool.env_check to see what FlexTool found.
  • Git (optional, but recommended for easy updates)

docs.title: 1. Install Python
docs.text:
Download and install Python from python.org. Make sure to check "Add Python to PATH" during installation on Windows.

Note: If you already have Python in your PATH (check with python --version in a terminal) and it is older than 3.11, you need to install a supported version. On Windows, you may need to use the full path to the new Python (e.g. C:\Python312\python.exe) unless you update your PATH to point to it.

docs.title: 2. Install Git (optional)
docs.text:
Git makes it easy to update FlexTool in the future. The alternative is to download zip files manually.

  • Download and install from https://git-scm.com/downloads or use your system's package manager.
  • Windows tips: During git installation, the defaults are fine for most questions. Exceptions:
  • Text editor: switch from VIM to Nano (scroll upward) — unless you know and like VIM.
  • Use Windows' default console window (unless you know what you are doing).

docs.title: 3. Get FlexTool
docs.text:
Either clone with Git (recommended): 

git clone https://github.com/irena-flextool/flextool.git

Or download and unzip from GitHub.

docs.title: 4. Enter the FlexTool directory
docs.text:
All the remaining steps must be run from inside the FlexTool directory:

cd flextool

(Substitute the extracted folder name if you used the zip download.)

docs.title: 5. Create a Virtual Environment
docs.text:
Linux (Debian / Ubuntu / Mint): The system Python may not include venv with pip by default. Install it first:

sudo apt install python3-venv

Create a virtual environment inside the FlexTool directory:

python -m venv .venv

Activate the virtual environment:

Linux / macOS: 

source .venv/bin/activate

Windows: 

.venv\Scripts\activate

docs.title: 6. Install FlexTool
docs.text:
Recommended — install FlexTool with Spine Toolbox (includes Spine DB Editor for editing input databases):

pip install ".[toolbox]"

This installs FlexTool with the built-in GUI, HiGHS solver (via highspy), and Spine Toolbox with its dependencies (Spine DB Editor, Spine Items, Spine Engine, PySide6, etc.).

docs.title: Lighter weight install (without Spine Toolbox)
docs.text:
If you prefer a leaner installation or have issues installing Spine Toolbox dependencies:

pip install .

This installs FlexTool and the GUI, but without Spine DB Editor. You can run scenarios and view results, but editing .sqlite input sources from the GUI requires Spine DB Editor. You can upgrade to the full install at any time by running the recommended command above.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
If you do not need a clone of the source tree, FlexTool can be installed directly from PyPI:

pip install flextool                # lean / GUI only
pip install "flextool[toolbox]"     # with Spine Toolbox

Test builds. TestPyPI sometimes carries pre-release test builds that are not yet on PyPI. To try one, point pip at the TestPyPI index, keep PyPI as a fallback for dependencies that are not mirrored on TestPyPI, and add --pre so pip accepts a pre-release:

pip install --pre \
    --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
    --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ \
    flextool

The PyPI install does not include the update_flextool.py initialization script or the example databases that live alongside it. If you need those — or want the update_flextool.py migration workflow described below — install from a clone instead.

docs.title: 7. Initialize FlexTool
docs.text:
Create the necessary database files and templates:

python update_flextool.py --skip-git

docs.title: 8. Verify the install
docs.text:
Confirm the CLI is wired up:

flextool-run --help

This should print the FlexTool CLI usage. If it does, the venv is healthy.

docs.title: 9. Launch FlexTool
docs.text:
Start the FlexTool GUI:

flextool-gui

(Equivalent to python -m flextool.gui.)

If you also installed Spine Toolbox, you can launch it with:

spinetoolbox

Then open FlexTool project from the menu: File... Open project... Choose FlexTool folder.

docs.title: Updating FlexTool
docs.text:
FlexTool update process will get the latest FlexTool version and then run a migration script that updates the databases to the latest version.

If you installed with Git:

cd flextool
source .venv/bin/activate   # Linux / macOS
.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
python update_flextool.py

If you installed from a zip file, download the latest zip, extract it over the existing directory, and run:

python update_flextool.py --skip-git

docs.title: From the GUI
docs.text:
Click Update FlexTool… in the top-right of the main window (next to UI settings…). FlexTool detects how it is installed and runs the right upgrade automatically — git pull plus an editable reinstall for a git checkout, or pip install --upgrade for a PyPI install — and streams the output to the Execution window. Restart FlexTool when it finishes for the new version to take effect.

The dialog has an Install Spine Toolbox checkbox. Spine Toolbox is a large, optional dependency that is required to open .sqlite input sources in the Spine DB Editor; leave it unticked if you do not need it. (It is ticked by default when Spine Toolbox is already installed, so updating keeps it.)

docs.title: Update notifications
docs.text:
By default FlexTool makes one lightweight check at startup — against PyPI, or your git remote for a git checkout — for a newer version. When one is available the Update FlexTool… button is highlighted. The check fails silently if you are offline or the network is restricted.

To disable it, untick Check for updates on startup in the Update FlexTool dialog (the choice is remembered), or set the environment variable FLEXTOOL_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to suppress the check entirely.

docs.title: "command not found: flextool-gui" / "flextool-run"
docs.text: Make sure your virtual environment is activated. The flextool-gui and flextool-run console scripts are only on PATH when the venv where FlexTool was installed is active.

docs.title: "No module named '_tkinter'" (macOS / Linux)
docs.text:
The FlexTool GUI uses tkinter, which is part of Python's standard library but depends on Tcl/Tk system libraries. Some platforms do not bundle these by default.

macOS (Homebrew Python): Install the Tcl/Tk binding for your Python version:

brew install python-tk@3.12

Replace 3.12 with your Python version (check with python3 --version).

Linux (Debian / Ubuntu): Install the system package:

sudo apt install python3-tk

docs.title: Import errors or missing modules
docs.text:
Try reinstalling: 

pip install . --force-reinstall

docs.title: Solver issues
docs.text:
FlexTool uses HiGHS by default — installed automatically via the highspy Python bindings, no additional setup needed.

It is also possible to wire in commercial solvers (e.g. CPLEX) for licensed users; see the documentation for details.

docs.title: Install FlexTool with Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
This page describes the Spine Toolbox installation path for IRENA FlexTool. Spine Toolbox is the heavier, multi-tool integration path: it wraps FlexTool as one node in a directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflow alongside other tools and data stores.

Most users do not need this path. If your work is centred on FlexTool itself — building scenarios, running them, inspecting results — follow Install with FlexTool GUI instead. The Spine Toolbox path is intended for users who already use Spine Toolbox or who combine FlexTool with other Spine-based models. See Choosing an interface for the side-by-side comparison.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.11 (see requires-python in pyproject.toml for up-to-date requirement)
  • 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, Linux or macOS. Windows 7 and 8.1 cannot run FlexTool 4 (its libraries need Windows 10). If a library reports "DLL load failed" on Windows, install the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable (x64, https://aka.ms/vs/17/release/vc_redist.x64.exe).
  • Processor (Intel/AMD): at least SSE4.2 and POPCNT (x86-64-v2: Intel Core i3/i5/i7 from 2009 on, AMD FX or Ryzen; Core 2 and Phenom II are not supported). AVX2 (most processors from 2013 on) runs the fastest build. Without AVX2 (for example Celeron/Pentium laptops up to about 2021, Intel Core before 2013, AMD FX), FlexTool uses the compatible build of the polars data library (about 10-30% slower): add the compat extra (pip install "flextool[compat]"). Without it, FlexTool says why it needs the compatible build and gives the pip command: in a terminal it asks before running it, the GUI asks at startup (in its terminal, or in a small yes/no dialog when started from a shortcut) before it loads polars and closes if you decline, a Spine Toolbox tool stops with the message, and flextool-update installs it. Run python -m flextool.env_check to see what FlexTool found.
  • Git (optional, but recommended for easy updates)

docs.title: 1. Install Python
docs.text:
Download and install Python from python.org. Make sure to check "Add Python to PATH" during installation on Windows.

Note: If you already have Python in your PATH (check with python --version in a terminal) and it is older than 3.11, you need to install a supported version. On Windows, you may need to use the full path to the new Python (e.g. C:\Python312\python.exe) unless you update your PATH to point to it.

docs.title: 2. Install Git (optional)
docs.text:
Git makes it easy to update FlexTool in the future. The alternative is to download zip files manually.

  • Download and install from https://git-scm.com/downloads or use your system's package manager.
  • Windows tips: During git installation, the defaults are fine for most questions. Exceptions:
  • Text editor: switch from VIM to Nano (scroll upward) — unless you know and like VIM.
  • Use Windows' default console window (unless you know what you are doing).

docs.title: 3. Get FlexTool
docs.text:
Either clone with Git (recommended): 

git clone https://github.com/irena-flextool/flextool.git

Or download and unzip from GitHub.

docs.title: 4. Enter the FlexTool directory
docs.text:
All the remaining steps must be run from inside the FlexTool directory:

cd flextool

(Substitute the extracted folder name if you used the zip download.)

docs.title: 5. Create a Virtual Environment
docs.text:
Linux (Debian / Ubuntu / Mint): The system Python may not include venv with pip by default. Install it first:

sudo apt install python3-venv

Create a virtual environment inside the FlexTool directory:

python -m venv .venv

Activate the virtual environment:

Linux / macOS: 

source .venv/bin/activate

Windows: 

.venv\Scripts\activate

docs.title: 6. Install FlexTool with Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
Install FlexTool and the toolbox extra. This pulls in Spine Toolbox alongside FlexTool's core dependencies (declared in pyproject.toml):

pip install ".[toolbox]"

The extra brings in Spine Toolbox itself, Spine DB Editor, Spine Items, Spine Engine, PySide6, and the rest of Spine Toolbox's runtime stack. On a slow link you may want --timeout=10000.

If you would rather install from PyPI than work from a clone, the same extra works there:

pip install "flextool[toolbox]"

docs.title: 7. Initialize FlexTool
docs.text:
Create the necessary database files and templates (skip the --skip-git flag if you cloned with git and want update_flextool.py to fetch upstream changes too):

python update_flextool.py --skip-git

docs.title: 8. Verify the install
docs.text:
Confirm the FlexTool CLI is wired up:

flextool-run --help

This should print the FlexTool CLI usage. FlexTool runs independently of Spine Toolbox, so this check passes even before Toolbox is launched — useful for isolating environment issues from Toolbox UI issues.

docs.title: 9. Launch Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
spinetoolbox

Then open the FlexTool project from the menu: File... Open project... and choose the FlexTool directory (not a file inside it).

docs.title: Updating FlexTool
docs.text:
The update flow mirrors Install with FlexTool GUI: pull the latest FlexTool, then migrate the input databases.

If you installed with Git:

cd flextool
source .venv/bin/activate   # Linux / macOS
.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
python update_flextool.py

If you installed from a zip file, download the latest zip, extract it over the existing directory, and run:

python update_flextool.py --skip-git

update_flextool.py brings the databases to the current schema version without destroying data (a backup is still good practice):

  • it migrates the database selected as Input data in the project, input_data.sqlite and templates/input_data_template.sqlite;
  • it rebuilds the example databases (templates/examples.sqlite, templates/time_settings_only.sqlite and the databases in how to example databases/) from the current templates.

To migrate any other database separately:

python migrate_database.py path/to/database.sqlite

Spine Toolbox itself updates separately. With the FlexTool venv active:

pip install --upgrade spinetoolbox

docs.title: Update troubleshooting
docs.text:
• If git reports merge conflicts, it is almost always because the template files were modified locally. Restore the tree with git restore . and re-run git pull, then python update_flextool.py.
  • results.sqlite only ever receives additive changes (to protect data), which leaves old parameter definitions lingering. To clear them, replace the database with a copy of the up-to-date templates/results_template.sqlite.

docs.title: "command not found: spinetoolbox" / "flextool-run"
docs.text: Make sure your virtual environment is activated. Spine Toolbox and the flextool-* console scripts are only on PATH when the venv where FlexTool was installed is active.

docs.title: Linux / macOS notes
docs.text:
FlexTool calls HiGHS through the highspy Python bindings, which install automatically as a dependency, so no separate solver binary is needed. Prebuilt highspy wheels cover x86-64 Linux, Windows and macOS, and ARM64 Linux and macOS (Apple Silicon). On other platforms you need to build HiGHS / highspy from source.

Spine Toolbox runs on Linux and macOS as well, with occasional minor graphical glitches on macOS.

docs.title: Import errors or missing modules
docs.text:
Try reinstalling:

pip install ".[toolbox]" --force-reinstall

docs.title: Solver issues
docs.text:
FlexTool uses HiGHS by default — installed automatically via the highspy Python bindings, no additional setup needed.

It is also possible to wire in commercial solvers (e.g. CPLEX) for licensed users; see the documentation for details.

docs.title: Choosing an interface
docs.text:
FlexTool offers two parallel ways to orchestrate runs and two parallel ways to edit data. This page helps you pick the right combination — most users settle in under two minutes by scanning the table below.

The two axes are orthogonal: any orchestration GUI can be paired with any data editor, and a terminal workflow can be layered on top of either combination for batches and automation.

docs.title: Pick by use case
docs.text:
You want to… Recommended stack Get started quickly / build a first model FlexTool GUI + Spine database editor Keep editing data in spreadsheets FlexTool GUI + Excel / LibreOffice Build multi-tool DAG workflows (FlexTool combined with other models) Spine Toolbox + Spine database editor Run batches on a server or in CI Terminal CLI (data editor irrelevant once the input DB is built) You're an experienced FlexTool v3 user / already use Spine Toolbox Spine Toolbox + Spine database editor

The rest of this page explains each choice and links to the installation and usage guides.

docs.title: FlexTool GUI
docs.text:
A standalone Tkinter application launched with python -m flextool.gui. It is the recommended starting point for new users and for anyone whose workflow centres on FlexTool itself.

What it gives you:

  • Project management with one or more input sources (.sqlite or .xlsx).
  • Double-click an .sqlite source to open it in the Spine database editor.
  • Scenario selection and an execution queue with a memory watchdog (per-job memory budget, system-memory floor, automatic kill of the most-over-budget job under pressure).
  • Auto-generated outputs after each run: scenario plots, scenario Excels, scenario CSVs, comparison plots, and comparison Excels — each toggleable.
  • Result viewer with keyboard navigation between scenarios and plot variants, plus a dedicated scenario comparison mode and a network graph view.

When to choose FlexTool GUI:

  • You are new to FlexTool, or your work is mostly FlexTool-centric.
  • You want one place to manage inputs, run scenarios, and inspect results.
  • You want the lightest installation footprint.

See Install with FlexTool GUI and the FlexTool GUI reference.

docs.title: Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
Spine Toolbox is a separate workflow manager that runs FlexTool as one node in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tools and data stores.

When to choose Spine Toolbox:

  • You build multi-tool pipelines (custom pre-processing, FlexTool, post-processing, another model downstream).
  • You need to integrate FlexTool with other Spine-based models.
  • You already use Spine Toolbox and don't want a second orchestration GUI.
  • You are more comfortable with the visual workflow than predefined options

See Install with Spine Toolbox and the Spine Toolbox interface guide.

docs.title: Spine database editor (default)
docs.text:
The Spine database editor is the native editor for FlexTool's input format. It opens from either GUI: double-click an .sqlite source in the FlexTool GUI, or open the data store from inside Spine Toolbox.

It understands FlexTool's entities, alternatives, scenarios, and parameter-value structure directly, so all relationships (e.g. a unit's input/output nodes, a node's commodity) are validated as you edit. This is the recommended editor for anything beyond trivial changes.

See the Spine database guide.

docs.title: Excel / LibreOffice (alternative)
docs.text:
If you would rather not learn a new editor, you can export an Excel template from the FlexTool GUI, edit the data in Excel or LibreOffice, and import it back. The same workflow is supported from the terminal.

See the Excel / spreadsheet interface.

Mix and match freely

You can edit some scenarios in the Spine database editor and others in Excel within the same project — they round-trip through the same input database. Use whichever fits the edit at hand.

docs.title: Scripting / automation (terminal CLI)
docs.text:
For batch jobs, CI pipelines, parameter sweeps, and headless servers, drive FlexTool from the command line. The CLI subcommands live under python -m flextool.cli.cmd_*, and the repository ships convenience wrappers such as run_flextool.py and execute_flextool_workflow.py.

When to choose the terminal CLI:

  • You want repeatable, scripted runs that don't need a GUI.
  • You're running on a remote server, a cluster, or in continuous integration.
  • You're sweeping many scenarios or chaining FlexTool into a larger automation.

The terminal workflow is orthogonal to the GUI axis: you can edit data in either the Spine database editor or Excel and still execute the same project from the terminal.

See the terminal workflow guide.

docs.title: What's not an interface any more
docs.text:
The FlexTool web / browser interface has been retired. It is preserved for historical reference in the archived browser interface notes, but it is no longer maintained and is not a current option for running FlexTool. This is also why some older video tutorials look quite different from the screenshots in this documentation — they were recorded against the retired web UI.

Still unsure?

Start with FlexTool GUI + Spine database editor. You can always switch later — the underlying data and scenarios are the same regardless of which orchestrator and editor you use.

docs.title: Model limitations
docs.text: FlexTool is a linear (or mixed-integer) optimisation model of an energy system. Like every model, it leaves some things out and simplifies others. This page lists the limitations that matter most in planning studies, with the usual way around them. Read it before you trust a result that depends on one of these features.

docs.title: Emissions
docs.text:
• CO2 is the only emission. Each commodity has one constant co2_content [tCO2/MWh]; other pollutants are not tracked.

    The emissions of a group come from the fuel its units draw from the group's commodity nodes. A cap or a price for a sector therefore needs separate fuel nodes for that sector. The emissions of a unit with several products (combined heat and power, cogeneration with desalination) are not split between the products.

  • A CO2 limit has no slack. If the system cannot meet co2_max_period or co2_max_total, the model leaves demand unserved at the node's penalty_up instead (or is infeasible when the node's penalty_method is off).

    Check the slack results of a run with a tight limit; see How to compare emission trajectories.

docs.title: Thermal units and unit commitment
docs.text:
• Linear commitment is an approximation. With startup_method linear, a part of a unit can be online: with min_load 0.5, a 500 MW unit can run at 25 MW with 50 MW (10 %) of it online.

    Minimum load and start-up costs apply only to the part that is online, so a large unit looks more flexible and cheaper to cycle than it is. binary commits whole units (a mixed-integer problem): it is exact, but slower. virtual_unitsize splits a fleet into smaller units to keep a binary model fast.

  • No start-up fuel. A start-up costs only startup_cost [CUR/MW]: it uses no fuel or heat, and there is no shut-down cost and no hot, warm or cold start.

  • Fuel use is linear in the output. With conversion_method min_load_efficiency, the fuel use is a straight line from minimum load to full load; there are no curved efficiency curves.

  • No parameter that keeps a unit online. A unit can be made to produce (a profile, a flow group floor), but there is no parameter that fixes its online status alone.

    A user constraint on the units online (constraint_online_coeff) sets a minimum number of units online; see How to make a unit run all the time.

docs.title: Inertia and reserves
docs.text:
• Inertia of units without online variables comes from their flow. A unit without online variables (no startup_method and no minimum_time_method) gives flow × inertia_constant, so a unit at half load gives half of its inertia.

    Give the synchronous units online variables (startup_method linear or binary) to count their inertia from the capacity online; see How to set a minimum inertia.

  • The inertia limit is entered, not computed. FlexTool reports the largest single flow into the group, but the inertia_limit does not follow it.

  • Upward reserve comes from online capacity. A unit with online variables holds upward reserve only from the capacity it has online. There is no separate reserve from offline units that can start fast.
  • Reserve activation is not modelled. The model holds the reserve capacity back; the energy of activating it and its cost are not part of the dispatch.

docs.title: Investment and adequacy
docs.text:
• The dispatch does not feed back into the investment. An investment solve does not see the results of the dispatch solves that follow it.

    If a dispatch check shows unserved energy or reserve shortfall, change the investment solve by hand: a better sample of representative periods, a capacity_margin or an energy margin, and run again; see Several milestones. The net-load re-selection of representative periods is the one loop that FlexTool runs for you.

  • The capacity margin is held by firm and VRE capacity only. Firm units count at capacity × availability, VRE at capacity × profile × availability; storage-backed units, connections and consumption count by their actual flow at the time step (see The capacity margin).

    Storage counts only with what it discharges at that step, which is conservative for a full reservoir or a long-duration store. Imports count only as their actual flow, so a group fed only by imports cannot hold a margin. A unit fed from a fuel or commodity node, or from a balance node with limited supply, counts at its capacity: the fuel is assumed to last through the peak. Connections and lossy units inside the group are left out, so the losses inside the group at the peak are not part of the requirement (add an estimate to the margin if they matter). Energy made by the balance slack of a node outside the group and exported into it is not taken back (that of a storage node feeding the group is). Under spatial Benders decomposition, a capacity-margin group with nodes in more than one region is an error.

  • Representative periods leave hours out. An investment made on a sample of weeks cannot see the hours outside the sample; check the plan with a full-year dispatch.

  • Costs count only within the model horizon. The annuity and the fixed cost of new capacity are paid in the periods it operates within the model; the years after the last period are not counted.

docs.title: Discounting
docs.text:
• Only inflation_rate discounts between periods. With the default 0, a cost in the last milestone weighs the same as in the first.

    In a model with real (constant-price) inputs, enter the social discount rate as inflation_rate. The per-technology discount_rate only turns investment costs into annuities; see Discounting between milestone years.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: • The standing loss is proportional to the content. self_discharge_loss is a share of the stored energy per hour. A loss that depends on the size of the storage (for example the heat loss of a hot tank) cannot be given.

docs.title: User constraints and policy targets
docs.text:
• Constraints on flows hold in every time step. A user constraint with flow, state or online terms is written for each time step, and its constant is a constant or a value per period, not per time step.

    There is no user constraint on a period's total flows, such as "renewables make at least 30 % of the year's electricity". The cumulative limits of a flow group (min_cumulative_flow, max_cumulative_flow) are absolute amounts (an average flow in MW), not shares: compute the amount outside FlexTool. See User constraints and Flow groups.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: • No AC power flow. A connection moves energy with losses as a share of the flow, or the network uses a linear DC power flow (dc_power_flow_with_angles). Voltages, reactive power and AC losses are not modelled.

docs.title: Time, foresight and uncertainty
docs.text:
• Perfect foresight within a solve. A solve knows its whole horizon, so storage and investments are planned with full knowledge of the future. Rolling and nested solves limit what each solve sees; see Solve sequences.
  • Forecasts differ only in time series. In a stochastic solve, the forecasts can differ only in the parameters marked "stochastic time" in the reference (profiles, inflow, availability and a few others); see How to use stochastics.

docs.title: Mathematics and solvers
docs.text:
• Linear or mixed-integer only. Every relation in the model is linear. A nonlinear effect has to be made linear (for example with several units or a profile) before it goes in.
  • Solver. The free HiGHS solver comes with FlexTool; commercial solvers can be used through Solvers. A large mixed-integer model can take long with any solver.

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text: A FlexTool run writes many result tables. This page says where to look first, in which order, and what the main tables and their units mean. Model outputs describes every result, and the Results catalogue lists every table with its files, columns and units.

docs.title: Where the results are
docs.text:
• Result viewer. In the FlexTool window, the Result viewer shows the plots of one scenario (key V) or compares several (key X); see Result viewer.
  • Files. Each run writes its tables to output_parquet/<scenario>/ (in the FlexTool window <scenario>_<source number>), and on request as CSV (output_csv/), Excel (output_excel/) and plots (output_plots/).
  • Plot data. With Write plotted data (CSV), each plot comes with a CSV file of the data drawn in it, which is often the easiest table to take into a report; see Plotted data as CSV.

Table names. The name says what a table holds: the entity classes first (unit, node, connection, group), then the resolution. __dt is per period and time step, __d per period. For example, unit__outputNode__dt is the output of each unit to each node in each time step, and unit_capacity__d the capacity of each unit in each period.

docs.title: Check the results in this order
1. Did the run succeed?
docs.text:
A run that did not finish has no usable results. The FlexTool window shows the run's state in the execution jobs; output_parquet/<scenario>/_run_status.json holds it, and _run.log the messages of the run. Read the warnings in the log: they name data that the model did not use as you may have meant.

summary_solve.csv (in the CSV output) gives an overview of each solve: the objective, the costs split into operations, investments, fixed costs and penalties, the discount factors of the periods, the CO2 total and every slack the model used.

docs.title: 2. Are there slacks?
docs.text:
A slack is a requirement the model could not meet, at a penalty cost: unserved demand, excess energy, a reserve, inertia or capacity margin shortfall. With a slack, the results show a system that does not work, so find the cause before reading on.

  • summary_solve.csv lists the slacks used and the Penalty (slack) costs. Its Created / Removed / Inertia / NonSync / Reserve lines are the period's slack summed over the time steps as Σ w·Δt·slack (time step duration Δt and timestep weight w, as the penalty in the objective): the amount over the time steps the model solves, not scaled to a year. With timeset weights or representative periods this is the represented sample (the weights have mean 1 by step count, so for equal step durations Σ w·Δt is the solved time). The CapMargin line is per period.
  • slack__upward__node_state__dt and slack__downward__node_state__dt [MW]: unserved demand (loss of load) and excess energy at each node; the __d tables give the period totals.
  • slack__reserve__upDown__group__dt, slack__inertia_group__dt, slack__nonsync_group__dt and slack__capacity_margin__d: the shortfalls of reserves, inertia, the non-synchronous limit and the capacity margin.
  • For a reserve shortfall, reserve__upDown__group__dt has, per reserve, direction, group and time step, the requirement of each method the group has (timeseries, dynamic, large failure), the reserve provided and counted, and the shortfall; reserve__upDown__group__d has their period averages and maxima, and reserve__group__provider__dt what each unit and connection counts. A large-failure requirement does not count the failing unit's own reserve, so compare the shortfall with requirement − counted, not with requirement − provided.
  • For an adequacy shortfall (the capacity margin of a group), the run log prints a line after each investment solve that leaves one (capacity margin shortfall: solve ..., group ..., period ...: ... MW at ...). capacity_margin__d has, per solve, group and investment period, the requirement at the binding time step, what each class of units and connections counts there and the shortfall; capacity_margin_entity__d has what each unit, connection and node counts. An investment solve keeps its rows under its own name, also when a dispatch solve realizes the period.

Penalties are large on purpose, so a small slack can dominate the costs. See Slack and penalty values.

docs.title: 3. What does the system cost?
docs.text:
• annualized_costs__d [M CUR per year]: the costs of one year of each period by category (investment annuities, fixed costs, fuel, CO2, other operating costs, start-ups, penalties). Use it to compare periods.
  • costs_discounted__d and costs_discounted [M CUR]: the same costs discounted with inflation_rate and multiplied by the years each period represents, per period and in total. This is what the model minimises.
  • cost_unit_annualized__d and the tables for connections and nodes: the costs of each entity.

See Costs and Discounting between milestone years.

docs.title: 4. What capacity is there?
docs.text:
• unit_capacity__d and connection_capacity__d [MW], node_capacity__d [MWh, storages]: the existing capacity, the capacity invested (coming online in the period), divested and the total in service.
  • invest_marginal: the value of one more kW of capacity (CUR/kW; CUR/kWh for a storage), in the units of invest_cost. Negative for a technology the model does not build: it does not pay off.

See Capacity and investment results.

docs.title: 5. How is it operated?
docs.text:
• unit__outputNode__dt and unit__inputNode__dt [MW]: the output and input of each unit in each time step; connection__dt the flows on connections.
  • node__dt [MW] and node__d [MWh per year]: the energy balance of each node by category (units, connections, storage losses, inflow, loss of load).
  • node_state__dt [MWh]: the content of each storage.
  • The dispatch plots of a node group with print_dispatch yes stack all flows into and out of the group.

See Energy flows and Energy balance in nodes.

docs.title: 6. Prices and emissions
docs.text:
• node_prices__dt [CUR/MWh]: the price of energy at each node and time step, the cost of one more MWh of demand there. A price at the level of the penalty means there was a slack.
  • group_CO2__d [t per year]: the CO2 of each CO2 group; co2.csv [Mt]: the CO2 total over the years the periods represent. The CO2 price of a binding cap is in the table co2_price_period_d_g [CUR/t].

See Prices and CO2 emissions.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Unit Used for MW flows and capacities, in each time step MWh storage capacity and content; flows summed over a period (__d), usually scaled to a full year M CUR costs per period and in total (millions of the currency of your inputs) CUR costs per time step (costs__dt) CUR/MWh prices t/a, Mt CO2 per year, CO2 over the whole run

Annualized or discounted. An annualized value is for one year of the period: the hours of the period are scaled to the 8760 hours of a year. A discounted value is a present value: it is multiplied by the years the period represents and by the period's discount factor.

Where the units are written. In the Excel workbook the first sheet, Units, gives the unit of every sheet; a sheet with several header rows has the unit of each column as its last header row (unit of measure), and a sheet with one header row has its units in a small block to the right of its data. In the CSV output, units.csv gives the unit of every column of every file. See Units in the files.

Your units. FlexTool does not convert units: a flow is in MW only if your inputs are in MW and MWh. A water node in m³ gives flows in m³/h. Set the node's unit_of_measure (m3) and the files, plots and the AI assistant label its results so (m³/h, m³, CUR/m³); a sum over nodes of different units says Mixed units of measure! (see Units of measure). A results database without the node parameter unit_of_measure comes from runs whose nodes were all MWh. The parameter units are in the Parameter catalogue.

docs.title: Unreleased (4.4.0) — capacity margin, units of measure, start-up inputs, period-total constraints, FT2 import and many fixes (schema v79)
docs.text: Input databases move to data version 79. The FlexTool window, the Spine Toolbox workflow and flextool-run --migrate migrate them; upgrading prints a notice for each behaviour change that affects the database. FlexTool now needs polar-high 3.12.4 or newer (installed with FlexTool).

docs.title: Behaviour changes — read before upgrading
docs.text:
Each line says what changes for a model that ran before and what to do; the details are in the sections below.

  • Capacity margin rewritten. Units count at capacity derated by availability (VRE by its profile), storage-fed units, connections and consumption by their flow, exports add to the requirement; an investment solve's shortfall and penalty are now reported in an investment → dispatch chain. Check the margin in the new capacity_margin__d.
  • discount_rate 0 now means 0 % (before: 5 %), a negative rate is an error, and an entity that invests or retires with a cost needs a lifetime. Set 0.05 to keep the old results.
  • A zero or missing invest_cost no longer blocks investment (nor a missing salvage_value retirement) where invest_method allows it. To forbid a period, use a _period method with invest_max_period 0, or not_allowed.
  • A solve-level new_stepduration combines every time series by rule (mean, harmonic mean for efficiency, sum for inflow and energy_margin_adder); before, most took the first time step's value. To keep the old energy_margin_adder demand, divide it by the number of time steps a solve step combines.
  • VRE curtailment, VRE potential and a flowGroup's cumulative_flow per period are MWh per year like the flows (a 2-day period: 182.5 times larger). Update scripts that read these tables.
  • A period-map limit that leaves out a period of the solve is an error (before: a CO2 cap of 0, no inertia requirement, no investment limit, ...). Fill in the missing periods.
  • A mistyped period key is an error (y2020 for p2020, numeric or time-step keys on a period parameter; before, the value was dropped). Correct the key; data for extra years goes in model.periods_available.
  • A profile link without profile data is an error (upper_limit or fixed; before, it held the flow at 0). Give the profile a value in the scenario's alternatives, or remove the link.
