docs.title: Units in the files
docs.text:
The unit of measure of every value column is written with the results; it follows the convention of Units of measure (a column without a unit, such as a share, says per unit).

  • Excel, a sheet with several header rows (a table with two or more column levels, such as unit__outputNode__dt with the levels unit and node; a scenario comparison adds the scenario level, so most of its sheets are such sheets): the last header row is unit of measure and gives the unit of each column right above its data. A sheet of a table without declared units gets no unit of measure row. pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=..., header=[0, 1, 2], index_col=[0, 1]) reads such a sheet back, with one more header row than the table has column levels.
  • Excel, a sheet with one header row (for example annualized_costs__d, node_state__dt, and in a scenario comparison a table such as costs_discounted whose only columns are the scenarios): the header row at A1 holds the column names, and the data is an Excel Table named tbl_<sheet name> (characters other than letters, digits, _ and . become _). The row index values are repeated on every row, not merged. To the right of the Table, one empty column apart, a small block gives the units: all value columns and the unit when every value column has the same unit, else one line per value column. Power Query reads the Table (Excel.Workbook(...){[Item="tbl_annualized_costs__d", Kind="Table"]}[Data]), so the unit block does not enter the query. pd.read_excel reads the whole sheet, the unit block included: pass usecols with the Table's columns, or drop the columns after the first empty one.
  • Excel, the first sheet Units: one row per result sheet with the sheet name (a link to the sheet), the table name, the unit(s) (a table whose units differ by column lists them with (by column)), the semantics (instantaneous, annualized, discounted, …) and a description. _output_metadata follows with one row per value column (unit, semantics, tooltip, formula; in a scenario comparison the scenario of the column in its own scenario column). The header cells carry no comments: LibreOffice cannot save a workbook with them.
  • CSV: the CSV files are written as before; units.csv next to them has one row per value column: file, position (the 0-based column of the file), header_1, header_2, … (the labels of the column in the file's header rows, empty below the file's last header row), unit and semantics. summary_solve.csv has one row (M CUR) for its costs. datapackage.json is a Frictionless descriptor of every CSV file: the field names are the labels of a column joined with | as a Frictionless reader joins them (coal|east; a label equal to the one above it is a merged cell and is not repeated, so the index column period of a file with three header rows is period|), a file with several header rows says so in its dialect (headerRows, headerJoin; header rows that are blank in every column, as in a wide file without value columns, are commentRows), and each value field has its unit. frictionless validate datapackage.json passes. The names units.csv and datapackage.json cannot be given to a result in the rename section of the output settings.

Nodes with their own unit of measure. When a node sets unit_of_measure (see Units of measure), the units of its results follow it in every file: a flow into a water node in m3 is m3/h, its storage m3, its annual flow m3/a, its price CUR/m3. A sum over nodes of different units (a nodeGroup's flows over an electricity and a water node, a connection's net flow and losses between them) is labelled Mixed units of measure!. Reserves, inertia, the non-synchronous share and the capacity margin stay in MW. A table whose rows are of different units (unit_capacity__d, connection_capacity__d, node_capacity__d, the nodeGroup and flowGroup tables) gets the units of each row: the Excel Table ends in a column unit of measure with the row's units (for the nodeGroup tables, whose columns differ, the units of the row's columns joined, for example m3; m3/a), units.csv gets a row column and one row per column and row entity, and the parquet footer holds them (flextool_row_units). With every node in MWh, none of these is written and the files are as before. The scenario's parquet folder then also holds _unit_context.json (the node units and which nodes each result follows), which the plots, the GUI and the scenario comparison read; a run whose nodes are all MWh, or a run that writes no parquets, deletes it. A replay (flextool-write-outputs) takes the units from the parquet footers. In a scenario comparison each scenario's columns keep that scenario's units, and the combined comparison parquets carry them in their footer; a column whose unit differs between the scenarios gets a note.

In the results database, a run with such a node defines the parameter node unit_of_measure (default MWh) and writes its value for the nodes that are not MWh; the descriptions of the other parameters give the units of an MWh node. A results database without this definition comes from runs whose nodes were all MWh.

The plot labels follow the nodes too. The labels of default_plots.yaml are unit templates: {A} is the node's amount unit, {R} its rate, {kR} and {kA} the per-kW and per-kWh forms ({A}/h, {A} (annualized), Currency/{A}, CUR/{kR}). For MWh nodes they read as before (MWh/h, MWh (annualized), CUR/kW). With a node in another unit each subplot gets the unit of its nodes; a plot that sums, stacks or averages nodes of different units says Mixed units of measure!, and lines of several units list them (MWh/h; m3/h). The dispatch plots' y-axis is m3/h for a water node and MWh/h by default. A label without tokens in your own plot_settings.yaml (or in a copy of the old default settings) is shown as written and does not follow the nodes.

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
• model entity cost_annualized parameter — M[CUR] (millions of user-chosen currency); annualized total cost broken down by category:

    • unit investment & retirement — M[CUR] cost of investing in unit capacity or salvage from retiring it
    • connection investment & retirement — M[CUR] same for connections
    • storage investment & retirement — M[CUR] same for node states (storages)
    • fixed cost pre-existing — M[CUR] fixed O&M for pre-existing capacity
    • fixed cost invested — M[CUR] fixed O&M for newly invested capacity
    • fixed cost reduction of divestments — M[CUR] fixed O&M removed by divestments
    • commodity cost / commodity sales — M[CUR] cost of buying / revenue from selling commodities
    • co2 — M[CUR] cost of CO2 emissions caused by commodities with CO2 content, net of the removal credit (negative cost) for flows into the same priced group's node(s)
    • other operational — M[CUR] other variable O&M costs
    • starts — M[CUR] start-up costs
    • ramps — M[CUR] ramp costs: the cost of changing the flow of units with a ramp_cost
    • upward / downward slack penalty — M[CUR] cost of involuntary demand reduction / increase
    • inertia slack penalty — M[CUR] cost of not meeting the inertia constraint
    • non-synchronous slack penalty — M[CUR] cost of not meeting the non-synchronous constraint
    • capacity margin penalty — M[CUR] cost of not meeting the capacity margin constraint
    • upward / downward reserve slack penalty — M[CUR] cost of not meeting the reserve constraint

    The annualized investment & retirement, fixed cost invested and fixed cost reduction of divestments are the yearly amounts of every vintage and retirement in effect in the period: an investment adds its annuity (the invest_cost annuity of the period the capacity starts to operate) and its yearly fixed cost in every period it operates within the run (within its lifetime, or every later period with reinvest_automatic); a retirement subtracts its salvage annuity in every period from the retirement until lifetime later, and the yearly fixed cost of the retired capacity in every period the retirement counts in (until the end of life of the existing capacity). They are reported only for capacity whose investment cost is reported (see the next section). For these columns the annualized value is therefore not the discounted value divided by the period's discount factor, which holds for the other columns.

  • model entity cost_t parameter — [CUR] (currency, not millions) same categories as above but per timestep: the cost incurred during the step, with the step duration and timestep weight applied but not scaled to a full year (no investment / fixed terms). The CSV / parquet output costs__dt has the same values and unit.

  • model entity cost_discounted_solve parameter — M[CUR] costs for the solve considering discounting and years represented (NPV currency)
  • model entity cost_discounted_total parameter — M[CUR] same, totalled over all realised periods
  • table years_represented__d (not in the results database) — [a] the years each period represents; an annualized per-period value times these years gives the period's total over the horizon
  • table period_share_of_year__d (not in the results database) — [per unit] for each realised period, the share of a year it covers (its complete hours / 8760, in the solve that realises it): the annualized per-period (…__d) results (flows, energy, annualized costs, emissions, start-ups) are the period's weighted sums over its time steps divided by this share; capacities, prices, averages, ratios and discounted costs are not scaled. A 48-hour period has 0.005479, so its annualized per-period values are 182.5 times its 48-hour sums; a full-year period has 1. Results saved before this version have no such table.

docs.title: Costs of a run of several solves
docs.text:
When model.solves holds several solves (a chain of investment solves, an investment solve and its dispatch solves, a stochastic solve and its realization solve), the reported costs are those of the run as a whole, the same as one solve over the same periods with the same decisions would report:

  • One discount base, the start of the run. Every discounted cost counts its years from the first period of the run, not from the first period of the solve that reports it.
  • Each realized period is reported once, by the solve that realizes it: its operating and penalty costs come from that solve's dispatch, except the capacity margin penalty.
  • The capacity margin penalty (and its slack, slack__capacity_margin__d) of a period is that of the solve that decided the period's investments, also when a later dispatch solve realizes the period (a dispatch solve has no capacity margin). The forecast branch periods of a stochastic fan are not realized, so their shortfalls and penalties stay out of the costs; capacity_margin__d has them.
  • New capacity is reported in the period where it starts to operate (the decision period without a construction_lead_time; during the lead time it is only in_construction, at no cost). Its investment cost (the annuity over the years it operates within the run, at the invest_cost, lifetime and discount_rate of that period) and the fixed cost over the same years come once, from the solve that decided it, and are reported only once a solve realizes the period it starts to operate in. Capacity carried from an earlier solve is therefore not charged again as existing capacity.
  • Retirements are reported in the retirement period: the salvage annuity over the years from the retirement until lifetime later, and the fixed cost saved in the periods the retirement counts in. The fixed cost of existing capacity (fixed cost pre-existing) is that of the capacity given in existing, aged over its lifetime, in every period of the run, also in the last solve's look-ahead periods that no solve realizes (the fixed cost of new capacity covers them too).
  • Inside a stochastic fan the investment cost and the fixed cost of the new capacity that operates in the fan's branch periods are reported, weighted by each branch's probability weight, at the fan's period label of the period the capacity starts to operate in (with or without a construction_lead_time, and also without a realization solve). A shared investment (stochastic_invest_method none) is one decision whose branch weights sum to 1, so it is reported at its full amount; under recourse each forecast's own investment is reported times its branch weight (the expected investment, as in the objective). Retirements in the branch periods of a recourse fan are not reported.
  • In a stochastic solve with a realization solve, the investments come from the stochastic solve and the operations and the fixed cost of existing capacity from the realization solve. A fan without a realization solve reports no operating or penalty costs; the fixed cost of existing capacity is reported in the fan's period labels.

The printed objective of each solve, the cumulative CO2 cap price and the investment duals (invest_marginal, the value of one more MW of capacity) stay discounted from the start of that solve, so cost_discounted_total is not the sum of the solves' objectives and the investment duals of later solves of a chain are on a later discount base. The CO2 price of a period is its dual divided by the discount factor of the solve that realizes the period. A CSV-dump reload has no run-level cost data: its reported costs are discounted from the start of each solve and its annualized investment, retirement and fixed costs of new and retired capacity are 0 (a warning is printed).

docs.title: Cost by entity
docs.text:
The system Costs above are also broken down per entity at the period level, so you can see which unit, connection or node drives each cost category. Six result tables are produced — one for each entity type (unit, connection, node) in each of two flavours:

  • annualized — M[CUR/a], scaled to a full year of operation (the same basis as cost_annualized)
  • discounted — M[CUR], net present value over the horizon (the same basis as cost_discounted_total)

Each table is indexed by (period, entity) — the entity level is named after its type (unit, connection or node) — and carries one column per cost category:

  • unit entity cost_annualized / cost_discounted parameters — per-unit cost break-down
  • connection entity cost_annualized / cost_discounted parameters — per-connection cost break-down
  • node entity cost_annualized / cost_discounted parameters — per-node cost break-down

The categories mirror the system Costs decomposition, restricted to those that apply to the entity type:

  • commodity cost / commodity sales — M[CUR] cost of buying / revenue from selling commodities
  • co2 — M[CUR] cost of CO2 emissions caused by the entity's flows
  • other operational — M[CUR] other variable O&M costs
  • starts — M[CUR] start-up costs (units)
  • ramps — M[CUR] ramp costs (units with a ramp_cost)
  • investment / retirement — M[CUR] cost of investing in unit / connection capacity or salvage from retiring it (named storage investment / storage retirement in the node table, where the capacity is node-state storage energy)
  • fixed cost pre-existing / fixed cost invested / fixed cost reduction of divestments — M[CUR] fixed O&M for pre-existing, newly invested and divested capacity
  • in the annualized tables, investment, retirement, fixed cost invested and fixed cost reduction of divestments are the yearly amounts in every period the capacity operates or the retirement applies, as in the system Costs
  • upward slack penalty / downward slack penalty (node table only) — M[CUR] cost of involuntary demand reduction / increase at the node

Attribution rules (matching the LP objective):

  • Fuel / commodity cost is attributed to the consuming process — the unit or connection that draws the commodity — not to the source node.
  • CO2 cost for a process is the sum over every priced group the process touches, so a flow that contributes emissions to several priced groups carries the full cost of each. A flow into a priced group's node (removal) carries a negative cost (credit) the same way.

By construction these tables are purely additive collapses of the same per-entity intermediates the system summary uses, so summing any category over all entities reproduces the system summary: the unit + connection + node contributions for a given category and period add up to the matching cost_annualized / cost_discounted_total category value (annualized_costs_d_p / costs_discounted_d_p in the parquet store).

These are period-level tables only — there are no per-timestep per-entity cost tables.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
• node entity price_t parameter — [CUR/MWh] the cost of one more MWh of demand at that node and time step (the dual of the node's energy balance; positive when more demand would cost more), for every node that maintains an energy balance. It is in the price base of the cost inputs: the inflation / discounting of the period and the years it represents are removed, and it is not weighted by the timestep weight (timeset_weights, representative-period weights) or by the branch probability — in a stochastic solve each forecast branch reports its own price, not its probability-weighted contribution (the cost outputs per step are probability-weighted, so price × flow is not the branch's cost row). A step that the objective does not weigh (e.g. a step that timeset_weights leaves out) has no price (empty). A node of a group with a coarser new_stepduration (and a bind_intraperiod_blocks storage node) has one balance per coarse step (per timeset block); its price is that balance's dual, the same at every time step of the coarse step when the steps have the same weight. Within a coarse step the energy may be moved freely between time steps, so for such a node the hour at which a slack (or any flow that only the coarse balance limits) is reported is one of several equally good choices; with a time-varying penalty the solver picks the cheapest hour. For a storage node the price is the value of stored energy.
  • table reserve_prices_dt_ppg (group__reserve__upDown, not in the results database) — [CUR/MWh] the cost of one more MW of reserve requirement held for one hour (in the same price base and with the same weights removed as price_t): the sum of the duals of the group's requirement constraints at the step (the timeseries requirement, the dynamic requirement and the large-failure requirement of every failing unit or connection), i.e. the cost of one more MW of every requirement of the group at once. Reported for every group with a requirement. When the requirement is not met it equals penalty_reserve.
  • table co2_price_period_d_g (group, not in the results database) — [CUR/tCO2] shadow price of the per-period CO2 cap (nominal currency, sign-flipped so a binding cap shows positive). In a rolling solve where a period's hours are split across more than one roll, the reported price is the hour-weighted average of the rolls that realize it (weighted by the hours each roll keeps of the period). In a stochastic solve each scenario path reports its own price, not its price times the path's branch probability.
  • table co2_price_total_d_g (group, not in the results database) — [CUR/tCO2] shadow price of the cumulative CO2 cap, per tonne over the represented years (NPV currency, broadcast across periods)

docs.title: Energy flows
docs.text:
• unit__node entity flow_annualized parameter — [MWh] cumulative flow from the node (if node is input) or to the node (if node is output), annualized to a full year
  • unit__node entity flow_t parameter — [MW] flow at each timestep
  • connection__node__node entity flow_annualized parameter — [MWh] annualized cumulative flow through the connection (left-to-right is positive)
  • connection__node__node entity flow_t parameter — [MW] flow through the connection at each timestep
  • table connection_losses_d_eee (not in the results database) — [MWh] annualized losses on the connection
  • table connection_losses_dt_eee (not in the results database) — [MW] losses on the connection at each timestep

docs.title: Optional output: output_connection_flows_separate
docs.text:
• connection__node__node entity flow_to_first_node_annualized parameter — [MWh] annualized cumulative flow only to the left (first) node
  • connection__node__node entity flow_to_second_node_annualized parameter — [MWh] annualized cumulative flow only to the right (second) node
  • connection__node__node entity flow_to_first_node_t parameter — [MW] flow to the left (first) node at each timestep
  • connection__node__node entity flow_to_second_node_t parameter — [MW] flow to the right (second) node at each timestep

docs.title: Capacity factors
docs.text:
• unit__node entity cf parameter — [per unit] average capacity factor of the flow: time-average of flow [MWh/h] divided by the unit's capacity [MW], which is on its output side; so the input cf of a unit at full load is 1/efficiency. One table per direction (unit_cf__inputNode, unit_cf__outputNode).
  • connection__node__node entity cf parameter — [per unit] average capacity factor of the absolute flow (flows in either direction count as utilization), divided by connection capacity

docs.title: Energy balance in nodes
docs.text:
• node entity balance parameter — [MWh] annualized period sum of all balance contributions: From units, From connections, To units, To connections, Self discharge, Loss of load (upward slack), Excess load (downward slack), Inflow
  • node entity balance_t parameter — [MW] same categories per timestep. Self discharge is the energy the storage lost in the step (the loss the optimisation used) divided by the step length; the loss of a coarse step (new_stepduration group) or of a bind_intraperiod_blocks block is spread evenly over its time steps.
  • node entity state_t parameter — [MWh] storage state of the node at each timestep (state nodes only; multiplied by entity_unitsize so the value is in storage MWh, not the scaled LP variable)

docs.title: Unit online and startup
docs.text:
• unit entity online_t parameter — [count] number of units online at each timestep
  • unit entity online_average parameter — [count] average online status over the period (weighted by step duration)
  • unit entity startup_cumulative parameter — [count] startups during the period scaled to a full year (weighted by rp_cost_weight to handle representative periods correctly)
  • unit__node entity startup_energy_t parameter — [MWh] energy that the unit's start-ups take from the node in each timestep (unit__inputNode startup_input_method startup_and_input or startup_only: startup_energy × MW started)
  • unit__node entity startup_energy_annualized parameter — [MWh] the same summed over the period and scaled to a full year. The start-up input is also in the unit's input flow from the node (flow_t, flow_annualized), the commodity cost, the CO2 emissions and the node balance; a startup_only arc has no other flow

docs.title: Connection online and startup
docs.text:
Only for connections with a startup_method:

  • connection entity online_t parameter — [count] units of the connection online at each timestep
  • connection entity online_average parameter — [count] average online status over the period (weighted by step duration)
  • connection entity startup_cumulative parameter — [count] startups during the period scaled to a full year (as for units)

docs.title: Unit curtailment and VRE potential
docs.text:
For VRE units (units that use an upper_limit profile) the model also reports curtailment and potential generation against each output node:

  • table unit_VRE_potential_outputNode_dt_ee (not in the results database) — [MW] potential VRE generation at the timestep (capacity × profile)
  • table unit_VRE_potential_outputNode_d_ee (not in the results database) — [MWh/a] potential VRE generation summed over the period's time steps (with the timestep weights) and scaled to a full year, like the flows
  • unit__node entity curtailment_t parameter — [MW] potential minus actual generation at the timestep
  • table unit_curtailment_outputNode_d_ee (not in the results database) — [MWh/a] curtailed energy summed over the period's time steps (with the timestep weights) and scaled to a full year, like the flows; the total plot multiplies each period by its years represented
  • table unit_curtailment_share_outputNode_dt_ee (not in the results database) — [0–1] timestep curtailment / potential
  • unit__node entity curtailment_share parameter — [0–1] period curtailment / period potential

docs.title: Node group results
docs.text:
group entities with print_indicators = yes produce indicator tables aggregating flows / inflows / slacks over their member nodes:

  • group entity indicator (period table) — gives a set of indicators for all node members. Each share is a ratio of two energies summed over the period, weighted by the time-step weights: share = Σ_t w·X / Σ_t w·Y (never a sum or an average of the time-step shares):
    • Loss of load share — [0–1] upward slack ÷ inflow over the period
    • VRE share of demand — [≥ 0] VRE generation into the member nodes ÷ inflow over the period (can exceed 1 when VRE is exported out of the group)
    • Excess load share — [0–1] downward slack ÷ inflow over the period
    • Curtailed VRE of demand — [≥ 0] curtailed VRE ÷ inflow over the period (can exceed 1 when the curtailment is larger than the demand)
    • Annualized inflow — [MWh] sum of inflow to member nodes scaled to a year
    • Curtailed VRE of potential VRE — [0–1] curtailed VRE ÷ potential VRE generation over the period, both on the arcs of the VRE units with an upper_limit profile into the member nodes (the group sum of unit_curtailment_outputNode and unit_VRE_potential_outputNode)
  • table nodeGroup_g_p (group_node__horizon, not in the results database) — the same indicators over the whole horizon: each share is the ratio of the energies over all periods, each period's weighted sum scaled to a year and multiplied by its years represented (Σ_d y·Σ_t w·X / share_d ÷ Σ_d y·Σ_t w·Y / share_d), not an average of the period shares; Inflow (horizon total) [MWh] replaces the annualized inflow. In a stochastic fan each branch period counts with its years, so the horizon total adds up all the paths
  • table nodeGroup_gdt_p (timestep table, not in the results database) — exposes the timestep-level building blocks of the above: Loss of load [MWh/step], VRE generation [MWh/step], Excess load [MWh/step], Curtailed VRE [MWh/step], Timestep inflow [MWh/step], Curtailed VRE of potential VRE [0–1], Annualized inflow [MWh], VRE share of demand [0–1]
  • group entity VRE_share_t parameter — [≥ 0] share of inflow served by VRE sources at each timestep (one column per node group; 0 at a time step without inflow)
  • table nodeGroup_VRE_share_d_g (not in the results database) — [≥ 0] VRE share of the period's inflow: VRE generation ÷ inflow, both summed over the period with the time-step weights (equals VRE share of demand above)
  • table nodeGroup_VRE_share_g (group_node_VRE_share__horizon, not in the results database) — [≥ 0] VRE share over the whole horizon: the total VRE energy ÷ the total inflow, each period scaled to a year and multiplied by its years represented
  • group entity flow_annualized parameter — [MWh] annualized sum of inflow to member nodes
  • group entity flow_t parameter — [MWh/step] timestep inflow to member nodes

group entities with print_dispatch = yes produce a multi-column dispatch table over the group:

  • group entity sum_flow_t parameter — [MWh/step] dispatch decomposed by (type, item) where type is one of: slack (upward/downward), from_unit, from_unitGroup, to_unit, to_unitGroup, from_connection, from_connectionGroup, to_connection, to_connectionGroup, inflow, internal_losses (units/connections/storages)
  • group entity sum_flow_annualized parameter — [MWh] same decomposition, annualized period totals

docs.title: Flow group results
docs.text:
flowGroup entities whose flow_aggregator is standalone_aggregator_only or both produce aggregate flow statistics over their member (process, node) legs (listed via flowGroup__unit__node / flowGroup__connection__node):

  • group_flow__d.csv — per-(flowGroup, period) totals:
    • cumulative_flow parameter — [MWh/a] sum of |flow| over the period for all member legs, with the time-step weights, scaled to a full year
    • average_flow parameter — [MW] average power (cumulative_flow / 8760 h)
  • group_flow__dt.csv — per-(flowGroup, period, time) signed net flow [MW] (sign convention: flow into the group's nodes is positive, flow out of them is negative). Intended for spreadsheet post-processing; because the values are signed they do not stack, so this series is not meant for stacked dispatch plots.

(For member flows shown as aggregated bands inside a node group's dispatch table, set flow_aggregator to dispatch_plots_only or both instead — see Node group results and the reference.)

docs.title: Capacity and investment results
docs.text:
• unit, connection, node entities capacity parameter — [MW or MWh] decomposed into:

    • existing — capacity assumed at the start of the period
    • invested — capacity that comes online in the period (without a construction lead time, the capacity invested in that period)
    • in_construction — capacity decided but not yet operating in the period; always present, empty without a construction lead time
    • divested — capacity the model decided to retire at the start of the period
    • total — capacity in service: existing + invested − divested, cumulated over the periods; capacity in construction is not included

    In combined solves (e.g. a chain of solves, or invest then dispatch), each realized investment is counted once, in the period it comes online.

    Period axis covers every period in which an investment or a divestment decision occurs (both the invest-eligible and divest-eligible periods feed into d_realize_invest), so divest-only periods are visible even when no new capacity is added.

  • unit, connection, node entities invest_marginal parameter — [CUR/kW, CUR/kWh for storage nodes, as invest_cost] effective dual of the investment decision: zero means the model is at the unconstrained optimum; positive means an active upper bound (per-entity, per-group, period, total or cumulative caps are summed automatically); negative means the entity is not built and is unprofitable to build (the v_invest column's own reduced cost) — this is the ordinary reading for an unbuilt entity, not an artefact; a numerical artefact instead looks like a non-zero value on a built (or at-bound) entity, or an inconsistent sign across these regimes, and is worth investigating

docs.title: CO2 emissions
docs.text:
• table CO2__ (not in the results database) — [Mt] horizon-total CO2 across all groups and units (uses years_represented_d to convert annualized emissions to horizon totals). In a stochastic solve with more than one scenario path this is reported per path (one column per path) instead of pooling every path's emissions into one number — the anchor's shared pre-reveal history and each forecast branch's own periods are alternative futures, not consecutive years to add together.
  • group entity CO2_annualized parameter — [t/yr] annualized CO2 emissions caused (or removed) by units and connections in the group
  • unit entity CO2_annualized parameter — [t/yr] annualized CO2 emissions of the unit's flows, by commodity and node

docs.title: Reserves
docs.text:
• unit__reserve__upDown__node and connection__reserve__upDown__node reservation_t parameter — [MW] reserve provision at each timestep
  • unit__reserve__upDown__node and connection__reserve__upDown__node reservation_average parameter — [MW] the time-step-weighted average MW over the period's realized steps: Σ_t w·Δt·MW / Σ_t w·Δt with w the time-step weight (representative periods weigh by the base periods they stand for). The steps of a solve that left reserves out (reduce_system_detail_method) are left out of both sums, not counted as 0 MW. This table does not multiply by reliability; the group tables below do.
  • group__reserve__upDown entity requirement_t parameter — the reserve requirement of each reserve, direction and group at each time step (reserve__upDown__group__dt, table nodeGroup_reserve_dt_eegp), from the group's requirement constraints evaluated at the solution, by quantity [MW]:
    • requirement_timeseries, requirement_dynamic, requirement_n_1 — the need of each method the group has (reserve_method; a column of a method the group does not have is left out): the reservation; the flows into and out of the group's nodes × increase_reserve_ratio plus the group's demand × its increase_reserve_ratio; the largest failure, the flow of a failing unit or connection × large_failure_ratio (one requirement per failing process; the raw parquet output_raw/reserve_group__<solve>.parquet names the largest one in n_1_process)
    • requirement — the need of the binding requirement, the one with the largest deficit (need − counted reserve; among equal ones timeseries, then dynamic, then the failing processes by name; the raw parquet names it in binding_method and, for a failure, binding_process). This is not always the largest need: when no requirement is short, the binding one is the one closest to being short, and its need can be below another method's. For example, a timeseries need of 90 MW with 100 MW counted (10 MW to spare) and a large-failure need of 80 MW with 85 MW counted (5 MW to spare) give requirement = 80 MW. The largest need of the group is the largest of the requirement_timeseries, requirement_dynamic and requirement_n_1 columns
    • provided — the reserve of the group's providers: Σ reserve × unitsize × reliability over the units and connections that hold the reserve at a node of the group (a provider at a node counts in every group that has the node)
    • counted — the reserve the binding requirement counts: provided, but for a large-failure requirement without the failing process's own reserve (it cannot cover its own failure). So shortfall = requirement − counted when there is a shortfall
    • shortfall — [MW] the requirement not met (the same as slack_reserve_t)
  • group__reserve__upDown entity requirement parameter — the same per period (reserve__upDown__group__d, table nodeGroup_reserve_d_eegp): requirement_avg, provided_avg, counted_avg and shortfall_avg are time-step-weighted averages over the period's realized steps (Σ_t w·Δt·X / Σ_t w·Δt, the steps of a solve that left reserves out not counted), requirement_max and shortfall_max the largest step values (not weighted). Compare requirement_avg with counted_avg, not with provided_avg: with a large-failure requirement the failing unit's own reserve is in provided but not in counted. requirement_avg averages the binding requirement, which can come from a different method at different steps.
  • The reserve price of the group (the sum of the duals of its requirements) is reserve_price__upDown__group__dt (table reserve_prices_dt_ppg, see Prices).
  • table nodeGroup_reserve_provider_dt_eegee (reserve__group__provider__dt, not in the results database) — [MW] the counted reserve (× reliability) of each unit or connection at each node for each reserve, direction and group at each time step; per group they add up to provided. With reliability below 1 it is less than the reserve the unit holds (reservation_t).

A step whose solve left reserves out has empty cells in these tables. A reserve held by storage with a reserve_duration adds no requirement; it shows as a lower provided. After each solve the run log prints reserve requirement check: solve ..., reserve ..., group ..., step (...): deficit ... MW, shortfall ... MW for a step where the evaluated requirement and the solver's shortfall disagree (that should not happen; on an accepted near-optimal solve it can be solver tolerance, and the line says so).

docs.title: Inertia and non-synchronous generation
docs.text:
• group entity inertia_t parameter — [MWs] total inertia in the group of nodes at each timestep
  • group entity inertia_largest_flow_t parameter — [MW] largest individual flow coming into the group of nodes with has_inertia
  • group entity inertia_unit_node_t parameter — [MWs] inertia contribution per (unit, node) at each timestep, one column per contributing (unit, node)

docs.title: Ramps
docs.text:
• unit__node entity ramp_t parameter — [MW] ramp of the unit input or output flow at each timestep: the change from the previous step (one table per direction: unit_ramp__inputNode__dt, unit_ramp__outputNode__dt). The ramp at a step with no previous step in the solve (the first step, the first step after a gap in the timeline, the first step of a representative period) is empty; at the first step of a rolling window it is measured from the previous window's last step. ramp_t is in MW per time step, while the limits ramp_speed_up / ramp_speed_down are a share of capacity per minute: a change may be at most ramp_speed_up × 60 × (average duration of the two steps in hours) × capacity (see Units), so on hourly steps a ramp_t of 30 MW on a 100 MW unit is a speed of 30 / 100 / 60 = 0.005.

The "ramp room" envelope on the node entity (additional headroom for upward / downward ramps from non-VRE units, VRE units, and connections) is currently not emitted by the new pipeline — it is on the roadmap for re-exposure once the corresponding post-processing is ported.

docs.title: DC power flow
docs.text:
When the network contains DC-power-flow connections / nodes (is_dc_power_flow = yes):

  • table dc_angle_dt_e (not in the results database) — [rad] voltage angle at each timestep
  • table dc_angle_diff_dt_e (not in the results database) — [rad] angle difference across the connection at each timestep

docs.title: Slack and penalty values
docs.text:
Slack uses are listed in the Energy balance in nodes section (Loss of load, Excess load and per-node slack_up / slack_down parameters with _t and annualized variants) and aggregated in Costs. Group-level slack tables:

  • group entity slack_capacity_margin parameter — [MW] capacity-margin shortfall in investment periods. It is the shortfall of the solve that decided the investments: in an investment → dispatch chain it is the investment solve's, shown under the investment solve, and its penalty is in the costs (capacity margin penalty). The forecast branch periods of a stochastic fan are not realized, so this table and the costs leave out their shortfalls; capacity_margin__d has them.
  • group entity capacity_margin parameter — the capacity margin of every solve with investment periods (capacity_margin__d, table nodeGroup_capacity_margin_d_g), per solve, group and investment period (look-ahead and forecast branch periods included, not only realized ones) at the binding step binding_time, the time step with the largest deficit (requirement − counted; on a group whose row is averaged over coarse steps, the first time step of the coarse step): margin [MW] (the capacity_margin, or capacity_margin_share × the peak), peak_demand [MW] (the peak demand of the group's nodes over the period's original timeline), demand [MW] (at the binding step), requirement [MW] (margin + demand), firm and vre [MW] (the counted capacity of firm units and of VRE units at their profile, with availability), storage_flow, unit_flow, connections_net and consumption [MW] (the flows of storage-backed units minus the slack energy of the storage nodes feeding the group, of the other units counted by their flow, of connections and of the group's consumption, signed as in the node balance), dumped [MW] (minus the downward slack), counted [MW] (their sum), shortfall [MW] (max(0, requirement − counted) at the binding step: 0 when the margin holds), penalty_cost [M CUR] (shortfall × penalty_capacity_margin × 1000 × inflation, as in the costs) and capacity_price [CUR/kW/a] (the shadow price of the margin: what one more kW of margin would cost; it equals penalty_capacity_margin while there is a shortfall, and is empty for a MIP). In the results database the binding step is not carried (the value is category → solve → period); it is in the CSV and parquet tables.
  • group entity capacity_margin_contribution parameter — [MW] what each unit, connection and node counts in the group's capacity margin at its binding step (capacity_margin_entity__d, table nodeGroup_capacity_margin_entity_d_g), by class: firm, vre, storage, storage_slack (minus the slack energy of a storage node feeding the group, per hour of the step), unit_by_flow, connection, consumption and dumped (a node's downward slack; a node that dumped nothing is left out). They add up to the columns of capacity_margin__d: firm → firm, vre → vre, storage and storage_slack → storage_flow, unit_by_flow → unit_flow, connection → connections_net, consumption → consumption, dumped → dumped. A row sums to counted. A unit that you expect to count but that is missing, or counts by its flow, shows which rule of the capacity margin applies to it.
  • group entity slack_inertia_t / slack_inertia — [MWs] inertia shortfall, timestep / annualized
  • group entity slack_nonsync_t / slack_nonsync — [MW] non-synchronous-share shortfall, timestep / annualized
  • group__reserve__upDown entity slack_reserve_t / slack_reserve — [MW] reserve shortfall, timestep / annualized; the requirement it falls short of, and what each provider counts, is in Reserves (reserve__upDown__group__dt)

For the sign / direction conventions of slacks, see Slack convention. For how block-aware solves (flex-temporal decomposition) and spatial Benders decomposition feed into these tables, see Decomposition — the result writers always operate on the fine-timeline, full-spatial solution, so the parquet tables look identical to a monolithic run.

docs.title: Plotted data as CSV
docs.text:
With Write plotted data (CSV) in the GUI's Png settings, --write-plot-data on flextool-run, flextool-write-outputs or flextool-scenario-results (Spine Toolbox users can add it to the tool's command-line arguments), or a top-level write_plot_data: true in the project's plot_settings.yaml, each plot file gets a CSV file next to it with the data drawn in it: output_plots/<scenario>/<plot>.png comes with <plot>.csv, a plot split into several files writes <plot>_01.csv, <plot>_02.csv, … with the data of each file, and the comparison plots and dispatch plots in output_plot_comparisons/ get theirs too. Any one of these turns it on. It is off by default and then costs nothing.

  • Rows are the x axis of the plot (the time steps, or the bars), with the row index levels (for example period, time) as the first columns. Only the plotted time window is written, and the gap rows that leave a gap in a line at a timeline break are not.
  • Columns are the plotted series (lines, stacks, bars), with one header row. When a series is named by several dimensions, its header is their values joined with |, in the order of the result's dimensions; the dimension names themselves are not written. For example, in a comparison plot of unit output with the scenario first and the unit second, the column base | coal_plant is unit coal_plant in scenario base. A series named like one of the first columns (for example an entity called time) gets (series) added to its name.
  • A leading subplot column names the subplot of each row when the file has more than one subplot.
  • Values are as plotted, after multiply_by (the unit is in the plot's axis label). For a stacked plot, each column is that series' own value, not the stacked total, so do not add the columns up again. Where a line is drawn as the sum over a dimension the plot does not show, the column is that sum. A cell that is empty in the results stays empty, also where a bar plot draws it as zero.
  • A dispatch plot's CSV has a period and a time column for the steps of the plotted time window (the periods one after another), the flows, and the demand line as a Demand column, as in the legend (Demand (line) if a flow is already called Demand). dispatch_data.xlsx (scenario comparison with --write-dispatch-xlsx) has one sheet per dispatch plot with the same period and time columns, a value on every row.
  • If a CSV cannot be written, the log has a warning naming the file, and the plots are still made.
  • In plot_settings.yaml, only write_plot_data: true (no quotes) turns this on; a quoted "true" or any value that is not true or false leaves it off with a warning.

The CSVs are removed with the plots when the plots are made again.

docs.title: Data structure in Spine databases
docs.text: Spine databases use Entity-Attribute-Value with Classes and Relationships (EAV-CR). Entity classes define the categories of data. These can be one-dimensional object classes (e.g. node or unit) or multi-dimensional relationship classes formed from the object classes (e.g. unit__node). Spine Toolbox user can define these classes to suit their modelling needs. For FlexTool the entity classes have been pre-defined. Instead, FlexTool user needs to add the entity instances: objects and relationships that define the particular network structure to be modelled (e.g. coal_plant unit or west node). Furthermore, each entity class (object or relationship) can hold only parameters that have been defined for that particular class. Again, FlexTool user does not need to add the parameter types - the user should just add needed parameter values for the entities the user has created.

docs.title: Database editor in brief
docs.text:
Spine Toolbox database editor can be used to modify data and to build scenarios. The figure below shows an example where parameter data from two alternatives have been selected for display (in the data table). The object tree on the left selects two nodes ('coal_market' and 'west') as well as one unit ('coal_plant'). Consequently, one can use both whole classes and individual entities (members of the classes) as data filters. The results of this filter are visualized in the graph on top. The mouse pointer is showing a relationship entity that connects the 'coal_plant' and its output node 'west'. The relationship entity is defined in a relationship tree, which is not visible here.

The scenario tree (on the right, below the alternative tree) shows that the 'coal' scenario is formed by taking all data from the 'init' alternative and then all data from the 'coal' alternative. If there would be same parameter defined for both scenarios, then the latter alternative would overwrite the first alternative.

Whenever data is modified, the data is staged in separate database tables (although not directly visible to user). The changes will be applied only once the user commits the changes and leaves a commit message to indicate what has been done. The commit can be done with ctrl-enter or from the database editor menu (triple bar at top-right).

The database editor menu has options for how to display the data: table view, different pivot views and a graph view. It also contains a tool to delete data (purge) and decrease database size by removing unused allocations (vacuum). You can also bring back dock windows that have been closed by the user. History will show the history of data changes based on the commits made by the user.

More on Spine Database editor in https://spine-toolbox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spine_db_editor/index.html.

docs.title: Parameter groups
docs.text:
Spine's parameter_definition table carries an optional parameter_group_name field — a lightweight category label that the database editor and other consumers use to group related parameters visually. FlexTool populates this field for every parameter: each parameter_definition row in the master template is tagged with one of the ~15 groups (timeline, model, basics, reserve, investment, retirement, output, …). The grouping has no semantic meaning to the solver — it is purely metadata.

The full list of groups, the rules for adding new parameters, and the migration mechanics are documented in:

  • Model parameters — the user-facing list with one-line descriptions per group.
  • Database schema and migration — how the field is populated and verified.

The FlexTool GUI's parameter-group picker (see FlexTool GUI → Add empty FlexTool input Excel) uses these groups to let users assemble a partial input Excel by ticking only the groups they need.

docs.title: IRENA FlexTool with Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
Spine Toolbox is an alternative orchestration interface for FlexTool. The other, simpler, interface is the standalone FlexTool GUI; Spine Toolbox is the heavier path that wraps FlexTool as one node in a directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflow alongside other tools and data stores. It allows not just to run FlexTool, but also to wrap it in more complex workflows (e.g. input data preparation or multi-tool pipeline) - when doing that, best to make a separate Spine Toolbox project in another folder or then freeze particular FlexTool installation to the purpose. The default workflow is part of FlexTool repository and you will get merge conflicts if you edit it and then try to pull repository updates.

See Install with Spine Toolbox for installation and Choosing an interface for the side-by-side comparison with the FlexTool GUI and the terminal CLI.

docs.title: When to choose Spine Toolbox
docs.text:
• You are combining FlexTool with other Spine-based models in a single workflow.
  • You want a DAG view of pre-processing, FlexTool, and post-processing steps, with the scenario filter visible on each connection.
  • You already use Spine Toolbox for other projects and would rather not run a second orchestration GUI alongside it.

For FlexTool-centric work (build scenarios, run them, inspect results in one place), the FlexTool GUI is the recommended choice instead.

docs.title: Opening the FlexTool project in Toolbox
docs.text:
The FlexTool repository ships a complete Spine Toolbox project under the .spinetoolbox/ directory at the repo root. After installing FlexTool with the [toolbox] extra and launching spinetoolbox, use File → Open project… and select the FlexTool root directory (not a file inside it). Toolbox reads .spinetoolbox/project.json and reconstructs the workflow, item positions, and connections.

The right-hand panel lists the scenarios discovered in the Input data database. Ticking scenarios there decides which ones run when you execute the workflow; Toolbox can execute several in parallel as long as the FlexTool item is configured to use work directories.

Each FlexTool run uses all available cores for its own data processing (at most 8 threads) unless told otherwise, and Toolbox does not pass a thread count. When Toolbox runs several scenarios at once, add --threads N to the FlexTool Tool's command-line arguments, with N about the number of cores divided by the number of runs executed at once. N covers FlexTool's data processing and the solver of each run.

docs.title: The shipped workflow
docs.text:
The workflow has no Export_to_csv step: the engine builds the LP in memory directly from the Spine database. CSV is an optional output renderer, not a hand-off format inside the workflow.

The items that actually ship in .spinetoolbox/project.json are:

  • Input data (Data Store) — the working .sqlite database that the FlexTool engine reads from. Double-click to open it in the Spine database editor. Replace the file (via the OS) or repoint the data store to use a different input database.
  • Examples (Data Store) — the read-only templates/examples.sqlite shipped with the repository. Holds the example scenarios used in the user guide.
  • Replace with examples (Merger) — copies selected example scenarios from Examples into Input data. The scenario filter on the connection chooses which ones are copied. This replaces the older Init / Initialize pair.
  • Migrate database version (Tool) — runs the migrate_database specification against Input data to upgrade it to the current FlexTool DB schema version. Use it after pulling a new FlexTool version.
  • Excel input (Data Connection) — points at a spreadsheet (example_input.xlsx by default) for the spreadsheet-fed flow.
  • Read input spreadsheet (Tool) — runs the Read tabular data specification to import the contents of Excel input into Input data. See Excel interface for the file format.
  • FlexTool location (Data Connection) — small user-local text file (templates/project_folder.txt) recording the project folder the run roots its outputs at. See Choosing the project folder below. (This replaces the older flextool_location.txt; you may rename the connection to "Project folder" in the Toolbox GUI if you like.)
  • FlexTool (Tool) — the solve step. Runs flextool/cli/cmd_run_flextool.py (the engine that the flextool-run console script supervises) as a subprocess. Receives the Input data, Output info, and Output settings database URLs as arguments.
  • Output info (Data Store) — output_info.sqlite, where the FlexTool run records what it produced (scenario list, output locations).
  • Output settings (Data Store) — output_settings.sqlite, holding render-side toggles consumed by FlexTool and Re-create results.
  • Re-create results (Tool) — runs the Process outputs specification to rebuild CSV / Excel / plot renderings from the parquets without re-solving.
  • Comparison settings (Data Store) — comparison_settings.sqlite, configuration for the scenario-comparison renderer.
  • Scenario comparison (Tool) — runs the scenario comparison specification to build cross-scenario dispatch plots and summary tables from the parquets in Output info.

docs.title: How FlexTool itself runs
docs.text:
The FlexTool workflow item is a Spine Toolbox Tool whose specification is a thin Python entry that calls flextool/cli/cmd_run_flextool.py — the engine that the FlexTool GUI runs and the flextool-run console script supervises. Once it starts, no Spine Toolbox code is in the loop (the run's _run.log holds FlexTool's own console output; the solver's native lines are only in the Tool's console):

  • The engine reads inputs from the Input data Spine database via SpineDBBackend.
  • Per-solve preprocessing produces polars frames in memory.
  • polar_high assembles the LP and HiGHS solves it in-process through highspy.
  • Solutions are written to parquet under output_parquet/<scenario>/, and CSV / Excel / PNG renderings are produced from those parquets on top.

There is no CSV hand-off between the workflow and the engine. The CSV files in solve_data/ only appear when --debug --csv-dump is passed, and they are not load-bearing for anything downstream. See Architecture for the full data-flow diagram.

docs.title: Project folders and results
docs.text: A Toolbox run roots all of its outputs — output_parquet/, results.sqlite, plots, and the per-project plot_settings.yaml — at a project folder you choose, instead of scattering them at the repo root. This makes the Toolbox track a peer of the FlexTool GUI: the GUI picks up Toolbox-produced results, and the Toolbox can run a GUI-made project.

docs.title: Choosing the project folder
docs.text:
The project folder is set by editing one line in the user-local, gitignored file templates/project_folder.txt (seeded for you by flextool-update):

projects/MyProject

The path may be absolute or relative to the FlexTool root. Leave the file blank (or with only comment lines) to send outputs to the FlexTool root — the old behavior. Because the file is gitignored, editing it never dirties git, so you switch projects simply by editing this line (and pointing the Input data Data Store at that project's input database).

docs.title: Producing the results SpineDB
docs.text:
To get a results SpineDB at <project>/results.sqlite, set output-spinedb = true in the Output settings database. Both steps honor it, with each scenario as a Spine alternative:

  • The FlexTool run writes it directly from the live solve (the usual case — the full results land in the DB as the scenarios run).
  • The Re-create results step (re)builds or augments it by replaying the processed parquet — no re-solve. Use this to add the SpineDB afterwards without re-running, or to reduce the scenario set via its alternative filter. Whatever else you tick in Output settings (output-plot / output-excel / output-csv) Re-create also (re)produces.

Two caveats apply to the replay path only:

  • The two inflation / discount-factor parameters are omitted (they need the live solve); the native run path writes the full set.
  • For a bidirectional connection the (source, sink) byname uses the parquet (node_1, node_2) geometry; one-directional connections are exact.

docs.title: Per-project plot settings
docs.text: Place a plot_settings.yaml in the project folder (projects/<Name>/plot_settings.yaml) to control plot colours and stacking order. It is honored automatically by both the per-scenario plots and the comparison plots in the Toolbox track. A top-level write_plot_data: true in it also writes the data drawn in each plot as a CSV file next to the plot (or add --write-plot-data to the tool's command-line arguments); see Plotted data as CSV.

docs.title: FlexTool GUI interoperability
docs.text: Outputs under projects/<Name>/output_parquet/<scenario>/ are discovered automatically by the FlexTool GUI — the folder name is the result identity. A Toolbox-produced scenario appears under "source 0" in the GUI, which is cosmetic. Conversely, the Toolbox can run a project built in the GUI: point the Input data Data Store at projects/<Name>/input_sources/<db>.sqlite and set templates/project_folder.txt to projects/<Name>.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
There is no forced migration — existing workflows keep working, and a blank project_folder.txt reproduces the old repo-root behavior. The only steps:

  1. Run flextool-update (or python update_flextool.py). It seeds templates/project_folder.txt and refreshes the settings databases (which already carry the output-spinedb option).
  2. Only if you forked or customized .spinetoolbox/project.json: update the FlexTool Tool's command argument from --flextool-location <project>/templates/flextool_location.txt to --project-folder-file <project>/templates/project_folder.txt. The legacy --flextool-location argument still works as a fallback.
  3. To direct outputs into a project folder, put its path in templates/project_folder.txt. To get results.sqlite, set output-spinedb=true in Output settings.

docs.title: Customising the workflow
docs.text: To experiment with workflow changes without touching the git-controlled .spinetoolbox/ in the FlexTool checkout, create a new Toolbox project in a separate folder, then use the toolbar's + From file… button to add the specifications from .spinetoolbox/specifications/ of your FlexTool checkout. The specifications stay in the FlexTool repository (and update with git pull / update_flextool.py), while the new project file lives wherever you put it.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The shipped workflow is tuned for the Spine database editor. One can use the tabular importer flow (imports Excel or LibreOffice that use specific format), but be careful to edit only in one place.
  • The Spine Toolbox UI itself sees occasional minor graphical glitches on macOS; the underlying FlexTool runs are unaffected.

docs.text:
• Install with Spine Toolbox

  • FlexTool GUI — the primary interface
  • Spine database — the SQLite input format
  • Excel interface — the parallel spreadsheet input flow
  • Terminal CLI — headless / CI usage
