docs.title: Running IRENA FlexTool from the terminal
docs.text: IRENA FlexTool can be run directly from the command line without Spine Toolbox or a web browser. This is useful for scripting, automation, running on servers, or when you prefer a terminal-based workflow.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+ with a virtual environment (e.g. ~/venv-spi/)
  • HiGHS solver, called from Python via the highspy bindings (installed automatically with the FlexTool package)
  • FlexTool installed: pip install -e . (add [toolbox] for Spine Toolbox integration)
  • See the install page for full setup instructions

Activate the virtual environment before running any commands:

source ~/venv-spi/bin/activate

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Run the example scenario base from the bundled example database:

python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    templates/examples.sqlite \
    output_info.sqlite \
    base

The database already exists, so the input-preparation phase is skipped automatically (it runs only when --tabular-file-path or --csv-directory-path is given). An input database older than this FlexTool is migrated first (a frozen one stops the workflow; see Migrate database schema). Phase 2 then runs the model and writes outputs in one pass. Results land in output_plots/base/ and output_parquet/base/.

docs.title: Scripts overview
docs.text:
Root-level scripts are backward-compatible wrappers that delegate to modules under flextool/cli/. To run the model, use the flextool-run console script:

# Console script (preferred for model runs)
flextool-run ...

# Root-level script (backward compat)
python run_flextool.py ...

# Module invocation
python -m flextool.cli.cmd_run_flextool ...

flextool-run runs the engine (flextool.cli.cmd_run_flextool) as a child process and writes everything the engine prints into the run's log, output_parquet/<scenario>/_run.log, including the solver's own lines and a crash dump. It takes the same arguments and exits with the engine's exit code. The other two forms run the engine in the same process; their _run.log holds only FlexTool's own console output.

docs.title: Workflow and execution
docs.text: Script CLI module Purpose execute_flextool_workflow.py flextool.cli.cmd_execute_flextool_workflow Unified entry point — runs the full workflow run_flextool.py flextool.cli.cmd_run_flextool (run it with flextool-run) Runs the optimization model and writes outputs write_outputs.py flextool.cli.cmd_write_outputs (Re-)generates plots, parquet, CSV, or Excel from results scenario_results.py flextool.cli.cmd_scenario_results Compares results across multiple scenarios

docs.title: Input preparation
docs.text: CLI module Purpose flextool.cli.cmd_read_tabular_input Parse Excel/ODS/CSV using JSON specification → write Spine DB flextool.cli.cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input Read self-describing Excel with embedded metadata → Spine DB flextool.cli.cmd_read_old_flextool Import old FlexTool v2 .xlsm files → Spine DB

docs.title: Export and maintenance
docs.text: Script CLI module Purpose migrate_database.py flextool.cli.cmd_migrate_database Upgrade DB schema to latest version — flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular Export Spine DB → Excel (.xlsx) update_flextool.py flextool.cli.cmd_update_flextool Git pull + project migration — flextool.cli.cmd_time_runs (flextool-time-runs) Time scenario runs phase by phase (Check that exercises run fast enough)

docs.title: Installed entry points
docs.text:
After pip install -e . or pip install ., these commands are available directly:

Command Entry point flextool-gui flextool.gui.__main__:main flextool-read-old flextool.cli.cmd_read_old_flextool:main flextool-migrate-database flextool.cli.cmd_migrate_database:main flextool-freeze flextool.cli.cmd_freeze_database:main flextool-project flextool.cli.cmd_project_package:main flextool-time-runs flextool.cli.cmd_time_runs:main

docs.title: execute_flextool_workflow.py — full workflow
docs.text:
This is the recommended entry point. It orchestrates two phases:

  1. Input preparation (optional) — convert tabular data (Excel/ODS/CSV) into a Spine database. Runs only when --tabular-file-path or --csv-directory-path is given; otherwise the existing input database is used as-is.
  2. Model execution + output write — run the FlexTool optimization model and write results in the requested formats. Parquet is always produced; --write-methods selects which additional formats (plot, csv, excel, spinedb) to generate alongside.

The two phases are fused because the in-memory FlexData + HiGHS solution are gone once the solver exits — there is no separate standalone "write outputs" step. (Use python run_flextool.py followed by python write_outputs.py --read-parquet-dir ... if you need to re-render artefacts from a previous run's parquets without re-solving.)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: python execute_flextool_workflow.py INPUT_DB_URL OUTPUT_DB_URL SCENARIO_NAME [options]

docs.title: Positional arguments
docs.text: Argument Description INPUT_DB_URL Input database URL or file path (e.g. sqlite:///input.sqlite or input.sqlite) OUTPUT_DB_URL Output database URL for storing result metadata SCENARIO_NAME Name of the scenario to execute

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Flag Description --tabular-file-path PATH Path to Excel/ODS input file (mutually exclusive with --csv-directory-path). Triggers Phase 1. --csv-directory-path PATH Path to directory containing CSV input files. Triggers Phase 1. --write-methods METHOD [...] Output formats to generate (default: plot parquet csv). Choices: plot, parquet, excel, csv, spinedb. Parquet is the canonical output and is always produced when this flag is omitted. spinedb dumps the processed results into a SpineDB using the FlexTool results schema (one Spine alternative per run, named after the scenario, so multiple runs coexist in one file). --output-subdir DIR Subdirectory for output files (default: scenario name) --output-config PATH Path to output configuration YAML (default: bundled flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml) --debug Forward --debug to the model run (enables verbose memory checkpoints and per-solve CSV diagnostics)

docs.title: Input sources
docs.text:
From an Excel or ODS file:

python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    input.sqlite output_info.sqlite my_scenario \
    --tabular-file-path my_input.xlsx

From a directory of CSV files:

python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    input.sqlite output_info.sqlite my_scenario \
    --csv-directory-path input_data/

From an existing Spine database (no --tabular-file-path / --csv-directory-path ⇒ Phase 1 is skipped automatically):

python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    sqlite:///input.sqlite output_info.sqlite my_scenario

docs.title: run_flextool.py — model execution
docs.text: Runs the FlexTool optimization model directly. This is called internally by execute_flextool_workflow.py but can also be used standalone. After solving, it writes outputs and records scenario information in the output database.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
flextool-run INPUT_DB_URL [OUTPUT_DB_URL] [options]

python run_flextool.py and python -m flextool.cli.cmd_run_flextool take the same arguments.

Each run writes two files into its output_parquet/<subdir>/ folder: _run_status.json (running, succeeded, failed, ...; each solve's outcome; the solver option files used: folder, and a SHA-256 of each; whether the parquet files there belong to this run) and _run.log (the run's console output). Under flextool-run, the GUI, the workflow runner and the calibrator the log also holds the solver's native output and any crash dump.

docs.title: Positional arguments
docs.text: Argument Description INPUT_DB_URL Input database URL OUTPUT_DB_URL Output database URL for result metadata (optional)

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Run control and I/O paths:

Flag Description --scenario-name NAME Scenario name to execute (if omitted, uses the active DB filter) --settings-db-url URL Settings DB consulted for post-processing defaults --migrate Migrate the input database to the current FlexTool version before the run, if it is older (see Migrate database schema). A frozen database is not migrated: the run stops with exit code 2. Without the flag, an older database is refused. --output-spreadsheet PATH Save results to a spreadsheet file --write-methods METHOD [...] Output formats: plot, parquet, excel, csv, spinedb (default: plot parquet) --results-db-url URL Target SpineDB for the spinedb write-method (default: <output-location>/results.sqlite) --output-config PATH Path to output configuration YAML (default: the bundled flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml) --active-configs NAME [...] Which plot configuration sets to use (default: default) --plot-rows START END First and last row to plot in time series (default: 0 167) --output-location DIR Override output location path --output-subdir NAME Subdirectory under output_parquet/ etc. (default: scenario name) --flextool-location PATH Spine Toolbox shim: directs outputs to the FlexTool repo root rather than the work directory --work-folder DIR Working directory for intermediate files (default: CWD). Enables parallel scenario execution by isolating each run --only-first-file-per-plot Only produce the first file for each plot (quick overview mode) --write-plot-data Also write the data drawn in each plot as a CSV file next to it (same name, .csv); see Results --input-source-file PATH The file the input database was made from (e.g. an Excel file), recorded in _run_status.json --run-launcher NAME Who started the run, recorded in _run_status.json (default direct; flextool-run adds flextool-run unless one is given)

Debug and diagnostics:

Flag Description --debug Enable verbose logging, per-checkpoint memory trace, and a solve_data/memory_diagnostics.csv per-solve CSV --csv-dump Preserve cascade debug artefacts on disk: input/, solve_data/, cross_solve/, and output_raw/ mirrors. Off by default (these directories are normally cleaned up after the run)

Scaling and solver tuning:

Each of these flags has an environment-variable twin for runs without a command line (Spine Toolbox, a script); a given flag wins over the variable, and the variable over the solve's database value. See Environment variables. flextool-run passes them to the engine unchanged.

Flag Description --scaling {off,solver_only,basic,full} FlexTool autoscaler strategy (see scaling.md). off disables all scaling including HiGHS' internal equilibration; solver_only keeps only HiGHS' default matrix scaling; basic adds FlexTool's Layer-1 range detection and Layer-3 user_*_scale recommendation without LP mutation; full (default) adds Layer-2 semantic per-type column/row/cost scaling. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SCALING --user-bound-scale N Pin HiGHS' user_bound_scale exponent (multiplies all column bounds and RHS by 2**N). Use the value HiGHS suggests in its scaling warning; clamped to [-10, 0]. Overrides the Layer-3 auto-pick. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_USER_BOUND_SCALE --presolve {on,off,choose} HiGHS presolve override. Default keeps the determinism-pinned on; off disables presolve (slower but useful for memory or numerical diagnostics). Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_PRESOLVE --threads N Threads for one FlexTool run: FlexTool's data processing and the solver. FlexTool's own processing (polars) uses at most N and at most 8 (POLARS_MAX_THREADS sets another limit below N); HiGHS gets threads=N with its parallel simplex off; a Benders solve runs at most N region solves at once. Default: the available cores, with HiGHS and Benders as before. When you run several FlexTool runs at once (for example an AI agent or a script starting them in parallel), give each about cores / runs, e.g. flextool-run input.sqlite --scenario-name base --threads 4. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_THREADS --highs-threads N Number of HiGHS solver threads (default 1). Values >1 enable HiGHS parallel mode and trade determinism for wall-clock speedup; at most --threads when that is given. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_THREADS --solver-time-limit SECONDS Time limit of each solve, on every solver (HiGHS time_limit, Gurobi TimeLimit, CPLEX timelimit, Xpress MAXTIME, COPT TimeLimit), a positive number (default: none; 0 or a negative value is ignored with a warning). Wins over a time limit in the solve's solver_arguments and in the solver's option file. A MIP stopped at the limit keeps its solution with a warning; an LP, or a solve without a solution, stops the run (see Time limit). Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_TIME_LIMIT (FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_TIME_LIMIT: HiGHS only) --solver-mip-gap GAP MIP relative gap for every solve of the run, on every solver (HiGHS mip_rel_gap, Gurobi MIPGap, CPLEX mip tolerances mipgap, Xpress MIPRELSTOP, COPT RelGap). Unset: each solve's solver_mip_gap, else the gap in the solver's option file. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_MIP_GAP (FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_MIP_GAP: HiGHS only) --solver-config-dir PATH Folder of the solver option files (highs.opt, gurobi.opt, ...). Unset: solver_config/ next to the input database, then in the workspace of a GUI project database, then in the Spine Toolbox project folder (--project-folder-file), then in the current folder; FlexTool's defaults with a warning when none has an option file. The run header's Solver config: line names the folder used; the run copies the files to <work folder>/solve_data/solver_config/ (see Where the option files come from). Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR --solver-log-level {silent,normal,verbose} Solver log output (default normal); silent also hides a commercial solver's log (still saved as solve_data/subprocess/<solve>.log); verbose is HiGHS only. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_LOG_LEVEL --save-memory Opt-in peak-RSS reduction: after the LP matrix is built, drop polar-high's polars/numpy source, write the LP to a temp MPS file, and solve it in a separate HiGHS subprocess (via cmd_solve_mps) so the solver's working set lives outside the FlexTool address space. Frees ~5-10 GB on large models at ~+90 s I/O per sub-solve. Also disables warm-LP reuse across cascade iterations. See architecture.md. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_SAVE_MEMORY=1 --warm-start Reuse a cached HiGHS basis for solves of the same model structure, in-process and with --save-memory (Benders solves excepted); any mismatch falls back to a cold solve. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_WARM_START=1 --basis-cache-dir PATH Folder of the --warm-start basis cache (default <work folder>/basis_cache); share one folder to reuse bases between runs. Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_BASIS_CACHE_DIR --benders-workers N Threads for the region solves of a Benders solve (default, or 0: the number of regions, at most cores minus one). Env fallback: FLEXTOOL_BENDERS_WORKERS

Decomposition (Benders):

Benders decomposition is selected per solve from the database, not via a CLI flag: set solve.decomposition = benders (plus the optional solve.benders_max_iter / benders_tolerance knobs) and declare at least two group.decomposition_method = benders_regional region groups. A single chain can mix schemes. See decomposition.md. The one remaining CLI flag is the filter-only inspector:

Flag Description --region GROUP_NAME Filter-only entry point: produce a per-region input directory input_region_<GROUP>/ for Benders decomposition and exit without solving. Cross-region processes are replaced with import/export half-flows; coupling variables are listed in solve_data/region_coupling.csv

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
flextool-run \
    sqlite:///templates/examples.sqlite \
    sqlite:///output_info.sqlite \
    --scenario-name base

Return codes: 0 = success, 1 = infeasible or unbounded, -1 = failure.

docs.title: write_outputs.py — output generation
docs.text: Generates plots, parquet files, CSV, or Excel outputs from existing model results. Useful for re-plotting with different settings without re-running the model.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python write_outputs.py [options]

All arguments are optional. When run from the terminal, you typically provide --scenario-name.

docs.title: Key options
docs.text: Flag Description --scenario-name NAME Scenario with raw outputs available (when re-plotting a single scenario from the terminal) --input-db-url URL Input DB with scenario filter (used when run_flextool.py chains into this command from Toolbox) --output-locations-db-url URL Output-locations DB holding paths of existing outputs (re-plotting from Toolbox) --settings-db-url URL Settings DB consulted for unset parameters --read-parquet-dir DIR Read from existing parquet files instead of raw CSVs (faster) --config-path PATH Output configuration YAML (default: the bundled flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml) --active-configs NAME [...] Which plot configuration sets to use (default: default) --write-methods METHOD [...] Output formats: plot, parquet, excel, csv, spinedb (default: plot parquet excel) --results-db-url URL Target SpineDB for the spinedb write-method (default: <output-location>/results.sqlite). Note: spinedb needs the native solve path, so it is skipped (with a warning) when re-rendering via --read-parquet-dir. --plot-rows START END First and last row to plot in time series (default: 0 167) --subdir DIR Subdirectory for outputs (default: scenario name) --output-location DIR Root directory for input/output locations (default: flextool root); overridden by --output-locations-db-url --plot-file-format {png,svg} File format for plots (default: png) --only-first-file-per-plot Only produce the first file for each plot (quick overview mode) --write-plot-data Also write the data drawn in each plot as a CSV file next to it (same name, .csv); see Results --single-result KEY CSV_NAME PLOT_NAME PLOT_TYPE SUBPLOTS_PER_ROW LEGEND_POSITION Process a single result (overrides --config-path). Use "null" for None values --debug Enable debug output

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Re-plot from raw CSV outputs:

python write_outputs.py --scenario-name base

Re-plot from existing parquet files:

python write_outputs.py \
    --scenario-name base \
    --read-parquet-dir output_parquet/base

Generate only Excel output:

python write_outputs.py \
    --scenario-name base \
    --write-methods excel

Plot a different time range (rows 0 to 500):

python write_outputs.py \
    --scenario-name base \
    --plot-rows 0 500

docs.title: scenario_results.py — cross-scenario comparison
docs.text: Reads results from multiple scenarios and generates comparison plots and optional spreadsheets.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: python scenario_results.py [DB_URL] [options]

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Flag Description --parquet-base-dir DIR Base directory containing per-scenario parquet subdirectories --alternatives NAME [...] Specify scenario/alternative names manually --dispatch-plots Generate dispatch area plots for nodes and node groups --write-to-xlsx Write combined results to Excel file --write-dispatch-xlsx Write dispatch data to Excel in the plot directory --write-to-ods Write combined results to ODS file --output-config-path PATH Plot configuration YAML (default: the bundled flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml, which also holds the comparison plots) --active-configs NAME [...] Which plot configuration sets to use (default: default) --plot-rows START END First and last row to plot in time series (default: 0 167) --plot-dir DIR Directory for comparison plots (default: output_plot_comparisons) --excel-dir DIR Directory for comparison Excel files --plot-file-format FORMAT File format for plots: png or svg --shared-legend Use shared legend across subplots --only-first-file-per-plot Only produce the first file for each plot --write-plot-data Also write the data drawn in each plot, dispatch plots included, as a CSV file next to it; see Results --show-plots Display plots interactively in addition to saving

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Generate dispatch plots for specific alternatives:

python scenario_results.py sqlite:///output_info.sqlite \
    --dispatch-plots --alternatives base high_RE

Compare scenarios from parquet directories (without output DB):

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_scenario_results \
    --parquet-base-dir output_parquet \
    --alternatives base network_all_tech \
    --dispatch-plots --write-to-xlsx

docs.title: Input preparation commands
docs.text: These commands convert tabular input data into a Spine database. They are called automatically by execute_flextool_workflow.py and by the GUI, but can also be run manually.

docs.title: Import self-describing Excel
docs.text:
The self-describing format embeds metadata (entity classes, parameter names, data types) directly in the Excel sheet headers. This is the recommended input format.

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input \
    my_input.xlsx sqlite:///input.sqlite
Argument Description xlsx_path Path to the self-describing Excel file target_db_url Target database URL --keep-entities Keep existing entities during purge (default: purge all) --no-purge Do not purge existing data before importing

docs.title: Import with specification file
docs.text:
The older format uses a separate JSON specification file to define how Excel/ODS/CSV columns map to database entities.

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_tabular_input \
    sqlite:///input.sqlite \
    --tabular-file-path my_input.xlsx
Argument Description target_db_url URL to FlexTool input database --tabular-file-path PATH Path to Excel or ODS input file --csv-directory-path PATH Path to directory containing CSV input files --migration-follows Accept version mismatch (migration will run after import)

docs.title: Import old FlexTool v2 files
docs.text:
Converts an old-format FlexTool 2 input data file (.xlsm, 18 fixed sheets) to a new FlexTool database. With --master, the sensitivities of the FlexTool 2 master workbook (the one with the run buttons and the Sensitivity definitions sheet) are imported in the same run, as alternatives and scenarios on top of base.

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_old_flextool \
    InputData/old_model.xlsm sqlite:///input.sqlite \
    --master flexTool.xlsm
Argument Description xlsm_path Path to the FlexTool 2 input data file (one of the master workbook's InputData/*.xlsm) target_db_url Target database URL. A new file is created. An existing FlexTool database is accepted only at version 56 (see below) --master PATH FlexTool 2 master workbook: import its sensitivities too --alternative-name NAME Name for the alternative (default: base) --no-purge Do not purge existing data before importing --no-migrate Leave the database at version 56 instead of migrating it --strict Stop with an error, and leave no database, when a value cannot be written (default: list it in the report) --verbose, -v Debug logging

The importer writes the data at a fixed database version (56) and then migrates the database to the current version. The sensitivities are written before the migration, so give --master in the same command. A database that is already at another version is refused: writing version-56 data into it would lose every value whose name or meaning changed since. So is a database that has data but is not a FlexTool database. flextool.cli.cmd_import_sensitivities MASTER BASE.xlsm sqlite:///db.sqlite adds sensitivities later only to a database left at version 56 with --no-migrate; migrate it afterwards with flextool-migrate-database db.sqlite. Giving the master workbook as the input file stops with a message that names the right files. A database the command migrates carries no behaviour-change notices: they describe changes between FlexTool 4 versions, which an imported FlexTool 2 model never ran on. A database left at version 56 with --no-migrate and migrated later with flextool-migrate-database does carry them; they can be ignored for an imported FlexTool 2 model.

Import report. The run ends with a report written for a reader who is not a modeller: what was written, every value the database refused, and, grouped by topic (time and costs, units, nodes and connections, sensitivities), every FlexTool 2 input that was not carried over or works differently in FlexTool 4, with the entities that use it and what to do. Check it before using the model. The inputs it lists:

FlexTool 2 input What differs master time_in_years that differs (by more than 1 %) from the hours the time series covers / 8760 FlexTool 2 scales the operating costs by the time the series represents (time_in_years); FlexTool 4 scales them by the hours the time steps cover, to a full year, and has no input to change that. The ratio of operating to investment costs then differs by the factor the line gives (e.g. 365 for 24 one-hour steps with time_in_years = 1), and so do the investments. Listed first. To keep FlexTool 2's balance, multiply the investment and fixed costs by that factor. cf and inflow series with steps not in use FlexTool 2 scales each series so that its mean over the steps in use equals its mean over the whole series (separately for the investment and the dispatch run); FlexTool 4 uses the values as they are. The line gives the factor. unit_type availability < 1 In FlexTool 2 it enters only the capacity margin; it does not reduce generation. In FlexTool 4 availability limits generation and derates the unit in the capacity margin together, so it is not imported: generation is as in FlexTool 2, and in a capacity margin the units count with their full capacity. master curtailment_penalty FlexTool 4 has no curtailment cost. master reserve_duration FlexTool 4 has reserve__upDown__group.reserve_duration, which the version-56 importer cannot write. Set it after the import. unit_type conversion eff The output / input ratio of a unit that takes its input from a node (e.g. a heat pump COP). Set the unit's efficiency to it, where the unit has no efficiency time series. units use min online (with its ts_unit min_online) FlexTool 4 has no time-series floor on the online capacity. The series of a unit whose flag is 0 is not listed: FlexTool 2 ignores it too. units fueluse increase eq x output2 FlexTool 2's fuel-use equation adds this fuel only when output2 is on the unit's own output node, so in a normal workbook it adds nothing in FlexTool 2 either; the import ignores it. gridNode import (MWh) The import series is not added to the node. a generation-limit flag on a storage unit Not carried over (the unit becomes a charger and a discharger). any other non-zero column the importer does not read Listed with a note to check whether it matters.

Sensitivity overrides that the sensitivity import does not translate are listed too, with their scenario (alternative), where the value can be set by hand.

Must-run and generation limits. In FlexTool 2, the units flags fix unit generation, use min generation and use max generation use the ts_unit series fix_generation, min_generation and max_generation of the same grid / node / unit: the share (0-1) of the unit's capacity it must generate, at least or at most. Each becomes a FlexTool 4 profile <unit>_<series> (a time series) and a unit__node__profile (unit, output node, profile) with profile_method fixed, lower_limit or upper_limit. The limit is on the primary output only; an output2 follows through the CHP constraints. A flag of 0 ignores the series, as in FlexTool 2. The report lists a flag without its series, a use max generation on a unit with a cf profile (FlexTool 2 ignores it there) and a flag on a conversion unit (FlexTool 2 bounds its input flow). FlexTool 2's max_generation also caps the online capacity of a unit with online variables; the FlexTool 4 profile caps only the generation, so the minimum load and start-ups of such a unit can differ a little where the series is below 1 (the report notes these units).

CHP (output2). FlexTool 2's output2 (e.g. the heat of a CHP unit) uses no fuel and is outside the unit's capacity, minimum load and ramp limits; it is tied to the primary output only by the output2 eq / gt / lt rows and output2_max_capacity_ratio. In FlexTool 4 the output2 edge gets conversion_flow_coeff 0 (out of the conversion equation and of the capacity limits), and each FlexTool 2 row becomes a user constraint <unit>_eq, _gt, _lt or _output2_max: output2 − coeff × output1 {=, ≥, ≤} constant × capacity, where the capacity is the unit's capacity in service in each solve: constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff (existing capacity, including what an earlier solve invested) plus constraint_invested_capacity_coeff (what the solve invests), both on the unit. So an invested CHP keeps its output2 in the dispatch solve that follows the investment solve. In older workbooks, which have the column output2 max capacity (MW) in place of output2 max capacity ratio, the eq / gt / lt constants are MW: the rows are output2 − coeff × output1 {=, ≥, ≤} constant, with no capacity term, output2 max capacity (MW) becomes a plain upper limit in MW, and the report says the constants were read as MW. The report also lists an output2 without any row: its output2 is free (no fuel, no limit), as in FlexTool 2.

Capacity. In FlexTool 2, invested capacity (MW) and invested storage (MWh) are capacity already built: they count in every capacity limit, in every mode, and are not part of the investment decision. So existing is capacity (MW) + invested capacity (MW) (units, chargers and dischargers, connections; for a connection the larger direction) and storage (MWh) + invested storage (MWh) (storage nodes). max invest (MW) / max invest (MWh) is the investment limit (invest_max_total). A sensitivity of either column changes the sum. FlexTool 2 also adds the investment annuity of the invested capacity to its total cost as a fixed amount; FlexTool 4 does not, so the report lists these entities (those with an investment cost, also when a sensitivity gives the capacity). The fixed kW/kWh ratio ties the invested MW to the invested MWh (MW = ratio × MWh), as in FlexTool 2; when only one max invest is given, the other is derived through the ratio, as FlexTool 2 does. A storage node stays a storage while it has capacity or can invest in it; a sensitivity that leaves it neither (e.g. invested storage (MWh) and max invest (MWh) 0, no storage (MWh)) makes it a balance node.

Time steps. The steps with in_use 1 on the ts_time sheet form the dispatch timeset, those with in_use_invest 1 the investment timeset (as FlexTool 2's model). A workbook whose solves have no step in use is refused with a message, before any database is written: FlexTool 2 would solve nothing either. (A FlexTool 2 master workbook can take ts_time from its time series folder, ts/<input file name>/ts_time.csv; the importer reads only the workbook, so copy the column into it.)

Storage start and finish. A non-zero storage start / storage finish fixes the first / last storage state at that share of the storage capacity (storage_start_end_method fix_start, fix_end or fix_start_end); 0 or empty fixes nothing (fix_nothing). The storage state wraps from the last step to the first (bind_within_solve), except when both are set (bind_forward_only), as in FlexTool 2.

docs.title: Export database to Excel
docs.text:
Exports a Spine database back to Excel (.xlsx) in self-describing format.

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular \
    sqlite:///input.sqlite output.xlsx
Argument Description db_url URL to FlexTool input database output_path Output Excel file path (.xlsx) --include-advanced Include advanced sheets (solve sequences, stochastic data) --old-format Use the old v1 format instead of self-describing v2

docs.title: Migrate database schema
docs.text:
Upgrades a database to the latest FlexTool schema version using the templates bundled under flextool/schemas/.

flextool-migrate-database input.sqlite
# or: python -m flextool.cli.cmd_migrate_database input.sqlite
Argument Description filepath Path to the database file (absolute, or relative to the current folder) --copy-to PATH Copy the database to PATH and migrate the copy; the original is not changed. For a frozen database. --allow-migrate-frozen Migrate a frozen database in place; its frozen marker is kept with the new version.

The model run (flextool-run, run_flextool.py, python -m flextool.cli.cmd_run_flextool) does not run a database that is not at the current FlexTool version: it stops with a message naming this command. With --migrate it migrates the database first, the same way as this command: a frozen database is not migrated, and the run stops with the frozen message and exit code 2. Runs started at the same time with --migrate on one database migrate it once: the migration holds a lock on <database>.migrate.lock next to the database (the file stays there; it can be deleted when no run is starting), and the other runs print "Waiting for another migration of ...", wait for it and then find the database current. Every in-place migration takes this lock: this command, the Toolbox Migrate database tool, the FlexTool window's refresh, --migrate and execute_flextool_workflow.py. A database that is already current does not wait for the lock and gets no lock file. On Windows a run waits for the lock at most 10 minutes (set FLEXTOOL_MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT to a number of seconds to change it; it is not read on Linux or macOS) and then stops with a message naming the lock file. A file system without file locks (some network mounts) stops the migration with a message: copy the database to a local folder. On a network folder that several machines share, the lock may only coordinate runs on one machine (CIFS, NFS mounted with local_lock): start the migration from one machine first. The settings databases (--settings-db-url, the output database) are not migrated. execute_flextool_workflow.py migrates the input database before it runs the model, the FlexTool window migrates its input sources when it refreshes them, and the Spine Toolbox workflow runs its Migrate database tool before FlexTool.

A frozen database older than this FlexTool (or at the current version but with an older SpineDB schema) is refused with exit code 2 and a message naming the two options: --copy-to NEW.sqlite migrates a copy (the copy is not frozen; it records the label, the old version and the SHA-256 of the frozen file it was made from) and --allow-migrate-frozen migrates the frozen file itself. A frozen database that is already current, or newer than this FlexTool, is left unchanged, also with --allow-migrate-frozen. If FlexTool cannot read the file to check for the marker (another program holds a lock on it), it does not migrate it and says so. flextool-update skips frozen databases and lists them, and execute_flextool_workflow.py stops on one.

docs.title: Freeze a released database
docs.text:
A released model (a reference case, a study's final input) can be frozen so that this FlexTool and later versions do not migrate it in place without being told to (older FlexTool versions do not know the marker). The marker is a row in the database's metadata table, so it travels with the file; it does not change the model. Only a database at the current version can be frozen.

flextool-freeze input.sqlite --label "Reference case 1.0"
flextool-freeze input.sqlite --status
flextool-freeze input.sqlite --unfreeze
Argument Description database The .sqlite file (a path or a sqlite:/// URL) --label LABEL Freeze with this label (at most 170 characters, no vertical bar) --status Print the data version, the frozen marker and, for a migrated copy, what it was migrated from --unfreeze Remove the frozen marker

Freezing writes into the file, so take the SHA-256 of the released file after freezing it. Editing a frozen database (in the database editor, or by importing data into it) is not prevented.

docs.title: Sharing a project
docs.text:
flextool-project writes a project to one file, checks such a file and imports it (the FlexTool window does the same from Manage projects… → Export… / Import…).

flextool-project export UAE_ref --results WOM_1,WEM_1 -o UAE_ref.flextool.zip
flextool-project verify UAE_ref.flextool.zip
flextool-project import UAE_ref.flextool.zip --name UAE_ref_received
Command / argument Description export PROJECT The project folder, or the name of a project in ./projects -o FILE The package file (default ./<Name>_<YYYYMMDD>.flextool.zip) --results none\|all\|RUN,RUN The result runs (folders of output_parquet/) to include; default none --no-external Do not copy the input files that the project reads from outside its folder --keep-run-records Ship each run's _run_status.json and _run.log as they are (default: this computer's folder paths, user name and host name are replaced in the record and the log is left out) --force Replace the package file when it exists (without it, an existing file stops the export) --solver-config-dir DIR Where the .opt files are read from (default $FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR, else ./solver_config) verify FILE Check every checksum and the versions, unpacking nothing; exit code 1 on a problem import FILE Unpack into ./projects/ (--projects-dir DIR for another folder) under the package's name or --name NAME; exit code 3 when the name is taken (the message suggests <Name>_2), 2 when the package is refused

The package holds the input sources (external input files copied in under their own source numbers), settings.yaml without the machine-specific settings (execution_limits, max_workers, scenario_resource_history, external_refs), plot_settings.yaml, the .opt files of the solver config folder, and the chosen result runs, with output_parquet/_axis_bounds.json cut to those runs. --results all leaves out a run that is still being written, and naming such a run stops the export. A run's record (_run_status.json) and log (_run.log) show this computer's folder paths, user name and host name: by default the record has them replaced by <project>, ~, <path>/, <host> and <user> and the log is left out (--keep-run-records keeps both as they are). Plots, CSV and Excel outputs, results.sqlite and the scratch folders are left out; flextool-write-outputs re-creates them from the results (--write-methods spinedb for results.sqlite). A .sqlite input with a -journal or -wal file next to it (a program may be writing to it) is copied through SQLite as a consistent database, others byte for byte; -journal, -wal and -shm files are never packaged, and a file that changes while it is copied stops the export. Names Windows cannot hold (CON, NUL, COM1…, < > : " | ? *, a trailing dot or space, names that differ only in case) stop the export, because a package must unpack on every system. The .opt files and plot_settings.yaml travel as they are, folder paths in them included. Its manifest.json records the FlexTool, polar-high, HiGHS, polars, spinedb_api and Python versions, the data version and frozen marker of each input database, the runs whose input changed after the run (stale_runs) and the SHA-256, size and modification time of each file. Export reads the databases read-only: nothing is migrated, and a frozen database stays frozen.

Import refuses member names that would leave the project folder or that Windows cannot hold, refuses a package that does not fit on the disk, checks every checksum before it writes anything, unpacks into a hidden projects/.<name>.partial/ folder, gives each file its recorded modification time back and then renames the folder into place. A database newer than this FlexTool is refused; an older one is migrated when the project is first opened, with the usual consent for a frozen one. The shipped .opt files go to imported_solver_config/ in the project and the workspace's own are never overwritten; the import message says whether they differ (with the lines that differ) and how to use them: copy imported_solver_config/*.opt to the workspace's solver_config/, or set FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR=<project>/imported_solver_config. It names any input left out of the package: its scenarios cannot be run again until that file is added. Errors such as a full disk or a folder that cannot be written are reported as one message (exit code 2); a stopped import leaves a hidden projects/.<name>.partial/, which the GUI does not list and the next import of that name removes. The checksums detect a file damaged on the way, not a deliberate change: the manifest is not signed.

Reproducing a delivered run. Send a project with the inputs and the one scenario run to be reproduced (--results WOM_1). The receiver runs flextool-project verify: it prints the versions the run was made with and one line, pip install flextool==X polar-high==Y highspy==Z polars==W, that installs the same FlexTool, solver interface, HiGHS and polars (the results depend on all four; import warns when the installed polar-high or highspy differs). The receiver then imports the package, makes the shipped solver options active as above, runs the scenario again, and compares the new results with the shipped WOM_1 (whose _run_status.json records the verdict, the solver and the input data version). Because the source number is kept, the re-run writes to the same WOM_1 folder name, so first move the shipped folder outside output_parquet/ (a renamed folder inside it shows up as another run), or compare against a copy of it kept elsewhere.

docs.title: Check that exercises run fast enough
docs.text:
For a course, flextool-time-runs runs scenarios one after another on the trainer's (or a participant's) computer and shows where each run's time goes. It prints the computer first (processor, cores, memory, system and FlexTool version), so the tables of different laptops can be compared. Before each run it prints the run's number and scenario, and the time when the run ends; the whole default set of examples takes several minutes.

flextool-time-runs                                  # every example and how-to scenario that comes with FlexTool
flextool-time-runs --source templates_examples --scenario coal "network_*"
flextool-time-runs --db projects/Course/input_sources/exercises.sqlite --scenario Ex1 Ex2 --target 30 --strict

Put a pattern in double quotes, as above: that works in bash, PowerShell and the Windows Command Prompt (which keeps single quotes as part of the name). On Windows, open the terminal with the FlexTool environment active (.venv\Scripts\activate, see Installation) so that flextool-time-runs is found.

The table has one row per run, slowest first, in seconds; ! marks a run over the target (default 60 s):

Column What it covers wall The whole run, started with the command and thread count the FlexTool window uses by default (see --threads) start-up Starting Python and loading FlexTool read input Reading the input database, preparing the input data and setting up the run preprocess Building each solve's data and its optimisation problem solve The solver outputs Writing the results (parquet) viewer The data the result viewer needs (also written with plots off) plots The scenario plots (png); zero with plots off untimed The rest. A Benders solve writes no per-solve problem-building, solving or result-writing times, so those land here Argument Description --db PATH Run the scenarios of this .sqlite input database (a path or a sqlite:/// URL; can be given several times) instead of the examples. The runs read a copy of it made in the temporary folder, so the file itself is never opened by a run --source JSON Build and run a JSON database: a file, or a shipped one by name (templates_examples, howto_demand, …) --scenario NAME [...] Scenario names or patterns (*, ?); default every scenario. A name that matches nothing is an error --plots off\|on\|both Write the scenario plots in the runs (default off); both runs each scenario twice --threads N Threads for each run, as Threads per run in the FlexTool window (default 1, the window's default). Give the value the course project uses --target SECONDS Mark runs longer than this (default 60) --strict Exit code 2 when a run is over the target. A failed run always gives exit code 1 --keep DIR Keep the runs' work folders, results and logs in DIR (default: a temporary folder that is removed) --csv FILE Also write the table to a CSV file

The runs go one after another, because runs in parallel slow each other down. The run times come from each run's timings.csv (in output_csv/<scenario>/), which every run writes. With --plots on, the runs draw the default plot set, not only the output configurations a project has made active, so the plots and viewer times can differ a little from that project's runs in the window.

Plots are off in the timed runs by default because they are the slowest part of a small model's run and an exercise does not need them: participants see every plot in the result viewer, which draws them from the results. Switch them off for an exercise project with the Auto-gen tick of Scenario pngs in the FlexTool window (see Outputs; the tick is saved in the project's settings.yaml, so a shared project keeps it), with --write-methods parquet on flextool-run, or with output-plot in the Spine Toolbox settings database.

docs.title: Update FlexTool
docs.text:
Pulls the latest version from GitHub and migrates project databases.

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_update_flextool

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text: These examples use the bundled templates/examples.sqlite database and the base scenario.

docs.title: 1. Run a full workflow from an existing database
docs.text:
# Run model and generate outputs (plots, parquet, CSV)
# No --tabular-file-path / --csv-directory-path → Phase 1 is skipped automatically
python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    templates/examples.sqlite \
    output_info.sqlite \
    base

# Output plots are saved to output_plots/base/
# Parquet files are saved to output_parquet/base/
# CSV files are saved to output_csv/base/

docs.title: 2. Import from Excel and run
docs.text:
# Self-describing format (recommended)
python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    input.sqlite output_info.sqlite my_scenario \
    --tabular-file-path my_input.xlsx

docs.title: 3. Re-plot outputs from parquet files
docs.text:
After running the model at least once, you can regenerate plots from the saved parquet files without re-running the model:

python write_outputs.py \
    --scenario-name base \
    --read-parquet-dir output_parquet/base \
    --write-methods plot

docs.title: 4. Compare multiple scenarios
docs.text:
First, run two scenarios to populate the output database:

# Run first scenario
python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    templates/examples.sqlite output_info.sqlite base

# Run second scenario
python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    templates/examples.sqlite output_info.sqlite network_all_tech

Then compare them:

python scenario_results.py sqlite:///output_info.sqlite --dispatch-plots

Comparison plots are saved to output_plot_comparisons/.

docs.title: 5. Import and convert an old FlexTool v2 model
docs.text:
# Import the old-format file (creates converted.sqlite; --master adds the sensitivities)
python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_old_flextool InputData/old_model.xlsm sqlite:///converted.sqlite \
    --master flexTool.xlsm

# Run a scenario from the converted database
python execute_flextool_workflow.py \
    converted.sqlite output_info.sqlite my_scenario

docs.title: 6. Export a database to Excel and re-import
docs.text:
# Export
python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular sqlite:///input.sqlite exported.xlsx

# Edit exported.xlsx in a spreadsheet editor...

# Re-import
python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input \
    exported.xlsx sqlite:///input.sqlite

docs.title: 7. Run several scenarios in a batch
docs.text:
To run a set of scenarios (for example the sensitivities of How to run a sensitivity) without the FlexTool window, loop over their names with flextool-run. Activate FlexTool's virtual environment first so that flextool-run is found.

Migrate the database first. flextool-run refuses an input database that is not at the current FlexTool version and names the command to run. Migrate it once before the loop:

flextool-migrate-database input.sqlite

or add --migrate to the flextool-run command; runs started at the same time then migrate it once.

Bash (Linux, macOS):

for s in coal coal_co2_price coal_fuel_price_high; do
    flextool-run sqlite:///input.sqlite sqlite:///output_info.sqlite --scenario-name "$s" --output-location results --work-folder "work/$s" --threads 2
    status=$?
    if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
        echo "Scenario $s did not finish (return code $status)"
    fi
done

PowerShell (Windows):

foreach ($s in @("coal", "coal_co2_price", "coal_fuel_price_high")) {
    flextool-run "sqlite:///input.sqlite" "sqlite:///output_info.sqlite" --scenario-name "$s" --output-location "results" --work-folder "work\$s" --threads 2
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        Write-Host "Scenario $s did not finish (return code $LASTEXITCODE)"
    }
}

Quoting. Put each scenario name and path in double quotes: a name with spaces then stays one argument in both shells. In a database URL, use forward slashes also on Windows, for example "sqlite:///C:/Users/me/flextool/input.sqlite" (three slashes, then the drive).

Return codes. 0 is success, 1 an infeasible or unbounded model, -1 another failure (bash shows it as 255). The loop goes on to the next scenario; each run's log is _run.log in its output_parquet/<scenario>/ folder, next to _run_status.json.

Runs at the same time. The loop above runs one scenario after another. To start several at once (for example from several terminals), give each run its own --work-folder and about cores / runs --threads (see the run_flextool.py options). Leave the output database out of runs that start at the same time and compare them from their parquet folders, as below.

Compare the results with scenario_results.py, from the output database or from the parquet folders:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_scenario_results --parquet-base-dir results/output_parquet --alternatives coal coal_co2_price coal_fuel_price_high --write-to-xlsx

The workbook is written to output_plot_comparisons/ under the parquet folder; --excel-dir and --plot-dir choose other folders.

To check that the runs are fast enough for a course, time them with flextool-time-runs.

docs.title: Output directory structure
docs.text:
After running the workflow, outputs are organized as follows:

<output location>/
  output_plots/<scenario>/          # PNG plot files
  output_parquet/<scenario>/        # Parquet data files
  output_csv/<scenario>/            # CSV data files
  output_excel/output_<scenario>.xlsx  # Excel workbook, one per scenario
  output_plot_comparisons/          # Cross-scenario comparison plots
  solve_data/                       # Solver progress and timing

The output location is the current directory, or the path given with --output-location. The FlexTool GUI writes into the project folder (projects/<Name>/), and its folder names carry the input source number (<scenario>_<src#>).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Output plots are controlled by YAML configuration files:

  • flextool/schemas/default_plots.yaml — the bundled plot configuration, for single-scenario plots and cross-scenario comparison plots alike (each plot's scenario_rule decides where it is drawn)

The file defines which results to plot, plot types, layout, and styling. You can create custom configuration files and pass them via --output-config or --output-config-path. An old setting that points to templates/default_plots.yaml or default_comparison_plots.yaml uses the bundled file.

Dispatch plot colors and stacking order are defined in the project's plot_settings.yaml (projects/<Name>/plot_settings.yaml), which is created from the bundled flextool/schemas/default_plot_settings.yaml and can be edited via the GUI or any text editor.

docs.title: IRENA FlexTool tutorial
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through building a small Coal + Wind power system from scratch over a 48-hour timeline. You will create one node at a time, add generation, connect a small transmission network, and watch each change move the dispatch and the slack penalties. Allow roughly 30–45 minutes the first time through. The tutorial assumes the FlexTool GUI is already installed — if not, follow Install with FlexTool GUI first.

Alternative execution interface: Spine Toolbox

If you prefer the Spine Toolbox workflow editor — typically for integrating FlexTool with other models, or for building custom input / output processing steps — the same Coal + Wind example can be built there. See Spine Toolbox and Install with Spine Toolbox.

Alternative data editor: Excel / LibreOffice

The model data shown in the screenshots below is edited in the Spine database editor, which the FlexTool GUI launches when you double-click an input source. If you would rather edit in a spreadsheet, export an Excel template, edit it, and re-import. See Excel as input/output. The modelling concepts in this tutorial are identical regardless of the editor.

Just want to see the finished version?

The same Coal + Wind scenarios are pre-built in templates/examples.sqlite. Add that file as an input source in a fresh project and you can run every scenario in this tutorial without building anything by hand. Building it step-by-step is the recommended way to learn the concepts.

docs.title: What you're building
docs.text:
A three-node electricity system with a coal plant, a wind plant, and three interconnections, dispatched over a two-day timeline:

The model grows one alternative at a time. Each alternative is a self-contained piece of data — the first node, the coal plant, the wind plant, the three-node network — and scenarios are assembled by stacking alternatives on top of each other. That way every step can be run on its own and compared to the previous one.

docs.title: Setting up the project
docs.text:
1. Launch the FlexTool GUI from the FlexTool installation directory, with its virtual environment active:

    flextool-gui

    (python -m flextool.gui does the same.)

  2. Create a new project. From the Project menu choose New project, name it tutorial, and pick a location. The GUI creates projects/tutorial/ with an empty input_sources/ folder and a settings.yaml.

  3. Add the seed input source. Click Add in the Input sources panel and pick templates/time_settings_only.sqlite from the FlexTool installation directory. The GUI copies the file into your project's input_sources/ (migrating it to the current schema version if needed) and renames it to whatever you typed in the dialog — tutorial.sqlite is a good name. This seed database already contains the basic time settings (init and init_2day-test alternatives) that every FlexTool model needs. See How to create basic time settings if you want to know how those were built.

  4. Open the input source in the Spine database editor. Double-click the tutorial.sqlite row in Input sources (or select it and press Edit). The Spine database editor opens in its own window — that is where the rest of the modelling steps happen. It comes with the recommended install (flextool[toolbox]); the lighter install without Spine Toolbox does not have it.

Always commit before running

The Spine database editor stages changes locally until you commit them with Ctrl-Enter (or Session → Commit… from the menu). Until you commit, the FlexTool GUI sees the previous, uncommitted state. Every step below ends with a commit reminder for this reason.

docs.title: Step 1 — A node with no units
docs.text: The first alternative holds nothing but a single demand node. Running it on its own forces the model to fall back on slack variables, which is a useful sanity check: it shows what happens when there is no way to meet demand.

docs.title: Add the alternative
docs.text: In the Alternative tree widget of the Spine database editor, add a new alternative called west. Every entity and parameter added in this step will live under this alternative, so it can be combined into scenarios cleanly later on.

docs.title: Add the entity
docs.text:
Right-click the node class in the Entity tree and choose Add entities. Name the new node west and click OK.

Open the Entity Alternative sheet and activate west in the west alternative. Entity Alternative decides whether an entity is part of a given alternative; parameter rows have their own alternative_name column and are independent.

docs.title: Add parameters
docs.text:
Set the following parameters on the west node, all under the west alternative:

  • inflow — a map of negative values, one per timestep, representing demand. Map-type parameters take a column of timestep names and a column of values. Typing 48 rows by hand is tedious, so the easiest way is to copy the column from templates/examples.sqlite (opened as a second input source) and paste it into your west node.
  • penalty_up — e.g. 9000. Cost of unmet upward demand. If nothing else can meet demand, the model "creates" energy at this price using an upward slack variable.
  • penalty_down — e.g. 8000. Cost of unabsorbed downward energy.
  • node_type — balance. Forces the node to maintain an energy balance at every timestep. This is the default, so it can be left blank.

Penalties and slack variables keep the LP feasible at every timestep even when supply and demand do not match. They default to 10000 if not set; you change them only when you have real values, or when you want one node to be preferred over another for last-resort balancing (Step 4 uses this).

Commit with Ctrl-Enter and write an informative commit message. Until you commit, the staged changes are invisible to the FlexTool GUI.

docs.title: Execute and inspect
docs.text:
Back in the FlexTool GUI:

  1. The Available scenarios panel rescans tutorial.sqlite automatically when you commit, but if it does not, press the Refresh button on the Input sources panel.

  2. You need a scenario to execute. Switch to the Spine database editor's Scenario tree and create a scenario Test-scenario that includes the alternatives init, init_2day-test, and west, in that order. Commit.

  3. In Available scenarios, check Test-scenario and click Add checked scenarios to the execution list (or press F9).

  4. Press Execute in the Execution jobs panel. The job appears in the queue and produces a parquet result tree under output_parquet/Test-scenario/ when it finishes.
  5. Press Results viewer under Output actions to inspect dispatch and slack. With no generators present, you should see the upward slack variable taking the full demand at penalty cost.

Alternative order matters

Lower alternatives override higher ones if they touch the same parameter. Test-scenario uses init_2day-test below init, so the 2-day timeset wins over init's full-year timeset — only 48 hours are solved.

docs.title: Step 2 — Add a coal unit
docs.text: Add a coal power plant feeding the west node from a fuel commodity.

docs.title: Alternative and entities
docs.text:
Add a new alternative coal. Then add the following entities (all under coal in Entity Alternative, except commodity which is active by default):

  • unit coal_plant
  • node coal_market
  • commodity coal
  • unit__inputNode coal_plant, coal_market — the coal plant draws from the coal market.
  • unit__outputNode coal_plant, west — and outputs electricity to west.
  • commodity__node coal, coal_market — links the coal commodity to its market node.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
On coal_plant (all under coal):

  • efficiency = 0.4 — 40 % thermal efficiency.
  • existing = 500 — 500 MW of existing capacity.

On the coal commodity:

  • price = 20 — €/MWh of fuel.

Commit with Ctrl-Enter.

docs.title: Execute and inspect
docs.text:
In the Spine database editor, create a new scenario coal with alternatives init, init_2day-test, west, coal (in that order), and commit. In the FlexTool GUI:

  1. Check coal in Available scenarios, Add checked to the queue, and Execute.
  2. Open the Result viewer and switch to comparison view (press X) to compare Test-scenario and coal side by side. The coal scenario should show the coal plant doing most of the work and the upward slack falling sharply.

docs.title: Step 3 — Add a wind plant
docs.text: Wind generation is modelled as a unit whose maximum output follows a time-varying profile instead of consuming a fuel.

docs.title: Alternative and entities
docs.text:
Add alternative wind, then:

  • unit wind_plant
  • profile wind_profile — time-varying capacity factor (no commodity).
  • unit__node__profile wind_plant, west, wind_profile — binds the profile to this unit and node.
  • unit__outputNode wind_plant, west

Add wind_plant to Entity Alternative under wind. profile is active by default and is only used when bound through unit__node__profile (or node_profile).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
On wind_plant (under wind):

  • conversion_method = constant_efficiency.
  • efficiency = 1.
  • existing = 1000 — 1000 MW of installed capacity.

On wind_profile:

  • profile — a map of hourly capacity factors (0–1). Copy this from templates/examples.sqlite the same way you copied the inflow map.

On the wind_plant, west, wind_profile relationship:

  • profile_method = upper_limit. The wind plant generates at or below the available capacity factor every hour.

Commit with Ctrl-Enter.

docs.title: Execute and inspect
docs.text: Create a scenario wind with alternatives init, init_2day-test, west, coal, wind. Commit, then in the FlexTool GUI check wind, queue it, and execute. With both coal and wind feeding west, the upward slack should be zero across all 48 hours — demand is fully met. In the Result viewer, compare coal against wind to see the wind output displacing coal during high-wind hours.

docs.title: Step 4 — Connect a three-node network
docs.text: The final alternative widens the model from one demand node to three, joined by three transmission connections of different capacities.

docs.title: Alternative and entities
docs.text:
Add alternative network. Then add:

  • node east
  • node north
  • connection east_north
  • connection west_east
  • connection west_north
  • connection__node__node east_north, east, north
  • connection__node__node west_east, west, east
  • connection__node__node west_north, west, north

Activate all five new entities (two nodes + three connections) in Entity Alternative under network.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
On east and north (under network):

  • node_type = balance (default, can be left blank).
  • inflow — a constant negative number (demand).
  • penalty_up, penalty_down — give north a lower penalty_up than east and west. The optimiser will then prefer to shed unmet demand at north whenever the transmission network is not strong enough to deliver everything, which makes the comparison plots more interesting.

On each of the three connections (under network):

  • existing — interconnection capacity (MW). Pick values that occasionally constrain flow.
  • efficiency = 0.9 — 90 % transfer efficiency.

Commit with Ctrl-Enter.

docs.title: Execute and inspect
docs.text:
Create a scenario network with alternatives init, init_2day-test, west, coal, wind, network. Commit, queue, execute. In the Result viewer:

  • Switch to comparison view and tick all four executed scenarios — Test-scenario, coal, wind, network.
  • Watch the dispatch shift: with a wider network and the north node providing the cheapest slack, you should see the model trade off transmission limits against slack penalty at north.
  • Use PgUp / PgDn to flick through plot variants (per-node, per-unit, totals).

Enable Auto-generate for repeated runs

The Auto-generate checkboxes in the main GUI window (Scenario plots, Comparison plots, Comparison Excel, …) run the same outputs automatically after each execution. Tick them once and every subsequent Execute produces a fresh set of PNGs and workbooks without further input.

docs.title: Step 5 — Let the model invest
docs.text: So far the model has only dispatched the capacity you gave it. Now let it decide how much wind capacity to build.

docs.title: Alternative and parameters
docs.text:
Add alternative wind_invest. On wind_plant (under wind_invest):

  • invest_method = invest_no_limit — the model may build any amount of new capacity.
  • invest_cost = 1000 — the overnight cost of new capacity [CUR/kW].
  • lifetime = 25 — years.
  • discount_rate = 0.04 — the cost of capital, 4 %.

The model turns the investment cost into a yearly payment (an annuity) over the lifetime: 1000 × 0.04 / (1 − 1.04^−25) ≈ 64 CUR/kW per year.

On the solve 2day-dispatch (under wind_invest):

  • invest_periods = an array with p2020 — the periods in which the model may invest.

Commit with Ctrl-Enter.

docs.title: Execute and inspect
docs.text:
Create a scenario wind_invest with alternatives init, init_2day-test, west, coal, wind, network, wind_invest. Commit, queue, execute. In the results:

  • Capacity. The unit capacity table (unit_capacity__d) shows the existing capacity of wind_plant, the capacity invested and the total. The model builds wind until one more MW would save less in fuel and penalties than its annuity.
  • Costs. The annualized costs (annualized_costs__d) now have a unit investment & retirement category: the annuity of the new capacity for one year, in M CUR.
  • Dispatch. Compare network and wind_invest in the comparison view: more wind output and less coal.

One period, two days

The model weighs one year of the annuity against the costs of the two days scaled to a full year. Two days are far too short a sample for a real investment decision: the investment how-tos use longer samples and several periods, and How to make investments (storage/unit) adds a battery (the scenario wind_battery_invest in templates/examples.sqlite).

See Reading results for the order in which to check the results of a run.

docs.title: Inspecting and comparing results
docs.text:
The Result viewer reads parquet directly, so it is always live: changing scenarios or plots does not re-run anything.

  • Single-scenario view (press V) — one scenario at a time. Use ↑ / ↓ to navigate plots; ← / → cycles through variants of the current plot.
  • Comparison view (press X) — Ctrl-A to select all rows, Alt-↑ / Alt-↓ to reorder. Useful for stacking Test-scenario, coal, wind, network and reading the convergence story top to bottom.

For static output:

  • Output actions → Re-plot scenarios writes PNGs into output_plots/<scenario>/.
  • Output actions → Scenarios to Excel dumps the parquet to output_excel/<scenario>.xlsx.
  • Output actions → Comparison to Excel writes a cross-scenario workbook into output_plot_comparisons/.
  • The same generators run automatically after each execution if their Auto-generate checkboxes are ticked.

If you want PNGs trimmed to a specific window of the timeline, open Png settings in the top-right of the central column and set Start timestep and Duration. The Result viewer ignores these settings — they only constrain pre-rendered PNGs.

docs.title: Cleaning up between runs
docs.text:
After many iterations the database accumulates committed alternatives and scenarios you no longer need. Two cleanup paths:

  • Inside the Spine database editor: Session → Purge…. Tick Select scenario items (and Select entity and value items if you want a full reset), purge, then Session → Vacuum to actually shrink the file.
  • From the FlexTool GUI: select an executed scenario and click Delete selected results irrevocably to drop its parquet plus any derived plots / Excel / CSV from disk. Input data is untouched.

docs.title: More functionality
docs.text:
You now have the building blocks: alternatives, scenarios, units, profiles, connections, commodities, and the FlexTool GUI's execute / inspect loop.

  • How-to recipes — small focused examples (storage, investments, reserves, CHP, hydro, …).
  • Model parameters — every entity class and parameter, organised by topic.
  • Reading results — where to look first in the results of a run.
  • Model outputs — what every parquet column means.
  • Advanced concepts — stochastics, representative periods, multi-year solves.
  • FlexTool GUI — full reference for the GUI used here.
  • Spine database — the data model behind the database editor.

docs.title: Browser interface in brief
docs.text:
The browser interface connects to an instance of FlexTool web interface. It can show and edit the same data as the Spine Toolbox. The workflow is not directly visible, but it is executed in the background when models are run.

The main page shows the projects available for the user.

The front page for the data editor shows all the data classes that can be shown and edited. Different data classes can be opened to separate browser tabs for convenience.

Parameter data can be shown and edited once the user chooses an object and an alternative.

On the 'Run' page, the user can select and execute scenarios.

Finally, the results page shows the model outputs taken from the result database. The results database can also be opened with Spine Toolbox for more control over the shown data as well as export capabilities.

docs.title: Installing IRENA FlexTool with a web server
docs.text:
The web server is outdated! Try at your own risk (probably needs some coding work to get working).

Installation instructions are in the FlexTool web server repository: here. The browser interface is shown here.

docs.title: Project Purpose
docs.text: IRENA FlexTool is an energy and power systems optimization model. It reads input data from a Spine database, derives per-solve preprocessing tables in polars, builds a linear/MIP program in memory via polar_high, solves it with HiGHS in-process via highspy, and writes results to parquet (with optional CSV, Excel, and plot renderings on top of the parquets). Inputs can be authored directly in the Spine database, populated from tabular input files (Excel / ODS / CSV), or imported from old FlexTool v2 .xlsm files. A Tkinter desktop application and a Spine Toolbox workflow provide the two user-facing GUIs.

docs.title: Top-level data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  excel["Excel / ODS / CSV+ old FlexTool .xlsm"] --> spdb
  manual["Spine DB editor"] --> spdb[("Spine input DB")]
  spdb --> backend["SpineDBBackend(EAV → polars frames)"]
  backend --> derive["input_derivation(per-solve preprocessing)"]
  derive --> provider["FlexDataProvider(in-memory transport)"]
  provider --> build["engine.build_flextool(polar_high.Problem)"]
  build --> solve["HiGHS via highspy(Problem / WarmProblem)"]
  solve --> handoff["SolveHandoff(Provider keys)"]
  handoff -->|next roll / sub-solve| derive
  solve --> outputs["process_outputs(read solution → calc_* → out_*)"]
  outputs --> parquet[("output_parquet//")]
  parquet --> renderers["CSV mirrors / Excel /PNG plots / GUI ResultViewer /scenario_comparison"]


Key invariants:


    

  • One backend. SpineDBBackend is the only input backend. Everything
  upstream (Excel, ODS, CSV, old .xlsm) is converted to a Spine DB
  before the engine sees it.
    • 

  • Lazy polars, in-memory. Frames stay as LazyFrame until they reach
  polar_high, which assembles the HiGHS matrix. Solver variables / duals
  are read back from the live highspy.Highs instance — no intermediate
  solver files.
    • 

  • Parquet is the canonical output. CSV / Excel / PNG / GUI plots all
  read from the parquets the cascade just wrote. Scenario comparison loads
  multi-scenario parquet sets and emits combined renderings.
    •

docs.title: CLI surface
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  root["Root wrapper scriptsrun_flextool.py, write_outputs.py,scenario_results.py, ..."] --> cli["flextool/cli/cmd_*"]
  cli --> engine["flextool/enginecascade + LP build + HiGHS solve"]
  cli --> backend["flextool/spinedb_backend"]
  cli --> derive["flextool/input_derivation"]
  cli --> decomp["flextool/decomposition"]
  cli --> inputs["flextool/process_inputs"]
  cli --> outputs["flextool/process_outputs"]
  cli --> plots["flextool/plot_outputs"]
  cli --> compare["flextool/scenario_comparison"]
  cli --> export["flextool/export_to_tabular"]
  cli --> update["flextool/update_flextool"]
  cli --> gui["flextool/gui"]

Each cmd_*.py is a thin argparse wrapper; the work lives in the linked packages. Every CLI command also has an installed entry point in pyproject.toml (the flextool-* names).

CLI module Entry point Purpose cmd_run_flextool flextool-run Run the cascade (run_chain_from_db / run_orchestration) plus output processing for a scenario. cmd_write_outputs flextool-write-outputs Replay process_outputs.write_outputs over an existing parquet folder. cmd_scenario_results flextool-scenario-results Combine parquets from multiple scenario folders into comparison plots / Excel. cmd_read_tabular_input flextool-read-tabular-input Parse Excel / ODS / CSV via JSON spec → Spine DB. cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input flextool-read-self-describing-tabular-input Self-describing Excel (embedded metadata) → Spine DB. cmd_read_old_flextool flextool-read-old Import old FlexTool v2 .xlsm files → Spine DB. cmd_read_matpower flextool-read-matpower Import a MATPOWER case → Spine DB. cmd_import_sensitivities flextool-import-sensitivities Import FlexTool v2 sensitivity scenarios into a version-56 import (flextool-read-old --master does both in one run). cmd_export_to_tabular flextool-export-to-tabular Export Spine DB → Excel (.xlsx). cmd_execute_flextool_workflow flextool-execute-workflow Two-phase workflow runner: optional input-prep (auto-triggered by --tabular-file-path / --csv-directory-path) followed by the fused model-run + output-write phase. cmd_migrate_database flextool-migrate-database Upgrade an input DB to the current schema version. cmd_update_flextool flextool-update git pull + project-side migration in one step. cmd_gui (via flextool.gui.__main__) flextool-gui Launch the Tkinter desktop application.

Two entry points are top-level modules outside flextool/cli/ ([tool.setuptools] py-modules), because they must act before import flextool: flextool_run_supervisor (flextool-run, see "Run record") and flextool_assistant_entry (flextool-assistant, see "AI assistant tools").

docs.title: Runtime options
docs.text:
flextool/run_options.py holds the one resolver for every operator option that has more than one form, and the registry of every environment variable FlexTool reads. Where a setting belongs:

  • database — what changes the model or its answer (a solve's scaling, solver_mip_gap, benders_in_out_weight, ...);
  • CLI flag — a choice for one run (threads, time limit, log level, --save-memory, --benders-workers);
  • environment variable — process-level settings that must exist before import (allocator, polars build), developer / CI switches, and the twin of a flag for callers without a command line (Spine Toolbox, a Python console, tests).

The contract:

  1. Several forms of one option resolve in the order flag > environment variable > database > default, through resolve() / RunOptions, one OptionSpec per option in OPTIONS.
  2. Flags of registry options default to None (a store_true flag gives True or None), so an unset flag lets the environment variable through.
  3. Nothing writes os.environ to carry an option. cmd_run_flextool builds RunOptions.from_cli(args) and passes it to run_chain_from_db(..., run_options=), which stores it on RunnerState.run_options; a library caller that passes none gets RunOptions.from_env(), resolved once per run. The database tier is added per solve with RunOptions.with_db (e.g. scaling).
  4. A child FlexTool process (GUI job, calibration iteration, workflow run) gets the parent's flag-given choices as flags (RunOptions.to_argv()) and inherits the parent's environment untouched. Benders region workers are threads and read the same RunOptions. The launcher label is a flag too (--run-launcher; the outermost one is kept). One exception: a pipe owner — the GUI's _run_job and the flextool-run supervisor (flextool_run_supervisor.py), which read the engine's output pipe and write _run.log — adds FLEXTOOL_RUN_LOG_OWNER=1, PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 and PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 to the env= copy of its direct child. They describe the pipe, not a run choice. The engine reads and removes FLEXTOOL_RUN_LOG_OWNER, so no process it starts inherits it; the owner's own os.environ is not changed. The calibrator, the representative-period iteration and the workflow runner start the supervisor with env=None. A second exception: FLEXTOOL_RUN_STOP_FILE is set only by the GUI, in the env= of an auxiliary job's process (a calibration, a representative-period iteration), passed on by inheritance and read only by the flextool-run supervisor, which drops it from the engine's env=. It is the job's stop channel (see "Run record"), never a run choice.
  5. Process-level variables (MALLOC_ARENA_MAX, _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF, POLARS_*) keep setdefault semantics: a value already in the environment wins. The exception is POLARS_MAX_THREADS while flextool/__init__.py imports polars: see "Thread budget" below.
  6. Solver options keep their own stack, the same for every solver (HiGHS: baseline < highs.opt; a commercial solver: <solver>.opt; then solve.solver_mip_gap < solve.solver_arguments < operator layer); the registry supplies only the operator layer (_operator_highs_overrides; _solver_dispatch._operator_native_overrides maps --solver-time-limit / --solver-mip-gap to the native names of _PARAM_MAP). The option files come from one folder per run, flextool/_solver_config_source.py (engine-free; not flextool/solver_config.py, which would shadow the template data folder): resolve_solver_config_source — explicit argument > --solver-config-dir > FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR > the bounded database layout (next to the database; <workspace> of a projects/<P>/input_sources/ database)

    the Toolbox project folder > cwd > packaged templates. snapshot_solver_option_files reads them once at run start into PathConfig.solver_option_files (every solve reads its layer from there, never from disk) and writes the record <work_folder>/solve_data/solver_config/. The GUI and the calibrator pass the folder explicitly.

  7. The run header prints RunOptions.summary_lines() — each option set by a flag or an environment variable, with its source — and the thread budget (Threads:), with polars' and HiGHS' thread counts.

Every other variable is an EnvKnob in ENV_KNOBS with its audience (user, dev, test) and page: user page, developer page, testing. tests/test_env_knob_registry.py fails on an unregistered read, an undocumented registered variable, or a documented variable that is no longer read.
