The basic level is meant for lookup questions. Standard adds interpret questions, and advanced adds diagnose questions. Every model answers every question at every level setting. This shows what a model does at its own level, and whether it escalates cleanly at a lower one.

docs.title: The grounding project
docs.text:
python tools/assistant_eval.py build --out DIR builds the project the questions are about and solves it (about half a minute). The project uses tests/fixtures/tests.json with three override alternatives:

  • h2_lookup: a storage node whose description gives its own units;
  • demand_update: a run that succeeds, after which the source is rewritten so that the next run fails in the input checks;
  • invest_2day: an investment version of the 48-hour solve.

The fixture's scenarios coal and coal_co2_price are solved as they are. The project folder name has a space and an ä in it.

build writes a marker file, .flextool_grounding_project.json. The marker holds a hash of the source database, the run id of each result folder, and a fingerprint of the source, the overrides and the run ids. run refuses a project without a valid marker, and one that has changed since it was built: another database, another input source, results of another run, or a run of its own made again. It also refuses a project built without its runs. Data from a real project therefore never reaches a calibration model.

Two builds are never the same project. The source database differs in its hash from build to build (the database records its own times), and every run gets a new run id. A rebuild therefore starts a new matrix: results folders made on an earlier build cannot be continued with --resume on the new one, nor summarised or sampled together with results of the new one. Keep the build for as long as its results are being run and graded.

docs.title: Running the models
docs.text:
python tools/assistant_eval.py run --project DIR/"Grounding project ä" --provider PRESET --model MODEL \
    --out _audit_reports/assistant_eval/MODEL_NAME [--levels basic,standard,advanced] [--accept-data-notice]
  • Keys are read from the system keyring or from the provider's environment variable. They are never given on the command line or in a file.
  • The data notice is the one the chat shows. --accept-data-notice accepts it for this run only, and only for a grounding project: nothing is kept, so every run on a remote service needs the flag (also with --resume), an acceptance in the chat does not cover a calibration, and the chat still asks. When the probe shows that a model is forwarded (an Ollama cloud model), that route's notice is asked as well.
  • One record per cell. A cell is one model at one level setting answering one question. The records go to the --out folder. They are redacted, and they stay local: _audit_reports/ is git-ignored. Each question gets a fresh conversation. The eight turns of S01 share one conversation, and S01 runs only at the model's automatic level. A finished cell's record holds its level setting (setting_key: the caps, the window, the history policy and the hashes of the instructions and tools, system_hash and tools_hash). summary and grade-ai warn when the cells of one model at one level were asked with more than one tools_hash or system_hash (a record written before the key was recorded counts as unknown, which warns only beside a known one): their grades are not of one setting. A new or changed tool changes the tools_hash of the levels that list it (explain_entity, 2026-11-12: standard and advanced): their kept checkpoints start again from the start, and their cells are asked again for grades of one setting; basic keeps its hash. A change of what the tools return that leaves their descriptions as they are bumps ASSISTANT_BEHAVIOUR (flextool/assistant/__init__.py, "b1" for the tools batch B1), which the key records as behaviour: the warning above covers it too (a record without it is unknown), and a checkpoint of another behaviour starts its cell again.
  • Local models (Ollama). Make one variant of the model for each context size. For example, write a Modelfile with FROM <model> (a model you have pulled) and PARAMETER num_ctx 32768, then run ollama create <model>-32k -f Modelfile. Do the same for -16k and -64k. Then pass --ollama-context basic=16384,standard=32768,advanced=65536. Before the first cell of each setting, the runner loads that setting's variant and records its context and memory use. If the variant runs with a smaller context than asked, or does not fit fully in graphics memory, every cell of that setting is recorded as "not applicable (context)" and not run. On a card whose memory is partly used by the desktop, a model may never fit fully. --allow-cpu-offload runs a variant that loaded with the asked context but is partly on the CPU. Each cell records the offload: the model's size, its size in graphics memory and the share on the CPU (cpu_offload in the cell and in its results.jsonl line, null when the model was fully in graphics memory). A variant whose context is smaller than asked is still not applicable.
  • OpenRouter free models. --relax-data-collection lets OpenRouter use providers that keep the data of the requests. The data is synthetic, and each cell records this. The runner stops after a daily number of requests: 45 for a :free model by default, or --max-requests-per-day N. When it stops, it prints "Daily request budget used. Run again with --resume --accept-data-notice tomorrow." (without the flag for a local model). The budget is checked before every request, also inside a cell: the cell's checkpoint is kept (below) and the next day continues it from that request, so a cell of more requests than one day allows (S01) finishes over two days. A provider's "quota used" reply stops it in the same way.
  • Errors. A cell whose answer was cut off, was still too long for the context, or was refused by the provider is a graded outcome and is saved. Any other error stops the run with exit code 1 (a daily quota: exit 0):
  • after a temporary one (a busy or overloaded service, a rate limit, Google's per-minute input-token quota, no connection, a timeout, a daily quota, a tool call the service could not read three times in a row — tool_call_unreadable, Ollama's "error parsing tool call", never a graded stop) the cell is kept: "G05__large__r1: kept up to turn 1, request 7; run again with --resume to continue it";
  • a tool call the service could not read is one answer's format problem, not the service's state: after it the run does not stop but goes on with the next cell, and at its end (also when the day's budget ends it) it names the kept cells — "2 cell(s) kept after a tool call the service could not read: G04__medium__r1, G05__medium__r1; run again with --resume to continue them." — and exits with code 1 (0 only when no cell is left kept or unsaved);
  • after any other (a key, permission, credit, model, routing, tools or history error, an internal fault) nothing of the cell is saved: "…: nothing was saved for this cell. Run again with --resume." Its next --resume asks it from the start. The requests a cell sent count towards the day's budget once each (spent.json in the results folder, the checkpoints and the records).
  • Checkpoints and --resume (item 216). Before every request the runner writes the cell's checkpoint, RESULTS/partial/<cell id>.json: the finished turns as they go into the record, the current turn's notices, failed attempts and seconds, the conversation and the turn's state, and requests_by_day (the answered requests it holds, by UTC day). --resume continues a kept cell from the request that failed: the finished turns (of S01, for example) are not asked again, and the failed request is sent again as it was (the same history, tool_choice and output limit, a fresh retry budget). A process that died (Ctrl-C, a crash) leaves a checkpoint with no stop: --resume continues it too and counts its pending request once on that day (it may have been sent). The checkpoint is removed when the cell's record is written. It is continued only when it is of this format, of this folder's model and project (identity), of the same level setting (level, model id sent, window, caps and result caps, compaction, history, free plan, route, the hashes of the instructions and tools) and when the restored conversation gives the same request byte for byte; else the cell starts again, with one line: "G01__medium__r1: started again from the start (the level setting changed: window)" (or "the instructions or tools changed", "the assistant's behaviour changed since this checkpoint", "a checkpoint of another format", "the checkpoint no longer gives the same request"). A checkpoint written by an older format or commit is never filled with defaults: a field missing or unknown is another format. A resume on another commit is allowed and recorded (the point's git and stopped_git), not prevented: the hashes guarantee only the next request, so such a cell can mix two code versions. The record's resume says how often and where the cell was continued: {"count", "points": [{"turn", "round", "request", "code", "provider", "lost_usage", "stopped_at", "resumed_at", "pace", "stream", "git", "stopped_git", "request_sha256", "body_sha256"}]} (0 points for a cell that never stopped); the stopped turn's failed_attempts hold the stopping attempts, as a retry would; results.jsonl gets resumes, resume_points ([[turn, round]]) and resume_codes. The graders never see any of it. A checkpoint holds what was sent, unredacted (0600): do not share a results folder with a partial/ in it; grade-ai, review and summary read only a checkpoint's position (to name an unfinished cell), calibrate never.
  • Google's per-minute input-token quota. Gemma on Google's free tier refuses every request whose input alone is over its per-minute input-token quota (CAL-FINDING 2026-11-10). That 429 has its own code, tpm_input (retried like a rate limit, never a graded stop). When the provider refuses the same request (the same request_sha256) twice in a row for it, the cell is "not applicable (provider quota per request)": its record keeps the finished turns, the quota (quota), the stops and every request it took, and has not_applicable_scope: "cell", so no later --resume asks it, whatever its setting. Every stop in spent.json and in a checkpoint names its request (request_sha256) and the request's corrected estimate (est_input). Another code that stops the same request three times in a row is only named ("the same request failed 3 times; --skip it or wait").
  • What the provider said. After FlexTool's own message the console shows the provider's own words: its HTTP status, its error code and its message, for example Google Gemini said: 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED — You exceeded your current quota. Quota exceeded for metric: …, then each different text of the cell's earlier failed attempts once (earlier attempts (2): 503 UNAVAILABLE — …). The stop's entry in spent.json keeps it: provider (the stopping answer: code, FlexTool's error code such as rpm or busy; status; provider_code; message) and attempts (every failed attempt of the cell in the same form, the stopping one last), with the run's pace and stream. A saved turn keeps its failed attempts too (failed_attempts; the turn's error has provider). The message is redacted (no key, no local path) and at most 300 characters. An error that came with no provider answer (no connection, a timeout, a stream that ended early) has null status, code and message.
  • --pace SECONDS keeps at least that many seconds between the starts of two requests of the run, on top of FlexTool's own pacing (the spacing is the largest of the pace, the interval learned from rate limits, the preset's seed and the provider's request-limit headers). The pace is not learned or kept for the chat. A provider that limits the tokens per minute refuses requests that are each small enough: every request of a cell carries about 5 000 tokens of instructions and tool descriptions, so a few back to back exceed the minute. For Gemma via Google (preset gemini) use --pace 20.
  • --no-stream asks for whole answers instead of streamed ones (the OpenAI-compatible providers; refused for Anthropic). The answer is read as the streamed one is: the same text (reasoning blocks such as Gemma's <thought> removed), tool calls with their provider data (Gemini's thought signatures), usage and error classification. Gemma via Google answered whole requests more reliably than streamed ones in manual tests.
  • --pace and --no-stream are part of the folder's record, not of its identity: run.json lists every run's pace and stream (runs), each cell records the ones it was asked with (in model), and a --resume may change them.
  • --resume skips finished cells, continues the kept ones and asks again the others that stopped. It also runs a cell recorded as not applicable once its setting fits. A saved cell that is asked again stays in the folder until its new record replaces it, so a stop on the way never leaves the cell missing. run.json records the questions, levels and repeats every run of the folder planned (its matrix), before any cell is asked. It refuses to continue a folder made with another model, provider, address, free-plan setting, Ollama contexts, CPU-offload setting, data-collection setting or project. Other levels, questions or repeats are fine.
  • Skipping a cell that never completes. A cell kept at a request that fails every time (the same request stopped again and again) does not finish. The owner can leave it out:
python tools/assistant_eval.py run --resume --project DIR/"Grounding project ä" --provider PRESET \
    --model MODEL --out RESULTS --skip S01__small__r1 --skip-reason "the endpoint breaks off"

with the other options of the folder's first run (its identity is checked as for --resume). --skip can be given more than once. Nothing is asked and no notice or key is needed: run.json records each cell as "not applicable (skipped by owner)" (its skipped entry) with the reason, the time and the attempts and requests spent.json and a saved record show (null when nothing tells). The skip is part of the folder's record, not of its identity, so a later --resume is not refused; it leaves the cell out. A cell id the folder cannot have is refused, with the closest ids named; a finished or not-applicable cell cannot be skipped. A skipped cell keeps its checkpoint (its requests are in the skip's count; the attempts are the stops of spent.json). --unskip CELL takes a skip back (the entry moves to unskipped) and the next --resume asks the cell again, from its checkpoint when it has one (a cell skipped before checkpoints, such as S01 of the first Gemma folder, starts once from the start). --unskip CELL also takes back a cell not applicable for the provider's quota per request: its record goes (its requests stay counted in spent.json, replaced) and the next --resume asks it from the start, for example after the provider's limit changed. grade-ai, review and summary accept a folder whose only gaps are skipped cells: a skipped cell is in no rate and no agreement figure. summary prints it apart ("skipped: 1", with the cell and the reason), summary --record appends it as outcome skipped (with skip_reason and skip_attempts) and calibrate lists it apart in the same way. - Usage. The requests are counted in the usage ledger under the provider's name with "(calibration)" added, apart from chat use.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) grades every cell, blind. The owner then either reviews part of the cells factually, always giving their own verdict before seeing Opus's (the owner's review is final), or leaves the facts to Opus and rates how helpful a small sample of answers is (the helpfulness review).

python tools/assistant_eval.py grade-ai _audit_reports/assistant_eval/{opus,gemini,gemma,gptoss} \
    --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2 --accept-data-notice
python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2      # repeat until done
python tools/assistant_eval.py summary --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2 --record
python tools/assistant_eval.py calibrate

All grading state lives in the grading folder (--dir): grading.json (the blind order and its seed, the results folders, the key version), cells/<n>.json (Opus's grading and the owner's review of cell #n), review.json (the review queue and its random sample) and agreement.txt. The results folders are only read. A grading folder made by the earlier grading (no "missing" verdict, no "incomplete" outcome) is refused: grade into a new folder.

docs.title: Items and outcomes
docs.text:
The automatic checks run against the answer key: facts with their units and SI prefixes, that every number in the answer comes from a tool result, forbidden claims, "the data does not answer" questions, the failed run and escalation. A check can only settle that an item is right. Every other finding is an item a grader judges, with the verdicts it allows:

  • right: the answer gets this item right;
  • missing: the answer does not give it, and says nothing false about it;
  • wrong: the answer says something false about it, or gives another value.

A number fact the check did not find is judged with the numbers that carry the fact's unit in the answer. A number with no tool source is right (a shown or plain calculation, or a general constant) or wrong (invented). A match of a forbidden pattern is wrong, or right when the answer does not claim it (for example, negated).

Each cell gets one outcome:

  • answered: nothing missing and nothing wrong;
  • incomplete: nothing wrong and no invented number, but something missing (a critical item too: the line lists critical_missing);
  • escalated: a clean hand-over to a higher level and nothing wrong (what it left out does not count);
  • failed: something wrong, an invented number, or no final answer.

A missing unit next to a right value, or a true claim not marked as an assumption, does not make a cell incomplete: it is counted as form_missing. A wrong unit or a false unmarked claim fails the cell. A cell whose final answer is empty (for example, cut off while the model was still reasoning) is failed without asking Opus (no_answer in its line). The tools called and the run's health are not items; the line keeps them as diagnostics.

Each cell also gets an understandability rating, which never changes the outcome: 1 = clear (the user gets the answer on the first reading), 2 = understandable with effort (the answer is there, but buried, out of order or needs a second reading), 3 = hard to follow.

docs.title: What the graders see
docs.text:
Opus and the owner see the same material: the question, the expected behaviour ("a full answer is expected" or "escalating to a higher level is acceptable"), the answer key, the items the checks found right, each tool call with its arguments and its result (folded to 4 000 characters), and the final message of each turn. Reasoning blocks (<thought>, <think>) are removed, and so are reasoning fields, continuation notes, notices, usage and times. The answer the graders see is the final message; text a model streamed between tool rounds is not recorded.

Grading is blind. The cells of every model are shuffled together, and a cell is shown as Cell #n. Model and family names become "[assistant]", phrases that name the level become "[level]", the level texts' fixed escalation sentences become "[escalation sentence]", and the sizes of cut tool results are hidden. Before anything is sent or shown, a leak scan checks every request as it would be sent; if something still names the model, the level, a cap or the time of a run, nothing is sent, and every cell it found is named. The blinding is partial: style, tool names (the basic level has fewer tools) and answer length can still hint at the model.

Answers and tool texts are data. Every text a model wrote or a tool returned is inside a fence <<<DATA tag>>> … <<<END tag>>> whose tag the model could not know; material that holds its own tag is refused. Opus's reply must be exactly the asked JSON (every item once, each verdict among the item's allowed ones, confidences, reasons of at most 200 characters). Two slips are accepted and recorded in the grade's relaxed list: a reason over 200 characters is cut to 200, and a verdict for an item the automatic checks found right is dropped. An otherwise invalid reply gets one retry that names what was wrong, field by field (only FlexTool's own item ids and field names); a second invalid reply is saved as unparsed and goes to the owner. An answer whose text, tool names or arguments seem to address a grader goes to the owner too, whatever Opus said.

docs.title: grade-ai
docs.text:
grade-ai sends one request per cell (none for a cell without an answer), through FlexTool's retries and pacing. A cell whose items the automatic checks all found right is sent too: its request asks only for the understandability. The key comes from the keyring or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; --accept-data-notice accepts Anthropic's data notice for this run only. The requests are counted in the usage ledger as "Anthropic (calibration)". Give it the results folders of every model; one folder alone is refused unless --single-model. The folder set is fixed by the first grade-ai. It refuses results folders that miss a planned cell (one of the run.json matrix; for a folder from before the matrix, any question, level or repeat another graded folder has) or have cells that are not finished (a cell the owner skipped with run --skip is no gap; a cell not applicable for the provider's quota per request is complete). The refusal names the cells and each folder's run --resume command; a cell with only a checkpoint is named "(unfinished: checkpoint at turn 2, request 7)". A cell that came back later would change the grading's cells, so grade-ai, review and summary refuse until every folder is complete.

Run the same command again to continue: a cell that was graded from the same material is skipped. If a cell's answer, the answer key or the rubric has changed since, grade-ai stops; --changed grades those cells again and keeps their earlier grading in the cell's history (their review starts over). An error that is not an answer stops the run with exit code 1 and saves nothing for that cell; an error during the retry keeps the first reply (already paid), and the next run sends only the retry. Grading requests are sent without prompt caching (each prompt is unique). grade-ai, review and summary --record lock the grading folder: two of them cannot work on it at once.

docs.title: Grading with Claude Code instead of the API
docs.text:
The same model can grade through Claude Code subagents (for example on a Max plan) instead of API requests. This needs a grading folder that grade-ai already started (its grading.json fixes the blind order). --start-only starts one without any request:

python tools/assistant_eval.py grade-ai _audit_reports/assistant_eval/{opus,gemini,gemma,gptoss} \
    --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2 --start-only
python tools/assistant_eval.py grade-ai _audit_reports/assistant_eval/{opus,gemini,gemma,gptoss} \
    --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2 --export-requests _audit_reports/assistant_eval/cc_grading
# subagents: read cc_grading/<n>.request.txt, write the JSON reply to cc_grading/<n>.reply.json
python tools/assistant_eval.py grade-ai _audit_reports/assistant_eval/{opus,gemini,gemma,gptoss} \
    --dir _audit_reports/assistant_eval/grading_v2 --import-replies _audit_reports/assistant_eval/cc_grading

--start-only runs every check of a first grade-ai (the folder set, every folder complete, one model only with --single-model, the leak scan of every request) and writes grading.json as the first API run would, its one seed drawn then; it needs no API key and no data notice, sends nothing and grades no cell. On a grading folder already started it says so and changes nothing; it is refused with --export-requests, --import-replies or --changed.

--export-requests OUT writes, for every cell grade-ai would send now, OUT/<n>.request.txt: a SYSTEM: section and a USER: section holding exactly the system and user parts of the API request, after the same blinding and leak scan (a leak refuses the export). OUT/index.json lists the tokens with their request hashes and the instructions for the agents; it names no model, level or results folder. Nothing is sent and nothing is written to the grading folder. A reply left in OUT for a request that changed since is set aside as .stale.

--import-replies OUT reads each OUT/<n>.reply.json (the raw reply text) through the same strict check as an API reply and records the cell as the API route does, with grader "claude-opus-5-5 via Claude Code (file route)", route file and no usage. A cell whose request hash changed since the export is refused: export again. A reply that fails the check is not recorded; OUT/<n>.retry.request.txt then holds the API's retry (the request, the first reply as ASSISTANT: and the same feedback as USER:), and a later import reads OUT/<n>.retry.reply.json (invalid again: saved as unparsed). The import reports how many cells it recorded, how many need a retry and how many replies are missing; run it again to continue. It never overwrites a graded cell unless the cell changed and --changed is given. The review queue, the summary and the agreement treat these grades like API grades; summary counts the AI grades per route, agreement.txt gives each route's agreement apart when both are used, and each results.jsonl line carries ai_route.

docs.title: review
docs.text:
review starts once Opus has graded every cell. The queue is drawn once:

  • every cell with a low confidence, an unparsed reply or an injection hint;
  • every cell with a number that has no tool source, whatever Opus said;
  • every cell written by claude-opus-5-5 (for self-preference);
  • a random sample of the rest: 15 % and at least 35 cells (all of them when fewer), drawn with the grading's seed;
  • a cell --changed graded again that is outside the sampled pool and no longer has another reason (changed).

For each queued cell, the owner sees the material and gives a verdict on each judged item (r / m / w, only the allowed letters) and the understandability (1 / 2 / 3). Only then are Opus's verdicts, confidences and reasons shown, with each disagreement marked. For each disagreement, Enter keeps the owner's verdict and a letter changes it. Both the first and the final verdicts are kept, and agreement uses the first. The reasons the cell was queued are never shown.

A sitting is 37 cells (--sitting N; 0 for no limit). q or Ctrl-C keeps the verdicts already given, and the next review asks the rest. --regrade #n reviews a cell again; the latest review wins. --all queues every cell (full manual grading).

docs.title: review in a markdown editor
docs.text:
The terminal shows the material as plain text. The same review can be done in files that a markdown viewer renders:

python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir GRADING --export-md REVIEW.md
# fill in the letters under "Your verdicts", then
python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir GRADING --import-md REVIEW.md
# the cells where Opus judged otherwise are now in REVIEW.final.md: keep or change your letters, then
python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir GRADING --import-md REVIEW.final.md

--export-md writes every queued cell not yet reviewed (no sitting limit) as # Cell #n, and the key file REVIEW.key.md: what the letters mean, in general and for each kind of item that has its own meaning (the same texts the graders read). The material is the graders' own, rendered and shortened: its sections are ### headings, the fences are gone, the question and the answers are blockquotes (their headings three levels lower), and the tool calls, the excerpts and the items-to-grade list are left out. Each cell ends with Your verdicts: each item the owner judges, with its text and the letters it allows (- `fact:x` (critical): statement: … [r / m / w]:), and the understandability; the owner writes the letter after the colon. The numbers (a number fact the check did not find, a number without a tool source) are left to Opus and not asked: the owner's grade of the cell carries Opus's verdicts for them, they count in the owner's outcome with Opus's verdict and they are in no item agreement pair. Nothing of Opus's is in this file, and every cell's material is leak-scanned as for the terminal.

--import-md records the letters as the owner's first verdicts; an empty line is asked again by the next export, so a file can be imported part-filled, as often as wanted. A first verdict once imported is never replaced (a different letter is reported and kept; --regrade in the terminal gives a later review). A cell whose first verdicts are complete and that Opus agrees with (or that has no readable reply of Opus's) is reviewed at once, as in the terminal. The other cells go to REVIEW.final.md: Opus's verdicts, confidences and reasons (blinded, as in the terminal) next to the owner's, then Your final verdicts with each differing line already holding the owner's letter (leaving it keeps it, as Enter does), then the material again. Its import records the final verdicts and the changes. A letter that is not allowed is reported and its cell left as it was (exit code 1). An export never overwrites a file that holds letters not imported yet; a cell whose material changed since the file was written is refused.

docs.title: The helpfulness review
docs.text:
The owner can leave the facts to Opus and rate instead how helpful the answers are, on a small sample of each level:

python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir GRADING --helpfulness --export-md HELPFUL.md [--per-level 8]
# rate each cell 1 / 2 / 3 and write notes, then
python tools/assistant_eval.py review --dir GRADING --helpfulness --import-md HELPFUL.md
python tools/assistant_eval.py summary --dir GRADING --record

The first --helpfulness draws the sample once into review.json (helpfulness) and makes Opus's factual grades final (opus_final): the factual queue no longer waits, and summary --record records every cell with Opus's grade (the owner's for a cell already reviewed factually). The sample is --per-level cells (default 8) of each level setting, drawn with the grading's seed from the cells with an answer and a readable grading of Opus's: a level's cells are taken by class in turn (diagnose, interpret, lookup), and each pick is of the model picked least often at that level so far. A sample is never drawn again; another --per-level is refused.

The file shows each cell blind (no model, no level): the question, the expected behaviour, the answer key, the final answers rendered as markdown (no tool calls, no items) and Opus's factual outcome with the items it found missing or wrong. Each cell ends with - `helpfulness` [1 / 2 / 3]: and Your note, free text of any length up to the next cell. 1 = helpful: the user gets what they need; 2 = partly: the answer is there but too long, unfocused or missing something useful (such as what to change); 3 = not helpful. An import saves the ratings and notes given, replacing earlier ones; a rating that is not 1–3 is reported (exit code 1). An export never overwrites a file with a rating or note not imported yet.

summary --dir prints the ratings by level setting and by model within it, and the notes with their cell, level, question and model. Each results.jsonl line carries helpfulness (the rating, or null); a rating given or changed after --record gives the cell a new line. The notes stay in the grading folder. calibrate shows the ratings per level setting next to the understandability.

docs.title: summary
docs.text:
summary --dir prints, per model, level setting and class: answered, incomplete, escalated, failed (and how many had no answer), the cells still waiting, the invented numbers and the understandability ratings; per model also the failed request attempts of its saved turns by code ("failed requests (service or format problems, not part of the grade): busy 1, tool_call_unreadable 3"), retried and recovered or not — a count of the service's and the format's problems, in no rate. It also writes agreement.txt: Opus against the owner's first verdicts, per item (3 categories), per outcome (4) and for understandability (also linear-weighted kappa), each with n, agreement, Cohen's kappa with a bootstrap interval by question, the confusion table and the lenient (Opus kinder) and strict counts. It reports:

  • the random sample: the estimate for the cells Opus alone graded. When the Wilson 95 % upper bound of the outcome disagreement is above 10 %, it says "Review every cell: review --all." With 35 cells this passes only with no disagreement (0 of 35: 9.9 %);
  • all reviewed cells;
  • self-preference: Opus's own cells that no other reason queued, against the random sample, as raw counts.

summary --record appends one line per cell to tools/assistant_eval_data/results.jsonl and refuses while cells still wait for review. A cell's grade is the owner's when reviewed, else Opus's. A later review or a --changed grading appends a new line, and the latest line of a cell is its grade.

A paid canary (a wrong answer that tells the grader to mark every item right, excluded from the results) would test injection resistance on the real model; the tests can only check the fences with a fake backend.

docs.title: The evidence for the owner
docs.text:
python tools/assistant_eval.py calibrate reads results.jsonl and prints a table for each model. The rows are the level settings, and the columns are the classes. Each entry gives three rates, each with n and a Wilson 95 % interval:

  • answered_rate: answered cells as a share of the cells that ran;
  • incomplete_rate: incomplete cells: nothing false said, but something left out. They are never counted as safe, because unlike an escalation they do not say what they left out;
  • safe_rate: answered or escalated cells with no invented number.

For each model it adds the cells incomplete on a critical item, the cells without an answer and how many cells the owner graded (the rest were graded by Opus alone). calibrate reads only grading v2 lines (line_format 2) and refuses a file with older lines.

It also prints, for each setting:

  • the calls, rounds and output tokens of the answered cells (median and 90th percentile);
  • cap hits, length stops, fit compactions and truncations;
  • the ratio of the reported to the estimated prompt tokens;
  • the understandability ratings and their median.

Free-plan cells are shown in a separate block and are not used for the caps.

Then it lists the evidence:

  • whether the models at each level answer that level's classes, and the models below escalate them;
  • a proposed number of calls per question for each level: the 90th percentile of the answered cells plus one, never below 3;
  • each model's evidence level next to its automatic level;
  • notes on the token estimates.

The starting bars are 60 % answered at basic, 75 % at standard and advanced, and no invented number. In the first round each class has only a few cells, so these tables are evidence for the owner's review, not decisions.

docs.title: The answer key
docs.text:
The oracle writes the key from tests/fixtures/tests.json, tests/assistant/grounding_projects.py, the user docs, flextool/process_outputs/_output_meta.py and the model's equation headers. It never runs FlexTool, the tools or the runner. Every value has a derivation.

The format is in the docstring of tools/assistant_eval_scoring.py. A number taken from a result table carries that table's unit, and tests/assistant/grounding/test_grounding_set_consistency.py checks this. A disputed value is derived again by a third agent. It is never edited to match a model or a tool.

docs.title: Reading results.jsonl over time
docs.text:
Each line is one graded answer: which model answered which question, at which assistant level, on which date, with which FlexTool version, and how it was graded. To see how a model does, take its lines with the latest date and group them by level and by question class (lookup, interpret, diagnose).

The date matters. Providers change models without changing their names, so an answer recorded under the same model name a few months later may come from a different model. Compare lines of one model only when their dates are close, and treat an old line as a record of that day, not of the model as it is now.

The question set and the answer key have version numbers. Compare scores only between lines with the same set_version and key_version. When either changes, run the models again before comparing.

A FlexTool upgrade can change answers too. The flextool_version and commit fields tell which version produced an answer.

Each line says who gave its grade (grader: owner when reviewed, claude-opus-5-5 otherwise, none for a cell without an answer or not run), why it was reviewed, and Opus's own outcome and understandability next to the final ones. When a cell has several lines, the latest is its grade. A line with outcome not_applicable is a cell that was not run because the model's context did not fit; leave it out of the rates. knobs_relaxed marks runs that allowed the provider to keep the synthetic data.

A single line is one try. Read rates over several questions, not one answer.

docs.title: Database schema and migration
docs.text:
FlexTool's input data lives in Spine databases (SQLite plus a thin Python layer from spinedb_api). The schema — entity classes, parameter definitions, value lists, alternatives — is template-driven: every JSON file under flextool/schemas/ (consolidated from the older top-level version/ and textual_templates/ directories) represents one snapshot of the schema. Migrations chain those snapshots forward, so a user's database can always be brought up to the latest version without losing data.

This page is a pointer for developers who need to read or modify the schema. For the user-facing meaning of individual parameters, see Model parameters. For where this DB sits in the overall data flow, see architecture.md.

docs.title: The current schema
docs.text:
The canonical, fully-populated snapshot is:

schemas/spinedb_schema.json

It lists every entity class, parameter definition, default value, value list, alternative, and parameter-group assignment that FlexTool knows about at the current version. New empty input databases are built from this file. The GUI's parameter-group picker (see excel_interface.md for the same groupings used in the Excel layer) reads its categorisation from here.

The current target version is the integer constant FLEXTOOL_DB_VERSION in flextool/update_flextool/__init__.py. The same constant is read at write time by flextool/process_inputs/write_to_input_db.py, so the schema version a fresh write announces matches the migration target.

Output-side databases use a parallel set of templates:

  • flextool_template_results_master.json — output DB schema
  • output_settings_template.json, output_info_template.json — output config seeds
  • comparison_settings_template.json — scenario-comparison config seed

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
flextool/update_flextool/db_migration.py walks a user's database forward through versioned steps. Each step either:

  • imports a small flextool_template_v<N>.json snapshot (e.g. flextool_template_rolling_window.json, flextool_template_lifetime_method.json), or
  • runs a hand-written Python step that adds/removes/renames specific entity classes, parameter definitions, value lists, or alternatives.

The chain is forward-only — there are no down-migrations. Each step bumps the model.version parameter stored in the DB so the migration is resumable from where it left off.

Idempotent commits

Migration steps wrap their commit_session calls in _commit_step, which swallows spinedb_api.exception.NothingToCommit. A step that was already hand-applied by an earlier partial run is treated as a no-op rather than a fatal abort, so the version bump still persists and later steps run normally.

Skim migrate_database in db_migration.py to see the full chain and the per-version diffs.

docs.title: Recent schema versions
docs.text:
A few recent steps worth knowing about (the chain in db_migration.py is the authoritative inventory):

  • v52 — multi-solver selection parameters. Adds the solve_advanced parameter group on the solve entity (solver, solver_io_api, solver_options, solver_time_limit, solver_mip_gap, solver_threads, solver_log_level) so each solve can dispatch to a different LP / MIP solver. (Several of these were later folded or removed at v56 — see below.) See Solver selection for the user-facing story.
  • v54 — storage_binding_method array → scalar. The previously array-valued parameter is collapsed to a single scalar via a priority-based reduction. Array values were previously summed silently in nodeBalance_eq; the v54 step rejects that pattern at ingestion and the single scalar enforces the one-method-per-node invariant.
  • v55 — storage_binding_method rename + value_list extension. Renames the three legacy members (bind_within_timeset → bind_within_timeblock, bind_using_blended_weights → bind_within_solve_blended_weights, bind_within_model → bind_within_solve) and adds two new variants (bind_within_period_blended_weights, bind_forward_only_blended_weights) plus the orthogonal aggregation method bind_intraperiod_blocks. The migration also refreshes the parameter description text. See Model parameters for the user-facing enumeration and silent-degrade behaviour.
  • v56 — solver-knob consolidation. Retypes solve.solver_arguments to a 1d-map (solver option name → value) and folds the v52-era per-solve solver knobs into it or onto CLI flags: solver_options folds into solver_arguments; highs_method / highs_parallel / highs_presolve fold into the solver / parallel / presolve keys of solver_arguments; solver_threads → --highs-threads, solver_log_level → --solver-log-level, solver_time_limit → --solver-time-limit, solver_io_api → --matrix-file-format (since removed: it had no effect), and use_row_scaling → the --scaling CLI flag (env FLEXTOOL_SCALING). The surviving solve_advanced DB parameters are solver, solver_arguments, solver_mip_gap, and solver_precommand (not used: never run, kept only so that older databases still read; item 236). See Solver selection.

A separate hand-coded step (independent of the numbered chain) migrates legacy databases that carried has_storage = yes without has_balance = yes, retagging the node as node_type = storage so the v4 single-node_type convention takes hold.

docs.title: CLI: flextool-migrate-database
docs.text:
flextool-migrate-database path/to/input_data.sqlite

Implemented in flextool/cli/cmd_migrate_database.py. Runs the migration chain idempotently against the given SQLite file. Re-running on an already-current DB is safe — every step is a no-op.

docs.title: initialize_database
docs.text:
flextool/update_flextool/initialize_database.py creates a fresh empty database from a JSON template (defaults to schemas/spinedb_schema.json). Used by:

  • the GUI's Add empty input DB action,
  • update_flextool when input_data.sqlite is missing,
  • session-scoped pytest fixtures that need a clean DB.

docs.title: update_flextool / self_update.py
docs.text:
The user-facing updater is implemented in flextool/update_flextool/self_update.py. On each run it:

  1. git pull the FlexTool source tree
  2. pip install --upgrade to refresh Python dependencies
  3. Run migrate_database against every .sqlite under templates/ and against the user's input_data.sqlite if present
  4. Initialise the input DB from the master template if it doesn't exist

This is what the GUI's Update button invokes.

docs.title: Adding a schema change
docs.text:
A typical workflow when introducing a new parameter or entity class:

  1. Pick the next free version number N (one above the current FLEXTOOL_DB_VERSION).
  2. Either add a small schemas/pre_v26/flextool_template_v<N>.json snapshot that imports cleanly via spinedb_api.import_data, or write a hand-coded add_parameters_manual / remove_parameters_manual / add_value_list_manual / add_relationships_manual step. Recent steps in db_migration.py are good templates.
  3. Append the new step to the while next_version <= new_version: chain in migrate_database.
  4. Bump FLEXTOOL_DB_VERSION in flextool/update_flextool/__init__.py.
  5. Mirror the change into schemas/spinedb_schema.json so freshly initialised DBs land at the new schema directly. The sync_master_json_template.py helper (CI runs it with --verify) checks that master is consistent with the migration chain.
  6. Add a test if the migration is non-trivial — see testing.md for where to put it.

A new value in a value list (for example a new combination of reduce_system_detail_methods) also needs a migration step and a version bump: value lists live in each database, so existing databases only get the value through add_value_list_manual. No data is rewritten. The engine side must accept the value too (for the two detail-reduction lists: REDUCE_UNIT_DETAIL_METHODS / REDUCE_SYSTEM_DETAIL_METHODS in engine/input/_solve_config.py, and UNIT_PARTS / SYSTEM_TOKENS in engine/preprocess/_reduce_detail.py).

Tip

Steps that touch existing rows should be tolerant of partial state: use update_item / add_update_item so re-applying the step on a DB that has already been migrated is a no-op.

docs.text:
• architecture.md — overall data flow from input DB through the engine to outputs
  • Model parameters — user-facing parameter docs that follow the schema groupings
  • excel_interface.md — where the parameter-group picker also surfaces

docs.title: Decomposition
docs.text:
Decomposition in FlexTool means splitting a monolithic LP into smaller solvable pieces, then recombining their solutions. FlexTool supports three independent flavours, all implemented natively in engine:

  • Spatial / Benders — partition the network into regions joined only by the inter-regional trade flows; a coordinating master holds those trade flows plus the trade-connection investment, and each region is an operational subproblem whose duals become optimality cuts the master accumulates until the optimality gap closes. Selected per solve from the database (solve.decomposition = benders); see §2.8.
  • Flex-temporal — balance some nodes at a coarser step than the solve (hourly power, daily hydrogen, …) in one LP; every flow stays on the solve's steps. Configured per node via group.new_stepduration.
  • Sequential / rolling / nested — split a long horizon into overlapping windows (rolling) or into an outer long-horizon solve whose decisions feed an inner short-horizon solve (nested). The user configuration is in solve.solve_mode / solve.contains_solves; the engine wiring is in solve/_recursive_solve.py + solve/_handoff.py.

Spatial and flex-temporal are LP-level decompositions (one solve, many sub-problems). Rolling / nested is a meta-level decomposition (one chain of solves, each with its own LP). They compose, with one exception noted in §6.

The engine-side overview of the per-solve pipeline and warm-start / Benders / cascade solve modes lives in engine.md; this page focuses on the decomposition mechanics themselves.

docs.title: 1. Picking a decomposition
docs.text:
Symptom Use Monolithic LP slow, but the system has clear regional structure (multi-country grid, sparse interconnections) Spatial / Benders Power demand needs hourly resolution but some commodities (long-duration storage, hydrogen, district heat) only need daily / weekly resolution Flex-temporal Long horizon (decades, full reanalysis years) that does not fit one solve Rolling Long-term storage needs a multi-year view, but dispatch needs intra-week resolution Nested Capacity-expansion at coarse resolution + intra-week dispatch at fine resolution Nested Multiple operational scenarios sharing the same realised path Nested + stochastic branches

The three flavours are orthogonal in intent (a decomposition along the geography axis, the time-resolution axis, and the horizon axis). §6 covers which combinations are actually wired today.

docs.title: 2.1 Concept
docs.text:
Benders decomposition splits the LP into a coordinating master and a set of operational subproblems, one per region. The complicating decisions — the inter-regional trade flows and the trade-connection investment — live in the master; everything inside a region (its own network, generators, storage, demand) is a subproblem solved with the master's trade schedule pinned. Each subproblem returns the duals of its pinned trade columns; the master accumulates those as optimality cuts and re-solves. The master objective is a valid lower bound on the true optimum; the incumbent feasible cost is the upper bound; the loop stops when the optimality gap (UB − LB) / |UB| drops below tolerance.

This replaces the earlier dual-subgradient (Lagrangian) scheme, which severed each cross-region arc into invest-less half-flows bounded near zero and collapsed greenfield trade to an autarkic solution with an invalid bound above the true optimum. Benders puts the trade investment and the trade flow / capacity coupling in the master, feeds each region the master's chosen flow as a pinned boundary injection, and returns a certified lower bound and the true optimum.

The master is built by build_flextool over a network-only reduced FlexData (_region_filter.master_network_data) — the SAME emit the monolith uses — so the master picks up the trade maxFlow capacity coupling, the invest annuity, and the connection flow cost natively and RP-weight-consistently: the master's trade flow cost and the regions' recourse costs are both weighted by the same representative-period / timestep weights build_flextool applies everywhere, so summing them is arithmetically the monolithic objective (no hand-rolled annuity, no weight mismatch). One recourse variable η_r per region carries that region's operational cost in the master objective.

flowchart TD
    A[FlexData whole system] --> B[_region_filter.splitregions + half-flows]
    A --> M0[_region_filter.master_network_datanetwork-only reduced FlexData]
    M0 --> M[Master = build_flextool + WarmProblemtrade flow f, invest C, recourse η_r]
    B --> C[Per-region Problembuild_flextool, trade pinned to f̄]
    M --> C
    C --> D[subproblem dualscol_dual of pinned trade cols]
    D --> E[master.add_cut_rowoptimality cut per region]
    E --> M
    M --> F{gap ≤ tol?}
    F -- iterate --> C
    F -- stop --> G[BendersResultregion_objectives, LB/UB, log]

docs.title: 2.2 Region declaration
docs.text:
Regions are group entities whose decomposition_method parameter equals the string benders_regional. The group's group__node / group__unit / group__connection memberships list the entities belonging to that region. The coordinator requires at least two such groups in the active scenario; one is treated as an error (use the monolithic path instead).

# Spine input DB fixture sketch.
entities += [("group", "region_A"), ("group", "region_B")]
parameter_values += [
    ("group", "region_A", "decomposition_method", "benders_regional", ALT),
    ("group", "region_B", "decomposition_method", "benders_regional", ALT),
]
for r in ("A", "B"):
    for node in [f"elec_{r}", f"h2_{r}", f"battery_{r}"]:
        entities.append(("group__node", (f"region_{r}", node)))

The reference catalogue entry is group.decomposition_method in Groups; the only accepted value is benders_regional (the _region suffix makes the geographic flavour explicit, leaving naming room for any future temporal variant). The source of truth is flextool/engine/solve/_region_filter.py:load_decomposition_method, which reads the sub-solve provider's input/p_group_decomposition frame (a provider is required; the work folder is never read).

docs.title: 2.3 Half-flow rewriting
docs.text:
Every connection whose endpoints straddle two region groups is rewritten into a pair of import / export half-flows through a virtual commodity node, one per region:

hf_<pipe>__export__<region_A>     (in region A, virtual sink node)
hf_<pipe>__import__<region_B>     (in region B, virtual source node)

Inside a region's standalone LP each half-flow is an ordinary v_flow column. The export and import sides of an arc carry the same flow at optimality. In the Benders scheme that consensus is enforced by the master: each iteration pins every region's forward cross-region half-flow to the master's current f̄ per (d, t) (reverse pinned to 0) before solving the region. The cut slope for (arc, d, t) is then the reduced cost of the pinned forward column (Solution.col_dual[pin_col_id] = ∂cost_r / ∂f̄, basis-correct, no monolith reference). The rewriter / half-flow metadata structure is in _region_filter (HalfFlow, Coupling, split); the arc / pin bookkeeping for the master lives in _benders._build_arcs.

Star topologies (more than two regions sharing one pipeline) are not supported; the rewriter asserts bilateral arcs only.

docs.title: 2.4 Algorithm — master + multi-cut Benders loop
docs.text:
The master is a single polar_high.Problem wrapped in a polar_high.WarmProblem, built ONCE and grown by appended optimality cut rows. The loop:

  1. Bootstrap f̄ = 0, solve every region, harvest the first cuts.
  2. Master solve → new trade schedule f̄ and invest C; the master objective is the lower bound LB (a valid global under-estimate — the whole point versus the old scheme).
  3. Subproblems: pin each region's forward trade columns to f̄, solve, read col_dual of the pinned columns.
  4. Cuts: append one optimality cut per region via WarmProblem.add_cut_row, bounding that region's recourse η_r.
  5. Upper bound: UB = master invest cost(C) + Σ_r cost_r(f̄); incumbent = best (min) UB.
  6. Repeat from 2 until gap = (best_UB − LB) / |best_UB| ≤ tol or the iteration cap is hit.

The recourse vars and cut rows are appended through the polar-high primitives WarmProblem.add_recourse_col and WarmProblem.add_cut_row; each region subproblem is solved with WarmProblem.solve(retry_on_unknown= …) so a transient HiGHS kUnknown is retried rather than aborting the run. Each η_r is lower-bounded by a large-NEGATIVE finite floor (NOT a hard η ≥ 0): FlexTool region costs can be negative, so a blind zero floor could cut off the optimum; the finite floor is a provably valid global under-estimate that keeps the cut-less iter-0 master optimal.

The two knobs:

DB parameter (solve entity) Default Meaning benders_max_iter 50 Outer-loop iteration cap benders_tolerance 1e-3 Relative optimality-gap threshold (gap normalised by the incumbent UB)

They are resolved per solve by SolveConfig.benders_config_for; a solve that authors neither falls back to these defaults.

docs.title: 2.5 Existing vs investable trade capacity
docs.text: The master handles existing and investable trade connections in ONE build. An existing-only arc (existing > 0, no invest_method) carries no invest variable; its flow is bounded by the existing unit count (existing_count = capacity / unitsize) through the FlexTool maxFlow RHS (p_flow_upper_existing). An investable arc gets a v_invest var and its capacity is bounded by existing + invested. A greenfield arc (existing = 0) is unchanged — all its trade capacity is invested C. Because the master is the SAME emit as the monolith, the existing-capacity term and the invest annuity drop in with no rescale, and the per-region half-flows are left uncapped (benders_uncap_cross_region=True) so a positive master pin is always feasible in the region.

docs.title: 2.6 Validity guard
docs.text: A monolith-free sandwich guard is always on: LB ≤ optimum ≤ best_UB must hold (best_UB is itself an upper bound on the optimum). An LB > best_UB is the genuine invalid-lower-bound pathology — exactly the bug this scheme fixes — and raises RuntimeError rather than reporting a wrong-but-plausible optimum. No external big-M is needed.

docs.title: 2.7 Diagnostics
docs.text:
Every outer iteration logs the iteration index, the master LB, the incumbent UB, and the current gap; the orchestrator also prints a final convergence + LB/UB sandwich summary. The same data is available on the returned BendersResult:

  • BendersResult.iteration_log — per-iteration dicts (LB / UB / gap trajectory)
  • BendersResult.lower_bound / upper_bound / gap — final values
  • BendersResult.region_objectives — per-region recourse cost at the incumbent
  • BendersResult.converged — True iff the gap dropped below tol before the iteration cap

Look for:

  • the gap closing monotonically (LB rising, UB falling toward each other); a stalled gap usually means benders_max_iter is too low or the cut slopes are degenerate (a region whose pinned trade column is basic returns a zero reduced cost)
  • region objectives broadly similar magnitude — one region dominating often means the cut placement is wrong (a major load centre ended up in a region with too little generation)

docs.title: 2.8 Selecting the scheme per solve
docs.text:
Decomposition is chosen per solve, from the database — there is no CLI flag. Set solve.decomposition = benders on the solve(s) you want decomposed, optionally overriding the two benders_* knobs:

solve parameter Value list / type Default Effect decomposition decomposition_schemes = {none, benders} none benders routes this solve through solve_benders; none solves it monolithically benders_max_iter float 50 Outer-loop iteration cap benders_tolerance float 1e-3 Relative optimality-gap threshold

Because the decision is per solve, a single chain can mix schemes — for example a Benders investment solve followed by a monolithic full-resolution dispatch solve. The orchestrator (engine.solve._orchestration) reads each solve's resolved decomposition value as it iterates model.solves. This is distinct from the group-level group.decomposition_method (none / benders_regional), which declares which groups are regions; solve.decomposition declares whether a given solve decomposes. Benders still requires at least two benders_regional groups.

Invest → dispatch handoff. A Benders investment solve assembles the owner-selected invested trade + in-region capacity into a whole-system SolveHandoff (the TIER-1 invest→dispatch chain) so a downstream rolling or monolithic dispatch solve consumes the realised capacity exactly as it would after any other invest solve. The orchestrator records which Benders solves produced an invest handoff and threads it forward; a downstream solve that would consume a Benders solve which produced none is rejected loudly rather than silently dropping the link.

The --region <GROUP_NAME> flag is a separate, filter-only entry point that emits a per-region input directory and exits without solving — useful for inspecting how the rewriter sees a given region.

docs.title: 2.9 Reference implementation
docs.text:
Symbol Module solve_benders(data, *, ...) — top-level entry flextool/engine/solve/_benders.py BendersResult — return type same Coupling, _build_arcs, the master + cut loop same master_network_data (network-only reduced FlexData for the master) flextool/engine/solve/_region_filter.py RegionSplit, HalfFlow, split same load_decomposition_method (reads decomposition_method from the provider's input/p_group_decomposition) same WarmProblem.add_cut_row / add_recourse_col / solve(retry_on_unknown=…) polar_high (external)

The per-solve routing lives in flextool/engine/solve/_orchestration.py (_PolarHighCascadeSolver._run_benders_solve, driven by SolveConfig.decomposition_for). The Benders path is also surfaced as a "Solve modes" entry in engine.md § Solve modes.

docs.title: 3.1 Concept
docs.text:
Mixed-resolution scheduling: some nodes (power demand, VRE, batteries) need fine timesteps; others (long-duration storage, hydrogen, district heat) only need a coarser energy balance. A node of a group whose new_stepduration is longer than the solve's step is a coarse node: it is balanced once per coarse step by summing its fine balance terms (nodeBalanceCoarse_eq), and a coarse storage node keeps one state per coarse step (stateConstantCoarse_eq). An arc between a fine and a coarse node stays on the solve's steps and enters both balances, so it conserves energy at both ends without any per-arc weights or filters.

A unit or connection whose every balance node is coarse is a coarse process (params._coarse.coarse_process_frames → processCoarse, process_coarse_step): its flows, units online, start-ups / shut-downs, reserve and the direction of an exact connection have one column per coarse step (model/_coarse_flows, §3.6). Only a process with a delay keeps the solve's steps (flex_data.coarse_process_exclusions), plus Benders cross-region arcs and master flows (§3.5), stochastic processes whose coarse step a forecast tie covers in part (flex_data.coarse_tie_straddles) and realization-solve processes whose pin varies within a step (flex_data.coarse_pin_varies); an info line names each with its reason.

This is structurally different from the Benders path: there is one LP, one HiGHS run, no outer loop.

docs.title: 3.2 Schema surface
docs.text:
Parameter Entity Effect solve.new_stepduration solve Solve-wide step (aggregates the solve's timeline) group.new_stepduration group The group's balance / storage nodes are balanced per coarse step of this length (when longer than the solve's step) group.decomposition_method group Benders region groups group__node (relation) The coarse nodes group__unit / group__connection (relation) No effect on time resolution (a warning names a listed process that touches a node outside the group — Q-c15-A)

Validation in validate_group_membership:

  • every entity may belong to at most one resolution-group
  • every entity may belong to at most one decomposition-group (the Benders region groups counted here too)
  • reserve participants may sit in a resolution-group (a coarse provider holds one reserve per coarse step; the requirement stays per solve step)

Validation in params._coarse.coarse_node_frames: a group step that is not a multiple of the solve's step, a fine step crossing the end of a coarse step, a coarse step that would straddle a representative period, and a bind_intraperiod_blocks node in a coarse group raise FlexToolConfigError; a group step shorter than the solve's step is ignored with a warning.

docs.title: 3.3 Block layout and coarse steps
docs.text:
emit/_blocks.py (production) and its port BlockLayout.build (in _block_layout.py) emit the per-solve block frames:

  • entity_block — (entity, block): each node's group, else default
  • block_step_duration — (block, period, step, step_duration)
  • overlap_set, block_step_previous, block_period_time_first/_last

The model reads the node → group map and the group step durations from these frames and the default block's period boundaries (nodeState_last_dt). The per-block aggregated timelines of the coarse blocks are a plain chunking of each period and do not feed the model.

The coarse steps come from one place, params._coarse.coarse_node_frames, called at the end of load_flextool for every solve, roll, nested and stochastic sub-solve. It takes the solve's own steps (dt in order, step durations, dtttdt), splits each period into runs of consecutive steps — a run ends where t_previous_within_timeset is not the step before (a gap, a timeset block start, a period or roll start), at every representative-block start (rp_block_first) and after the period's last realized step (a roll's realized end, so the state a roll hands over excludes look-ahead flows) — and chunks each run from its start: a coarse step closes once its fine durations add up to the group step (a run that is not a multiple ends with a shorter step). Result: nodeCoarse (n), node_coarse_step (n, d, b_first, t) and node_coarse_interior (n, d, t, t_previous).

docs.title: 3.4 The coarse balance
docs.text: nodeBalanceCoarse_eq[n, d, b] is nodeBalance_eq summed over the fine steps t ∈ b: flows, slacks, the state change of the node's binding method, the fix_start and roll-continuation start terms and self-discharge, with the summed −inflow as RHS. With the state constant inside the coarse step the state terms telescope to v_state[b⁻] − v_state[b], so every storage binding method applies. Same orientation and units as nodeBalance_eq: its dual is the node's price over the coarse step. bind_intraperiod_blocks nodes have the same summed row per timeset block (nodeBalanceBlock_eq) with the block lag dtttdt_block_lag (the blocks of a period form a loop; in a rolling solve the blocks also end at the roll's realized end, and in a period the roll holds only in part — period_block_chain, from solve_data/roll_period_whole — the lag is the bind_forward_only lag, so the blocks chain forward and the roll carry starts the chain).

docs.title: 3.5 Paths
docs.text:
• Rolling / nested / stochastic: every sub-solve builds its own coarse frames from its own steps; nested fix_price reads the coarse row's dual for a coarse parent node.
  • Benders: region subproblems and the master filter the coarse frames by node; half-flows enter coarse rows like any arc, so a region↔master boundary may join nodes of different resolutions. Cross-region arcs and master flows stay on the solve's steps (_region_filter); a process inside one region may be coarse in its subproblem.
  • Warm start: the coarse frames are in the fingerprint.

docs.title: 3.6 Coarse processes and the row rule
docs.text:
model/_coarse_flows (module docstring is the reference):

  • Levels (v_flow(_back), v_online_*, v_reserve, v_exact_forward; v_angle of a coarse-angle node, vq_inertia / vq_non_synchronous of an averaged row) are registered at each coarse step's first fine step b_first and read through alias, which maps every fine row to its step's column.
  • Events (v_startup_*, v_shutdown_*) live at b_first only and are not aliased; minimum up / down times count whole coarse steps.
  • Arc-local rows (capacity, conversion, profiles, online capacity, minimum load, start-up / shut-down reduction, reserve limits) are written once per coarse step as the twin family <family>_coarse, the Δt-weighted average of the fine row (add_cstr).
  • Row rule (add_row_rule_cstr, row_partition; flex_data.coarse_row_members / COARSE_ROW_FAMILIES): a row coupling several entities (capacity margin, inertia, non-synchronous, flow-group instant flow, user constraint, forecast storage-use tie, DC power flow) whose every member is coarse is one averaged <family>_coarse row per coarse step; a row with a fine member stays per solve step and reads the coarse terms at their constant value. The reserve requirement (reserveBalance_*) is always per solve step.
  • Ramps run between coarse steps (ramp_rows, reserve_room_rows).
  • The behaviour notice coarse_process_flows (upgraded databases only) names coarse processes whose result can differ from the fine model (flex_data.coarse_process_reasons).

docs.title: 3.7 Outputs
docs.text: Every reader of a coarse variable expands it to the solve's steps through engine/output/_coarse_flows (COARSE_VARS: copy for levels, first for events — the whole start-up at the step's first fine step, 0 at the others, so totals and costs are the LP's); a grep gate in the tests keeps direct reads out. A coarse storage state is constant within its coarse step. Coarse-node prices are the nodeBalanceCoarse_eq duals broadcast to the fine steps of each coarse step (read_highs_solution._broadcast_block_node_duals).

docs.title: 3.8 Caveats
docs.text:
• A process with a delay keeps the solve's steps (its flow is shifted by solve steps).
  • An averaged row sees step means: a capacity margin covers the mean net demand of the step, not its peak.

The engine-side overview of flex-temporal lives in engine.md § Flex-temporal decomposition.

docs.title: 4. Rolling / nested solves
docs.text: These are user-facing patterns documented in Solve sequences, rolling and nested solves; this section covers the engine wiring.

docs.title: 4.1 Rolling
docs.text:
A long horizon is split into overlapping optimisation windows. Each window ("roll") is its own LP; the next window starts at the previous window's "jump" point with the storage state at that point fixed.

Schema:

  • solve.solve_mode = rolling_window
  • solve.rolling_solve_jump — interval between roll start points (also the output interval per roll)
  • solve.rolling_solve_horizon — length of the roll's optimisation horizon (> jump; the overlap is horizon - jump)
  • solve.rolling_duration — optional total horizon length; -1 (or unset) means "until the active time list is exhausted"

Engine wiring:

  • RecursiveSolveBuilder.create_rolling_solves in _recursive_solve.py expands the parent solve into a sequence solve_roll_0, solve_roll_1, … with per-roll active-time and realized-time lists.
  • Per-roll storage carry-over rides SolveHandoff.roll_end_state (solve/_handoff.py), routed to the sub-solve that continues from it by solve/_carry_routing.py.
  • Every roll builds its own LP: the in-process polar_high.WarmProblem is reused only for an identical sub-solve (every FlexData field, labels included, and the solver configuration), and a roll's dt labels always shift. See engine.md § Warm-start cascade.

docs.title: 4.2 Nested
docs.text:
An outer long-horizon solve fixes long-term decisions (capacity, long- term storage state at chosen anchor periods); an inner short-horizon solve dispatches within those decisions.

Schema:

  • solve.contains_solves — array of child solves run after the parent using the parent's realised data
  • solve.fix_storage_periods — periods where the parent's last storage value becomes a target for the child
  • node.storage_nested_fix_method — how the child handles the fix-storage target (fix_quantity / fix_price / etc.; fix_price requires storage_state_reference_price)

Engine wiring:

  • The RecursiveSolveBuilder walks the solve tree at define_solve_recursive time and threads ParentSolveInfo into nested children.
  • The parent's realised capacity / storage state rides SolveHandoff.realized_invest / realized_existing / fix_storage / fix_storage_timesteps.
  • The child's preprocessing reads from state.handoffs[parent_name] (in memory; there is no disk fallback).

The single-matching-period rename quirk: when a child solve's period set intersects its parent's by exactly one period, the child is renamed solve + "_" + period and duplicate_solve carbon-copies the parent's lockstep dicts under the new name. Preserved verbatim from the legacy preprocessor.

docs.title: 4.3 Stochastic branches
docs.text:
Each branch is itself a sub-solve in the chain. solve.stochastic_branches is a 4-D map that decorates affected periods with branch-suffixed clones (y2025 → y2025, y2025_low, y2025_high). Only the realised branch contributes to realized_time_lists and fix_storage_time_lists; the other branches' LP variables exist for the optimisation but do not enter the realised outputs.

The wiring lives in _stochastic.StochasticSolver (called from RecursiveSolveBuilder); non-anticipativity constraints are emitted by _non_anticipativity.py (add_dispatch_constraints, add_invest_constraints). See engine.md § Stochastic branches.

docs.title: 5. RELEASE notes context
docs.text:
The 3.29.0–3.33.0 release cycle is the relevant window for these features. Quick map (full text in release.md or CHANGELOG.md):

  • 3.29.0 — Flex-temporal decomposition lands. v50 migration moves new_stepduration from timeset to solve. v51 adds group-level new_stepduration + decomposition_method.
  • 3.30.0–3.32.0 — Block-aware emitters complete (then known as writer ports); output expansion stabilises.
  • 4.0.0 (v60 migration) — spatial decomposition becomes DB-driven and per-solve: solve.decomposition plus per-solve knobs. The global --decomposition CLI flags are removed; the orchestrator routes each solve from its DB value.
  • 4.0.0 (v62 migration) — the spatial scheme switches from the dual-subgradient (Lagrangian) coordinator to Benders. The decomposition_schemes value lagrangian → benders and the group method lagrangian_region → benders_regional; the old lagrangian_alpha / lagrangian_max_iter / lagrangian_tolerance knobs are dropped and replaced by benders_max_iter (50) / benders_tolerance (1e-3). Existing DBs are auto-migrated (breaking schema change, DB version 62). The Benders invest solve threads its realised capacity into a downstream dispatch solve (TIER-1 invest→dispatch handoff).

docs.title: 6. Where they compose
docs.text: Combination Supported Notes Benders + flex-temporal Yes Region subproblems and the master filter the coarse-step frames by node; a region↔master boundary may join nodes of different resolutions (the half-flows are hourly on both sides). Benders + rolling No One Benders solve is the unit of work for the outer rolling loop. Not currently wired; would require per-roll cut warm-start. The TIER-1 invest→dispatch handoff threads a Benders invest solve into a downstream rolling dispatch solve, which is the supported pattern. Benders + nested Partial The outer (parent) solve can be Benders, but the parent's handoff to children propagates only the invest→dispatch capacity, not per-region operational state. Treat as untested beyond the invest→dispatch chain. Flex-temporal + rolling Yes Each roll cuts its own coarse steps; a coarse step ends at the roll's realized end, and the roll carry reaches the first coarse row. Flex-temporal + nested Yes Each parent / child solve builds its own coarse steps; fix_price reads a coarse parent node's coarse-row dual. Flex-temporal + stochastic Yes Every branch period gets its own coarse steps; a branch's first coarse row starts from the trunk's state. Rolling + nested Yes The legacy "more than one solve in a rolling solve" raise still trips for unsupported sibling-rolling-children patterns. Rolling + stochastic Yes Each roll can carry branches; the realised branch chains forward.

  • scaling.md — auto-scaling pipeline; runs per sub-problem, so each region / each roll / each block gets its own scaling pass.

docs.title: The engine pipeline
docs.text:
flextool/engine/ is FlexTool's in-memory optimization engine. It reads a Spine input DB (or a CSV workdir, or an in-memory test fixture) into a single typed dataclass, runs ~150 derived-parameter helpers to populate the rest of the dataclass, builds an LP feature-by-feature on top of the upstream polar_high eDSL, and hands the HiGHS-via-highspy solution off to either the next solve in a cascade or to process_outputs.

This page is the developer-side deep dive — the folder map is in flextool/engine/README.md and the feature table on architecture.md; here we walk the pipeline in the order a bug or extension actually traverses it.

Two repositories

polar_high is the standalone LP eDSL — sets, parameters, variables, lazy constraint composition, warm-LP machinery, and the Benders cut / recourse primitives. engine is the FlexTool-side glue: it knows the on-disk layout of the input/ + solve_data/ CSVs and the shape of FlexTool's optimization model. polar_high knows nothing of FlexTool.

docs.title: Per-solve pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  src["Spine input DB(or CsvSource / InMemoryReader)"] --> reader
  reader["SpineDbReaderInMemoryReader"] --> overlay
  overlay["_apply_db_overrides(direct + derived ports)"] --> emit
  emit["preprocess/emit/ + preprocess/params/(~150 sets & params, Provider-first)"] --> provider["FlexDataProvider(in-memory transport)"]
  provider --> flex["FlexData(polars frames + Params)"]
  flex --> build["build_flextool(m, d)feature-gated LP build"]
  build --> prob["polar_high.Problem(or WarmProblem)"]
  prob --> highs["HiGHS via highspy"]
  highs --> sol["Solution"]
  sol --> capture["capture_post_solve→ SolveHandoff"]
  capture -->|next sub-solve| overlay
  sol --> outputs["process_outputs.write_outputs"]

Side-paths off this trunk:

  • Rolling-horizon / nested: every iteration loops back through overlay carrying a SolveHandoff. When the LP shape is unchanged the cascade re-uses the live WarmProblem; when it isn't, the cascade cold-rebuilds.
  • Stochastic branches: _stochastic.py decorates per-solve active-time lists with branch-suffixed periods before overlay sees them. Branched periods get LP variables; only the realized branch contributes to handoff carriers.
  • Spatial Benders: _benders.solve_benders slices a single FlexData into per-region copies via _region_filter, builds a coordinating master (trade flows + trade invest + one recourse per region) plus one operational sub-problem per region, and accumulates the sub-problems' duals as optimality cuts until the optimality gap closes.

docs.title: Solve-level detail reduction
docs.text:
solve.reduce_unit_detail_method / reduce_system_detail_method (user docs: entities_and_time.md "Leaving out detail in a solve") are applied in one place: preprocess._reduce_detail.apply_reduce_detail(d, unit, system), called by the cascade right after load_flextool for every sub-solve (_orchestration._drive_cascade). Every consumer after it reads the reduced data: the online / ramp carry check (check_online_ramp_carry, moved out of load_flextool so that it sees the reduced online set), the realization checks, the Benders split, the cold and warm build, the handoff and the per-roll outputs. The per-roll emit and the input derivation are not changed.

  • Copy, not replace. The transform returns a copy.copy of the FlexData with the changed fields set, not dataclasses.replace.

    A shallow copy keeps the extra attributes that the cascade and the emit hang on a FlexData (the axis vocabulary, output_static_data, reduced_output_features); dataclasses.replace would rebuild the object from its fields only and drop them. Unchanged frames are shared. A level that changes nothing returns the same object, so the LP is byte-identical.

  • Only clears, prunes, relaxes or folds. Each part sets its fields to None (the field lists RAMP_FIELDS, ONLINE_FIELDS, RESERVE_FIELDS, ... in _reduce_detail.py), except relax_integrality (integer online columns continuous), the min_load_efficiency fold (p_slope + p_section, p_section = 0) and the pruning of online variables without a use.

    Under the integers* levels, online_uses lists, on the data after the level's removals, the uses of each process's online variables (ONLINE_USES: start-up cost, min load / capacity_min_coeff floors, min up / down times, the min_load_efficiency section, a written user constraint with constraint_online_coeff, a reserve, inertia, ramp limits, the parent's commitment pin; non-anticipativity ties are no use). The processes without a use lose their online variables: _prune_online filters the rows of PRUNE_FIELDS (the online sets and their parameters, the carry and pin, the min-time sets, p_startup_cost) to the other processes, and clears dt_online_carry with the last carried commitment (ReduceReport.removed["online_unused"]). The reserve use is conservative: maxFlow and the connection reserve rows hold the same reserve terms without the units online, so a reserve-only unit could be pruned too; it keeps its online variables, as the user docs say. test_reduce_detail_online_uses.py classifies every model reader of the online sets / variables (a new reader must be added as a use or as no use) and checks that pruning gives the optimum of the same units authored as no_startup.
