FLEXTOOL_PHASE_TIMING unset (off) 1 Per-iteration rows (preprocessing / lp_build / solve / handoff, warm_used) in timings.csv. warm_used is a flag in the seconds column (1 = warm start used), not a time. Always-on rows: read_input, preprocessing_global, roll_setup, all_solves, write_outputs/*, total. FLEXTOOL_PHASE_PROFILE unset (off) 1 One epoch-stamped RSS line per orchestration phase on stderr (aligns with the sampler log). FLEXTOOL_PYRAMID_PROFILE unset (off) 1 One [pyramid profile] RSS line per preprocessing emit on stderr. FLEXTOOL_AUTOSCALE_PROFILE unset (off) 1 RSS markers around the autoscale steps. FLEXTOOL_BUILD_PROFILE unset (off) 1 One RSS line per model-build step on stderr. FLEXTOOL_LOADFLEX_PROFILE unset (off) 1 One RSS line per data-load step on stderr. POLAR_HIGH_LAYER2_PROFILE unset (off) 1 One [layer2-bucket profile] line per term of the autoscale Layer 2 coefficient walk. Read by FlexTool's engine/autoscale/_layer2.py, not by polar-high. POLAR_HIGH_RANGES_MAX_FAMILY_ROWS 1000000 integer Only with a polar-high that has no bounded coefficient walk: constraint families with more rows are skipped in Layer 2 bucketing. Read by FlexTool's _layer2.py.

Example — find a transient RSS peak the per-phase recorder misses:

FLEXTOOL_MEM_SAMPLER=1 FLEXTOOL_MEM_SAMPLER_INTERVAL_MS=50 \
    python run_flextool.py input.sqlite output_info.sqlite --scenario-name base

docs.title: Run record
docs.text:
Each run writes _run_status.json and _run.log into its output_parquet/<run>/ folder. _run.log is written by the process that holds the run's output pipe, when there is one.

Variable Default Set to What it does FLEXTOOL_RUN_LOG_OWNER unset 1 Set by the GUI and flextool-run in the environment of the engine run they start (only that direct child; the engine removes it, so no run it starts sees it). It tells the engine that its parent writes _run.log from the output pipe, with the native solver lines and crash dumps: the engine prints one marker line for the parent instead of copying its own console output into the log. Not for use by hand. FLEXTOOL_RUN_STOP_FILE unset a file path Set by the GUI in the environment of a calibration or representative-period job, and inherited by every flextool-run supervisor that job starts. When the file appears (the GUI writes the reason into it when the job is stopped), the supervisor kills its engine and records the run as killed with that reason; a supervisor that finds it before its engine starts runs nothing. The supervisor leaves it out of the engine's environment. Not for use by hand.

docs.title: User folders
docs.text:
FlexTool keeps its per-user files (the AI assistant's settings, saved chats, usage ledger, key file and caches) in the platform's user config and cache folders, found with platformdirs.

Variable Default Set to What it does FLEXTOOL_USER_HOME unset (the platform's folders) folder FlexTool's user config folder becomes <folder>/config and its user cache folder <folder>/cache. The test suite sets it for every test process and every process a test starts (tests/user_dirs_guard.py), so no test reads or writes the real user folders.

docs.title: Process level
docs.text:
Set when flextool is imported, with setdefault semantics: a value already in the environment wins.

Variable FlexTool sets What it does POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY in-memory polars' engine choice. FlexTool's results are verified only on the in-memory engine; the streaming engine changes row order and summation order. _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF dirty_decay_ms:1000,muzzy_decay_ms:0 Settings of polars' jemalloc allocator: return freed pages to the system, which roughly halves peak memory on long runs. When polars was imported before flextool, FlexTool sets the decay at run time instead.

docs.title: Injecting parameters between solves
docs.text: Reference for the programmatic override_provider hook on run_chain_from_db. This is the supported mechanism for feeding data from an external tool — another optimisation model, a market simulator, a Python data step — into a FlexTool cascade between sub-solves of the same run.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A FlexTool cascade runs several sub-solves in sequence; each one passes a typed SolveHandoff (realised investments, end-of-horizon storage state, cumulative emissions, …) to the next. The override hook lets a Python wrapper substitute values for any of those handoff carriers before the next sub-solve's preprocessing reads them.

Typical wrappers:

  • An outer model in a bi-level setup writes a Parquet file with target capacities; the wrapper reads it and overrides realized_invest.
  • A market simulator runs between two operational solves; the wrapper feeds an updated cumulative_co2 or cumulative_commodity ladder into the second solve.
  • A Python data step rewrites end-of-horizon storage state from an observed (rather than optimised) trajectory to validate roll-forward behaviour.

The mechanism is programmatic only — there is no CLI flag. The wrapper script imports run_chain_from_db and passes a callable.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
from flextool.engine import run_chain_from_db

run_chain_from_db(
    input_db_url,
    scenario_name,  # required: None or "" raises FlexToolConfigError
    work_folder=None,
    *,
    override_provider=None,  # Callable[[], dict[str, pl.DataFrame]] | None
    ...,
)

The override_provider callable takes no arguments and returns a dict mapping a whitelisted K.HANDOFF_* constant to a polars.DataFrame. It is invoked once per sub-solve iteration, after the natural handoff translators and before preprocessing. Returning {} (or None) means "no override this iteration".

Full source: flextool/engine/solve/_orchestration.py (entry point), flextool/engine/solve/_run_model.py (invocation site), flextool/engine/preprocess/_provider_translators.py (translate_overrides_to_provider, read_handoff_frame, dump_provider_sources).

docs.title: Whitelisted handoff keys
docs.text:
Only the 11 keys below are overridable. Supplying any other key raises ValueError in translate_overrides_to_provider. The constants live in flextool.engine.preprocess._provider_keys; import as from flextool.engine.preprocess import _provider_keys as K.

Key constant What it overrides Required columns K.HANDOFF_REALIZED_INVEST Realised investment decisions carried into the next solve's "previously invested capacity" entity, period, value K.HANDOFF_REALIZED_EXISTING Realised existing (non-decision) capacity adjustments entity, period, value K.HANDOFF_DIVEST_CUMULATIVE Cumulative divestments carried forward entity, value K.HANDOFF_ROLL_END_STATE End-of-horizon storage state (downward roll) node, value K.HANDOFF_UPWARD_ROLL_END_STATE End-of-horizon storage state (upward roll) node, value K.HANDOFF_CUMULATIVE_CO2 Cumulative CO2 per group/period for the next emission cap group, period, value K.HANDOFF_CUMULATIVE_COMMODITY Cumulative commodity-ladder realised MWh commodity, tier, period, p_ladder_cum_realized_mwh K.HANDOFF_CUM_SIM_HOURS Cumulative simulated hours per period (commodity ladder denominator) period, p_ladder_cum_sim_hours K.HANDOFF_FIX_STORAGE_QUANTITY Fixed storage quantity at specific steps node, period, step, p_fix_storage_quantity K.HANDOFF_FIX_STORAGE_PRICE Fixed storage price at specific steps node, period, step, p_fix_storage_price K.HANDOFF_FIX_STORAGE_USAGE Fixed storage usage at specific steps node, period, step, p_fix_storage_usage

The column shapes match the empty-frame schemas in _provider_translators._HANDOFF_EMPTY_SCHEMAS; the value columns are read as Utf8 and cast on consumption (the legacy CSV-roundtrip contract). Building the frame as numeric Float64 also works — polars casts on the consumer side. Match the natural handoff carrier's schema if in doubt; the easiest pattern is to start from a captured SolveHandoff.<field> frame and transform it (see the example below).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
At the start of each sub-solve iteration, the orchestrator runs the following steps in order:

  1. Sequential handoff translation. The previous sub-solve's SolveHandoff is fanned into handoff/* Provider keys (translate_handoff_to_provider). A realised-dispatch roll takes only PIN_FIELDS from its UC roll and ROLL_FORWARD_FIELDS from the previous dispatch roll.
  2. Parent handoff translation. In nested cascades, the parent's handoff is translated next, PIN_FIELDS only (realised investment / existing / divest, fixed online, the nested storage fixes).
  3. Routed carriers. The carriers tied to the realised end — the storage state (handoff/roll_end_state, handoff/upward_roll_end_state) and the step carriers (online state, last flow, last step, online history) — are written by the carry router (solve/_carry_routing.py): the latest state realised before this sub-solve at its nesting level or deeper, or empty when the sub-solve is the first of its level. The running totals (cumulative_*, cum_sim_hours) are not routed: every sub-solve passes them on, so they come from the sequential predecessor.
  4. Override callable. If state.override_provider is non-None, it is invoked. The returned dict is fanned into the parallel override/* Provider keys (translate_overrides_to_provider).
  5. Preprocessing. Per-solve preprocessing reads handoff values via read_handoff_frame, which checks the override/* slot first and falls back to handoff/*. Consumers stay key-stable.
  6. Solve. The LP is built (cold) or updated (warm) and dispatched to the solver.
  7. Produced handoff. After the solve, the sub-solve's own SolveHandoff is written under produced_handoff/* (translate_produced_handoff_to_provider). The handoff/* keys keep the values the solve consumed, so a LP rebuilt from the post-solve provider is the LP that was solved; read produced_handoff/* for what the solve passes on (e.g. a roll's final running totals).

The callable is invoked on every iteration including the first. Return {} whenever no override applies — that iteration falls through to the natural handoff carrier with no Provider writes and no log output. If the callable raises, the exception propagates and the cascade aborts; clean error handling is the wrapper's responsibility.

Each invocation that returns a non-empty dict logs at INFO::

[override] applied N keys at iter=I solve=SOLVE_NAME

with the sorted key list at DEBUG.

docs.title: Warm-path interaction
docs.text:
Under warm=True (the default) an LP is reused for iteration N only when iteration N's FlexData — computed after the override callable has fired and preprocessing has read the overridden handoff — is identical to iteration N-1's in every field, labels included, and the solver configuration is the same (_reuse_blocker in solve/_warm.py). Concretely:

  • An override that changes anything preprocessing computes (for example K.HANDOFF_REALIZED_INVEST at iteration N changes p_entity_previously_invested_capacity) makes iteration N's FlexData differ, so iteration N builds its own LP: the override always reaches the LP matrix, the objective and the right-hand sides.
  • An override that changes nothing in FlexData leaves the LP identical, and reusing it is equivalent to rebuilding it.

No warm=False run is needed for overrides to take effect.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
Set FLEXTOOL_AUDIT_SOURCES=1 (see Environment variables) to enable the per-sub-solve audit dump. Every Provider key written with a non-None source tag is appended to <work_folder>/audit_sources.log as one tab-separated line per write::

<solve_name>\t<provider_key>\t<source_tag>

Override writes carry the tag external_override and the key prefix override/. Useful for confirming the wrapper fired on the iterations it was meant to (and didn't fire on the ones it wasn't).

docs.title: Example wrapper
docs.text:
A wrapper script that reads override frames from a directory of Parquet files. Each file is named <scenario>__<solve_name>.parquet and contains a single override frame for realized_invest. Files that don't exist are treated as "no override for that iteration".

"""Run a FlexTool cascade with realized_invest overrides supplied
by an external tool that drops Parquet files into a watch directory.

Usage:
    python run_with_overrides.py path/to/input.sqlite scenario_name
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import polars as pl

from flextool.engine import run_chain_from_db
from flextool.engine.preprocess import _provider_keys as K


WATCH_DIR = Path("overrides_in")
WORK_FOLDER = Path("work_overrides")


def _make_override_callback(scenario: str, solve_order: list[str]):
    """Return a callable suitable for ``override_provider=``.

    Captures the cascade's expected solve order so the callback knows
    which iteration index maps to which solve name (the orchestrator
    does not pass that into the callable; the wrapper tracks it).
    """
    iter_state = {"i": 0}

    def fetch_override() -> dict[str, pl.DataFrame]:
        i = iter_state["i"]
        iter_state["i"] += 1

        # First sub-solve has no prior carrier — nothing to override.
        if i == 0:
            return {}

        solve_name = solve_order[i] if i < len(solve_order) else None
        if solve_name is None:
            return {}

        parquet = WATCH_DIR / f"{scenario}__{solve_name}.parquet"
        if not parquet.exists():
            # No file from the external tool for this iteration —
            # fall through to the natural handoff carrier.
            return {}

        frame = pl.read_parquet(parquet)
        # Ensure the schema matches what the handoff translator wrote
        # for an empty realized_invest carrier:
        #     (entity, period, value).  Cast value to Utf8 to match
        # the CSV-roundtrip contract (polars also accepts Float64).
        frame = frame.select(
            pl.col("entity").cast(pl.Utf8),
            pl.col("period").cast(pl.Utf8),
            pl.col("value").cast(pl.Utf8),
        )
        return {K.HANDOFF_REALIZED_INVEST: frame}

    return fetch_override


def main() -> None:
    db_path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    scenario = sys.argv[2]

    # The wrapper must know the solve order ahead of time to map
    # iteration index → solve name.  Alternatives:
    #   - hard-code the chain when it is fixed (as below);
    #   - read it from a prior dry-run and persist it;
    #   - gate purely on file existence (drop the solve_order list and
    #     name the Parquet files by iteration index instead).
    solve_order = [
        "y2020_5week", "y2025_5week", "y2030_5week", "y2035_5week",
    ]

    WORK_FOLDER.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    results = run_chain_from_db(
        db_path,
        scenario_name=scenario,
        work_folder=WORK_FOLDER,
        override_provider=_make_override_callback(scenario, solve_order),
    )

    for name, step in results.items():
        print(f"{name}: optimal={step.optimal} obj={step.obj}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Set FLEXTOOL_AUDIT_SOURCES=1 when running this to verify the override fired on the expected iterations.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The override callable is arbitrary Python supplied by the wrapper author. Whoever invokes run_chain_from_db already has full Python execution privileges in the same process, so the override hook introduces no new injection surface — anything the callable could do, the wrapper script itself could already do. The 11-key whitelist constrains what cascade state the returned dict can substitute, not what code can run inside the callable. No eval / exec / importlib machinery is involved on the FlexTool side; the callable is just invoked with () and its return value is consumed.

If you are integrating FlexTool into a service that accepts untrusted input, the trust boundary is the wrapper around run_chain_from_db itself, not this hook.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• tests/engine/test_override_provider.py — end-to-end test of the override path plus the audit-dump variant. Useful as a reference for additional patterns (capturing a real handoff frame, scaling it, asserting the propagated effect).
  • specs/architecture_provider_and_future_duckdb.md (internal design notes, not in the public repository) (sections on Phases 5 and 6) — design rationale for the override/* namespace, the override-aware read_handoff_frame lookup, and the audit-dump format.
  • Environment variables — FLEXTOOL_AUDIT_SOURCES for inspecting which iterations were overridden.

docs.title: FlexTool scaling user guide
docs.text: Short, practical reference for the numerical scaling that runs on every FlexTool solve. Paired with the deeper reference in slack_convention.md and the architecture overview in architecture.md.

docs.title: What is scaling doing for me?
docs.text:
FlexTool builds an LP / MIP whose matrix, cost row, and bound-vector coefficients can span many orders of magnitude when a user mixes entities of very different physical scale (tiny heat pumps next to multi-GW coal plants, multi-year invest horizons next to hourly dispatch, etc.). Wide coefficient spreads make the solver scale the problem badly, miss symmetry, slow down, or — in extreme cases — declare false infeasibility.

The autoscaler does three things on every solve, then writes a YAML audit so you can see what it did:

  1. Layer 1 — detect. Walks the assembled LP and computes log10 ranges for the matrix, cost row, bound vector, and RHS, plus a cross-group max-ratio. Always runs; results land in the YAML. When the spread is comfortable HiGHS handles the LP on its own and Layers 2/3 are no-ops.
  2. Layer 2 — semantic per-type scaling. Buckets matrix columns by physical quantity-type (energy, capacity, monetary, etc.) and multiplies each bucket by a power-of-2 scaler that compresses the median value onto O(1). The output writer applies the inverse so downstream consumers see absolute units.

Both readouts (the Layer 1 ranges and the Layer 2 magnitude buckets) are memory-bounded. Rather than materialise the whole coefficient product just to read a statistic, they walk the constraint / column spine in fixed row-batches — only one batch's coefficients are ever held in memory at once. This requires polar-high >= 2.4.0, which FlexTool now depends on; on the large RETO-Africa DES scenario it cuts the autoscale peak working set roughly in half. There is no longer a size cap that skips very large families: every family's coefficients are read and folded into the scaling decision, so no family is silently left out. 3. Layer 3 — HiGHS native + escape-tier folding. Picks an integer user_bound_scale exponent (within HiGHS's safe range) and folds the unbounded-slack escape valve into the same pass.

The autoscaler never changes the LP optimum — every transform is reversible and the reverse is wired into the output writer.

docs.title: How do I enable / disable it?
docs.text:
The autoscaler is on by default. Two ways to turn it off:

python run_flextool.py <input.sqlite> <output_info.sqlite> \
    --scenario-name <name> --scaling=off

Or set the environment variable:

export FLEXTOOL_SCALING=off

--scaling takes one of off, solver_only, basic, full (default full). With --scaling=off, Layer 1 still runs (the YAML audit is always written) but Layers 2 and 3 are skipped — the LP arrives at HiGHS in raw user units, and HiGHS' own equilibration is also disabled. The intermediate modes are solver_only (HiGHS-internal equilibration only), basic (Layer 1 + Layer 3 bound-scale, no Layer 2 column rewriting), and full (the default — all three layers).

docs.title: Manual user_bound_scale override
docs.text:
When the auto-pick for Layer 3 misses a value you know works better (e.g. HiGHS itself nudged with "Consider setting the user_bound_scale option to N"), pin it explicitly:

python run_flextool.py ... --user-bound-scale 6

Or per-solve in the DB via solve.user_bound_scale. A non-zero integer disables the auto-pick and the value is clamped to the HiGHS-safe range.

docs.title: The YAML audit
docs.text:
Every solve writes solve_data/autoscale_<solve>.yaml. Three top-level sections:

Section Contents layer1 matrix / cost / bound / RHS log10 ranges; cross_group_max_ratio; trigger flag (whether Layers 2/3 fired). layer2 per-quantity-type power-of-2 exponents; post-Layer-2 ranges per type; list of quantity-types actually present in the LP. layer3 user_bound_scale exponent applied to HiGHS; escape-tier plan.

A single-line console summary echoes after each solve. When a solve is rejected and its post-autoscale LP is still wide-ranged, a hint also prints — framed as a possibility, since a wide range does not by itself explain a non-optimal status; the YAML shows which layer (or which quantity-type) could not compress the spread. (Note a solve HiGHS could not certify as optimal is not automatically rejected — see the solve acceptance policy in _solve_acceptance.py.)

docs.title: Limitations to be aware of
docs.text:
The autoscaler is a numerical tool, not a model fixer. Some things it cannot do:

  • Compress within-type spread. Layer 2 scales whole quantity-types uniformly. If two capacity entities differ by 6 decades inside the same type, no single power-of-2 scaler shrinks both onto O(1).
  • Cure composite physical models. A 10 kW residential heat pump directly connected to a 10 GW continental grid forces both sides into the same node-balance row at their physical magnitudes. The fix is structural — aggregate the small-side units (e.g. 1000 buildings as one), or run the two subsystems as sequential models (invest → dispatch handoff). The Layer 1 ranges will flag this; the YAML's quantity-type sections will show the wide pre-/post-L2 range.
  • Help when the Rivendell guard fires. Layer 2 has a guard that refuses to over-shrink columns carrying mixed-magnitude coefficients on a single row (the Rivendell case). When the guard activates, Layer 2 leaves those columns alone — the YAML records that the scaler was clamped.

docs.title: Small coefficients rounded to zero
docs.text:
Two cutoffs remove near-zero coefficients before any scaling (both are judged on the coefficient's own, unscaled value):

  • Matrix and right-hand side — model.small_number_threshold (default 1e-4; polar-high Problem.coef_zero_threshold). A constraint coefficient or RHS term with |value| < threshold becomes 0. It does not apply to the objective.
  • Tiny cost coefficients (objective) — polar-high Problem.obj_coef_zero_rel_threshold, which FlexTool sets to OBJ_COEF_ZERO_REL_THRESHOLD = 1e-14 (flextool/engine/model/core.py, not a database parameter). A variable's total cost coefficient below 2**floor(log2(1e-14 · max|cost|)) becomes 0. Layer 3 centres the objective on the cost range [min|c|, max|c|]; one float leftover such as a 1e-17 cost (from an algebraic cancellation) stretched that range to 17 decades, Layer 3 then scaled the objective by 2**25 and HiGHS' dual simplex failed with "excessive dual values" (#140). The cutoff is applied to the cost vector the solver gets, the pre-solve range readout that Layer 3 uses, and the warm-start cost updates.

The cutoff is relative to the largest cost on purpose. Costs legitimately span many decades. Across the LP-snapshot fixtures the smallest real cost is 4.1e-5 (slack penalties of rolling_separate_dispatch), so reusing small_number_threshold (1e-4) would delete real costs. The widest real spread is min/max = 1.4e-12 (11.8 decades). 1e-14 is about 100 machine epsilons below the largest cost: below every real spread, above cancellation residue. Being relative, it also scales with scale_the_objective. It changes none of the snapshot LPs.

docs.title: Legacy LP row-scaling
docs.text: Separate from the autoscale package, FlexTool still ships an LP row-scaling family that multiplies node-balance / group-balance rows by node_capacity_for_scaling / group_capacity_for_scaling derived from connected-entity unitsizes (rounded to powers of 10 to preserve HiGHS symmetry detection). The former per-solve solve.use_row_scaling DB parameter was removed; row scaling is now controlled by the --scaling CLI flag (env var FLEXTOOL_SCALING) alongside the rest of the autoscaler. Every solve emits p_use_row_scaling=0 by default, so the legacy family is off unless forced via the FLEXTOOL_FORCE_ROW_SCALING test hook. Output un-scaling is wired into process_outputs/read_highs_solution.py either way.

docs.title: Input values are not rounded
docs.text: FlexTool passes every input value to the model at full double precision; nothing rounds parameter values before the LP is built. (An earlier --precision-digits option claimed to round inputs to 10 significant figures, but it never reached a normal run; it was removed.)

docs.title: Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• "My objective doesn't match a pre-scaling reference." Compare with --scaling=off: the scaled and unscaled solves agree within the solver tolerance, not bit for bit.
  • "HiGHS reports non-optimal." Read the console hint and open solve_data/autoscale_<solve>.yaml. The post-Layer-2 ranges show whether Layer 2 compressed the spread; the layer3 section shows what user_bound_scale HiGHS received. Try pinning a different value with --user-bound-scale N.
  • "The solver runs slowly but says optimal." Inspect layer1 ranges. A wide cost or matrix range that survives Layer 2 (look at layer2.post_l2_ranges) is the most common cause.
  • "My model is a 10 kW heat pump next to a 10 GW grid." This is the composite case. The autoscaler will record the wide cross-group ratio but cannot fix it numerically — aggregate the small-side units or stage the subsystems sequentially.
  • "I want the legacy row-scaling on top of autoscale." The solve.use_row_scaling DB knob no longer exists; the legacy family is off by default and only reachable via the FLEXTOOL_FORCE_ROW_SCALING test hook. For production scaling use the --scaling CLI flag; the output writer un-scales whatever was applied.

docs.title: Slack convention
docs.text:
Reference for how every vq_* slack variable in flextool.mod is declared, bounded, penalised in the objective, and written to output CSV.

This document is the single source of truth when adding a new slack or editing an existing one.

docs.title: One-line summary
docs.text: Single-variable slacks; the user-supplied penalty is the valve. Every vq_* is a single non-negative variable (with a scaler-relative <= 1 upper bound where that was historically natural). The penalty coefficient already keeps the slack quiescent on well-posed inputs and also lets the solver absorb pathological inputs without returning false infeasibility. Outputs un-scale row-scaled slacks back to the user's absolute units so downstream consumers see no change.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: An earlier design split each slack into a bounded primary (<= K_rel) plus an unbounded escape at 1000x penalty, with the idea that the primary tier kept the LP matrix bounded and the escape tier absorbed pathological input. In practice the existing high penalty already performs both roles on its own: a large penalty is preferred over infeasibility, and the solver will drive slack to zero when there is any feasible alternative. Two columns with identical constraint coefficients but different objective weights are also a degeneracy generator; removing the escape tier eliminates that.

docs.title: Convention
docs.text:
For a slack vq_foo whose row appears in constraint R[i, ...] with row-scaler S[i, ...]:

# Declaration — single variable
var vq_foo {...indices...} >= 0;                # unbounded
# or, where historically bounded ``<= 1`` makes physical sense
var vq_foo {...indices...} >= 0, <= 1;

# In the constraint row
s.t. R {...indices...}:
    ...
    + vq_foo[...] * S[..., d] * step_duration[...]
    ...
    ;

# In the objective — single sum
  + sum {...} pdt_branch_weight[d, t]
            * vq_foo[...]
            * S[..., d]
            * pdGroup[..., 'penalty_foo', d]
            * step_duration[...]
            * p_rp_cost_weight[d, t]
            * p_inflation_factor_operations_yearly[d]
            / complete_period_share_of_year[d]

docs.title: The slack roster
docs.text:
Seven vq_* slacks. "No t" means period-only indexing (no time dimension).

Slack Index set Row scaler (internal) Upper bound vq_state_up (n, d, t) for n in nodeBalance ∪ nodeBalancePeriod node_capacity_for_scaling[n, d] none vq_state_down (n, d, t) for n in nodeBalance ∪ nodeBalancePeriod node_capacity_for_scaling[n, d] none vq_reserve (r, ud, ng, d, t) for (r, ud, ng) in reserve__upDown__group pdtReserve_upDown_group[r, ud, ng, 'reservation', d, t] <= 1 vq_inertia (g, d, t) for g in groupInertia pdtGroup_inertia_limit[g, d, t] <= 1 vq_non_synchronous (g, d, t) for g in groupNonSync group_capacity_for_scaling[g, d] none vq_capacity_margin (g, d) for g in groupCapacityMargin — no t group_capacity_for_scaling[g, d] none vq_state_up_group (g, d, t) for g in group_loss_share group_capacity_for_scaling[g, d] none; penalised indirectly through vq_state_up via group_loss_share_constraint

docs.title: Output CSV convention
docs.text: For every slack, the written value per row is the single-variable value expressed in absolute units — multiplied by the row scaler and step duration where the writer does so. The file name, column headers, row structure, and numerical scale are identical to the pre-scaling-project output so downstream pandas readers (process_outputs/read_variables.py, scenario analysis, plotting) work unchanged. Row scaling un-scaling (× node_cap or × group_cap) is applied by the writer when p_use_row_scaling=1 (the legacy LP row-scaling family — independent of the autoscale/ package; the former solve.use_row_scaling DB parameter was removed, so this is now only forced via the FLEXTOOL_FORCE_ROW_SCALING test hook); in Mode A the scaler defaults to 1 so the factor is a no-op.

docs.title: Editing checklist when adding a new slack
docs.text:
1. Declaration — one var line, >= 0 and optionally <= 1 where the historic row structure justifies a relative cap.
  2. Every constraint row that includes the slack — add a term multiplied by the row scaler.
  3. Objective — one sum term with the user-supplied penalty.
  4. Output writer — write vq_foo.val multiplied by whatever row-scaler factors are in effect so the CSV stays in absolute units.
  5. Parquet registry — add a VariableSpec in flextool/process_outputs/read_highs_solution.py; set unscale_by="node_cap" or "group_cap" if the slack appears in a row-scaled constraint.
  6. Baseline comparison — run the engine gate and confirm no material delta on objective, slack totals, matrix range.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
FlexTool has a multi-layer test pyramid: fast unit/integration tests on the engine building blocks, scenario goldens built on demand from JSON fixtures, and end-to-end scenario runs that compare output CSVs against committed reference files. This page is a developer pointer — where the tests live, how the JSON-fixture architecture works, how the CI verify chain enforces drift detection, and how the markers gate CI.

For the high-level test-layout inventory see architecture.md ("Test layout and fixture architecture"). For the engine internals being tested see engine.md. For the JSON-fixture rollout narrative see the CHANGELOG.md entry for v3.47.0.

docs.title: Layer 1 — engine unit & integration
docs.text:
Lives under tests/engine/. Covers the LP build path, derived parameter expansion, writer port, scaling pipeline (see scaling.md), decomposition (see decomposition.md), warm-start handoff, fast load, stochastic / PBT pieces, and the Surface A audit subdirectories:

  • loaders/ — A-tier loader tests (test_a01_a02_temporal_node.py, test_a03_a11_a12_process_topology.py, …) covering temporal-node, topology, online-ramp, storage-handoff, invest, costs/CO2, user-cstr/stochastic, groups/reserve/ladder, delay/dc loaders.
  • constraints/ — B-tier constraint tests (test_b01_b02_balance_storage.py … test_b09_b10_b11_dc_co2_user.py, plus emission / storage-handoff wiring).
  • objective/ — B16–B20 objective-term tests (varcost, invest cost, slack & reserve penalties, delay/DR/ladder).

Each subdirectory has its own conftest.py and a test_fixtures_solve.py that exercises the shared fixture solve fixtures.

Tests range from millisecond-class unit tests (block layout, derived params) to solver-touching parity tests. Synthetic flextool-flavoured fixtures live in tests/engine/fixtures/ and are auto-added to sys.path by tests/engine/conftest.py so test modules can from flex_toy_<feature> import … directly.

Meta-provider invariants. tests/engine/test_meta_provider_invariants.py enforces the Provider-only cascade contract as executable tests, not convention:

  • test_no_disk_csv_reads_in_cascade — fails if a cascade module re-introduces a csv.reader / open(...).read() against a CSV path without an explicit justification entry in the allowlist.
  • test_no_photocopier_lru_cache — fails on module-level @lru_cache over frame-returning helpers (cross-test contamination trap).
  • test_no_module_level_frame_globals — fails on module-level pl.DataFrame / pl.LazyFrame globals.
  • test_provider_or_shims_have_justification — every disk read still in the cascade must be accompanied by a documented reason.
  • test_allowlists_cover_only_existing_files — the allowlists themselves cannot drift past the files they reference.

A cascade module that reads from disk silently is a meta-test failure, not a code-review catch.

docs.title: Layer 2 — scenario fixtures, goldens, and parity
tests/fixtures/*.json is the single authoritative source
docs.text:
Every SQLite DB used by tests is built on demand from a JSON fixture. The previous ~521 MB of tracked / gitignored SQLite + CSV fixtures has collapsed to ~5 KB of JSON plus the on-demand cascade. Schema migration covers the fixture set via flextool.update_flextool.test_fixtures.migrate_all, and the CI verify chain (see below) fails the build if any fixture drifts from the current FLEXTOOL_DB_VERSION.

Canonical fixtures currently in tests/fixtures/:

Fixture Role tests.json Main fixture; tests/scenarios.yaml and most engine tests build their work-folders from here. Also the source for the generated templates_examples.json canonical DB. stochastics.json Stochastic / forecast-branch scenarios. Source for the generated howto_stochastics.json canonical DB. stochastics_pbt_inflow.json PBT inflow scenarios (period-block-time stochastic inflow). lh2_three_region.json LH2 three-region monolithic + Benders parity fixture (see decomposition.md). h2_trade_parity.json H2-trade Benders parity fixture. multi_ts_branch1.json Multi-timeseries branch-1 fixture. branch2_parent_period.json Branch-2 / parent-period stochastic fixture. case14_dc_power_flow.json PGLib IEEE case14 MATPOWER export (~8200 lines), used by test_flex_dc_power_flow.py.

The _augment_*.py, build_*.py and regen_lh2_three_region.py scripts alongside these JSONs are builders / overlays kept for provenance, not runtime dependencies. They take the schema sections from spinedb_schema.json (fixture_schema.schema_sections), and tests/update_flextool/test_fixture_builders.py checks that each still reproduces the data of its committed fixture. Every fixture carries exactly the schema's sections (test_fixture_schema_drift.py).

docs.title: scenario_workdir — on-demand cascade fixture
docs.text:
scenario_workdir(scenario_name, db_fixture="main"), defined in tests/conftest.py, is the session-scoped fixture that replaced the historical tests/engine/data/work_*/ snapshot pattern. It shares one cached run with scenario_run (which returns the tests._support.load.ScenarioRun instead of the folder). For a requested (scenario, db_fixture) pair it:

  1. Resolves db_fixture against the per-fixture session-scoped DB (built once per session from the matching JSON).
  2. Runs the full cascade (tests._support.load.run_scenario: csv_dump=False, keep_solutions=True) in a tmp_path_factory work folder.
  3. Copies the DB to tests.sqlite and snapshots the last step's provider into input/ + solve_data/, for tests that read those files. Nothing in a run reads them back: to get a sub-solve's FlexData, use scenario_run + load_scenario (the production loader call: the step's provider + a DB reader).
  4. Caches the result per (scenario, db_fixture) — each scenario pays its ~2 s cascade cost once per test session regardless of how many tests consume it.

Valid db_fixture keys map 1:1 to the JSONs listed above (main, stochastic, lh2, case14, h2_trade_parity, multi_ts_branch1, stochastics_pbt_inflow, branch2_parent_period).

def test_foo(scenario_workdir):
    work = scenario_workdir("coal_ladder_annual", db_fixture="main")
    # work is a Path to a populated workdir with input/output CSVs.

The two tests/engine/data/work_<scenario>/ directories that survive after Stage 4 (work_lh2_three_region, work_test_a_lot) hold only a single golden_obj.json golden objective each. No migrated test depends on the gitignored bulk CSV snapshot pattern; the entry stays on .gitignore for back-compat only.

docs.title: extend_tests_fixture — agent-friendly append-only edits
docs.text:
flextool.update_flextool.extend_tests_fixture is a YAML-delta workflow for append-only additions to tests/fixtures/*.json — new entities, alternatives, scalar parameter values, and scenarios. It exists because rewriting authoritative JSON by hand is risky:

  • Validates every name against spinedb_schema.json with did-you-mean suggestions.
  • Rejects edits to existing entries (append-only enforcement).
  • Rejects structured (Map / time-series) values, pointing the caller at the SpineDB editor for those.
  • Eight unit tests under tests/spinedb_backend/ lock the contract.

Agents add to fixtures without rewriting them; structured / curated edits remain a human-with-SpineDB-editor job.

docs.title: generate_canonical — projected canonical DBs
docs.text:
flextool.update_flextool.generate_canonical projects authoritative fixtures into derived canonical JSONs. The recipes in flextool/schemas/canonical_databases/_recipes.yaml declare two projections today:

  • tests/fixtures/tests.json → templates_examples.json
  • tests/fixtures/stochastics.json → howto_stochastics.json

The remaining howto_*.json files plus templates_time_settings_only.json stay individually authoritative — purpose-specific minimal teaching examples whose curation goals differ from test-coverage curation. generate_canonical --verify fails when a projected canonical drifts from its source.

docs.title: Golden objectives & scenario goldens
docs.text:
tests/scenarios.yaml defines a parametrised end-to-end scenario set that runs in tests/test_scenarios.py:

  1. Build the session-scoped SQLite DB from tests/fixtures/<fixture>.json.
  2. Run FlexToolRunner for the scenario in an isolated tmp workdir.
  3. Compare selected output CSVs against tests/expected/<scenario>/*.csv.
  4. If the scenario YAML entry sets expected_objective, assert that summary_solve.csv lands within expected_objective_tolerance (default 1e-3, often tightened to 1e-5 for stable scenarios).
  5. If time_budget_seconds is set, assert the full write-input → solve → write-outputs cycle finishes in budget.

Standalone golden integration tests live alongside (e.g. tests/test_lh2_three_region.py pins the LH2 three-region monolithic objective against tests/expected/lh2_three_region/objective.json at relative tolerance 1e-4). The same fixture also backs the native Benders gap-to-monolithic check — see decomposition.md and slack_convention.md.

docs.title: Layer 3 — full integration
docs.text:
The tests/test_scenarios.py driver above covers Layer 3 for the in-tree scenarios (tests/scenarios.yaml parametrises it, goldens live in tests/expected/<scenario>/). The separate execution_tests/ directory contains Spine Toolbox workflow execution tests (test_execution.py, tool.py) that exercise the same scenarios through the Toolbox DAG rather than the Python runner directly.

Three-tier gate cadence (matches the architecture.md wording so contributors converge on the same loop):

  • Inner loop — module-specific tests after every edit, typically pytest tests/engine/<area>/. Run continuously while iterating.
  • Broader gate — pytest tests/engine/ full sweep, once per commit batch (~27 minutes on a recent reference run).
  • Activation truth — pytest tests/ (Layer 1 + scenario integration suite + tests/model/ + tests/gui/ + tests/spinedb_backend/), run rarely (overnight / pre-release).

Inner loop ≠ confidence to merge; activation truth is the only gate that signals end-to-end health.

docs.title: CI verify chain
docs.text:
.github/workflows/tests.yml::template-check enforces four drift checks before any Linux/Windows/macOS test job runs. The same commands are valid as pre-push sanity locally:

Step Command What it checks Master template parity python -m flextool.update_flextool.sync_master_json_template --verify schemas/spinedb_schema.json matches the migration chain (see db_schema.md). Test fixtures schema python -m flextool.update_flextool.test_fixtures verify All tests/fixtures/*.json are at the current FLEXTOOL_DB_VERSION. Generated canonicals python -m flextool.update_flextool.generate_canonical --verify Generated canonical JSONs (templates_examples.json, howto_stochastics.json) match what generate_canonical would emit from the current authoritative sources. Canonical schema python -m flextool.update_flextool.canonical_databases verify The authoritative canonical JSONs themselves are at the current schema.

A drift in any of the four is a failed workflow, not a code-review catch. See the architecture.md "verify hooks" tail for the same chain in the higher-level inventory and db_schema.md for the migration-chain side of the contract.

docs.title: Markers and gating
docs.text:
Defined in pyproject.toml and re-asserted in tests/conftest.py:

Marker Meaning smoke Layer-1 + scenarios on the per-commit CI gate (<1 min) solver Touches a real solver (HiGHS), 5–60 s each slow >~30 s — nightly only decomposition Tier 8 objective-decomposition parity (tests/test_scenarios.py) perturbation Tier 6 single-multiplier perturbation tests emission Tier 7 MPS row-count emission tests csv_reload CSV reload contract tests in tests/csv_reload/ — opt-in gui Opens a real Tk window — opt-in with --run-gui (see "GUI tests" below)

The smoke marker is attached automatically to scenarios in scenarios.yaml that set smoke: true.

csv_reload is attached by tests/csv_reload/conftest.py to every test in that folder: tests that load a CSV work folder (a provider snapshot, a dump_csvs tree, hand-written CSVs) with the unsupported flextool.engine._csv_reload.load_from_dump (a provider seeded from the folder's CSVs), which production never does: load_flextool needs the sub-solve's provider and a DB reader, and never reads the work folder. The default addopts (-m 'not csv_reload') deselects them, and because a command-line -m replaces that one, the conftest also skips them unless the -m expression names csv_reload. Run them with pytest -m csv_reload tests/csv_reload/.

.github/workflows/ci.yml defines the three-tier CI gate:

  • smoke — every push and PR; runs pytest -m "smoke or (not slow and not solver)" with a 1-minute timeout.
  • full — push to master and nightly cron; full Layer-1 plus Layer-2 MPS parity (30-minute timeout).
  • slow — nightly only; -m slow.
  • gui-tests — every push and PR, a required check: the Tk tests under xvfb (see "GUI tests" below).

docs.title: GUI tests
docs.text:
The tests that open a real Tk window are the modules listed in _GUI_DISPLAY_MODULES (tests/conftest.py) and the tests marked gui (pytestmark = pytest.mark.gui, e.g. every module of tests/gui/assistant/). They are skipped unless --run-gui is given; --gui-only deselects everything else. Never run them on your own display — they move windows and the keyboard focus. Run them under xvfb, with openbox as the window manager as the CI job does (mapping, focus, grabs and the work area then behave as on a desktop):

xvfb-run -a sh -c 'openbox & sleep 1; python -m pytest tests/gui --run-gui --gui-only -n 0'

The gui-tests job of ci.yml runs exactly this on Linux (Python 3.14, --timeout 300). It runs serially: the focus is one per display, so tests in parallel processes on one display take it from each other. A test that checks where the focus went asks the window (focus_lastfor()), not the display (focus_get()). A dialog is transient to its parent, and a window manager never maps a transient of a withdrawn window: open dialogs over a mapped window. The Tk-free modules of tests/gui/ run in the sharded Tests workflow. Windows and macOS Tk are checked by hand.

docs.title: Test-suite environment variables
docs.text:
Opt-in switches read by the test suite only (registered with audience test in ENV_KNOBS, flextool/run_options.py). The runtime developer switches the suite also uses, such as FLEXTOOL_AUTOSCALE_STRICT and FLEXTOOL_SKIP_SOLVER_PROBE, are in Environment variables (developer).

Variable Default Set to What it does FLEXTOOL_NATIVE_PARITY_SWEEP unset (skipped) 1 Run the slow parity sweep of tests/engine/test_orchestration.py over every fixture (about 5 min per fixture). FLEXTOOL_TEST_RSS_BUDGET_MB 1500 MB RSS budget of the input-derivation memory test tests/spinedb_backend/test_memory_budget.py, for machines with unrelated memory pressure. FLEXTOOL_TEST_KEYRING_LOG set by the suite file Set by the root conftest.py in the first process of a session and inherited by the xdist workers: every process appends a call that reached a system keyring backend, or a store or removal on the default keyring, to this file, and the session fails when it is not empty (tests/user_dirs_guard.py). Not for use by hand. FLEXTOOL_SHIM_RECORD set by the tests file Set by tests/engine/commercial_shim/test_item230_commercial_shims.py (opt-in, -m commercial_shim): each commercial-CLI shim in tests/engine/commercial_shim/shims/ appends one JSON line per call to this file (arguments, stdin script, the parameters as the solver package reports them after the solve, status, MIP gap); the tests assert on it. Not for use by hand.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
pytest -m smoke              # the CI smoke gate, fast
pytest -m "not solver"       # everything that doesn't touch a solver
pytest tests/engine/  # broader gate — engine layer
pytest tests/                # activation truth (slow)

Regenerate a single scenario's golden CSVs in place:

pytest tests/test_scenarios.py --regenerate coal

This runs only the matching scenario parametrize-case, writes fresh CSVs into tests/expected/coal/, and lets you commit the diff.

docs.title: Determinism guards
docs.text:
engine emitters keep cross-solve determinism through explicit polars sort keys on every set / parameter frame before it enters the polar_high.Problem. The downstream LP row / column IDs are then assigned in canonical order regardless of Python hash randomisation.

The autouse fixture _reset_flextool_module_caches in tests/conftest.py clears the LP-scaling module cache around every test so scenarios that share solve names cannot cross-contaminate.

docs.title: Adding a new test
docs.text:
• Engine unit test. Drop a test_*.py file into tests/engine/ (or the matching loaders/ / constraints/ / objective/ subdirectory) — pytest auto-discovers.
  • New scenario golden. Append a scenario entry to tests/scenarios.yaml, then pytest tests/test_scenarios.py --regenerate <name> and commit the resulting tests/expected/<name>/ directory.
  • New fixture content (append-only). Use flextool.update_flextool.extend_tests_fixture with a YAML delta rather than editing the JSON by hand.
  • Marker discipline. Mark fast tests with smoke only if they belong in the per-commit gate; mark anything that builds and solves an LP with solver; mark anything over ~30 s with slow.

docs.title: Recorded provider replies
docs.text:
The AI assistant's backend tests run on synthetic payloads (tests/assistant/llm/payloads/). The real answers of each AI service are kept as recordings under tests/assistant/llm/recorded/<preset>/<case>.json, made by hand with tools/record_llm_replies.py and checked in CI by tests/assistant/llm/test_recorded_replies.py (skipped while there are none). A recording is made only against the synthetic test project that the tool builds itself (tests/fixtures/tests.json with the runs of the assistant tests), never against a user's project.

To record one service:

  1. Make its key findable as the chat finds it: the preset's environment variable (GEMINI_API_KEY, …) or flextool-assistant --set-key --provider <preset>. The key is never given on the command line. For a local server, start it with the model loaded the way users run it (for Ollama, OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384).
  2. Run, from the repository root: 
    python tools/record_llm_replies.py --preset gemini --model <a model from flextool-assistant --list-models>
python tools/record_llm_replies.py --preset ollama --model <a pulled model that supports tools>
python tools/record_llm_replies.py --preset openai_compatible --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 --model <name>
    The tool asks two fixed questions (one about input data, one about a result) through the real session, so the service is billed for a few requests. It writes the file only when both questions were answered, the model made at least two rounds of tool calls, the scrubbed recording passes the scrub check and it replays to the same answers; otherwise it says why and writes nothing (exit 1).
  3. Look through the file before committing it, then run pytest tests/assistant/llm/test_recorded_replies.py.

What the scrub does before writing: no request header is recorded; message, call, response and request ids (chatcmpl-…, msg_…, toolu_…, gen-…, call_…, req_…) become placeholders of the same format, the same everywhere in the file; organisation and project ids, run ids, e-mail addresses and the key are replaced; the FlexTool redaction removes the project folder, the home folder, user and host names and other absolute paths; the address of a custom endpoint becomes https://endpoint.example.test/v1. Any other address than the preset's own or one on this computer keeps its scheme, port and route kind with a placeholder host (192.0.2.1 or [2001:db8::1] on the local network, endpoint.example.test elsewhere) and the preset's path; a remote_host outside the known services becomes forwarded.example.test. In every text, the top-level fields included, an IP address outside loopback and the documentation ranges becomes a numbered documentation address (192.0.2.N, 2001:db8::N, never the endpoint's), and a host name of the local network (*.lan, *.local, *.home, *.internal, *.intranet, *.corp, *.localdomain, *.home.arpa, or a one-label host after ://) becomes host-N.example.test; a one-label endpoint host is replaced only as a host (://gpu, gpu:11434), never inside a word. Public host names in texts stay. Of the model server's own answers only the fields the probe reads are recorded (Ollama /api/show: capabilities, remote_host, parameter size, architecture and context length; /api/ps: the recorded model's name, context, size and graphics memory, no digest; LM Studio: the recorded model's context, load state and capabilities), and a model list keeps only the recorded model. Signatures and thinking text stay, because the replay needs them. Response headers are kept only from an allow-list (content-type, retry-after, retry-after-ms, x-ratelimit-*, anthropic-ratelimit-*).

What the scrub check (in the tool and in CI) refuses: a key-like text (sk-, sk-ant-, sk-or-, AIza…), a run of 32 or more letters and digits outside a signature field, an absolute path, an e-mail address, a request header, x-stainless-*, openai-organization or openai-project anywhere, a project name other than the fixture's, an IP address outside loopback and the documentation ranges, a host name of the local network or a one-label host after ://, a base_url or remote_host outside the known services, and (in the tool) the endpoint's own host left anywhere — a one-label one as a whole word. The check's patterns are its own and looser than the scrub's, and it also reads each streamed answer joined, so an address the scrub missed, or one split over two pieces, is refused rather than written.

When a recording settles a point the design marked unverified (for example the shape of Ollama's remote_host or of LM Studio's model list), correct the code and its tests in the same change.

docs.title: Unit floors, input shares and reserve shortfall
docs.text: Engine notes for _unit_floors.py, model/core.py::_eq_min_input_share and _reserve.reserve_shortfall_scale. User-facing semantics are in docs/reference/units.md and docs/reference/reserves.md (min_load, capacity_min_coeff, input_share_min, Reserves).

docs.title: Output measure
docs.text: unit_measured_arcs(d) — the arcs that define a unit's capacity: the conversion_flow_coeff ≠ 0 output arcs of an indirect unit (the maxOutputSum arc set, _indirect_sum_arcs), the single capped arc of a direct unit (including the (p, src, p) arc of a sink-less unit). Inputs of indirect units are never in it.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
name over row minFlow_minload_<kind> (p,d,t) ∈ p_idx, online ∩ min_load units Σ_A v_flow ≥ v_online·min_load + Rdn_p minFlow_output_floor_<kind> (p,p,k,d,t), units with ≥ 2 measured outputs, capacity_min_coeff_k > 0 v_flow ≥ v_online·min_load·cmin_k + Rdn_k minFlow_reserve (p,d,t), units with a reducing reserve on A, not covered above Σ_A v_flow ≥ Rdn_p minFlow_reserve_arc (p,s,k,d,t), reducing reserve on an arc of a multi-output unit or outside A v_flow ≥ Rdn_a minInputShare (p,s,p,d,t), indirect units with ≥ 2 conv≠0 inputs, share_s > 0 conv_s·in_s ≥ share_s·Σ conv·in

Rdn = reserve that reduces the arc: down at the sink node, up at the source node. Factor 1 when v_flow is the flow at that node (sink side; an indirect unit's input; a sink-less unit); 1/slope for a source-side reserve on a direct input→output arc. All rows are dimensionless (unit-count flow units) in the autoscale registry.

Decisions: the floor is not scaled by availability; connections are excluded; an indirect unit's input-side up reserve gets only the zero floor on that input arc (expressing "the input cut takes the outputs below min load" needs the conversion mix), so combined with output-side down reserve such a unit can end up below min_load.

docs.title: Upward reserve and online capacity
docs.text:
Upward reserve held at a node a process delivers into (b.reserve_up_to_sink, b.reserve_up_sink_parts from core._reserve_coupling) sits on the LHS of the capacity rows, with coefficient 1 (v_flow and v_reserve are both in output units of unitsize):

  • built capacity, units: maxFlow (per arc) and maxOutputSum (sum of an indirect unit's outputs). On an indirect unit's INPUT arc maxFlow's M (core._max_flow_rhs) uses x(availability) in place of plain availability — the min-load section is drawn per unit online, not per available unit, credited only to a unit with an online variable (#102; same x as maxInputFlow_online below, computed once and shared);

  • online capacity, units with online variables (_online.py): maxFlow_online_<kind>: v_flow + Σ_r Rup ≤ v_online·avail·cap_max_coeff per capped arc, and maxOutputSum_online_<kind>: Σ_k v_flow + Σ_k Σ_r Rup ≤ v_online·avail.

maxFlow / maxFlow_negCap / maxFlow_online_* read the units-only aggregate b.reserve_up_to_sink_units; a connection's reserve is limited by its own rows (connection_reserve_*, "Connections and reserve" below). profile_flow_upper_limit keeps the term for every process (b.reserve_up_to_sink). Hand-built data without process_unit keeps the process-generic coupling.

So an offline unit holds no upward reserve (spinning reserve). The built-capacity rows keep their term for online processes too (redundant while online ≤ built; they carry the invest/divest terms). reserve_process_upward (max_share) still uses the built capacity. Together with the floors the online band is v_online·min_load + Rdn ≤ Σ out ≤ v_online·cap·avail − Rup.

docs.title: Source-side reserve and capacity
docs.text:
The mirror of the floors: reserve that raises a unit arc's flow. _unit_floors.increasing_source_selectors(d, arcs) gives (down_src_flow, down_src_eff) keyed (p, r, ud, source) over all unit arcs (all_unit_arcs): down reserve at the source node of an arc whose v_flow is the input (sink == p: an indirect unit's input, a sink-less unit; φ = 1) or of a direct input→output arc (source ≠ p ≠ sink; φ = 1/slope, _inverse_slope). core._reserve_coupling turns them into b.reserve_down_at_source (per arc (p, source, sink, d, t), converted by φ) and b.reserve_down_input_arcs; the reducing up source selectors give b.reserve_up_at_source for profile_flow_lower_limit.

row term maxFlow + Σ_r v_reserve_down[p,r,s]·φ; a bound input arc carrying the reserve gets a row too (the v_flow bound stays, redundant) maxFlow_online_<kind> same term against online capacity maxInputFlow_online_<kind> (new) an online indirect unit's input arc with the reserve: v_flow + Σ_r v_reserve_down ≤ v_online·x(avail)·p_indirect_input_cap, x(y) = (slope·W(y) + section)/(slope·W(1) + section) — the min-load section is drawn per unit online, so avail·p_indirect_input_cap would cap the derated full output (x = avail without a section) profile_flow_upper_limit / _lower_limit + down at the source / − up at the source, × φ reserve_process_{upward,downward} max_share · c, c = input capacity per unit at an input node (_reserve._input_capacity_factor: p_indirect_input_cap, slope + section, 1)

Per-arc simplifications (as the floors): a direct unit with several outputs has one arc per output from the same input, and the reserve term joins each of them on (p, source), so the reserve needs headroom on every output arc (conservative; _input_capacity_factor de-duplicates (p, n)). An indirect unit's up reserve at an output (maxOutputSum) and down reserve at an input (maxFlow on the input arc) are the same "burn more" action but are checked in separate rows, so the headroom can be counted twice; a multi-input indirect unit is only kept within each input's own capacity. The reverse arc of a two-way unit (2way_2var) is a direct arc in process_source_sink_eff: down reserve at its node is headroom on the arc that draws from the node and a floor on the arc that feeds it. Connections have their own rows ("Connections and reserve" below).

docs.title: Reserve and ramp rows
docs.text:
core._eq_ramp adds the reserve of an arc to its ramp rows, from the same _reserve_coupling aggregates as maxFlow and the floors (no new selector):

row reserve term meaning ramp_{sink,source}_up_constraint + b.reserve_up_to_sink (up at the arc's sink) + every b.reserve_down_at_source entry (down at its source, ×φ) R↑: raises the arc's flow ramp_{sink,source}_down_constraint − b.reserve_down_to_sink − every b.reserve_up_at_source entry (×φ) R↓: lowers it

Sink-side and source-side rows of a direct arc limit the same v_flow and both carry the terms. The rule is per arc, as the floors: upward reserve at an indirect unit's output does not load the ramp room of its input arcs. For a unit WITHOUT online variables (or a built-only row) the row is v_flow[t] − v_flow[t′] ± R ≤/≥ ±ρ·c·cap with ρ the room of the pair of steps (ramp_speed·60·(Δ′+Δ)/2) and cap = existing_count (±invest/divest); a unit ramping down from t′ to t can hold its decrease in addition as upward reserve (that is what "reserve reduces the ramp room" means per model step; activation-time-scaled room is item 81).

For a unit WITH online variables (c14c part C, design §3) the room is on the units online, split by state, instead of on existing_count flat: the existing_count/invest/divest terms drop out of that row entirely and are replaced (per UC class linear/integer) by

up:    + c·ρ̄·v_online + c·(SU − ρ̄)·v_startup − F[t′]·v_shutdown
down:  − c·ρ̄·v_online + (c·ρ̄ + F[t])·v_startup − c·SD′·v_shutdown

(SU/SD′ as in "Startup / shutdown capacity reduction" below, this row's own side only — not the min over sides maxFlow_online keeps). F is the arc's OWN per-unit-online floor (_unit_floors.arc_floor_share, the same sets minFlow_minload / minFlow_output_floor use):

arc F the only arc of the unit's output measure A_p (a direct unit's single arc, or a single-output indirect unit's output) min_load an output of a multi-output unit with capacity_min_coeff > 0 min_load · capacity_min_coeff any other (other outputs, input arcs, units without min_load) 0

A single-input indirect unit's own fuel (input) arc also gets F = 0 here, by design, not oversight (c14c critique item 10): conversion_indirect plus the output floor already give input ≥ (slope·ml + section)·on = c·ml_in·on structurally, so F_in = c·ml_in would be a valid, tighter floor there too (closing the same pair-gain gap the output-side table closes). c14c's own target was single-output arcs only; the input-arc floor is left for a follow-up (see "Follow-ups" below, item 6), not adopted silently.

So a continuing unit's online capacity changes by at most ρ̄ each step, a starter reaches at most SU (reusing maxFlow_online's startup-step limit) and a stopper floors at F at the predecessor step; downwards a stopper drops at most from SD′ and a starter rises at least to F. v_startup / v_shutdown are relative to the SAME online predecessor online_change uses, so a start/stop pair with online unchanged gains at most c·(ml − ½·ρ·Δ) − F ≤ 0 of room on a single-output arc (strictly negative: no free room from declaring a pair there); an input, or one output of a multi-output unit, can still gain up to the min-load share, paid by the startup cost (research_backbone_startup_ramp.md §1/§3).

On a continuation roll's carry row (the period's first step ramping from the previous roll's realized flow, dt_ramp_carry) the predecessor is history, not this roll's data: the up row's stopper floor is F = 0 (no v_shutdown term at all there — the carried step's min_load isn't in this roll), and the down row's stopper allowance is SD′_carry = max(1, f̂ / (c·ĉ)) (f̂ = the carried flow, ĉ = p_roll_continue_online; 1 where ĉ = 0, no stoppers then) — exact and always feasible for any history the previous roll realized, unlike a fixed κ/c guess (critique item 3). Starters at the carry row keep SU/F as usual (this roll's own data).

Steps without a predecessor (dt_ramp_link / dt_ramp_carry), where the arc holds reserve in that direction (prundt: at its sink in the same direction, at its source in the opposite one), get a reserve-only row R ≤ ρ·c·cap with ρ = ramp_speed·60·Δ (the linked row with v_flow[t′] = v_flow[t]); cap = v_online for a unit with online variables, existing_count otherwise. Rows inside a period with ρ ≥ 1 are dropped also with reserve: maxFlow* carries the same R↑ and the floors (minFlow_*) the same R↓. Declaring a startup or shutdown no longer buys extra ramp or reserve room by itself (the c14a flat + v_startup / − v_shutdown term is gone; Q-c14a-B is resolved by this split, not left open). Connections have no ramp parameters.

docs.title: Startup / shutdown capacity reduction
docs.text:
_online._cap_reduction (Q8, item 49): for an online unit's arc with a ramp limit on a side (process_source_sink_ramp_limit_*, docs: "if the unit also has ramp limits"; GMPL keyed it on the speed alone), SU = min(1, ml + ½·ramp_speed_up·60·Δt) (the tighter side when both), red_su = max(0, availability − SU); SD / red_sd with the down speed at the pre-shutdown step. The half step is the step average of a unit synchronising at min load (owner question Q-c14a-A; GMPL used the full step). Availability correction: GMPL subtracted (1 − SU)·v_startup from availability·online, limiting started units to availability − 1 + SU; red_su gives them min(availability, SU) (identical at availability 1).

Rows (maxFlow_online_<kind>, and maxInputFlow_online_<kind> on an indirect unit's input arc):

row reduction base row κ·red_su·v_startup[t] + κ·max(0, red_sd − red_su)·v_shutdown[t⁺] …_shutdown_<kind> (where red_sd > 0 and t has a UNIQUE successor t⁺) κ·red_sd·v_shutdown[t⁺] + κ·max(0, red_su − red_sd)·v_startup[t] …_shutdown_branch_<kind> (one row PER successor, where t has SEVERAL successors — a branch point) κ·red_sd·v_shutdown[t⁺] + κ·max(0, red_su − red_sd)·v_startup[t]

The pair is the exact aggregate bound for any mix of starts at t and stops at t⁺ (one-step runs get min(SU, SD)); GMPL's single row with both reductions is the minimum-uptime ≥ 2 form and forbids one-step runs. t⁺ ranges over every successor whose dt_ramp_link predecessor is t (c14c #98 / critique item 1): the same period (the original case), or the next period continuing the timeline (two periods on consecutive parts of one timeline, or a mid-horizon branch continuing from its trunk step) — none at a period's last step that does not continue, before a gap, a representative-block start or a roll's last step. At a branch point (several mid-horizon branches continuing from the same trunk step) the shutdown cross-term cannot be split across the single base row (one v_flow[t] variable, one row): the base row keeps only its startup term there (a valid, looser bound) and …_shutdown_branch_<kind> gives the tight bound per branch instead — summing the branches' v_shutdown into one row would let several mutually-exclusive branches each buy back a whole unit of ramp room from the shared trunk step. κ = capacity_max_coeff on capped arcs, p_indirect_input_cap on input arcs. ml: min_load on output-measured arcs (direct arcs: also for an input-side ramp, v_flow is the output); on an indirect unit's input arc the input drawn at min load per unit of input limit, x / input_share_max with x = (slope·W(min_load) + section)/(slope·W(1) + section) (W(y) the output fuel width filled to y, as p_indirect_input_cap), so a started unit can always draw its min-load input. A ramp-limited input arc of an online indirect unit gets maxInputFlow_online rows even without reserve. On input arcs availability is replaced by x(availability) in the row and in red = max(0, x(availability) − SU_in) (_online._input_availability_share). Per arc: maxOutputSum_online of a multi-output unit is not reduced (as GMPL; ramps are arc attributes).

docs.title: Reserve shortfall multiplier
docs.text:
vq_reserve ∈ [0, 1] (bounded for numerics) is multiplied by reserve_shortfall_scale(d) in every reserveBalance_* row, in the objective penalty and in process_outputs (calc_slacks):

  • timeseries: reservation — returned as the very same Param when no dynamic / n-1 group exists (byte-identical LP);
  • dynamic: Σ p_flow_upper·unitsize·increase_reserve_ratio over the flows of the dynamic RHS (sink and source side);
  • n-1: max_f Σ p_flow_upper·unitsize·large_failure_ratio, the sum over the failing flows of one process f, maximised over the failing processes (_flow_requirement_bound(per_process_max=True)): the largest single n-1 row;
  • source side (a flow out of the group's node, dynamic and n-1 down): the bound of an arc in process_source_sink_eff is multiplied by the full-load draw slope + section (_with_full_load_draw; section only for min_load_efficiency units with online variables), because the rows count the flow drawn from the node as nodeBalance_eq does (_reserve._drawn_terms: v_flow·unitsize·slope + v_online·section·unitsize on an efficiency arc, v_flow·unitsize elsewhere); v_online ≤ p_flow_upper makes it a valid bound;
  • dynamic group demand: group_demand_requirement(d) = ratio_g · Σ_{n∈g} max(−inflow, 0) / Δt (exact, a constant), the same Param as the RHS term of reserveBalance_dynamic_eq. The inflow is p_negative_inflow_unmargined: the energy-margin emitters write solve_data/pdtNodeInflow_unmargined (the inflow before the margin) whenever a solve applies a margin, and keep it equal to pdtNodeInflow in later solves sharing the Provider; without the key the field is p_negative_inflow. Benders: the field is not region-filtered (like penalty_reserve); a subproblem joins it with its filtered group_node, so each region gets its own nodes' demand;
  • authored reservation is added for any group; methods add up.

p_flow_upper is the structural bound (existing + max invest by that period, per unit size); unlimited invest and conversion_flow_coeff = 0 arcs carry max_flow_for_unconstrained_variables, so the multiplier stays finite. Rows with a zero multiplier are dropped (no coefficient).

Activation (_reserve_methods.demanded_reserves, shared by _derived.prundt_from_source and emit/_reserve_sets): a reserve's relationships are active when the (reserve, up/down) has a requirement — a non-zero reservation on some group, a dynamic group driven by an increase_reserve_ratio at one of its nodes (or by its own group ratio), or an n-1 group with a large_failure_ratio at one of its nodes: dynamic and n-1 requirements are reserve demand by themselves. A dynamic / n-1 group without a driving ratio stays inactive. An n-1 ratio on a process without a flow in the failing direction activates the reserve with no n-1 row (inert columns).

docs.title: n-1 rows
docs.text:
reserveBalance_{up,down}_n_1_eq[r, ud, g, p_fail, d, t]: one row per failing process p_fail (a process with large_failure_ratio at a node of g and a flow into, for up, or out of, for down, that node). LHS: v_reserve_total[r, ud, g, d, t] minus the reserve of p_fail at every node of g (× unitsize × reliability) plus the group's shared vq_reserve · scale; RHS: p_fail's failing flows × unitsize × ratio. The shared slack prices the largest deficit once (.mod parity).

v_reserve_total (POWER column, no cost) exists for every group with an n-1 row and at least one provider; reserve_total_upper bounds it by the reserve of all providers: v_reserve_total − reserve_sum ≤ 0. Eliminating the total gives back the per-provider form (each n-1 row counts every provider except p_fail), so the reformulation is an exact projection. The inequality suffices because the total enters only ≥ requirement rows, with a positive sign, and has no cost. It needs reserve_sum ≥ 0, which holds because providers have reliability > 0 (process_reserve_upDown_node_active) and unitsize > 0; otherwise v_reserve_total ≥ 0 would add a constraint. A group without providers (or without reliability data) has no total: its rows are vq_reserve · scale ≥ failure.

The reserveBalance_timeseries_eq / reserveBalance_dynamic_eq rows of a group that has a total use v_reserve_total in place of reserve_sum (exact by the same projection; groups without n-1 rows keep reserve_sum). This roughly halves the reserve block of groups combining n-1 with another method. The value function in the timeseries right-hand side is unchanged, so the reported reserve price (the timeseries row duals) is the same wherever it is unique.

Nonzeros per (r, ud, g, d, t), with P provider pairs (p, n), and per failing process f its own provider pairs own_f and failing arcs a_f: (P + 1) + Σ_f (2 + own_f + a_f) (the per-provider form had Σ_f (P − own_f + 1 + a_f)), so they grow with providers plus failing processes. HiGHS presolve keeps the total columns (measured with HiGHS 1.14: presolve neither removes the total columns nor re-densifies the rows).

Results: the objective and every value that is unique at the optimum are those of the per-provider form; v_reserve is costless, so its split among providers is often not unique and may differ between the two forms. The n-1 row duals keep their meaning; when the total is positive, the magnitude of the reserve_total_upper dual is the sum of the duals of the group-step's rows that use the total (HiGHS reports the ≤ row with the opposite sign to the ≥ rows). The total is not written to the outputs.

docs.title: Connections and reserve
docs.text:
_reserve._add_connection_reserve_constraints. Connections are the processes of process_source_sink that are not in process_unit (_common._connection_procs; process_unit None — hand-built data — keeps the old process-generic coupling; an empty process_unit makes every process a connection, so the DB projection keeps it empty instead of None). maxFlow, maxFlow_negCap and maxFlow_online_* carry the upward reserve of units only (b.reserve_up_to_sink_units).

At a reserve node n a connection p has at most one in-channel (a flow variable arriving at n: v_flow[p,m,n], or v_flow_back[p,n,m] of a one-variable / DC arc) and at most one out-channel (v_flow[p,n,m] drawing slope·v_flow on an efficiency arc, or v_flow_back[p,m,n]); more raises. Flows are measured where they arrive; s_out is the power drawn at n per unit of the out-channel. Net-position rule:

R↑_n ≤ (C_in − x_in) + s_out·x_out        R↓_n ≤ x_in + s_out·(C_out − x_out)
up:   x_in − s_out·x_out + R↑ ≤ C_in                  (connection_reserve_up)
down: x_out − x_in/s_out + R↓/s_out ≤ C_out           (connection_reserve_down)

One row per capacity bound of the channel whose capacity the reserve uses (in-channel for up, out-channel for down): built (C and the invest / divest terms of that arc's maxFlow / maxFlow_back), _online_{linear,integer} (κ·availability·v_online), _exact (Ū·y on the forward arc, Ū·(1−y) on the reverse arc), so each row holds a single channel's capacity and is exact. A missing channel contributes nothing (C = 0, s_out = 1): a one-way connection gets the floor R↑ ≤ s·x_out at its sending node and x + R↑ ≤ C (the old maxFlow coupling) at its receiving node; a one-variable connection gets R↑ ≤ C − f, R↓ ≤ C + f for its signed flow f into n; reserve at a node the connection does not link is 0. The same capacity may back upward reserve at one end and downward reserve at the other (one action serves both), as for units (separate up / down rows).

Kept as they were: reserve_process_* (max_share × built capacity, c = 1 for connections) and profile_flow_upper_limit, which keeps the upward-reserve term on the in-arc of a connection with a connection__profile — conservative: it does not count reserve from stopping the out-flow.

The reverse flow v_flow_back also counts in the dynamic and n-1 requirements, their shortfall scale and the storage energy rows (reverse orientation of a one-variable connection to a storage node, slope 1), with the orientation of nodeBalance_eq (into the arc's source, out of its sink).

docs.title: Follow-ups (not implemented)
docs.text:
1. (Done: "Source-side reserve and capacity" above.)
  2. (Done: "Connections and reserve" above.)
  3. reserveBalance lacks the .mod's slope factor for source-side reserves of direct units; _unit_floors._inverse_slope follows the current convention and must change with it (tripwire: test_down_reserve_floor.py::test_direct_unit_input_side_up_reserve).
  4. Connection delay is not implemented. Connections are never in process_indirect, and the delayed input term exists only in conversion_indirect; the .mod had the same gap (its nodeBalance delay term is commented out). The delay used to mark the connection delayed anyway, which made it fork_yes, moved its arcs from process_source_sink_eff to _noEff (efficiency losses dropped) and turned a regular connection one-way. Now every reader of delay reads unit.delay only (input_derivation/_specs.py delay tables, input_derivation/_process_method.py, _derived _classify_process_method / _delay_distributions_from_source, _projection.process_delayed), so a connection is modelled as if no delay were set, and _validators.validate_connection_delay warns once per connection with a non-zero delay (tests/engine/test_connection_delay_ignored.py). Applying a connection delay needs a delayed term in the node balance; when it is added, drop the filters and the warning.
  5. (Done: v_flow_back in the dynamic and n-1 rows, see "Connections and reserve".)
  6. A single-input indirect unit's fuel (input) arc gets F = 0 in the ramp-row table above (c14c critique item 10) instead of F_in = c·ml_in, which conversion_indirect plus the output floor would justify structurally. Deliberately left: c14c's target was single-output arcs; see specs/github_issues.md §3 item 178.

docs.title: Basics: time, VRE, network and demand
How to create basic temporal structures for your model
docs.text:
(time_settings_only.sqlite)

FlexTool allows to build models for different kinds of purposes and has therefore a flexible temporal structure, which requires some learning at first. To get you started, this how-to creates three different timelines: a full year, a 48h timeline and a timeline with five one-week periods to represent a full year. To be able to choose which of these are used in a given scenario, three alternatives are created: init, init_2day-test, init_5week-invest.

The names of these alternatives hint at the intended use of each timeline. Even when you are building a large model with a long timeline, it is better to use a short 48 hour timeline for testing purposes when building the model. Using five one-week periods, i.e. "a representative periods", in an investment model is a method to reduce the model size and consequently solve time. More about that in How to run solves in a sequence (investment + dispatch)

To define a temporal structure for a model instance, you need to create the following entities:

  • timeline entity called y2020 with a map-type parameter timestep_duration that defines the timeline the time series data in the model will need to use. It contains, in the first column, the name of each timestep (e.g. t0001 or 2022-01-01-01) and, in the second column, the length of the timestep in hours (e.g. 1.0). The timestep names here must match the timestep names in other time series like inflow or profile. Here all of the three options use the same full year timeline i.e. timesteps from t0001 to t8760 with a step size of one hour.
  • timeset entities called full-year, 2day and 5week. Each of them need a map-type parameter timeset_duration to define a timeset using a timestep name to indicate where the timeset starts and a number to define the duration of the timeset in timesteps: (t0001, 8760) for the full-year and (t4001 and 48.0) for the 48h. The timeline is larger than the 48 hours, but this way the solver uses 48 hours specified. The 5week needs five starting points t2521, t4538, t5041, t7057 and t8233 with all having the length of 168.0
  • timeset needs to be connected to the timeline. This is done by adding the timeset parameter timeline. Each of the three timesets include the value y2020.

  • solve entities called full-year-dispatch, 2day-dispatch and 5week-invest. In addition, they need the following parameters:

  • a map-type parameter period_timeset to define the timeset to be used by each period. Here each of the three use their timeset to describe the same period p2020. The first column of the map has the period: p2020 and the second column the timeset: full-year, 2day or 5week

  • an array-type parameter realized_periods to define the periods that are realised from the solve named by the entity (the first column of an array is an index number starting with 0, the second column contains the period to be realized in the results: p2020 for all the solves here)

  • a parameter solve_mode, to be set to single_solve in these examples

  • Finally, a model entity will define the solves to be included in a one model instance. They are defined in the array parameter solves. For these examples, the model name is flextool and for each solve the name of the solve should be given in the solves array (distinguished by the alternative): full-year-dispatch, 2day-dispatch or 5week-invest.

Be careful when choosing datatypes! Maps need to be maps not arrays. You will see a red exclamation mark if you are using the wrong datatype. (In the future, an update is coming to toolbox to ensure compliance.)
