The tool includes some assumptions about the time structure, in case something is missing. These will work if there is only one option for the model to choose. The assuptions are the following:

  • If timeset: timeline is not set and only one timeline is defined, it is used
  • If no timeset is exist and only one timeline is defined, create a full timeline timeset
  • If period_timeset is defined, but no realized_periods or invest_periods exists, all periods are realized
  • If period_timeset does not exist and only one timeset exists, create timesets for all realized_periods and invest_periods
  • If model: solves does not exist, and only one solve exists, that it is used
  • If a solve in model: solves does not exist, create a solve where all periods_available are realized

docs.title: How to create a PV, wind or run-of-river hydro power plant
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: wind) init - west - wind

These three power plant types don't use any commodities (i.e. fuels), but are instead dependant on a timeseries profile. To create these plants one needs an output node, an unit and a profile.

The unit needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The unit only needs parameters:

  • existing: [The maximum capacity of the plant]

Additionally these parameters should be at their default values:

  • conversion_method: constant_efficiency
  • efficiency: 1

The profile entity only has one parameter: profile. It is a timeseries map which tells what fraction of the capacity the plant can produce at each timestep.

The other entities

  • unit__outputnode: (plant|output node) and
  • unit__node__profile: (plant|output node|profile) need to be both created.

The unit__node__profile entity needs a parameter profile_method that has three options: upper_limit, lower_limit and exact. It states how the profile is considered. In most cases the upper_limit option should be used as it allows the plant to curtail the production if there is more supply than demand. Otherwise the output node might have to use downward_penalty to spill energy.

The same profile can be used for multiple unit__outputnodes (and that is why the profile is not a unit parameter but its own entity).

docs.title: How to connect nodes in the same energy network
docs.text:
(connections.sqlite)

Typically nodes are used to maintain an energy balance and therefore they are used to represent a location with demand or a storage. The nodes can pass energy to each other through a connection entity. This is often an electricity connection but it can be any form of energy (or matter) moving between two nodes. To create a connection one needs:

  • two nodes
  • connection
  • connection__node__node to tie these three together.

The connection and nodes need to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The connection needs parameters:

  • existing: The maximum capacity of the connection [MW]. Applies to both directions.
  • efficiency: represents the losses in transferring the energy. Same in both directions.

Optional parameters:

  • is_DC: yes, flag if the connection is counted as non-synchronous for the possible non-synchronous limit. If is_DC (direct current) is yes, then the connection is non-synchronous. More at: How-to create a non-synchronous limit
  • transfer_method: Five options: regular (default), exact, variable_cost_only, no_losses_no_variable_cost, unidirectional.

In most cases regular should be used. The downside of it is that it allows the flows to both directions at the same time, but the model does this only in specific circumstances when its beneficial to leak energy through the connection losses. For example, if connection capacity is 500 and efficiency 0.8, both nodes can receive 500, but send 625 (500 / 0.8), reducing the incoming energy by 125 in both nodes without any cost. Typically the model does not want to produce extra energy as it usually has costs, but it can happen if there is a cost to curtailing energy generation from a free source or if a unit is forced to generate at some level ('e.g. using profile_method: 'equal'). If non-synchronous constraint is used with a node using this connection, use exact instead as regular connections can circumvent this limit.

Exact method does not allow flow in both directions at the same time: it uses one binary variable per connection and time step, so in each time step the whole connection transfers in one direction only. This is computationally heavier (especially if the model would otherwise be fully linear).

Variable_cost_only can be used when there are no losses associated with the flow. It allows costs related to the flow, but if losses are to be included, it should not be used.

The no_losses_no_variable_cost can be used when the connection has no losses and no variable costs accociated with the flow. It is computationally the most efficient method, as it uses only one variable for the flow (the variable becomes negative for the other direction, but this can work only when there are no losses or variable costs). It also prevents simultanoues flow to both directions.

The unidirectional method restricts the flow to one direction only (from the first node to the second node in connection__node__node). It uses a single non-negative variable and supports efficiency and other_operational_cost in the usual way. Useful for one-way transmission such as controllable HVDC links or commodity pipelines.

A group can also carry a transfer_method that overrides the per-connection choice for every connection between its member nodes. Set it to any of the connection options above, or to dc_power_flow_with_angles to activate B-theta DC power flow on the subnet (which additionally needs reactance on each connection). An is_DC connection between the group's nodes is not a DC power-flow line: it keeps its own transfer_method. See the Groups section of the reference for details.

The results of connections can be seen from the node_balance table. However, these are the results from all the connections connected to the node. If you want summary metrics for an individual connection or a collection of them, create a flowGroup, add the relevant flowGroup__connection__node members, and set flow_aggregator: standalone_aggregator_only on the flowGroup. This produces a flow-group summary (per-period cumulative_flow MWh/a, scaled to a full year, and average_flow MW, plus a signed net-flow timewise series) for the group.

The example database shows a connection between a two node system where the other node has a wind power plant and the other node has a coal power plant.

docs.title: How to set the demand in a node
docs.text:
(demand.sqlite)

The demand in a node is set with the inflow parameter. When the node is consuming energy or matter, the values should be negative and when the node is supplying energy (or matter) the values should be positive. The inflow parameter accepts two types of data:

  • Constant
  • Timeseries map

If the model is using multiple periods, then the same timeseries profile is used for every period. However, the inflow can be scaled for different periods with the inflow_method parameter:

  • scale_to_annual_flow: This will multiply the demand with a constant to make the summed inflow to match the annual_flow. This requires the node parameter annual_flow that is a map of periods containing the annual flow for each period. The sum of inflows is divided by the period's share of the year (hours in period /8760) before scaling (so that the annual energy demand/supply matches the annual_flow no matter what parts of the year are used to represent the full year).
  • scale_in_proportion: calculates a scaling factor by dividing annual_flow with the sum of time series inflow (after it has been annualized using timeline_duration_in_years). This does not force the demand/supply to match annual flow in case the representative periods are not representing the full year, but the time series will still be scaled to capture the proportional change in the annual_flow parameter.
  • scale_to_annual_and_peak_flow: The inflow scaled so that the peak is at the given peak_flow and the inflow sums to annual flow of the period. This is done by the following equation:
new_inflow = (peak/peak_old)*(1+c)*old_inflow-peak*c

where c = 
[(peak/peak_old)*(8760/hours_in_period)*sum(old_inflow) - annual_flow] 
/ [peak*steps_in_period*(8760/hours_in_period) - (peak/peak_old)*(8760/hours_in_period)*sum(old_inflow)]

peak_old is the largest (by magnitude) inflow of the period's own time steps, so each period's peak reaches its peak_inflow. steps_in_period is the number of time steps in the period (= hours_in_period on 1 h steps). peak_inflow is, like inflow, energy per time step; with timeset_weights or representative periods the sums and the step count are weighted.

Examples of all these options are shown in the demand.sqlite.

docs.title: How to create a delay between two nodes
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: water_pump_delayed)

Sometimes a flow between two nodes needs to be delayed, for example water flow in river systems can take hours between two power plants. This can be approximated using the delay parameter of units (connections do not apply delay yet — a connection delay is ignored with a warning — so use a unit for a delayed flow). Delay can be expressed using a constant value (hours) or as a weighted map of time delays (index: time delay in hours, value: weight). Each weight indicates its share of the original flow and the weights should sum to 1. Delay requires that the time resolutions in the model are always integer multiples of these time differences.

docs.title: How to use timeset weights (non-RP weighted timesteps)
docs.text:
timeset.timeset_weights lets each timestep within a timeset carry a custom weight that is applied to the cost and slack terms in the objective. The typical use case is a coarse, OSeMOSYS-style timeslice structure where some timesteps cover more year-hours than others (wet vs. dry season, peak vs. off-peak day-types) — timeset_duration already controls how long each step is, but timeset_weights is what scales the contribution to the annual cost when those slices are uneven.

The parameter is a flat Map on the timeset entity: index is the timestep name, value is a float. Weights are normalised per period to sum to 1 and then re-scaled by the number of active timesteps, so uniform input reproduces weight = 1 per step (the default behaviour) and the absolute magnitude of the weights does not matter — only the relative shape does. Decoder lives in flextool/engine/input/_timeline.py (_decode_timeset_weights) and the per-period normalisation is documented under TimelineConfig.timeset_weights in the same file. See also the timeset_weights entry in Reference.

Mutually exclusive: timeset_weights and representative_period_weights

A single timeset may carry either timeset_weights (per-step weights for non-RP timeslice models) or representative_period_weights (per-period weights for RP-clustered models), not both. The runner errors out if both are set on the same timeset.

docs.title: How to run a sensitivity (one alternative on top of a scenario)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenarios: coal and coal_co2_price)

The idea. A sensitivity changes one or a few input values and leaves the rest of the model as it is. In FlexTool, put the changed values in an alternative of their own and add that alternative on top of the scenario you want to vary. The new scenario then differs from the original only in those values, and the difference in the results is the effect of the change.

Make the alternative. Add an alternative, for example fuel_price_high, and give it only the values that change: here price 30 on the commodity coal (instead of 20). Do not copy the other data into it.

Make the scenario. Make a new scenario with the same alternatives as the original, in the same order, and add the new alternative last. An alternative lower in the list overrides the ones above it when they set the same parameter (see the tutorial), so the last alternative wins. Make one scenario for each sensitivity: coal and coal_fuel_price_high side by side. To combine two changes, add both alternatives.

An example. In examples.sqlite, the scenario coal_co2_price is the scenario coal with the alternative co2_price on top. That alternative sets co2_method price and co2_price 50 CUR/t on the group co2_price. The three scenarios of How to compare emission trajectories are built the same way.

Things to know.

  • A value in the sensitivity alternative replaces the whole value of the alternatives above it, not a part of it. If you give a period map, give every period of the solves: for many parameters a missing period is an error (the parameter descriptions say which).
  • An entity that exists only in the sensitivity (a new unit, for example) needs its entity alternative set to active in that alternative.
  • Check that the two scenarios differ only where you meant: the AI assistant's compare_inputs lists the input differences between two scenarios (see The AI assistant).

Compare the results. Run both scenarios and open them together in the comparison view of the Result viewer (key X), or make comparison plots with scenario_results.py. To run many sensitivities from the terminal, see Run several scenarios in a batch.

docs.title: How to add CO2 emissions, costs and limits
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: coal_co2 ) init - west - coal - co2_price - co2_limit

Carbon dioxide emissions are added to FlexTool by associating relevant commodities (e.g. coal) with a co2_content parameter (CO2 content (tons per MWh) of energy contained in the fuel). The other CO2 parameters are handeled through a group of nodes (Here coal_price or coal_limit groups). Therefore one needs to create a group and add all the nodes that supply these commodities (eg. coal_market) to a group with a group_node entity. (Here the entity co2_price--coal_market) To set a price one needs to create set the co2_method parameter to price (constant) and create the co2_price parameter with the desired value. This price is added to the price of the commodity.

Alternatively one can set a limit on the co2 used by setting the co2_method parameter to period or total and setting the co2_max_period (periodic map [tCO2/a], annual emissions in each period) parameter or co2_max_total (constant [tCO2], emissions over the whole solve: annual emissions times years_represented, summed over the periods) parameter.

A flow into a node of the same group (instead of out of it) is treated as CO2 removal: it earns co2_content × co2_price as a credit against the price, and it is subtracted from the group's co2_max_period / co2_max_total emissions. This is how a direct-air-capture or bio-energy-with-carbon-capture process should be modelled — as a process whose output flow delivers into the group's CO2-content commodity node.

There methods can be combined by setting the co2_method to price_period, price_total, period_total or price_period_total.

docs.title: How to compare emission trajectories
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenarios: co2_without_measures, co2_existing_measures, co2_additional_measures) init - west - coal - co2_trajectory_system - (one trajectory alternative)

The idea. Put the system in one set of alternatives and each emission trajectory in an alternative of its own, on top of it. A scenario per trajectory then differs only in the CO2 limit, so the results show what the trajectory costs. The examples use the usual reporting terms: without measures, with existing measures and with additional measures.

The system. The alternative co2_trajectory_system has:

  • a solve y2020_2035_2day_dispatch with solve_mode single_solve, four periods p2020, p2025, p2030 and p2035 in period_timeset (each → 2day) and in realized_periods, years_represented 5 in each period, and the model's solves set to it;
  • a constant demand of 300 MW at west;
  • coal_plant (from coal), 50 CUR/MWh, which emits 0.34 / 0.4 = 0.85 t of CO2 per MWh of electricity;
  • a carbon-free clean_plant (existing 500 MW, conversion_method none), turned on in this alternative, with a unit__outputNode (clean_plant, west) and no input; its other_operational_cost of 80 CUR/MWh is on that flow;
  • co2_method period on the group co2_limit, whose member is coal_market.

The objectives below assume no inflation_rate (0).

The trajectories. Each trajectory alternative sets co2_max_period on co2_limit as a period map [tCO2/a]:

Alternative p2020 p2025 p2030 p2035 co2_without_measures 3.0 Mt 3.0 Mt 3.0 Mt 3.0 Mt co2_existing_measures 2.0 Mt 1.8 Mt 1.6 Mt 1.4 Mt co2_additional_measures 2.0 Mt 1.5 Mt 1.0 Mt 0.5 Mt

No limit is a large value. The system alternative sets co2_method period, and a group with that method must have a co2_max_period: no value is an error, and so is a period missing from a map. The scenario without measures therefore gives a value that never binds; a constant is enough (the example uses a map with the same value in each period). Coal alone would emit 300 MW × 0.85 t/MWh × 8760 h = 2 233 800 t/a, so 3.0 Mt/a does not bind. Another way is to set co2_method in the trajectory alternatives only.

The scenarios. Each scenario is init, west, coal, co2_trajectory_system and one trajectory, with the trajectory ranked last so that it overrides the others (see the tutorial on alternative order).

The results. Below 2 233 800 t/a the limit binds, so coal makes exactly the limit's worth of electricity and clean_plant makes the rest. A tonne less of CO2 costs (80 − 50) / 0.85 = 35.29 CUR, which is the CO2 price that the model reports in every period where the limit binds.

Scenario Emissions [Mt/a] CO2 price [CUR/t] Objective [M CUR] co2_without_measures 2.2338 in every period 0 2628.0 co2_existing_measures 2.0, 1.8, 1.6, 1.4 35.29 3004.8 co2_additional_measures 2.0, 1.5, 1.0, 0.5 35.29 3322.45

Compare them. Run the three scenarios and open them together in the comparison view of the Result viewer (key X), or make comparison plots with scenario_results.py --alternatives co2_without_measures co2_existing_measures co2_additional_measures. The plots Emissions CO2 per nodeGroup and CO2 period limited shadow price show the emissions and the CO2 price per period.

Things to know.

  • The limit is annual (t/a): each period's emissions are scaled to a full year, whatever the length of its timeset. Use co2_max_total with co2_method total for a budget over the whole horizon (see CO2 costs and limits).
  • In a rolling solve, each roll may use the part of the period's limit that its horizon reaches, minus what earlier rolls already emitted in that period.
  • CO2 is the only emission that FlexTool tracks, and co2_content is a constant per commodity.
  • The limit has no slack. If the system cannot meet a trajectory, the model meets it by leaving demand unserved (the node's upward slack at penalty_up; with penalty_method off on the node, the model is infeasible instead), so check the slack results of a tight trajectory.

docs.title: How to create a non-synchronous limit
docs.text:
(non_sync_and_curtailment.sqlite) (scenario: non_sync)

Non-synchronous limit is a property of a group of nodes. It states that the non-synchronous flow to the group of nodes cannot exceed a set share of the input flows at any timestep. To demonstrate this, we have set a system with a coal plant, a wind plant and a single demand node. However, it can be done to a group of nodes with unlimited number of plants or connections connected. So, one can limit the non-synchronous share of individual nodes or of the whole system. The flows between the nodes of the group are excluded.

The non-synchronous limit is set to a group of nodes with one or multiple members. Note: These are set to the group with group_node entity, not with group_node_unit entity!

Create a group (here nodeA_group) and set a group_node entity (nodeA_group |nodeA). Then add parameters:

  • has_non_synchronous: yes
  • non_synchronous_limit: 0.5
  • penalty_non_synchronous: 4000

This forces the non-sync flow to be at max 50% of the incoming flow to the nodeA. The penalty should be always set as in some cases there is no other way to keep the constraint feasible (and it will be difficult to find the reason why the model does not solve). The existence of the non-synchronous penalty in your results indicates that this constraint has been violated and you should investigate the reason for this in your system. If the penalty_non_synchronous is lower than the upward_penalty of the demand node, the system will prefer breaking the non-sync constraint instead of the node balance equation. In other words, it will not curtail the production of profile plants if the demand is not satisfied even though it will break the non-synchronous penalty. If it is higher, the curtailment will take place instead.

When having a connection to a storage from a node with this constraint, the best practice is to add this storage node to the group as well. This excludes the flows to and from the storage in the calculation of the non-synchronous ratio. However, if you want to have these flows in the calculation, you have two options depending on if you want the flow to be synchronous or not. If it is non-synchronous, just set the connection parameter is_DC: yes. If it is synchronous (e.g., some flywheels), an issue arises with the reqular connection as it now can reduce the ratio with equal simultaneous flow in both directions. To prevent the simultaneous flow to both directions you need to set the transfer_method: exact. This will increase the solving time significantly as it will use integer variables (so, better to add the storage node to the node group with a non-synchronous limit).

Then set which plants and connections are considered non-synchronous by adding parameters:

unit_outputNode:

  • is_non_synchronous: yes

Connection_node_node:

  • is_DC: yes

Here the (wind_plant|nodeA) relation has the is_non_synchronous parameter and battery connection is_DC parameter. Because the battery node is in nodeA_group, the battery connection runs inside the group and its is_DC has no effect; it would count if the battery node were left out of the group.

A connection between a node of the group and a node outside it counts in both directions: its flow into the group is infeed (non-synchronous if the connection is is_DC), its flow out of the group is supply. A regular connection (at the cost of its losses) and a no_losses_no_variable_cost connection (at no cost) can flow both ways at the same time, which raises the supply side and so loosens the limit. Use transfer_method: exact for a synchronous connection that crosses the boundary of a group with a non-synchronous limit. FlexTool warns about a no_losses_no_variable_cost connection across the boundary (not when it is is_DC: then flowing both ways only tightens the limit).

With several groups that have a non-synchronous limit, each group counts its own boundary: wind exported from one group over an AC connection arrives in the neighbouring group as synchronous infeed (it is not counted against that group's limit), while over an is_DC connection it counts as non-synchronous there too.

If you want summary metrics per flow in the results, create a separate flowGroup for each flow (or collection of flows) and add flowGroup__unit__node entities to it. The flowGroup needs the parameter:

  • flow_aggregator: standalone_aggregator_only

This emits the flow-group's own outputs (per-period cumulative_flow MWh/a, scaled to a full year, and average_flow MW, plus a signed net-flow timewise series) for the members. It is summary output — for per-timestep decomposition of a node's flows, use print_dispatch on a group__node group instead (see "How to create aggregate outputs").

Here we have coal_flow flowGroup with flowGroup__unit__node relation coal_flow|coal_plant|nodeA and wind_flow flowGroup with flowGroup__unit__node relation wind_flow|wind_plant|nodeA.

docs.title: How to set a minimum inertia
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: coal_wind_inertia) init - west - coal - wind - inertia

The idea. Synchronous machines store energy in their rotating mass, and this inertia slows the fall of the frequency after a large plant trips. A minimum inertia keeps enough synchronous machines running when wind and solar cover most of the demand. In FlexTool it is a limit on a group of nodes.

The limit. Give the group (with its nodes as group__node entities, here electricity with west, east and north):

  • has_inertia: yes
  • inertia_limit [MWs]: the minimum inertia, here 200. Constant, period, time or period+time.

  • penalty_inertia [CUR per MWs and hour]: the cost of a shortfall, default 5000.

    A time map can set the requirement hour by hour. It must give a value for every time step of the solve (a missing one is an error); give 0 for an hour without a requirement. A period map must give a value for every period of the solve.

Which machines give inertia. Give each synchronous machine an inertia_constant [MWs/MW] on the arc to the node it is connected to: on unit__outputNode for a generator (here coal_plant 5, coal_chp 4), on unit__inputNode for a synchronous motor load such as a pump (here water_pump 3). Wind, solar and batteries get none.

How the inertia is counted. It depends on whether the unit has online variables:

  • With online variables (startup_method linear or binary): online capacity × inertia_constant.

    A unit gives its full inertia whenever it is online, also at minimum load. This is the physically right measure, and it lets the model keep a plant online at low output to provide inertia.

  • Without online variables: flow × inertia_constant.

    A unit at half load gives half of its inertia, and a unit with no output gives none. This underestimates the inertia of part-loaded plants, and the model can only get inertia by producing. In coal_wind_inertia, coal_plant has no online variables, so in the hours when wind could cover the demand it still runs at 40 MW: 40 MW × 5 MWs/MW = 200 MWs.

A unit with an inertia_constant on both its input and its output arc counts on both sides.

A synchronous condenser. A condenser gives inertia without producing power. Make it a unit with only an electricity input:

  • unit sync_condenser with existing [MW] and startup_method linear (or binary for whole machines), and no unit__outputNode
  • unit__inputNode (sync_condenser, west) with inertia_constant, for example 4

  • min_load, for example 0.02, for its losses

    A unit without outputs has its capacity on its input, so the condenser draws at least min_load × online capacity from west while it is online. The model takes it online when inertia is needed: with existing 100 and inertia_constant 4, 50 MW online gives the 200 MWs and draws 1 MW. The online variables are needed, since a condenser without them has no flow and so no inertia.

The penalty. The limit can be broken at penalty_inertia per MWs of shortfall and hour. Set the penalty well above what the model pays to keep machines online, and check that the shortfall is 0. A shortfall means that the system does not have enough synchronous machines; a cheap penalty lets the model buy its way out of the limit.

The results.

  • group_inertia__dt (group inertia_t) [MWs]: the inertia of the group in each time step.
  • group__unit__node_inertia__dt (inertia_unit_node_t) [MWs]: the part of each unit.
  • slack__inertia_group__dt and slack__inertia_group__d (slack_inertia_t, slack_inertia) [MWs]: the shortfall; its cost is the category inertia slack penalty in the costs.
  • group_inertia_largest_flow__dt (inertia_largest_flow_t) [MW]: the largest single flow into the group. FlexTool reports it, but it does not set the limit from it: compute the limit from your largest infeed and enter it.

Things to know.

  • With a new_stepduration (longer time steps), the limit is averaged over each new time step.
  • An investment solve with reduce_unit_detail_method online (or another value that leaves out the online variables) counts the inertia from the flows. With reduce_system_detail_method inertia (or one of the values that include it), the solve has no inertia limit. See Leaving out detail in a solve.
  • The parameters are in Groups and in Units.

docs.title: How to make investments (storage/unit)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: wind_battery_invest) init - west - wind - battery - battery_invest

Here we will use the previous battery scenario to represent the investment options in the tool.

The solve will invest only if it has an array of invest_periods set, telling the periods where it is allowed to make investment decisions. In a multi solve investment model (rolling investments) it can be useful to separately set realized_invest_periods so that the investment results get reported only from the chosen periods from each solve (in order to avoid overlapping reporting of investment decisions that are replaced by investment decisions in later solves). Furthermore, realized_periods will define the solves and periods from which the dispatch results are output into results.

A period in realized_invest_periods must also be in the same solve's invest_periods; FlexTool stops with an error naming the solve and the periods otherwise. Each period's investments should be realized by only one solve: do not list the same period in the realized_invest_periods of two solves. If you do, FlexTool logs a warning naming both solves and the period. Dispatch timesteps, on the other hand, may be realized by more than one solve (for example an investment solve and a dispatch solve nested inside it that both have the same period in realized_periods). For the overlapping timesteps the solve that runs later is kept and the earlier solve's results are not reported. FlexTool logs one warning per pair of solves and period, giving the number of overlapping timesteps. Timesteps that only the earlier solve realizes are still reported from the earlier solve.

First, the investment parameters need to be included both for the battery_inverter and battery entities:

  • invest_method - the modeller has options to limit the investment and retirement. Options are not_allowed, invest, retire or invest and retire. These have the sub options of no limit invest_no_limit, limit the amount per period: invest_period, limit the total amount invested invest_total or limit both the total investment and the investment per period invest_period_total.

  • If the investment is limited, it requires the corresponding maximum/minimum investment (power [MW] or energy [MWh]) to the virtual capacity. This can be set to individual entities or groups of entities:

    • invest_max_total
    • invest_max_period
    • invest_min_total
    • invest_min_period
    • retire_max_total
    • retire_max_period
    • retire_min_total
    • retire_min_period

  • invest_cost - overnight investment cost new capacity [currency/kW] for the battery_inverter and [currency/kWh] for the battery. Other one can be left empty or zero, since they will be tied together in the next phase. Here we will assume a fixed relation between kW and kWh for this battery technology, but for example flow batteries could have separate investments for storage and charging capacities.

  • discount_rate - discount rate (WACC) [e.g. 0.05 means 5%] for the technology that reflects the financing cost and risk. Should be nominal when model inflation_rate > 0, real when inflation_rate = 0.
  • lifetime - technical lifetime of the technology to calculate investment annuity (together with the discount rate)

Additional parameters:

  • lifetime_method: Model can either be forced to reinvest when the lifetime ends (reinvest_automatic), have a choice (reinvest_choice), or be restricted to a one-shot build that retires after its lifetime without rebuild (no_investment — for physical one-off additions like plant refurbishments).
  • construction_lead_time [years]: time from the investment decision until the capacity starts to operate. The start is rounded to the start of a period by construction_lead_time_method (below), on the periods of the whole model (all its solves). Constant or period (a map may set a different lead time per decision period). Default 0. Applies to unit, connection and node investments, deterministic and stochastic alike.
  • Terms. The investment decision is taken in a period of the solve's invest_periods. The capacity is in construction from the decision period until it comes online at the start of operation; from then on it is in service. Without a lead time, the capacity comes online in the decision period.
  • Results. In the capacity results (unit_capacity__d, connection_capacity__d, node_capacity__d) invested is the capacity that comes online in the period and in_construction the capacity decided but not yet operating (empty without a lead time); total is the capacity in service and does not include capacity in construction. Over combined solves (a chain of solves, invest then dispatch) every realized investment is counted once, in the period it comes online.
  • Limits. invest_max_period / invest_min_period (also of groups) count the capacity coming online in the period; the investment is decided earlier. invest_max_total / invest_min_total count every investment decision.
  • Costs. invest_cost is the overnight cost: construction time costs with their interest must be included in it. The annuity and the fixed_cost of new capacity are paid only over the years it operates within the model horizon, and the invest_cost (and lifetime, discount_rate) of the period it comes online is used. The lifetime starts when the capacity comes online.
  • Horizon. An investment whose rounded start of operation is after the end of the solve (including its look-ahead periods) or after the model horizon is not offered, with a warning naming the entity, the lead time and the solve. A chain of myopic solves whose horizon is not longer than the lead time therefore never invests in that technology: use a longer solve horizon or construction_lead_time_method = immediate.
  • construction_lead_time_method: how the start of operation (decision year plus construction_lead_time) is rounded to the start of a period:
  • immediate — no lead time; the capacity operates from the decision period. This is also the effective default when no lead time is set.
  • closest_seam — the nearest period start; a tie goes to the later one. This is the effective default once a lead time is set but no method is chosen.
  • previous_seam — the period start before.

  • next_seam — the period start after.

    Construction lead time and stochastics compose automatically. Under recourse (stochastic_invest_method = recourse) with an invest non-anticipativity window (shared_invest_periods, see the stochastics how-to), a long-lead technology that must be online after the branch reveal has to be ordered before it — in a pre-reveal, tied period — so its investment is a single shared here-and-now decision, while a short-lead technology can be ordered at/after the reveal and react per scenario. This staging is emergent (no extra parameter): set the window to the pre-reveal periods and the lead time stages the technologies for you. Note the two knobs stay orthogonal — the window is the information boundary (which order periods are shared), the lead time is the physics (how early you must order); you need both, set consistently, for staging.

  • salvage_value: Sets the extra value that can be gained for retiring [CUR/kW]. Only capacity that existed before the model run (existing) can be retired, until its end of life; the retirement saves its fixed cost over the periods it counts in and earns the salvage value as an annuity over lifetime (see retirements).

  • fixed_cost: Annual cost for capacity [CUR/kW]

In many cases some of the investment decisions are tied to each other. Here the battery capacity and the connection capacity of the battery_inverter will be tied as they are simultaneously limited by the choice of the battery technology to be invested in.

To model this, a new constraint needs to be created that ties together the storage capacity of the battery and the charging/discharging capacity of the battery_inverter.

A new constraint entity battery_tie_kW_kWh is created and added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

It is given parameters constant and sense. Constant could be left out, since it is zero. The sense of the constraint must be equal to enforce the kw/kWh relation.

Both battery_inverter and battery need a coefficient to tell the model how they relate to each other. The equation has the capacity variables on the left side of the equation and the constant on the right side.

sum_i(`constraint_invested_capacity_coeff` * `v_invest`) = `constant`
      where i is any unit, connection or node that is part of the constraint

When the constraint_invested_capacity_coeff for battery is set at 1 and for the battery_inverter at -8, then the equation will force battery_inverter v_invest to be 8 times smaller than the battery v_invest. The negative term can be arranged to the right side of the equation, which yields:

1 x *battery* = 8 x *battery_inverter*, which can be true only if *battery_inverter* is 1/8 of *battery*

constraint_invested_capacity_coeff is not a parameter with a single value, but a map type parameter (index: constraint name, value: coefficient). It allows the entity to participate in multiple constraints. (In older databases this parameter was constraint_capacity_coefficient; migration renames it.)

To tie cumulative, built-up capacity rather than the current period's new build, use constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff. It takes the capacity in service at the start of the period: existing capacity plus the capacity that came online in earlier periods, minus earlier retirements. Capacity coming online in the period itself is in the invested term (constraint_invested_capacity_coeff, the capacity that comes online in the period; without a construction lead time, the capacity invested in that period). Paired with constraint_invested_capacity_coeff, it expresses period-over-period growth limits:

v_invest[e, d] <= growth_rate * pre_built[e, d]

is written as: constraint_invested_capacity_coeff = { c: 1.0 } and constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff = { c: -growth_rate } on entity e, with constraint c having sense = less_than and constant = 0. A 10% growth cap starting from 1000 MW of existing wind would allow 100 MW in period 1, 110 in period 2, 121 in period 3, and so on.

To tie the capacity in service in the period (the capacity that limits the flows, for example for a share of the fleet or a ratio between technologies), use constraint_capacity_coeff; for the capacity retired in the period, constraint_retired_capacity_coeff; for the capacity in construction (decided but not yet operating, only with a construction lead time), constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff. Capacity in service = pre-built + invested − retired, with or without a construction lead time; capacity in construction is not in service.

Finally, FlexTool can mix several types of constraint coefficients: constraint_invested_capacity_coeff, constraint_retired_capacity_coeff, constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff, constraint_capacity_coeff, constraint_state_coeff, constraint_online_coeff and constraint_flow_coeff allowing the user to create custom constraints between any types of entities in the model for the main variables in the model (flow, state, online as well as invest). So, the equation above is in full form:

  + sum_i [constraint_invested_capacity_coeff(i) * v_invest]
           where i contains [node, unit, connection] belonging to the constraint
  + sum_i [constraint_retired_capacity_coeff(i) * v_divest]
  + sum_i [constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff(i) * pre_built]
           where pre_built = existing + Σ v_invest of earlier periods still in service − Σ v_divest of earlier periods
  + sum_i [constraint_capacity_coeff(i) * capacity_in_service]
           where capacity_in_service = existing + Σ v_invest still in service − Σ v_divest up to this period
  + sum_j [constraint_flow_coeff(j) * capacity]
           where j contains [unit--node, connection--node] belonging to the constraint
  + sum_k [constraint_state_coeff(k) * capacity]
           where k contains [node] belonging to the constraint
  + sum_m [constraint_online_coeff(m) * v_online]
           where m contains [unit, connection] with online variables belonging to the constraint,
           and v_online is the number of units online in the time step (of virtual_unitsize;
           without it, the largest existing capacity, else 1000 MW)
  =
  constant (a constant, or a period map giving each period its own value)

  where 'capacity' is existing capacity plus invested capacity

docs.title: How to create a multi-year model
docs.text:
A multi-year model is constructed from multiple periods, each presenting one year. In the example case, each year is otherwise the same, but the demand is increasing in the west node. This means that all periods can use the same timeset 5weeks from the same timeline y2020, but one can also make separate timelines for each year, if data is available for this. The inflow time series are scaled to match the value in annual_flow that is mapped for each period. The model is using the inflow_method scale_to_annual in order to achieve this (default is use_original that would not perform scaling). There should also be an inflation_rate parameter set for the model entity flexTool if something else than the model default of 0 is to be used (set to expected inflation when inputs are in nominal terms).

Discounting later years. Only inflation_rate discounts the costs of later periods; with the default 0, a cost in the last period weighs the same as in the first. In a model in real terms, set inflation_rate to the social discount rate to get present values. See Discounting between milestone years.

A multi-year model could be solved at one go (multi_year_one_solve) or by rolling through several solves (multi-year) where each solve has a foresight horizon and a realisation horizon. Next we will go through both options.

docs.title: Multi year with one solve
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: multi_year_one_solve)

In this example, one solve is used for all the four periods. All the four periods need to be added to the solve arrays invest_periods and realized_periods. Here the same timeset is used for all the four periods, so only difference between them is the increasing inflow set above. The parameters that need to be added to the solve entity:

  • years_represented parameter is used by the model to calculate the discounting factors for the periods in the model (often future years). It should state the number of years each period will be representing. For example, a period for 2025 could represent the years 2025-2029 if its years_represented is set to 5. Any investments would be taking place at the start of 2025 and discounted to the beginning of 2025, but the operational costs would accrue from each year in 2025-2029 each with a different discounting factor (decreasing based on the interest rate).
  • invest_periods the periods in which the model is allowed to make investments.
  • realized_periods the periods that will be realized in this solve (outputs dispatch results for these periods).
  • period_timeset defines the set of representative 'periods' (timesets in FlexTool) to be used in each FlexTool period.

docs.title: Multi year with rolling solves
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: multi_year)

If the solving time gets too big, there is an option to split the timeline into overlapping parts and solve them separately. This shortens the solving time as it increases exponentially as the model grows. Therefore, collection of smaller solves is faster. The drawback is that the accuracy will be affected if there are dependencies with a larger time interval than the split size.

When dealing with investments the splitting only works if the different periods are similar, in most cases complete years. If the first solve is really windy, it would invest too much on wind which wouldn't produce enough energy in later solves and then it would need to invest again to something else. It can also be challenging to consider lifetimes. If the option of retiring is allowed, it might retire something that is needed for later solves. In this example, the periods are complete years and the only difference between periods is increased demand.

The model rolls through several solves and therefore, the model entity flexTool has four values in the solves array. Each value represents one solve and it's position in the sequence of solves. The next figure illustrates the realization (blue) and foresight horizons (grey). The first solve will solve both the year 2020 and year 2025, but it will only output the year 2020. The next will solve both 2025 and 2030 but only output 2025.

Next figure shows the values needed to define one solve (out of the four solves in the example). Each of these need to be repeated for each solve in the model.

  • years_represented parameter is used by the model to calculate the discounting factors for the periods in the model (often future years). It should state the number of years each period will be representing. For example, a period for 2025 could represent the years 2025-2029 if its years_represented is set to 5. Any investments would be taking place at the start of 2025 and discounted to the beginning of 2025, but the operational costs would accrue from each year in 2025-2029 each with a different discounting factor (decreasing based on the interest rate).
  • invest_periods the periods in which the model is allowed to make investments. To be given for each solve.
  • realized_periods the periods that will be realized in this solve (outputs dispatch results for these periods). To be given for each solve.
  • realized_invest_periods parameter states the periods that will realize the investment decisions. If not stated, it will use the realized_periods that are also invest_periods.
  • period_timeset defines the set of representative 'periods' (timesets in FlexTool) to be used in each FlexTool period.

Note the the solve_mode: rolling_window is not used! This is not for investment runs (without nesting) as it rolls freely, and investments should only be made at the start of the period. This example is called 'manual rolling' later when those are discussed.

In the examples.sqlite, the solve entities can carry solver options in the solver_arguments map (e.g. solver, parallel and presolve for HiGHS). They only affect the speed and not the results, but usually the default values are good enough and the user should only change them if they understand how the solvers work.

docs.title: How to model CSP with thermal storage
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenarios: csp_without, csp_existing, csp_fixed_design, csp_optimised_design, csp_gas_backup) init - west - coal - csp_system - (plant and design alternatives)

Three entities. A concentrating solar power (CSP) plant with thermal storage is three generic entities: a solar field unit that makes heat from a profile, a heat storage node, and a turbine unit that turns the heat into electricity. Each has its own capacity and its own investment, so the model can choose the solar multiple and the storage hours itself, or you can fix them with user constraints. The heat storage is a storage node like a battery (see How to add a storage unit and Using nodes as storages). Storing MWh of heat is the same model as a two-tank molten-salt system at fixed temperatures. To have the results say so, set unit_of_measure MWh_th on csp_heat: its storage is then labelled MWh_th, the field's output and the turbine's input MW_th, its price CUR/MWh_th and its investment cost CUR/kWh_th, while west stays in MW (see Units of measure). The numbers do not change.

The example system. The alternatives init, west and coal are the tutorial's system: the 48-hour solve y2020_2day_dispatch, the node west and the 500 MW coal_plant (coal 20 CUR/MWh of fuel, efficiency 0.4: 50 CUR/MWh of electricity), which is the backup. The other alternatives add:

Alternative Entity Parameter Value csp_system node west inflow −150 [MW] csp_system profile csp_field_yield profile a time series: 1.0 for t0007–t0018 and t0055–t0066 (clear days), 0.4 for t0031–t0042 (cloudy day), 0 otherwise csp_plant unit csp_field conversion_method, existing none, 500 [MW_th] csp_plant unit__node__profile (csp_field, csp_heat, csp_field_yield) profile_method upper_limit csp_plant node csp_heat node_type, existing storage, 2500 [MWh_th] csp_plant node csp_heat storage_binding_method bind_within_timeblock csp_plant node csp_heat penalty_up, penalty_down 1000, 1000 [CUR/MWh] csp_plant unit csp_turbine conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 0.4, 100 [MW_e]

Entities. csp_plant turns on csp_field, csp_heat and csp_turbine (Entity Alternative). csp_field has no input and one unit__outputNode (csp_field, csp_heat). csp_turbine has a unit__inputNode (csp_turbine, csp_heat) and a unit__outputNode (csp_turbine, west).

The field-yield profile. The profile is the heat the field delivers to the storage per MW_th of its design output, with the optical and receiver losses already taken off. Prepare it outside FlexTool, from the direct normal irradiance (DNI) of the site or from the hourly output of a plant simulation tool. The upper_limit lets the field deliver less than the profile: that is curtailment (defocusing), and it costs nothing.

The results. Totals over the 48 hours; the objective is the 48-hour cost × 8760 / 48 / 10⁶ plus the annuities.

Scenario Field used / curtailed [MWh_th] Turbine [MWh_e] Coal [MWh] Objective [M CUR] csp_without – – 7200 65.700 csp_existing 7900 / 500 3160 4040 36.865 csp_fixed_design 7900 / 500 3160 4040 50.809 csp_optimised_design 12 000 / 2000 4800 2400 43.353 csp_gas_backup 7900 / 500, boiler 4100 4800 2400 31.877

Only totals are unique. The field's heat is free and coal costs the same in every hour, so the model does not care when the turbine runs. The totals, the capacities and the costs are unique; the hourly dispatch and the storage state are not. Compare scenarios with period results (unit__outputNode__d, unit_capacity__d, node_capacity__d, the costs), not with hourly ones.

docs.title: Existing plant
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: csp_existing) init - west - coal - csp_system - csp_plant

What it does. On the clear day the field makes 500 MW_th for 12 hours, 6000 MWh_th. The turbine takes 250 MW_th (100 MW_e / 0.4) directly, 3000 MWh_th, and the tank stores the rest until it is full at 2500 MWh_th; the last 500 MWh_th are curtailed. After sunset the tank runs the turbine for 10 more hours. On the cloudy day the field makes 200 MW_th for 12 hours, 2400 MWh_th, and all of it is used. The turbine makes 0.4 × 7900 = 3160 MWh_e, and coal makes the other 4040 MWh.

docs.title: Fixed design: solar multiple and storage hours
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: csp_fixed_design) init - west - coal - csp_system - csp_plant - csp_invest_common - csp_fixed_design

Investment data. csp_invest_common sets invest_periods [p2020] on the solve y2020_2day_dispatch, and on each of the three entities existing 0, invest_method invest_total, lifetime 25 and discount_rate 0.07:

Entity invest_max_total invest_cost unit csp_turbine 100 [MW_e] 500 [CUR/kW_e] unit csp_field 1000 [MW_th] 150 [CUR/kW_th] node csp_heat 5000 [MWh_th] 15 [CUR/kWh_th]

The recipe. The solar multiple (SM) is the field's thermal capacity divided by the turbine's thermal input at design point, and the storage hours (h) are the tank capacity divided by the same input. The turbine's thermal input is its capacity divided by its design efficiency η_d. So the ties are field − (SM / η_d) × turbine = 0 and tank − (h / η_d) × turbine = 0. With SM 2, 10 hours and η_d 0.4 the coefficients are −5 and −25.

The data. csp_fixed_design adds the two constraints, both with sense equal and constant 0:

Entity Parameter Value constraint csp_solar_multiple, csp_storage_hours sense, constant equal, 0 unit csp_field constraint_capacity_coeff (csp_solar_multiple | 1) node csp_heat constraint_capacity_coeff (csp_storage_hours | 1) unit csp_turbine constraint_capacity_coeff (csp_solar_multiple | −5), (csp_storage_hours | −25)

Use the capacity, not the investment. constraint_capacity_coeff ties the capacity in service: existing + invested − retired. constraint_invested_capacity_coeff ties only the new build of a period, so it breaks the ratio when there is existing capacity or when the parts are built in different periods. The rows have only capacity terms, so they are written once per period (see user constraints).

Use the design efficiency. η_d in the coefficients is a constant, the turbine's efficiency at its design point, even when the turbine's efficiency is a time series (for example lower on hot days with dry cooling). For a solar multiple in a range instead of a fixed value, use two rows: greater_than with SM_min and less_than with SM_max.

The results. The plant pays: it saves 288 350 CUR per MW_e and year of coal, against 139 442 CUR of annuities, so the turbine is built to its bound of 100 MW_e. The ties then give a field of 500 MW_th and a tank of 2500 MWh_th, the plant of csp_existing, with the same dispatch. The annuities are (100 × 500 + 500 × 150 + 2500 × 15) × 1000 × 0.0858 (7 % over 25 years) = 13.944 M CUR, so the objective is 36.865 + 13.944 = 50.809 M CUR.

docs.title: Optimised design
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: csp_optimised_design) init - west - coal - csp_system - csp_plant - csp_invest_common

What it does. Without the ties the model chooses the three capacities within their bounds. It can still build the fixed design, so its objective can only be lower or the same: 43.353 against 50.809 M CUR. Here it builds the turbine and the tank to their bounds (100 MW_e and 5000 MWh_th) and a field of 833 MW_th: a solar multiple of 3.3 and 20 storage hours, with the turbine running in every hour.

Which bound decides what. Two bounds bind. Each extra MW_e of turbine still pays: it saves 438 000 CUR of coal a year against about 285 000 CUR of turbine and field annuities. A tank MWh_th is cheaper than the field it replaces, so the tank also runs to its bound. The field of 833 MW_th is then set by the tank bound: a smaller tank needs a larger field to carry the cloudy day.

Without the bounds. With the tank bound lifted, the costs alone would choose a field of 714 MW_th and a tank of 5571 MWh_th (solar multiple 2.86, 22.3 h). With the turbine bound lifted, free heat against the flat 50 CUR/MWh of coal makes every MW_e pay until the plant meets the whole demand.

What to do. Set invest_max_total from real limits (land, grid connection, the planned plant size) and use realistic costs. If a bound binds without such a reason, the design is the bound's, not the model's: raise or remove the bound, or fix the ratios with the ties of the previous section. Check unit_capacity__d and node_capacity__d against the bounds you set.

docs.title: Gas backup
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: csp_gas_backup) init - west - coal - csp_system - csp_plant - csp_gas_backup

The data. csp_gas_backup adds a gas boiler that heats the storage node:

Entity Parameter Value commodity natural_gas price 12 [CUR/MWh] node natural_gas_market node_type commodity unit csp_backup_boiler conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 0.9, 250 [MW_th]

csp_gas_backup turns on natural_gas_market and csp_backup_boiler. The boiler has a unit__inputNode (csp_backup_boiler, natural_gas_market) and a unit__outputNode (csp_backup_boiler, csp_heat), and the commodity__node (natural_gas, natural_gas_market) links the price.

What it does. Boiler heat costs 12 / 0.9 = 13.3 CUR/MWh_th, which is 33.3 CUR/MWh_e through the turbine, less than coal. So the turbine runs at 100 MW_e in every hour. The field still delivers 7900 MWh_th (the tank is still full on the clear day) and the boiler makes the other 4100 MWh_th from 4555.6 MWh of gas. Coal makes 2400 MWh, and the objective is 31.877 M CUR.

A share of the yearly output. Rules such as "the boiler makes at most 15 % of the plant's heat over the year" are a user constraint with constraint_period_method period_total: one row per period over the year's total, not one per time step. Add a constraint csp_gas_share with sense less_than, constant 0 and constraint_period_method period_total, and the coefficients constraint_flow_coeff (csp_gas_share | 0.85) on unit__outputNode (csp_backup_boiler, csp_heat) and (csp_gas_share | -0.15) on unit__outputNode (csp_field, csp_heat). The row is boiler ≤ 0.15 × (field + boiler) over the year, written as 0.85 × boiler − 0.15 × field ≤ 0. The boiler may then make at most 15 % of the heat that the field and the boiler make together, in whichever hours it is most useful. (For a share of the field's heat alone, use 1 on the boiler.) See Period total for how the row is weighted.

PV and an electric heater. Another hybrid is a unit from the electricity node to csp_heat (an electric heater, efficiency about 0.99). Cheap PV power can then charge the tank in the middle of the day.

docs.title: Plant summary from the outputs
docs.text:
One plant, three entities. FlexTool reports the field, the tank and the turbine separately. The plant's figures come from the outputs as below; the values are those of csp_existing (the costs of csp_fixed_design). Mind the units: the __d tables are scaled to a full year (× 8760 / 48 here, one 48-hour period); divide by 182.5 for the sums over the 48 hours.

Figure Output Value Field potential unit_outputNode_VRE_potential__d (csp_field, csp_heat) 1 533 000 MWh_th/a (8400 × 182.5) Field curtailed unit_curtailment__outputNode__d (csp_field, csp_heat) 91 250 MWh_th/a (500 × 182.5) Curtailment share unit_outputNode_VRE_curtailment_share__d 91 250 / 1 533 000 = 5.95 % Field used unit__outputNode__d (csp_field, csp_heat) 1 441 750 MWh_th/a (7900 × 182.5) Turbine output unit__outputNode__d (csp_turbine, west) 576 700 MWh_e/a (3160 × 182.5) Capacity factor unit_cf__outputNode__d (csp_turbine, west) 3160 / (100 × 48) = 65.8 % Tank cycles the decreases of node_state__dt (csp_heat) summed, divided by the tank capacity at least 1 in the 48 h (the 2500 MWh_th stored on the clear day: day 1 must store ≥ 2500 MWh_th because the turbine can take only 3000 of the 5500 used) Plant cost the investment columns of cost_unit_annualized__d (csp_field, csp_turbine) and storage investment of cost_node_annualized__d (csp_heat) 6.4355 + 4.2905 + 3.2179 = 13.944 M CUR/a Levelised cost plant cost / turbine output 13.944 M / 576 700 = 24.2 CUR/MWh Average price received Σ turbine flow × node_prices__dt (west) / Σ turbine flow 50 CUR/MWh (coal sets the price in every hour)

Not unique. The tank cycles depend on the hourly timing, which is free in this example, so they are not unique. The levelised cost is the plant's own cost, not its value to the system: show the average price received next to it.

Keep the heat out of the electricity indicators. The field is a unit with an upper_limit profile, so FlexTool counts its curtailment as VRE curtailment. Do not put csp_heat in a group with print_indicators for electricity, or the field's curtailment counts in that group's VRE curtailment.

docs.title: Caveats and limitations
docs.text:
• Net or gross output. Use the net turbine efficiency (after the plant's own electricity use), so the turbine's output is the net output. For the own use as a separate flow, give the turbine a second input from the electricity node and tie it to the output with a user constraint.
  • Capacity margin. The turbine runs from the heat tank, so the capacity margin counts it by its actual flow at each time step, not at its capacity. With a gas backup input whose input_share_max is 1 (the gas can run the turbine alone), it counts at its capacity.
  • Representative periods. The tank cycles every day. Use hourly representative days or weeks with a *_blended_weights storage_binding_method (see Nested Rolling window solves); a long new_stepduration loses the daily cycle.
  • Annual fossil share in rolling dispatch. A period_total share (see Gas backup) holds in an investment solve, in a single dispatch solve and in a rolling dispatch solve whose rolling_solve_jump is a whole number of periods. A rolling dispatch solve whose rolls are shorter than the period leaves it out, with a warning in the run log; if no solve of the run enforces it, the run stops with an error.
  • Start-up heat. A turbine that warms up on tank heat before it delivers power: give it online variables (startup_method linear or binary) and set, on its unit__inputNode (csp_turbine, csp_heat), startup_input_method startup_and_input and startup_energy [MWh_th per MW_e started]. Each start-up then takes that heat from the tank on top of the turbine's flow, and the tank's reported input to the turbine includes it. See How to give a unit a start-up fuel or start-up heat.
  • Standing losses. self_discharge_loss is a share of the content; a loss proportional to the tank's size is not available.

docs.title: How to see the VRE curtailment and VRE share results for a node
docs.text:
(non_sync_and_curtailment.sqlite) (scenario: curtailment)

When the system has profile-units with the profile_method: upper_limit, the model can curtail the unit's flow to avoid penalties.

The curtailment could take place for several reasons:

  • the supply is higher than the demand and the energy cannot be stored or transferred (further)
  • non-synchronous limit
  • extra flow constraints have been set
  • other unit specific constraint affecting how VRE units or other units are forced to behave (ramp, start-up ...)

To see the curtailment results you need a group with group__node members (not a flowGroup with flowGroup__unit__node members!). The group then needs the parameter:

  • print_indicators: yes

This produces the node-group summary indicator metrics — loss-of-load share, VRE share, curtailment share, excess-load share and annualised inflow — written to the Results database as group: indicator and to Excel as the group_summary table. print_indicators is the "summary" output for node groups; pair it with print_dispatch if you also want the per-timestep decomposition of the same nodes.

These changes were done to the previous non-sync example database.

Note: Curtailed VRE of demand is the curtailment in relation to the inflow (demand), so it can exceed 100% as seen in the figure. Curtailed VRE of potential VRE is the curtailment in relation to the potential VRE generation and stays within 0–100%.

The figures show the layout of the results. Their values come from an earlier version, in which the battery connection inside nodeA_group still counted towards the non-synchronous limit (the battery cycled to loosen it); the current version gives less battery cycling, less wind and more coal in this example.

docs.title: How to create aggregate outputs
docs.text:
It is often desirable to output results that focus on particular aspects of the model. For example, you may want all flows going in and out of all electricity nodes, without the corresponding flows for other energy carriers (e.g. fuels used to produce the electricity). And if the model is large, some of those flows are easier to read when aggregated into a single column.

FlexTool splits these two concerns across a node group and a separate flowGroup:

Intent Set this Role Members Pick a set of nodes and get a per-timestep decomposition of every flow crossing them (one column per contributing process/connection) print_dispatch: yes on group the decomposition — produces group_flow_t group__node Re-bucket a set of flows so they appear as a single aggregated band inside that dispatch output flow_aggregator: dispatch_plots_only on flowGroup a dispatch-band re-bucketer — no output on its own flowGroup__unit__node or flowGroup__connection__node

Together they work like this: print_dispatch builds the dispatch table for its node group; while doing so it inspects every flow touching those nodes, and if any of those flows are in a flowGroup whose flow_aggregator is dispatch_plots_only (or both), their columns are collapsed into a single band named after the flowGroup. A dispatch_plots_only flowGroup produces no output of its own — it only reshapes a dispatch table that a node group is producing.

Avoid double-counting. If the same flow arc belongs to two flowGroups that are both dispatch-bound (dispatch_plots_only or both), that arc is counted twice in the node group's dispatch balance and the model emits a loud validation warning. For overlapping thematic aggregates, use standalone_aggregator_only instead — overlap is harmless there because those flowGroups report their own outputs and never feed a node-group dispatch table.

Concretely, to build a focused dispatch view for a collection of nodes:

  • create or re-use a group (e.g. electricity)
  • set the group's parameter print_dispatch to yes
  • add the relevant nodes via group__node (e.g. electricity__west)

Then, to collapse a collection of flows inside that dispatch view:

  • create or re-use a separate flowGroup (e.g. all_VRE)
  • set the flowGroup's parameter flow_aggregator to dispatch_plots_only
  • add the flows via flowGroup__unit__node or flowGroup__connection__node (e.g. all_VRE__wind1__west)

(Contrast with flow_aggregator: standalone_aggregator_only, which produces the flowGroup's own outputs — per-period cumulative_flow (MWh/a, scaled to a full year) / average_flow (MW) plus a signed net-flow timewise series — and does not interact with the dispatch table.)

"How to database" (aggregate_output.sqlite) aggregates results for the nodeA and nodeB. Both of the nodes have a wind power plant and nodeA has a coal power plant. The demand is divided to the electricity, heat and irrigation needs. This means that, besides an internal demand (inflow), both nodes output to the heat node while nodeA also outputs to the irrigation node. Additionally the nodes are connected to each other and the node_country_y1. The nodeA is connected to the node_country_x1 and nodeB is connected to the node_country_x2.

For the sake of the example, we are only interested in the nodeA and nodeB. Therefore, group focus_nodes is created and the nodes are added to it with group__node entities. To simplify the results, the flows from the two wind plants are aggregated as one. Same applies to the heat pumps. This is done by creating the flowGroups wind_aggregated and heat_aggregated. The flows are added to each flowGroup with flowGroup__unit__node.

Note that here the node has to be either nodeA or nodeB, not the heat node. The flowGroup only collapses columns whose node is inside the dispatch group's node set — e.g. wind_aggregated__wind_plant_1__nodeA is collapsed because nodeA is in focus_nodes. A flowGroup__unit__node row whose node is outside the dispatch group's nodes is simply ignored for that dispatch table.

Connections are simplified by creating flowGroups connections_country_x and connections_country_y and adding the relevant connections with flowGroup__connection__node. Again the node must be nodeA or nodeB to be collapsed in the dispatch output.

The focus_nodes group needs print_dispatch: yes and the unit and connection flowGroups need flow_aggregator: dispatch_plots_only.

The resulting table has the flows to the focus_nodes group from units and connections. Additionally, the internal losses of the group are calculated. These are the flows between the nodes of the group and the storage losses. Here the losses come from the connection between nodeA and nodeB. Possible slacks to balance the nodes are included too.

docs.title: How to enable/disable outputs
docs.text:
Some of the outputs are optional. Some of these optional outputs are output by default while some are not (see below). Removing outputs speeds up the post-processing of results. The user can enable/disable them by changing the following parameters of the model entity:

  • output_node_balance_t: Default: yes. Produces detailed inflows and outflows for all the nodes for all timesteps. Mainly useful to diagnose what is wrong with the model.
  • output_connection__node__node_flow_t: Default: yes. The flows between the nodes for each timestep.
  • output_unit__node_flow_t: Default, yes. The flows from units to the nodes for each timestep.
  • output_ramp_envelope: Default, no. Includes seven parameters that form the ramp room envelope. Shows the actual ramp as well as different levels of available ramping capability in a given node - for both directions, upward and downward. The first level includes ramproom in all the units, except VRE. The second level adds ramping room in VRE units (typically only downward, unless they have been curtailed. Finally, the last level adds potential ramping capability in the connections, which reflects only the ramproom in the connections themselves - the units/nodes behind the connection may or may not have capability to provide that ramp. (Parameter node_ramp_t)
  • output_connection_flow_separate: Default, no. Produces the connection flows separately for both directions.
  • output_unit__node_ramp_t: Default, no. Produces the ramps of individual units for all timesteps.
  • output_horizon: Writes a raw dump of every LP variable and constraint over the whole horizon (forecast branches and rolling look-ahead included) to output_parquet/<scenario>/horizon/. The normal outputs are unchanged. Useful when constructing a stochastic or rolling model.

To get the numbers behind a plot, turn on Write plotted data (CSV) in the GUI's Png settings (or --write-plot-data in the terminal, or write_plot_data: true in plot_settings.yaml): each plot file then gets a CSV with the same name and the data drawn in it. See Plotted data as CSV.

docs.title: How to read the LP scaling diagnostic report
docs.text:
Every solve runs the auto-scaling pipeline before handing the LP to the solver and writes a single audit artefact into solve_data/:

  • autoscale_<solve>.yaml — YAML audit (Layer 1 ranges, Layer 2 per-quantity-type plan, Layer 3 user_bound_scale + escape-tier plan)

A 1-line console verdict is also printed after each solve. The YAML covers (in order):

  • Layer 1 — matrix / cost / bound / RHS log10 ranges and the cross-group max-ratio that gates whether Layers 2/3 fire
  • Layer 2 — per-quantity-type power-of-2 column scalers (energy, capacity, monetary, …) with post-Layer-2 ranges
  • Layer 3 — the user_bound_scale exponent HiGHS receives and any escape-valve folding

Auto-scaling never changes the LP optimum: every variable and constraint is unscaled back to the user's units before the solution is written out. The audit is purely diagnostic. Read it when:

  • the solver runs slowly or hits its time limit
  • HiGHS reports numerical trouble (ill-conditioning warnings, suspect infeasibility)
  • you are about to file a bug — attaching the YAML saves a round-trip
  • you are tuning a freshly-converted model and want to spot unit-mix mistakes early
  • a rejected solve's hint flagged the post-autoscale LP as still wide-ranged (scaling may be implicated) — the YAML shows which layer (or which quantity type) could not compress the spread

The autoscale package lives at flextool/engine/autoscale/ (_ranges.py / _layer2.py / _layer3.py / _report.py). For the user-facing guide and tuning tips, see dev/scaling.md.

docs.title: How to export a partial Excel template (parameter-group picker)
docs.text:
When you only need a subset of the parameter universe — say, a small dispatch sandbox without investments or stochastics — you can export an Excel template restricted to selected parameter groups instead of the full reference template. The CLI supports this via the --groups flag on the export-to-tabular command:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite \
    partial_template.xlsx \
    --groups "vre,storage,reserves"

The flag takes a comma-separated list of parameter_group names. Parameters outside the listed groups are dropped, and sheets with no surviving parameter columns are removed unless they are explicitly listed in always_include_with_groups in flextool/export_to_tabular/export_settings.yaml.

The following groups are always kept regardless of the --groups selection (declared as required_groups in export_settings.yaml):

  • timeline
  • model
  • solve_basics
  • basics

These provide the structural backbone of any FlexTool model. Implementation: flextool/cli/cmd_export_to_tabular.py and flextool/export_to_tabular/sheet_config.py. The FlexTool GUI exposes the same picker under the "Add empty FlexTool input Excel" action (3.32.0). See also Excel interface for the Excel-as-input workflow.

docs.title: How to replace a dataset and keep the old one as an alternative
docs.text:
The idea. When new data arrives (a new demand forecast, updated cost assumptions), keep the old data and put the new values in an alternative of their own. A scenario with the new alternative on top then uses the new data, the old scenario still runs as before, and the two can be compared. Excel is handy for entering a large set of new values.

1. Export a partial template. Export only the parameter groups that hold the data you replace, as in How to export a partial Excel template:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_export_to_tabular sqlite:///input.sqlite new_demand.xlsx --groups basics

2. Edit the workbook.

  • On each sheet, keep only the rows you replace and delete the others.
  • Write the name of the new alternative, for example demand_2024, in the alternative column of those rows.

  • Enter the new values. A new entity also needs entity existence TRUE in the new alternative.

    Rows that keep the name of an existing alternative do not change the database (see step 3), so they can stay, but deleting them keeps the workbook easy to check.

3. Import into the same database, without purging. Copy the database first. Then:

python -m flextool.cli.cmd_read_self_describing_tabular_input new_demand.xlsx sqlite:///input.sqlite --no-purge

Always give --no-purge when adding data

Without --no-purge, the import first deletes the entities, alternatives, scenarios and parameter values of the database and then writes the workbook's data: only the rows of your partial workbook would be left.

With --no-purge, the import adds the new alternatives, entities and values. A value that the database already has for the same entity, parameter and alternative is not changed: the import prints a message for it and goes on. So an edit under the old alternative name has no effect; the new values must be in the new alternative.

4. Make the scenario. Add a scenario with the alternatives of the old scenario and demand_2024 last, in the Spine database editor or in the scenario sheet of the workbook before the import (a new column: the scenario name in the top row, then base_alternative and the other alternatives in order). The old scenario stays as it was.

5. Run and compare. Run both scenarios and open them in the comparison view of the Result viewer (key X). The AI assistant's compare_inputs checks that the two scenarios differ only in the new data, and compare_runs shows how the results differ (see The AI assistant). The same set-up runs one value change as a sensitivity: see How to run a sensitivity.

docs.title: How to make a data dictionary for your model
docs.text:
A project team that builds a model from its own data often needs a list of every input parameter: what it means, its unit, the shapes it accepts and its default, with room to note where the team's value comes from. FlexTool writes that list, the parameter catalogue, from its own database schema, so it always matches the installed version. The same table is on the web as the Parameter catalogue (web docs) page; the FlexTool assistant answers the same questions per parameter with its describe_parameter tool.

Write it as an Excel file, and mark the parameters your input database gives values to. The command runs in FlexTool's Python environment (see Terminal workflow for how to open a terminal with it):

python -m flextool.docs_build --xlsx catalogue.xlsx \
    --input-db input_data.sqlite --scenario base

The file has three sheets:

  • Read me: what the file is, the FlexTool and database versions, the input database, and one line per column of the parameters sheet, including what to write in Source and How to replace.
  • parameters: one row per parameter (class, parameter, definition, unit, quantity type, allowed shapes, default, allowed values, parameter group) and three empty columns for the team: Source, How to replace and Notes. The header row and the class and parameter columns are frozen, so they stay visible when you scroll; the header has filters, so you can show, for example, only the parameters the database uses.

  • classes: what each entity class (unit, node, unit__outputNode, ...) is.

  • --input-db (optional) is the input database, as a file path or as a URL (sqlite:///input_data.sqlite). It adds the columns used in DB (yes when any entity has a value), entities (how many) and alternatives (in which). Only the keys of the stored values are read; the file is opened read-only, so it is not changed or migrated.

  • --scenario (optional) counts only the values in the alternatives of that scenario. An entity that the scenario switches off (its entity alternative) still counts.
  • A parameter that the database has but this FlexTool does not define gets its own row marked not in this FlexTool version. That happens with an older database whose parameters were renamed since: the command says so and names flextool-migrate-database; migrate the database (or a copy of it) to see its values under the current names.

The catalogue is a dictionary, not an input template: to fill in data, use a partial Excel template or the Excel interface.

docs.title: How to use CPLEX as the solver
docs.text:
CPLEX remains wireable as an advanced option for licensed users. Using CPLEX requires that you have installed the software, have a licence for it and have added it to PATH or to the environment where you are using the FlexTool, so that the tool can find the solver.

CPLEX is invoked via the solve parameter solver. FlexTool builds the LP in memory through polars + polar-high. The CPLEX path passes the problem to the Interactive Optimizer and produces two additional files in the work directory: a CPLEX log file and the solution file in CPLEX format.

Additional parameters:

  • solver_precommand is not used. FlexTool 3 put it in front of the cplex call (for example to reserve a floating licence); FlexTool 4 never runs commands stored in a database, for safety, and warns when one is set (the parameter is kept only so that older databases still read). Use the solver's own licence server setup, or reserve the licence before starting FlexTool; see Solver precommand.
  • solver_arguments is a map of CPLEX parameter names to values (for example mip.tolerances.mipgap → 0.001), set on top of the option file; a file or folder parameter takes only a plain file name there (see What the database may set). See Authoring solver_arguments.

docs.title: How to make the Flextool run faster
docs.text:
The list below contains potential ways to decrease the run-time of FlexTool models.
