External changes (results will remain the same):

  • Keep both the input database and Flextool on the same drive. If the database is on a different drive, it can slow the process. Avoid network drives.
  • Try to ensure that there is sufficient memory available by closing other programs that use lot of memory. Linear optimization problems can require lot of memory.
  • Use as fast computer as available. Both faster processors and more processors can decrease computation time.

Model changes (results will remain the same):

  • Disable outputs that you don't need. This will speed up the result processing. See: How to enable/disable outputs
  • Switch off the scenario plots (png) when the result viewer is enough; it shows every plot from the results. To see where a run's time goes, phase by phase, use flextool-time-runs. See: Check that exercises run fast enough
  • When using HiGHS solver: in your solve's solver_arguments map, you can set presolve = on and parallel = on to speed up the optimisation. However, it can be better to turn HiGHS parallel off when executing multiple scnearios in parallel.
  • Especially with MIP problems, considering using a commercial solver like CPLEX (license required). See: How to use CPLEX as the solver

Model changes (results will be affected):

  • Get rid of integer variables. Mixed integer programming can increase the solving time manyfold compared to the linear version especially if commercial solver is not available. MIP parameters are:
  • transfer_method: exact, change to reqular

  • startup_method: binary, change to linear

  • Set virtual_unitsize to the actual sub-unit size of the modeled plant when startup_method = binary. If you do not set it, FlexTool uses the full existing capacity as the commitment granularity — every on/off decision moves the entire plant at once. For a large plant (say 1000 MW), that granularity is usually too coarse for the MIP to close to a useful tolerance in reasonable time: a realistic 3-day 3-representative-period UC problem with ~1 GW whole-unit commitment may run up against solver time limits at several percent MIP gap, while the same plant modelled with virtual_unitsize matching its real sub-units (e.g. five × 200 MW boilers → existing = 5, virtual_unitsize = 200) closes to < 0.2 % in about a minute. virtual_unitsize is not a free tuning knob — picking an arbitrarily small value (say 50 MW for a plant with no 50 MW sub-units) would let the solver commit fractions that don't physically exist, mis-representing minimum load and startup behavior. Choose the value that reflects the actual physical unit granularity of the modeled entity (e.g. individual boilers / turbines / strings). The clustered unit-commitment approach (Palmintier & Webster 2012) is just this: represent each real sub-unit as one unit in the integer count. When the modeled entity is inherently a single indivisible plant, leave virtual_unitsize unset (or use existing = 1 with virtual_unitsize = the plant size) — and you may have to accept that the MIP is slow, use startup_method = linear, or aggregate differently.

Model changes (potentially large changes to the results --> need to understand how the particular analysis will be affected):

  • Use representative periods for investment decisions. See: How to create a multi-year model
  • Split the timeline into parts. The solving time increases exponentially with the model size. Multiple smaller solves can be faster. Splitting is best done with Rolling window solve and Nested rolling solve. See: How to use a rolling window for a dispatch model, How to use Nested Rolling window solves (investments and long-term storage)
  • Aggregate data. Technological: Combine power plants that are using the same technology. Spatial: Combine nodes. Temporal: Use longer timesteps.

docs.title: How to use Benders decomposition (spatial)
docs.text:
Large systems that naturally split into regions (e.g. an interconnected pan-continental network where each country's internal grid is cheap but the joint solve is large) can be solved with a spatial Benders decomposition. A coordinating master holds the inter-regional trade flows and the trade-connection investment plus one recourse variable per region; each region is solved as an operational subproblem with the master's trade fixed, returning duals that become optimality cuts the master accumulates. The master objective is a valid lower bound and the loop converges on the optimality gap.

Set up the regions in the database:

  • create one group per region, list its node members via group__node
  • set the group parameter decomposition_method to benders_regional on each region group
  • declare at least two such region groups in the active scenario

See the group.decomposition_method parameter in Groups and the algorithm write-up in dev/decomposition.md.

Then turn on Benders decomposition on the solve itself — set the solve parameter decomposition to benders on the solve(s) you want decomposed (optionally tuning benders_max_iter and benders_tolerance; they default to 50 / 1e-3). Then run normally:

flextool-run \
    sqlite:///input_data.sqlite \
    --scenario-name multi_region

The choice is per solve, so a single chain can mix schemes (e.g. a Benders investment solve followed by a monolithic dispatch solve — the Benders invest solve's realised trade + in-region capacity threads into the downstream dispatch). The per-solve routing is in flextool/engine/solve/_orchestration.py and the coordinator (master + cut loop) in flextool/engine/solve/_benders.py. benders_max_iter caps the cut loop and benders_tolerance is the relative optimality-gap threshold for declaring convergence. Use Benders when the per-region solve is cheap but the monolithic solve is expensive; if the regions are tightly coupled (i.e. cross-region flows dominate the dispatch) the cut loop may need many iterations and a monolithic solve is usually better.

Connections between regions (or between a region and the master) are replaced by trade flows in the decomposition, so they cannot have a startup_method, the exact transfer method or reserve: the run stops with an error naming them. Binary online variables or exact connections inside a region make the region subproblem a mixed-integer problem; the cuts are then not exact (a warning is printed), so prefer startup_method linear in decomposed solves.

docs.title: Solve sequences, rolling and nested solves
How to run solves in a sequence (investment + dispatch)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: 5weeks_invest_fullYear_dispatch_coal_wind)

In this example, investment decisions are made using a five week sample of a year and then the dispatch is solved with the full year timeline using these investments.

To do this you need two solves:

  • Investment solve
  • Dispatch solve

Both solves should solve the same periods using different timeset to represent these periods. This example has only one period p2020 describing a year. The investment solve uses a representative sample timeset 5weeks to do the investment decisions. These are then passed to the dispatch solve that uses complete timeline fullYear.

Investment solve requires the parameters:

  • Invest_periods: Array of periods where investments can be made
  • realised_invest_periods: Array of periods that are output for investment decisions
  • period_timeset: Uses the 5weeks as the timeset

Note that the realized_invest_periods is used instead of realized_periods, because we want the investment solve to only output investments. Additionally some of the units, connections or storages will need investment parameters (invest_cost, lifetime...) see How to make investments (storage/unit)

The dispatch solve requires the parameters:

  • realized_periods: Array of output periods
  • period_timeset: Uses the fullYear as the timeset

The sequence of solves is defined by the model parameter solves. Here it is an array where the first item is an investment_solve 5weeks_only_invest and the second is the dispatch solve y2020_fullYear_dispatch. This is enough for the model to know to pass the investment decisions of the period to the period of the same name in the second solve.

Note that the picture has two model: solves parameters defined one for each alternative. Only the parameter from the 5weeks_only_invest is used as the lower alternatives in the scenario tree override the values from the higher alternatives and only one model can be run.

Check the investment solve's capacity margin. A group's capacity margin (capacity_margin_method) applies only in a solve with investment periods, so here only the investment solve has it; the dispatch solve does not check it again. When the investment solve leaves a shortfall (the plan does not hold the margin, because the penalty is cheaper than the capacity or the capacity cannot be built), the run log says so right after that solve:

capacity margin shortfall: solve <solve>, group <group>, period <period>: <MW> MW at <time step> (penalty <M CUR> M CUR)

A period that is a look-ahead period of one investment solve and an investment period of the next gets a line from each solve that leaves a shortfall in it: the solve name says which plan the line is about.

The results then show:

  • slack__capacity_margin__d: the shortfall [MW] of the period, also when a later dispatch solve realizes the period, and its penalty in the costs (capacity margin penalty in costs_discounted__d).
  • capacity_margin__d: the capacity margin of each solve with investment periods, under that solve's name, for each group and investment period (look-ahead and forecast branch periods included) at its binding step (the time step with the largest deficit): the margin, the demand, the requirement, what firm and VRE units, storage, other units, connections and consumption count, the shortfall, its penalty and the shadow price of the margin.
  • capacity_margin_entity__d: what each unit, connection and node counts at that step, to see which capacity is missing or does not count.

See Slack and penalty values.

docs.title: How to make an LP investment and a detailed dispatch check
docs.text:
Unit commitment (startup_method binary), min loads, ramps and reserves make an investment solve slow, and an investment solve over many periods or a long sample may not finish at all. A common way out is to make the investment solve an LP with less detail and then check the plan with a dispatch solve that has all the detail.

Set up the two solves as in How to run solves in a sequence: an investment solve that realizes the investments only (realized_invest_periods) and a dispatch solve that realizes the operations (realized_periods). Then set on the investment solve:

  • reduce_unit_detail_method: online (or online_ramps to also leave out ramp limits and ramp costs).

    The investment solve has no units online: no start-ups and start-up costs, no min load, no minimum up and down times. min_load_efficiency units run at their full-load efficiency, and exact connections behave as regular. Use integers instead to keep the units online but make them continuous (linear unit commitment), which keeps start-up costs and min loads.

  • reduce_system_detail_method: reserves (or reserves_inertia_non_synchronous to also leave out the inertia and non-synchronous limits).

Leave both at none on the dispatch solve. The dispatch solve then commits the invested units with integer units online, ramps and holds the reserves.

An example to start from. In examples.sqlite, the scenario 5weeks_invest_fullYear_dispatch_coal_wind has the investment solve invest_1year_5weeks (alternative 5weeks_only_invest) and the dispatch solve y2020_fullYear_dispatch. Give coal_plant startup_method binary (as the alternative coal_min_load_MIP does), and set the two parameters on invest_1year_5weeks.

What to check. Read the investment solve's info line in the run log: it lists what was left out, for which units and groups, and what that means for the detail that was kept (for example "the reserves of ... now come from built capacity"). Then look at the dispatch solve's slack and penalty results (slack__* tables, the reserve shortfall). A shortfall there means the plan does not hold with the detail the investment solve left out: reserves in particular drive investment in flexible capacity, so an investment solve without them invests less in it. Then add the detail back step by step (for example integers instead of online, or keep the reserves) until the dispatch check passes.

In the results the investment solve realizes no operations, so the dispatch solve's tables are complete. If a solve that realizes operations leaves a feature out, its cells of that feature are empty, not 0 (see Leaving out detail in a solve).

docs.title: Several milestones: representative-period investment, then a full-year dispatch of each
docs.text:
A multi-year plan often makes the investments on representative periods (a few sample weeks per milestone year) and then checks each milestone with an hourly dispatch of the whole year (8760 h). FlexTool passes the investment decisions of a period to the period of the same name in the solves that follow, so the dispatch solves see the capacity built up to their milestone. There are two ways to set this up.

Sequential: one dispatch solve per milestone. List the solves in the model parameter solves, the investment solve first: for example [invest_rp, dispatch_2030, dispatch_2040, dispatch_2050].

  • The investment solve has every milestone in invest_periods and realized_invest_periods, the representative timeset of each milestone in period_timeset, and years_represented for each milestone. Leave realized_periods out.

  • Each dispatch solve has one milestone in period_timeset (with the full-year timeset) and in realized_periods, and the same years_represented for it as the investment solve.

    A dispatch solve that realizes a later milestone gets the capacity invested in all the milestones up to it. One dispatch solve may also hold all the milestones, but its LP is then that many full years at once.

Nested: the investment solve contains the dispatch solve. Put only the investment solve in model solves and give it contains_solves: dispatch_solve. The dispatch solve lists every milestone in period_timeset (each with the full-year timeset) and in realized_periods, and it can be a rolling solve (solve_mode rolling_window) so that each LP stays small. A storage solve can sit between the two for long-term storage. With several investment solves (myopic investment, set with 2D maps of invest_periods and realized_invest_periods), the same dispatch solve runs after each of them for the periods that investment solve realized. See How to use Nested Rolling window solves.

Leave detail out of the investment solve. Set reduce_unit_detail_method and reduce_system_detail_method on the investment solve and keep the full detail in the dispatch solves, as in How to make an LP investment and a detailed dispatch check (the options are in Leaving out detail in a solve).

Choose the representative periods with care. Hours the sample leaves out can be short of capacity in the full-year dispatch. The sections below help: force-include adequacy-critical weeks, cluster on net load and add an energy margin. The investment solve does not see the dispatch results: if a dispatch solve shows unserved energy or reserve shortfall, change the sample or the margins and run again.

Examples. In examples.sqlite, 5weeks_invest_fullYear_dispatch_coal_wind is the sequential set-up with one milestone, and multi_fullYear_battery_nested_multi_invest is a nested set-up with four milestones, investment solves (each on the sample timeset of two milestones), a storage solve at 6 h steps and a rolling dispatch. To run in seconds, these examples use short stand-ins: their fullYear timeset is 72 hours and 5weeks is five blocks of 4 hours. In a real model, the dispatch timeset covers the 8760 hours of the year and the sample holds whole weeks.

docs.title: How to use a rolling window for a dispatch model
docs.text:
A rolling window can be used for example when a dispatch model gets too big to be solved on one go. It splits the problem into multiple consecutive smaller problems.

The rolling window solve splits the time dimension into overlapping parts and solves each one of them separately but in a sequence (and can therefore pass state information from the previous solve to the next one). For example, instead of a solving the full year in one go, you can split the year into six four-month long solves where each solve outputs only the first two months. The solves would therefore include the months:

  • Roll: Solve months -> Output months
  • 1: [1,2,3,4] -> [1,2]
  • 2: [3,4,5,6] -> [3,4]
  • 3: [5,6,7,8] -> [5,6]
  • 4: [7,8,9,10] -> [7,8]
  • 5: [9,10,11,12] ->[9,10]
  • 6: [11,12] -> [11,12]

The rolling solve could be setup also manually as described in the 'How to run a multi year model' - just using shorter periods.

However, this would be tedious if there are many solves. In a rolling window model, the user can set the rolling_solve_jump and rolling_solve_horizon parameters, which are expressed in hours.

  • rolling_solve_horizon: sets the length of the whole solve, in hours. In previous example 4 months (2880 hours). Horizon allows the model to see bit further in the future to improve the decision making for the period that will be output.

  • rolling_solve_jump: sets the interval for the length of each 'jump' the model takes forward in reach roll. It is then both the interval of roll starting points and the length of the output for each roll. The rolling_solve_jump must be smaller than the rolling_solve_horizon. In the previous example the rolling_solve_jump would be 2 months (1440 hours).

In addition, the user can set the duration for how long the model will roll:

  • rolling_duration: Optional (hours), the length of combined rolls. In the example, it could be set to 8640 hours which would divide evenly, or 8760 hours which means that the last roll will be shorter than the others. It is nicer to use rolling_solve_jump that is divisable with the rolling_duration to keep rolls even. If rolling_duration is not set, it defaults to rolling through the whole timeline.

When using rolling window solve, you are solving the model with less information. Therefore, the results will be less optimal since the model will not have the full information at once. It is therefore important to know how this could affect the results and what things to consider when implementing a rolling window model. It will have an impact on time dependant parts of the model: for example, storages or cumulative flow constraints. If the model can see only a few months to the future, it can't see how much energy needs to be stored after that.

Investments should not be used with this free rolling solve (solve_mode: rolling_window) as investments should only be done at the start of the periods. Both the long-term storage and the investments can be taken into account with nested rolling solves that have a separate how-to.

Short term storages also are operated less optimally in a rolling window model. There is a positive side to this as well, since perfect foresight linear optimization models are 'too optimal'. They don't reflect the forecast errors present in real life. So, a rolling window model might operate a bit more realistically than a single_solve model. A single_solve model can consider things happening far in the future when setting the storage level at present, even though in reality that information is not available. So, the total cost of a rolling_window model should always be higher than the total cost from a complete single_solve model that has perfect information.

To set a dispatch rolling window model you need to set the entity solve parameters:

  • solve_mode: rolling_window
  • rolling_solve_jump: Hours, the desired length of the solve interval
  • rolling_solve_horizon: Hours, the desired length of each roll solve
  • rolling_duration: (Optional) Hours, the length of the combined outputs. If not set, the whole timeline is used.

Considerations on the rolling times:

  • The rolling_solve_jump and rolling_solve_horizon must be large enough to make the model faster. If too small intervals are used, the creation of solves and moving data from solve to another might take too much time.
  • If you are not using 1-hour timesteps, preferably use multiples of the timestep you are using as the rolling_solve_jump and rolling_solve_horizon. The steps included in each solve are calculated by summing the step durations until they are larger or equal to the hours given. So, if multiples are not used, the rolls might not be exactly the same size.
  • The model can roll over timeset and period jumps, which might cause some issues if storage constraints are used. Using timeset length or its multiples is therefore recommended. For example, the rolling_solve_jump could be a half of a timeset and the rolling_solve_horizon whole timeset or rolling_solve_jump a timeset and rolling_solve_horizon three timesets. Of course, when running e.g. a full year dispatch, there is only one timeset of 8760 hours, which makes the choices more simple.

Considerations on storage parameters:

  • storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value or use_reference_price are the preferred means to bind storage values. They can be used together with the storage_state_start_end_method: start, which would then set the initial storage state. These methods bind either the storage value or the storage price at the end of horizon (not the end of jump). This allows the storage to use the part of the horizon that is not output to improve the behaviour of the storage in the part that is output (as defined by rolling_solve_horizon and rolling_solve_jump).
  • bind_within_timeblock does not work correctly if the rolls don't include whole timeblocks. Instead, it will bind the first step of the roll (whatever it is) to the end of the timeblock. Do not use in nested solves if you are not using whole timeblocks or its multiples as rolling_solve_jump. The storage level is not carried from roll to roll for this method (nor for bind_within_period and bind_within_solve): each roll cycles on its own, so the storage level jumps at each roll start, and the reported state change at that step is that jump.
  • the same applies to the bind_within_period (but in relation to periods - do not use this unless you are rolling_solve_jump is as long as a period or its multiples).
  • bind_intraperiod_blocks loops the blocks of a period only in the rolls that hold the whole period. In a period that a roll holds only in part, the blocks chain forward and the storage level is carried from roll to roll, as for bind_forward_only. The blocks of a roll also end at the end of its realized part. Use a rolling_solve_jump of a whole number of periods to keep every realized period looping (otherwise a warning is given).
  • The representative-period variants (bind_within_solve_blended_weights, bind_within_period_blended_weights, bind_forward_only_blended_weights) are not applied in a rolling solve on representative periods: their base-period chain spans the whole period and cannot be cut into rolls. Those nodes bind forward only (bind_forward_only) and the storage state is passed directly from roll to roll; a warning names them once per solve.
  • storage_start_end_method can be used to set the first timestep of the first roll and/or the last timestep of the entire model (in conjunction with storage_state_start and storage_state_end); the end value applies in every roll whose horizon contains the model's last timestep (usually the last roll only). Every later roll starts from the storage state realised by the previous roll. It is meant for simple models: storage_state_reference_value with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value is usually the better choice.
  • bind_within_solve binds the start state to the end state of each roll not the start and end of the whole model timeline. Use with caution (and probably best not to use together with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value).

docs.title: How to use Nested Rolling window solves (investments and long-term storage)
docs.text:
The basic rolling solve can have problems in dealing with long term storage and with investments. If the model only sees a few weeks to the future, it really can't see how much energy should be stored in long term storages. Problems with investments can also be serious: If the first roll is really windy, the model would overinvest in wind power that is not profitable in the later rolls. Similarly, if the model is allowed to retire capacity, it might retire something that is actually needed in the later rolls.

Nested solve sequences can first solve the investments and long-term storage levels and pass them to the dispatch solve. Both storage solve and dispatch solve can be rolling solves. The dispatch solves can then send the end storage values to the investment and long-term storage solves as start values to reduce the error of these solves.

When to use nested solves?

  • Dispatch model is taking too long to solve, but simple rolling window solve would not represent the long-term storages correctly. (Nesting without the investment solve)
  • Investment model takes too long to solve, even with manual rolling How to create a multi-year model. With nesting you can have smaller rolls for dispatch solve than the investment solve. (Nesting without the storage solve)
  • Investment model takes too long and you have long term storages to consider. (Three level nesting, graph below)

However, the obvious issue is that investment and storage solves cannot be solved using the old complete solve as it wouldn't make the solve time any shorter. Therefore, we need to decrease the information for investment and storage solves as well. There are a few options for this:

  1. Use lower resolution (longer timesteps). This can work quite well for a long-term storage.
  2. Use representative periods from the full timeline when performing investments. There is a large body of literature and methods on how to pick the representative weeks.
  3. Split the investment timeline (myopic investments) by manually creating a solve sequence for the investment solves like in: How to create a multi-year model section. This can be combined with the first or second option.

Each of these have their pros and cons:

  • Using the lower resolution can speed-up the model considerably, but it also means that everything that happens faster than the new timestep duration will be lost as the timestep varying parameters are averaged or summed for the new timestep. For example, consider a model with investment options to solar and storage. If the step duration is changed to 24 hours, the model won't invest in enough storage to mitigate the diurnal variation in PV. When these investments are then passed to the dispatch solve, the invested portfolio will have trouble meeting the demand.
  • Using the sample can be effective if the sample is chosen well, but all the needs that are not in these samples are not included. The speed is heavily dependent on the number and size of those samples.
  • Splitting the investment timeline for multi-year models can be seen as a relatively realistic approach, since investment decisions would have a lot of uncertainty in the longer time frame anyway.

The investment decisions with less information are always less optimal than with complete solves. Therefore, when they are passed to the dispatch solve, it will in some cases cause penalties in the results when the invested portfolio is not sufficient to meet the demand at all times.

The long term storage solve can be implemented using a lower resolution solve. The storage state behaviour from the storage solve is used as a target for the dispatch solve. There are three options for doing this:

  • fix_quantity creates a constraint that forces the end storage state to be the same as in the storage solve at this timestep.
  • fix_usage does the same but not taking into account the inflow or slacks. Forces the summed usage of the storage during the dispatch solve to be the same as during the same time span in the storage solve. This avoids infeasibilities when modelling inflow stochastics in comparison to the fix_quantity.
  • fix_price takes the storage node's price (price_t, the value of one more MWh of stored energy) from the storage solve at the end timestep of the dispatch solve and uses it in the objective function to give a value to the stored energy at the end of the horizon.

The rolling_solve_jump and rolling_solve_horizon in the storage solve have to be longer than in the dispatch solve. You can set which storages are included as "long term storages" whose value will be transferred to the dispatch solve.

To create a nested solve sequence, you need two or three solve entities. Either the investment solve or the storage solve can be left out. When using nested solve sequence, the sequence is not set with the model: solves parameter. Only the topmost solve is put there. Instead, the nested levels are set by the solve parameter contains_solves: solve_name. The investment solve is always on the top followed by the storage solve and dispatch solve:

  • investment_solve solve parameter contains_solves: storage_solve_name
  • storage_solve solve parameter contains_solves: dispatch_solve_name

To create a storage solve:

  • solve parameter fix_storage_periods: Array of periods where the storage values are fixed in the lower solve. Should be the same as realized_periods for the dispatch solve.
  • node parameter storage_nested_fix_method: fix_quantity, fix_price or fix_usage

To create an investment_solve:

  • solve parameter invest_periods: Array of periods where the model can invest.
  • solve parameter realized_invest_periods: Array of periods where the model will realize investment decisions to the lower solves and results.
  • solve parameter realized_periods: Should not be used in this solve! You don't want the dispatch results from this solve, but from the dispatch solve.

In addition, the rolling dispatch solve should be created as in the How to use rolling window solve for dispatch. To set a dispatch rolling window model you need to set the entity solve parameters:

  • solve_mode: rolling_window
  • rolling_solve_jump: Hours, the desired length of the solve interval
  • rolling_solve_horizon: Hours, the desired length of each roll solve
  • rolling_duration: (Optional) Hours, the length of the combined outputs. If not set, the whole timeline is used.
  • realized_periods: Array of periods that are realized

The other model parameters apply to all of the solves. Therefore, the considerations of the storage value binding that were discussed in the How to use a rolling window for a dispatch model should be taken into account here as well.

  • Storage levels can be fixed with storage_solve_horizon_method: use_reference_value or use_reference_price, these will fix the end of each horizon not each jump.
  • storage_start_end_method fixes the start of each solve level (the first step of the first roll) and/or the end of the entire model. The end value applies to the last timestep of the model in every solve whose horizon contains it: the investment, storage and dispatch solves when each of them reaches the end of the model, but not a solve (or roll) that ends earlier. It is meant for simple models: in nested solves storage_state_reference_value with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value is usually the better choice. The start applies where a level appears for the first time; every later solve or roll of a level (also the first dispatch roll under a later storage roll, and the next investment or storage solve of a split investment timeline) starts from the latest storage state realised before it at that level or below (usually by the dispatch solve). The upper solves only fix the end of a lower solve's horizon (storage_nested_fix_method). At the model's last timestep in a lower-level solve, an upper-level fix_quantity or fix_usage overrides storage_state_end; a fix_price only values that end, so storage_state_end still applies.
  • In most cases the bind_storage_method should be left as bind_forward_only
  • Do not use bind_within_timeblock if you are not using full timeblock or its multiples as the rolling_solve_jump in the dispatch model, otherwise you might cause an infeasible problem.
  • Do not use bind_within_period if you are not using full periods or its multiples as the rolling_solve_jump in the dispatch model, otherwise you might cause an infeasible problem.
  • Do not use bind_within_solve

The recommended storage parameters with nested solves are:

  • storage_start_end_method: fix_start
  • storage_solve_horizon_method: fix_quantity
  • storage_state_start and storage_state_reference_value: use the same value

This way the start and end states of the system are the same. Each end of the horizon (not the output) has that value as well, which keeps the model from emptying the storages at the end of the roll. In the dispatch solve, the fixed storage value from the storage solve overrides the horizon end value if a conflict exist.

How to create the three lower information solve types for investment and storage solves discussed above?

To create a lower resolution (longer timesteps) solve:

  • Make a new timeset, but use the same timeline and timeset_duration for it as with the high resolution solve
  • In the solve use this new timeset in the period_timeset
  • Set solve parameter new_stepduration: Hours

The model will create a new timeline for this solve with the new_stepduration. Each time series gets one value per new time step, by a rule that depends on the parameter (see new_stepduration in the reference): inflow and energy_margin_adder are summed over the time steps that form each new time step (a constant counts once per time step it combines); prices, costs, limits, availability, min_load, penalties, reservations, self_discharge_loss, weights and profiles are averaged over them, weighted by their durations; efficiency and efficiency_at_min_load take the mean of 1/efficiency (exact fuel use at a constant flow); storage_state_reference_value takes the value at the new step's end. Stochastic (branch) time series are combined the same way, branch by branch. peak_inflow stays per time step of the timeline: scale_to_annual_and_peak_flow scales each time step of the timeline as without new_stepduration and a new time step gets their sum, so the peak is matched by the timeline's time step, not by the average of a new time step. The new_stepduration must be a whole multiple of the timeline's time steps; on a timeline with time steps of different lengths every new time step must end where a time step of the timeline ends. FlexTool stops with an error otherwise. Steps are aggregated from the start of each block of the timeset_duration; if a block is not a multiple of the new_stepduration its last timestep will be shorter than the rest. A gap between two blocks stays a gap, so storage, ramps and on-line status treat the blocks as they do without new_stepduration. When several timesets of the solve share a timeline (e.g. one timeset per period), each period keeps its own timesteps; if a block of one timeset starts or ends inside a timestep of another timeset's block, that timestep is cut there (a warning names both timesets). A timeset used by a solve with new_stepduration cannot also be used by a solve without it, or by a solve with a different new_stepduration: give such solves their own timesets.

Some nodes can also be balanced at a coarser step than the rest of the solve: put them in a group with its own new_stepduration (e.g. hydrogen and its storage at 24 h while electricity stays hourly). Each node of the group is balanced once per coarse step, summing its flows over the step, and a storage node of the group keeps one state per coarse step. A unit or connection with a node outside the group keeps the solve's time step: an electrolyser between an hourly electricity node and a daily hydrogen node uses electricity in every hour it produces hydrogen. A unit or connection whose nodes are all coarse (e.g. a hydrogen liquefier or a hydrogen pipeline between daily nodes) has one flow per coarse step, which makes the model smaller. Its limits (capacity, availability, profiles, efficiency) apply to their average over the step, and ramp limits apply between coarse steps. The result is the same as with hourly flows when at most one limit of each flow varies within the step and its cost and efficiency do not; otherwise it can differ a little. A unit with online variables between coarse nodes decides its units online, start-ups and shut-downs once per coarse step, and its minimum up and down times count whole coarse steps; with ramp limits, its start-up and shut-down capacity reduction uses the coarse step (the average output over the whole step of a unit that starts at its start, ramping up from minimum load). A unit or connection between coarse nodes that provides reserves holds one reserve per coarse step: its reserve limits apply to the average over the step (with the average availability or profile), its reserve ramp room is the smallest of the step's time steps, and the reserve requirement is still checked at every time step of the solve, so it must be met by the step's one reserve in each of them. Nodes of a coarse group can be in reserve groups. An exact connection between coarse nodes chooses its direction once per coarse step, and DC power-flow lines between coarse nodes have one flow per coarse step (with one voltage angle per coarse step at the nodes of a DC network whose lines are all coarse; a DC network with an hourly line keeps every angle hourly). Rows that combine several units and connections — capacity margin, inertia and non-synchronous limits of a group, flow group instant limits, user constraints and DC power flow — are averaged over the coarse step when all their units and connections use it: they then see the step mean of demand, inflows, profiles and limits (a capacity margin on daily steps covers the mean net demand of the day, not its peak hour). A row that mixes coarse and hourly units or connections is still checked at every time step, with the coarse flows constant through their step. Only units and connections with a delay keep the solve's time step (and, in a Benders decomposition, flows that cross regions or live in the master; in a stochastic solve, those whose coarse step is tied between the forecasts over only part of it). An info line names the units and connections that keep the solve's step and the reason, and a database upgraded from an earlier FlexTool version prints a notice naming the coarse ones whose results can differ from hourly flows. Results are written at every time step: flows, units online and reserves hold the same value through the coarse step, and start-ups and shut-downs are written at the first time step of their coarse step. Listing a unit or connection in such a group has no effect on time resolution. The group step must be a multiple of the solve's time step.

Note that if the last timestep of the dispatch horizon is not in the storage solve timeline, it will use the last available timestep to fix the storage. This can happen at the end of the timeline when the dispatch solve with a lower step size can fit an extra step after the last time step of the storage solve. Other reason might be that both dispatch and storage solves are aggregated with the new_stepduration. In that case, it is usually best to use values for the new_stepduration that are dividable.

To create a sample solve with representative periods:

The tutorial contains an example of representaive periods under alternative 5weeks where the year is represented with five sample weeks. It is done with the timeset parameter timeset_duration where instead of choosing the whole timeline by setting the first timestep and the duration of whole timeline, you choose multiple starting points with smaller durations. The example for the 5weeks is below.

To create an investment solve sequence, you have two options:

  • Create manually a series of solves and set the invest_periods and realized_invest_periods individually for the solves. How to create a multi-year model has an example of this with the difference that here you use realized_invest_periods instead of realized_periods and that each of the higher level solves requires the contains_solves parameter.

If you have many splits, this option can get tedious and prone to mistakes.

The other option is to use only one investment solve entity:

  • The invest_periods and realized_invest_periods should then be set with a 2D map where the first column tells the solve (you don't have to create separate solve entities for these) and the second column tells the period. To get a 2D map, choose the parameter type as Map and then right click the table and choose Insert column after/before. The value column does not matter. The model will generate these solves, with the periods given. Note that the solve names should match in both 2D-maps.

You can use the same lower level solve with each the investment solves as the lower level solves will exclude the periods that are not included in either of the upper level realized periods: realized_invest_periods or fix_storage_periods. So, the lower level solve should have all the periods that it is used for in any the solves.

Note that the results of a nested rolling solve run are not fully optimal, because the information in the model is decreased. This is the price you pay for the speed. Therefore, the results should not be taken as they are, instead it is important to know how to interpret the results: What phenomena are missing? How will they affect the results? Where should extra investments go to satisfy the demand (there is a possibility to use the capacity_margin method to force extra investments)?

In the examples.sqlite there are four example scenarios related to this:

  • multi_fullYear_battery: The four period full year single solve, with coal, wind, battery storage with unlimited investment possibilities. Running this is still possible but takes a few minutes. This is here as a reference for the nested solves.
  • multi_fullYear_battery_nested_24h_invest_one_solve: This has the nested structure and the investment solve is done with 24h timesteps and storage solve 6h timesteps.
  • multi_fullYear_battery_nested_sample_invest_one_solve: This has the investment solve as 5weeks sample but all the four periods are included in the same investment solve. Nested structure with 6h storage solve timesteps.
  • multi_fullYear_battery_nested_multi_invest: This has split the investment to four solves with each having two period 5weeks sample period horizon. Nested structure with 6h storage solve timesteps.

The 24h timestep is clearly too long as it invests too little for storage and coal. A large upward penalty ensues.

The sample one solve invest also invests too little, as the largest demand-supply ratio weeks are not in the five week sample. However, the investments are spread more accurately.

The split sample investment run produces in this case similar results as the one solve sample run. This is not always the case! Here the only difference between the periods was linearly increased demand.

docs.title: How to force-include adequacy-critical weeks in representative-period selection
docs.text:
When a nested solve builds its investment stage on representative periods (see How to use Nested Rolling window solves), those periods are picked by greedy convex-hull clustering, which optimises a whole-year approximation of the shape of the profiles and inflows. A sustained low-VRE / high-demand stress week can have an unremarkable within-period shape and so never get selected — the investment stage then never sees that week as a hard balance constraint and under-builds. Force-include fixes the representation: it injects the worst base period under an explicit net-load signal so the stress week becomes a hard row in the invest LP. This is complementary to the energy-margin lever below — force-include corrects which weeks the invest stage sees, whereas the energy margin applies a deliberate margin on top of whatever weeks are chosen.

The selection runs from the command line:

python -m flextool.representative_periods.preprocess <db_url> <scenario> <n_rp> <period_length> [options]

The force-include options (all off by default):

  • --force-highest-net-load — force-include the base period with the greatest sustained net load (Flag B, energy-adequacy — the main fix; rewards a whole low-VRE / high-demand week rather than one spiky hour).
  • --force-peak-load — force-include the base period with the highest instantaneous net load (Flag A, capacity-adequacy; noisier for energy-constrained systems).
  • --force-window N — sub-window length in timesteps for the sustained score (default: the whole period).
  • --vg-weight W — convex blend in [0,1] between the VG-shortfall term and the inflow-demand term of the net-load signal; the inflow term gets 1 - W (default 0.5).
  • --region-groups G1,G2,… — opt-in node-group demand-weighting of the VG term (see below).

The VG-shortfall term of the net-load signal has two weighting modes. By default it is the unweighted, system-coincident mean shortfall over all profile series — best for a simple system or when no node-group information is available. With --region-groups G1,G2,… each region's VG shortfall is instead weighted by that region's demand D_r, so a coincident trough in the high-demand regions dominates the selection. The mapping is derived structurally — profile→node via unit__node__profile, node→region via group__node membership, and D_r = Σ|scalar demand| over the region's member nodes — with no name conventions. Each named region group must therefore contain BOTH the VG (profile) nodes and the demand nodes of that region.

For example, on the H2_trade model:

python -m flextool.representative_periods.preprocess <db_url> y2050_rp 5 168 --force-highest-net-load --region-groups decomp_AUS,decomp_JAP,decomp_KOR

forces the low-VRE week starting 2050-10-15 (base period 41), which the unseeded hull ({3, 8, 14, 22, 49}) misses entirely, and the timeset is written as hull_5rp_168h+f1. Without --region-groups on this multi-region trade model the top-scoring week happens to already be a hull pick, so the timeset name is unchanged — a documented limitation of the unweighted signal on such systems; use --region-groups there.

Forced periods seed the greedy hull: they are guaranteed into the set as its initial vertices, and the clustering then fills the remaining slots to complement them (never re-selecting a period a forced extreme already represents). The total stays pinned at n_rp — a forced period consumes one of the n_rp slots, it never grows the set beyond n_rp. The +f{n} suffix counts the forced periods that displaced a clustered pick (i.e. that the unseeded hull would not have selected). With no --force-* flag the run is byte-identical to the pure-hull selection and keeps the plain hull_{n_rp}rp_{period_length}h timeset name, so force-include never overwrites the pure-hull timeset.

docs.title: How to cluster representative periods on net load
docs.text:
By default the greedy hull clusters on the shape of every normalized profile and inflow series. --netload-clustering instead clusters on a real-MW net-load signal — demand minus available VRE — so the selected periods are the ones the net demand actually stresses rather than the ones with the most distinctive individual profile shapes:

python -m flextool.representative_periods.preprocess <db_url> <scenario> <n_rp> <period_length> --netload-clustering [--vre-penetration P]
  • --netload-clustering — cluster on demand − Σ VRE·availability. VRE is any generation unit whose unit__node__profile arc uses profile_method = upper_limit (the default). The iteration-0 VRE fleet is sized by a demand-match default (each aggregation unit's investable VRE is grown until its energy plus existing VRE energy covers the unit's demand energy). The timeset is written as netload_{n_rp}rp_{period_length}h.
  • --vre-penetration P — scale the demand-match energy-share target (1.0 = full-energy match; default 1.0). Ignored without --netload-clustering.

Per-group vs per-node granularity. Set the group.use_for_representative_periods (yes_no) flag to yes on one or more region groups to sum each flagged group's member-node net load into a single regional signal; when no group carries the flag, each node is clustered as its own net-load signal.

Iterating on solved capacities. The single-shot mode above sizes VRE with the demand-match default. To instead feed a solve's realised investments back into the selection, use the iteration driver, which reselects and re-solves until the representative set stabilises:

python -m flextool.representative_periods.netload_iterate <db_url> <scenario> --n-rp 5 --period-length 168 --iterations 3 [--keep-best]

Each iteration runs an invest-only solve and feeds its invested capacities into the next net-load selection; the loop stops early once the selected set stops changing. --keep-best additionally dispatches each mature iteration over the full year and keeps the representative set with the lowest full-year cost. Run ... netload_iterate --help for the full flag list (--invest-solves, --dispatch-solves, --vre-penetration, --work-dir, --output-location, --alternative-name, --warm-start).

docs.title: How to add an energy margin for investment adequacy
docs.text:
In a nested solve the investment stage is optimised over representative periods and the full-year dispatch is solved separately. The representative periods can be systematically optimistic about variable-renewable (VRE) availability: their average VRE availability tends to exceed the true annual average. The investment stage then under-builds, and the full-year dispatch has to cover the shortfall with large forced unserved-energy (upward-slack) penalties.

The energy-margin lever lets you de-rate a node's energy balance in the investment stage so that it builds enough capacity to meet the true demand under the true (lower) annual VRE availability. It is set per node with a method and one of two value parameters:

  • energy_margin_method - none (default, off), inflow_multiplier, or inflow_adder.
  • energy_margin_multiplier - the factor (default 1.0). When energy_margin_method = inflow_multiplier, the node's demand (inflow) is multiplied by this factor in the investment solve only — the dispatch solves always see the true demand. A value of 1.1 makes the investment stage build for about 10% more demand, so the real capacity is enough to meet the real demand under the true annual VRE. A value of 1.0 has no effect.
  • energy_margin_adder - the extra demand in MWh per time step of the timeline (default 0.0). When energy_margin_method = inflow_adder, this many MWh of extra demand (negative inflow) is added to every time step at the node in the investment solve only; the dispatch solves always see the true demand. When the investment solve has new_stepduration, a solve step gets the sum over the time steps it combines, like inflow. A value of 0.0 has no effect.

For example, to build about 10% more into a demand node, set energy_margin_method = inflow_multiplier and energy_margin_multiplier = 1.1 on that node.

The energy margin enters only the node balance. The reserve requirement, the non-synchronous limit and the capacity margin of a group follow the real demand; use capacity_margin for a capacity surplus. Combined with a capacity margin, the energy margin does not lower or raise the capacity requirement: storage and imports count with the power they deliver at a step, also when it serves the energy margin's added demand, and firm output that serves it leaves the capacity margin unchanged.

Use inflow_adder as the additive alternative to the multiplier. Because the multiplier scales the node's existing demand, it is a no-op on a node whose native inflow is zero — a common shape for a bare adequacy / slack node that carries no demand series of its own. inflow_adder instead adds a fixed block of demand at the node: it deepens the node's demand where it already has inflow and, crucially, creates the demand where the node had none, adding the same MWh to every investment-stage time step (a constant adder; on a timeline of 24 h time steps a margin of 10 MW needs a value of 240), or placing per-period values if authored as a period map. Set energy_margin_method = inflow_adder and energy_margin_adder = <MWh> on the node to raise investment-stage adequacy headroom without touching dispatch demand.

The margin is extra demand for the investment decision only, not load: it does not raise reserve requirements (a reserve group's increase_reserve_ratio follows the un-margined demand).

The energy margin is a per-node lever for regions whose adequacy gap is driven by VRE optimism and can be closed by building more of an investable response (more VRE, storage, or imports). It cannot help a region whose VRE collapses to near zero during the stress period when the only investable response is more VRE that serves the same demand — those regions need firm capacity or imports instead.

It is complementary to the capacity_margin_method (see the group reference): capacity_margin_method targets peak-capacity adequacy (firm and VRE capacity above the demand at every time step), whereas the energy margin targets sustained-energy adequacy across the year.

docs.title: Peak memory in long rolling and nested chains
docs.text:
The cascade keeps several solves' worth of state alive in RAM at once — the LP and its solution while outputs and the hand-off to the next roll are written, the next roll's input data, and the parked Provider state from earlier sub-solves. On continental-scale rolling or nested chains this can push peak RSS into the 10-30 GB range. Two CLI knobs help when peak RSS is the bottleneck rather than wall time:

  • --save-memory (or FLEXTOOL_SAVE_MEMORY=1) — after each LP is built, drops polar-high's polars/numpy LP source, writes the LP to a temp MPS file, and solves it in a separate HiGHS subprocess (via cmd_solve_mps) so the solver's working set lives outside the FlexTool address space. Frees ~5–10 GB on large models at a cost of ~+90 s I/O per sub-solve. Also disables warm-LP reuse, so every sub-solve cold-rebuilds. Use when the machine OOMs, not as a default.
  • --presolve off — HiGHS' presolve is the largest single contributor to peak RSS on highly-structured LPs (continental power grids, dense capacity-expansion). Turning it off slows the solve but can free several GB. Pair with --save-memory for the largest savings.

Both flags are documented in Terminal / CLI. The FlexTool GUI's side menu has a Save memory checkbox that passes --save-memory through to each scenario run.

docs.title: How to use representative-period clustering with scalar profiles
docs.text: The representative-period preprocessor in flextool/representative_periods/preprocess.py builds its clustering matrix from time-varying profile and node.inflow series. Constant-valued (scalar) profiles and inflows are dropped from the clustering input: a constant series has zero variance and contributes no information to the period-similarity distance. The preprocessor prints a one-line note such as Skipping 3 scalar profile(s) and 1 scalar inflow(s) — clustering only considers time-varying series. so you can see exactly how many series were filtered out. There is nothing to configure: scalar profiles and inflows are still used by the model as constants, they just do not take part in choosing the representative periods.

docs.title: How to use stochastics (representing uncertainty)
docs.text:
(stochastics.sqlite)

Stochastics are used to represent the uncertainty of the future in the decision making. The main idea is to represent the distribution of possible futures by a set of discrete, probability-weighted forecast branches. The branches fan out from a common branching point, and each carries a probability weight; the weights sum to one. The model minimises the expected (probability-weighted) cost across all the forecast branches.

Because the decision maker does not yet know which future will occur, decisions that must be committed before the uncertainty is revealed cannot differ between the forecasts. A non-anticipativity constraint therefore forces the forecast branches to agree with each other on those here-and-now decisions over the committed part of the horizon — and that agreement is the (non-anticipative) realization of each such decision. The tied decision types are investments, storage usage and unit online (commitment) status; energy flows are always left free so each forecast dispatches them independently. (min_uptime, min_downtime and ramp limits are separate physics, always active within each branch's own trajectory — they are not part of the non-anticipativity tie.)

There is no "realized" branch among the weighted forecasts. "Realized" is an optional designation — at most one branch per branching point — that marks which branch's data are treated as the actuals; it is never a weighted member of the fan. The stochastic solve optimises over the forecasts only, so its operations inside the fan have no realized answer of their own. With a designated branch, FlexTool runs a realization dispatch right after the stochastic solve: a deterministic solve over the same committed window that reads the designated branch's data, keeps the stochastic solve's investments and inherits the units online and the reserves tied across the forecasts (the value of the first forecast branch in sorted order). Its results are the realized operational results. Without a designation (a forecasts-only fan) the results hold the investment decisions and the operations of the periods before the reveal, but no realized operation inside the fan. A solve reports only these committed / realized results, never the individual forecast branches (the output_horizon debug option, below, writes them to a separate raw dump).

For the stochastics to have an effect on the results, the system needs parameters that change between the forecast branches. These could be e.g. wind power generation or fuel prices. The model then carries separate variables in every branch for all the decisions it can take (e.g. investment, storage state, online, flow), and minimises their probability-weighted (expected) cost. The committed decisions — tied across the branches as described above — therefore hedge against the whole distribution of forecasts rather than optimising for any single one.

In this example, we show two ways to use stochastics: single solve and rolling horizon. They all share the same test system that includes:

  • A demand node
  • Coal, gas and wind power plants
  • Hydro power plant with a reservoir and a downriver nodes

The demand and the downriver nodes have a constant negative inflow. Therefore, the hydro plant capacity is partly in use at all times. The varying timeseries are the wind profile and the water inflow the reservoir. The coal commodity is more expensive than the gas, so the system will try to use the reservoir water to minimize the usage of coal. This will be affected by the forecast of the wind and the forecast of the water inflow. These are the stochastic timeseries in these examples.

You can have stochastics in multiple timeseries in the same solve, but these will have to share the branches. This means that for example if you have two wind plants with two different stochastic wind profiles with three branches (upper, mid and lower estimates) you need to think if it is best to use only three branches and put both of the upper estimates to the same 'upper' branch or should you use combinatorics to make nine branches. However, note that the tool will not do the combinatorics for you and the solving time will be heavily affected by extra branches. Consequently, the usual practice is to present all the stochastics using just e.g. three branches and consider the correlations between the stochastic parameters in the pre-processing of the input data.

Notes about the storage options with stochastics:

  • The best options to use are:

  • storage_state_start_end_method: fix_start or fix_start_end (and the their values)

  • storage_solve_horizon_method: fix_value or fix_price (and their values)

  • storage_binding_method works per path of the stochastic tree (a path runs from the solve's first step through the trunk periods, the shared periods before the split, to the end of one forecast branch). With bind_within_solve the cycle closes once per path: the last step of every forecast branch ends at the level the solve's first step starts from. When the fan opens in the solve's first period, each forecast's first step continues from the last step of its own path, and since all the paths end at the same level, all the forecasts start from it too. With bind_forward_only (the default) a fan that opens later continues from the trunk's last step, and the forecasts of a fan that opens in the solve's first period all start from the same level: the solve's start state (the storage_state_start value, or the state carried in from the previous roll or solve), or, with neither (fix_nothing), one free level shared by all the forecasts. With storage_start_end_method fix_start (or fix_start_end) the start of each forecast is pinned to the given share (storage_state_start) of that forecast's own storage capacity, so where the capacity differs by forecast (investment or divestment per forecast) the starting energy differs although the share is the same; without a fixed start all the forecasts start from the same level.

  • Representative periods (a timeset with representative_period_weights) work in stochastic solves: each forecast branch period uses the representative periods of the period it branches from (all branches share that selection). The _blended_weights methods follow the same rules per branch: the first branch period continues from the last base period of the trunk period (the shared period before the split), a later one from the previous period of the same branch; bind_within_solve_blended_weights closes once per path, so every branch's last period ends at the level the trunk period starts from; bind_within_period_blended_weights closes each branch period on itself. When the fan opens in the solve's first period, the forecasts start from the same level (the fan has only forecasts, no realized member, so this equal start is what ties them). For a node in an include_stochastics group the start levels of the representative blocks are tied across the forecasts inside the non-anticipativity window, like the storage state.

docs.title: What the model ties across branches (dispatch vs. investment defaults)
docs.text:
Wherever the branches still share the same information — the committed part of the horizon, before the forecast is revealed — the model ties some decisions so that all forecast branches agree on them (the branches are tied to each other, not to any realized branch) and lets the rest diverge. What is tied depends on whether the solve invests.

Any stochastic solve (dispatch or investment) assumes, by default:

  • Storage state, unit commitment (online status) and reserves are tied across the forecast branches over the solve's committed periods — every branch must take the same storage and start-up decisions while they still share information, so these decisions are genuinely non-anticipative. In a single solve whose committed periods span the whole horizon this ties them over the whole horizon (so only the flows differ between branches); in a rolling solve the tie covers only each roll's committed (jump) slice, and the branches operate freely in the forecast horizon beyond the reveal.
  • Energy flows are always free — each forecast dispatches its flows independently.
  • Continuity is ordinary temporal carry-in. Only the model's very first timestep starts from the given history / initial state; every later timestep continues from the previous one. At a branching point each child branch continues from its parent branch's last step, so sibling branches start from the same state simply because they share a parent.

An investment solve additionally assumes, by default:

  • A single, shared here-and-now investment plan for all branches (stochastic_invest_method = none) — you commit one set of investments regardless of which future occurs.

So a plain dispatch solve = commit the committed part (shared storage / online / reserve), forecast the rest, flows free. An investment solve = the same operational tie plus one shared investment plan.

Overriding the defaults:

  • Investment — set stochastic_invest_method = recourse for per-scenario (wait-and-see) investment, or declare a mid-horizon reveal for a genuine two-stage hedge (see Stochastic investment below).
  • Operations — set the solve array parameter shared_operation_periods to change the operational tie window: an empty array frees operations from the first timestep (each forecast operates freely — combined with a single shared investment this is the classic two-stage capacity-expansion model), or a list of periods ties operations only over those periods. See Stochastics over multiple periods for the details.

docs.title: Single solve stochastics
docs.text:
(stochastics.sqlite scenario: 2_day_stochastic_dispatch)

In this scenario a near-term operating window is committed with an uncertain forecast for the following day over a 48-hour timeset. To set up a stochastic solve, we need three things: the stochastic branch information, the stochastic timeseries, and choosing which parts of the model use stochastic timeseries.

The information about the branches is set with the solve parameter stochastic_branches. This is a 4-dimensional map. (Edit -> choose map -> right click -> add columns.) The columns are: period, branch, analysis_time (starting time of the branch), realized (yes/no), and the value is the branch's probability weight. In this example we have forecast branches (e.g. mid, upper and lower) representing the wind forecasts. The weights set each branch's probability in the objective function (expected model cost) and are normalized so that the total weight is always one across the forecast branches at each start time. The realized flag is optional: at most one branch per start time may be flagged yes, and it only designates which branch's data are the actuals used by the realization dispatch (above) — a realized-flagged branch is not counted among the weighted forecasts. In this example all four branches (realized, upper, lower and mid) are forecasts and none is flagged yes: the fan is pure forecasts, so the solve reports no realized dispatch (its normal results are empty apart from the objective), and the example sets output_horizon (below) to write the forecast branches to the raw dump. Flag one branch realized: yes to get a realization dispatch of the 48 hours.

The stochastic wind timeseries are set with the same profile parameter profile, but with a three-dimensional map instead of the regular one-dimensional one. The tool recognizes a stochastic timeseries from the dimensions of the data. The three dimensions are: branch, analysis_time and time. The model reads the branch-specific series for each forecast branch; where a branch has no stochastic data available for part of the horizon, it falls back to the profile's non-stochastic value, if one is given. A forecast branch period reads the series whose analysis_time is its own first time step and, for a time step that series does not cover, the series whose analysis_time is the solve's fan start (the step at which the solve branches). A series given only at the fan's analysis_time therefore serves every later period of the horizon; a series given at a later period's first step overrides it there. A period before the reveal never reads the fan-start series. The other parameters documented as "stochastic time" in the reference (availability of units and nodes, unit efficiency and min_load, other_operational_cost of unit inputs and outputs, reservation, penalty_up and penalty_down, node inflow) take the same three-level map and are read the same way; an entity's value is read regardless of whether it is in an include_stochastics group — the group changes HOW it is read, not whether it is read at all (below). Giving a value to only some of a reveal's forecast branches and leaving the rest out is a configuration error (naming the entity, the parameter and the branches left out); give every branch a value, or none.

The parts of the model that will use stochastic data per branch are chosen with a group parameter include_stochastics: the units, nodes and connections added to this group read the matching forecast branch's own value on every branch period (if available). Here we add the unit wind_plant to this group. A profile is read per profile, not per user: when any unit, node or connection that uses a stochastic-time profile is in an include_stochastics group, every user of that profile reads the forecast branch's own series, including users outside the group. To keep one of two wind plants on a single series, give it its own non-stochastic profile. An entity with a stochastic-time value that is in no such group still reads the series — every one of its branch periods reads the single value of the designated realized branch rather than its own branch's value. A forecasts-only fan (no branch flagged realized: yes) has no such value, so a stochastic-time value of an entity outside every include_stochastics group is a configuration error there, naming the entity and the parameter — add the entity to the group, designate a realized branch, or give the parameter a non-stochastic value. Inside the group a forecasts-only fan is valid: every forecast reads its own branch. The period label (the original name of the period that opens the fan, see "Stochastics over multiple periods") has no dispatch, so it needs no value of its own. The realization dispatch reads the designated branch's value for every entity. A deterministic solve that declares no stochastic_branches at all takes the designated realized branch's value too, so authoring a stochastic-time value there without one is a configuration error, unless a realized branch elsewhere (e.g. the stochastic solve whose realization dispatch it is) was projected onto it.

An option exists to look at the stochastic (forecast-branch) horizons for debugging your system: the model parameter output_horizon. It does not change the normal results (they hold the realized rows only, with or without the option); instead output_parquet/<scenario>/horizon/ gets one raw parquet per LP variable and constraint with every row of every solve (forecast branches and rolling look-ahead included), a realized column marking the rows that reach the normal results, and the raw primal values, reduced costs and duals (see Results). The values are raw solver values, without cost processing.

If you change the weights of the stochastic branches, you should see the results change.

The figure shows the dispatch of the forecast branches; those rows are in the raw horizon/ dump, not in the normal results or plots.

docs.title: Stochastics over multiple periods
docs.text:
When the solve's horizon spans periods beyond the branching period, the branches extend through all the remaining periods: every forecast branch with a nonzero weight gets a synthetic <period>_<branch> copy of the branching period and of each later period, and the operations of the stochastic solve live only on these copies. The real period names of the periods from the reveal onwards are period labels: they hold only period-level bookkeeping — the shared investment (under stochastic_invest_method = none, seen by every forecast), the years represented and the discounting — and have no dispatch (no time-step rows, empty operational results). Under recourse a period label has no investment either: every forecast invests on its own. The designated realized branch gets no copy: its data feed the realization dispatch, which dispatches the real period names. Only a period strictly before the reveal falls back to the lexically-smallest forecast branch for its own (necessarily pre-branch, undivided) data. The branch probability weights carry forward along each branch, so the weighting is constant along a branch's period chain and sums to one across the forecast branches of each period.

Notes for multi-period stochastic solves:

  • If years_represented is defined for the solve, it must cover all of the solve's periods. A configuration that defines it for only some periods fails with a configuration error (older versions silently ran on a truncated horizon instead).
  • The forecast branch weights are normalized to sum to one across the forecasts at each period; a realized designation adds no weight to the fan (it is not a weighted member).
  • In a single solve whose committed periods span the whole horizon, the non-anticipativity constraints cover the whole horizon: the shared decision types (storage usage, online status, reserve) stay tied across the forecast branches through the later periods, and post-branching divergence shows up only in the flow variables. Use a rolling solve when the branches should be free to commit differently after the information is revealed — each roll then commits only its jump slice and the non-anticipativity window ends at the reveal.
  • To free the operational branches within a single solve (without moving to a rolling solve), set the solve array parameter shared_operation_periods. Left unset (the default) it keeps the behaviour above — the operational non-anticipativity window equals the realized-dispatch timesteps (plus any fix_storage timesteps), so operations stay tied across the whole committed horizon. Set it to an empty array to free operations from the first timestep: the shared decision types then branch freely per forecast while the investment plan is still a single shared decision (stochastic_invest_method = none) — this is the classic two-stage capacity-expansion structure (one here-and-now investment, wait-and-see operations). Set it to a list of periods to tie operations only over those periods (e.g. a mid-horizon reveal: tie the pre-reveal periods, free the rest); the listed periods' timesteps are intersected with the solve's active timeline, and a curated list replaces (does not add to) the default realized-dispatch window. The dispatch output window is unaffected — realized_periods still governs which periods are reported.
  • A realized: yes row placed at a later period's first timestep does not re-branch the model, but it selects which branch's timeseries the realization dispatch uses from that period onwards. This can be used deliberately for per-period series selection; if you did not intend a series swap, keep the realized: yes row only at the solve (or roll) start.
  • The branching period's label has no dispatch, so it reads no stochastic-time value; its forecast copies read their own branch's value, and the realization dispatch reads the designated branch's.
  • Each forecast copy of a later period reads its branch's series at its own first time step and, for a time step not covered there, the series given at the fan's analysis_time (the realization dispatch and the entities outside every include_stochastics group read the realized branch the same way). One forecast per branch at the fan's analysis_time, covering the whole horizon, is therefore enough. In a rolling solve the order is the other way round (see "Rolling horizon stochastics").
  • When a solve commits time steps inside a forecasts-only fan and a later solve (e.g. the next roll) continues from them, the units online and the reserves on the tied steps are the same in every forecast: the next solve continues from them (the first forecast branch in sorted order). Storage state, ramp-limited flows, the cumulative commodity ladder, the CO2 total cap and recourse investment are decided per forecast there, so such a run stops before the LP with an error naming the solve and these families: designate a realized: yes branch (FlexTool then adds the realization dispatch), configure a realization solve right after it, or end the committed window before the reveal.

docs.title: Rolling horizon stochastics
docs.text:
(stochastics.sqlite scenario: 1_week_rolling_wind)

In this scenario we extend the previous timeline to one week and roll through it one day at a time with additional three day stochastic horizon:

solve: rolling_solve_jump = 24 and rolling_solve_horizon = 96.

The stochastic data should be given so that it can serve the rolling structure: rolling_solve_jump dictates the duration of the committed (jump) part of each solve and the interval of forecast updates. So, for every analysis_time there needs to be a time series in each forecast branch that extends to the end of the horizon (as defined by rolling_solve_horizon). The branches continue to the end of the horizon without branching again. Each roll fans at its first step into the forecast branches; the non-anticipativity tie covers the committed jump slice, and the branches then diverge over the forecast tail. Only the committed jump is carried forward to the next roll as the realized state.

For the solve parameter stochastic_branches this means an analysis_time at each roll start (here t0001, t0025, t0049, t0073, t0097, t0121 and t0145).

Look-ahead periods. A roll uses only the forecasts available when it decides, at its fan's analysis_time. Every period of the roll after the fan's period (the look-ahead periods, and also the later committed periods of a multi-period jump) reads the forecast given at the roll's own fan analysis_time, even where a later roll's forecast is given at that period's first time step. The roll's fan forecast must therefore cover the roll's whole horizon, look-ahead included: where it has no value for a time step of such a period but a forecast given later (at the period's own first time step) has one, the run stops before the roll is solved with an error naming the entity, the parameter, the roll and the uncovered time steps. A time step that no forecast covers reads the non-stochastic value, as before. The realization dispatch of a rolling solve reads the designated branch the same way. Data that is not stochastic (a plain time series) is read as before. A single (non-rolling) solve keeps the rule above: a forecast given at a later period's own first time step overrides the fan forecast there.

Each roll fans at its first step, so its committed jump lies inside the fan. In this example branch realized is designated realized: yes at every roll start: FlexTool runs a realization dispatch after each stochastic roll over that roll's jump, with the designated branch's data, and the next roll continues from the realization dispatch's end state (storage, units online, ramps). Without a designation the jump is realized only for the families tied across the forecasts (units online and reserves); a model with storage (as here), ramp limits or cumulative caps then stops with a configuration error (see "Stochastics over multiple periods").
