A fan that opens only in a roll's look-ahead needs no designation: the next roll continues from the committed steps before the reveal. The solve parameter dispatch_realization_method sets how the realization runs:

  • within_solve (default): no second solve unless a branch is designated realized: yes, which adds the realization dispatch as described above (with stochastic_invest_method = none; under recourse a warning says that no realization dispatch is added).
  • separate_dispatch: always splits realization into a dedicated downstream dispatch pass (committed investments/decisions fixed) as a separate realized-dispatch solve. It dispatches the branch designated realized: yes; without such a branch the run stops with an error naming the solve. This is the 2-stage seed of a future multi-stage sequential-market structure.

The selection is engine-managed rather than something you normally set per roll; separate_dispatch's automatic-selection defaults are still being refined.

Otherwise there is no difference to the previous example.

docs.title: Stochastic investment
docs.text: By default (solve.stochastic_invest_method = none) a stochastic model makes a single investment plan shared by every branch — one plan for all futures. The stochastic-investment modes below differ in what is decided before the uncertainty is revealed.

docs.title: Standard two-stage stochastic investment (the main mode)
docs.text:
The usual goal is a genuine two-stage plan: one shared here-and-now investment decision, made before the uncertainty resolves, with every scenario then operating that fleet freely from the first timestep according to its own realization. The investment is the first-stage (non-anticipative) decision; all operations are second-stage recourse — nothing operational is tied across the branches.

For a model that invests in a single period this is available today: keep stochastic_invest_method = none (one shared investment) and set shared_operation_periods = [] (operations branch freely from t0 — see What the model ties across branches above). The result is the classic stochastic capacity-expansion model — commit one fleet, minimise the probability-weighted cost of operating it across the scenarios.

For a multi-period investment horizon the ideal is that only the first period's investment is shared (the genuine here-and-now decision) while later-period investment adapts per scenario (recourse), since by then some uncertainty has resolved. This is delivered by the investment non-anticipativity window — the solve array parameter shared_invest_periods. Compose three knobs:

  • stochastic_invest_method = recourse (so per-branch investment variables exist to tie);
  • shared_invest_periods = [<first period>] (tie the first period's v_invest/v_divest across branches — a single shared here-and-now decision — while later periods invest per-branch);
  • shared_operation_periods = [] (operations branch freely from t0).

The result is the standard two-stage stochastic capacity-expansion structure: shared first-period investment + per-branch (recourse) investment later + free operations. Set shared_invest_periods to more than one period to extend the shared window (e.g. [p2035, p2040] shares the first two periods, recourse from the third). Left unset (the default) or set to an empty array it adds no tie — recourse stays per-branch everywhere, byte-identical to before. Both invest and divest are tied over the window, so the net first-stage capacity (existing + invest − divest) is genuinely shared. The window requires recourse; on a none solve it is a harmless no-op (investment is already shared across all periods).

docs.title: Per-scenario (wait-and-see) investment
docs.text: stochastic_invest_method = recourse lets each forecast branch invest on its own data at and after the branching period, with probability-weighted investment costs and per-branch limits. When branches start at the solve's first step this is a wait-and-see analysis — each forecast has perfect foresight, so the objective is an EVPI lower bound, not a committed plan (it typically costs less than any single plan can). Useful for scenario screening and per-branch capacity ranges; it is not a plan you can build. Forecast-branch (unrealized) investments are not in the normal results; they are in the raw dump of model.output_horizon (a debug flag). Committed results report the committed / realized region. recourse is incompatible with Benders decomposition (the solver rejects the combination).

docs.title: Hedged mid-horizon reveal (first periods deterministic for investment and operations)
docs.text:
A third structure keeps the first periods fully deterministic — single shared pre-reveal periods for both investment and operations — and lets the branches fan out only from a later period. Set the branching period of the stochastic_branches map to that later period, with the branches' analysis time at that period's first step (the reveal must fall on a period boundary — investment is period-granular).

The pre-reveal periods stay single real-named periods with one shared v_invest and one shared operational schedule — non-anticipativity holds by construction (there is only one variable per pre-reveal period, so nothing to tie). The post-reveal periods fan per branch (second-stage recourse). Note how this differs from the standard mode above: here the near-term operations are shared (committed) too, not just the investment — appropriate when the first periods genuinely are deterministic (a committed near-term operating schedule) rather than a first period that should already be operated per forecast. The objective sits strictly between the wait-and-see bound and the deterministic mean-value plan (positive EVPI and VSS); only the pre-reveal periods' committed results and the investment decisions are output (plus the realized operation of the fan when a branch is designated realized). Mid-horizon reveal is a general stochastics capability — it works for dispatch-only hedged stochastics too, not only for recourse investment.

docs.title: How to add a storage unit (battery)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite, scenario: wind_battery) init - west - wind - battery

In the Init SQLite database, there is a scenario wind_battery. In the example, the wind_plant alone is not able to meet the load in all conditions, but the battery will help it to improve the situation.

In FlexTool, only nodes can have storage. Nodes can therefore be demand nodes, storage nodes or both.

The node needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

To make a storage node one the required parameters are:

  • node_type: storage
  • existing: The maximum storage size of battery as the potential energy [MWh]
  • penalty_up: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere
  • penalty_down: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere

Additional parameters:

  • self_discharge_loss The fraction of energy lost in each hour (0.01: the content shrinks by 1/1.01 per hour). It is applied continuously, so it is exact for time steps of any length; energy charged within a step is treated as spread evenly over the step.

Storage states can be tied to a value. For this three methods are introduced:

  • storage_start_end_method: Fixes start and/or end state of the storage to a chosen value. This is for the start and the end of the whole model timeline (not for individual solves in case the model is rolling forward): the end value applies to the model's last timestep in every solve whose horizon contains it. It is meant for simple models; with several solves or rolls storage_state_reference_value with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value is usually the better choice. A later roll or a later solve of a solve sequence starts from the storage state realised at the end of the realised part of the previous roll or solve.
    • storage_state_start and storage_state_end set these values.
  • storage_bind_method: Forces the start and end values to be the same for the chosen time interval (timeset, period or solve)
  • storage_solve_horizon_method: Fixes the state of the storage at the end of the solve horizon or sets a price for the stored energy at the end of the solve horizon
    • storage_state_reference_value and storage_state_reference_price set these values

Note on end-of-horizon valuation. When storage_solve_horizon_method = use_reference_price is set, the storage_state_reference_price is applied in the solver objective (the model sees a credit for leaving energy in the storage at the end of the horizon). However, this credit is not included in the calculated cost totals reported in costs_discounted_* and summary_solve.csv — end-of-horizon storage valuation has several valid interpretations (reference price × end state, difference between initial and final state priced at an average commodity price, opportunity cost, or simply book value) and is typically done as post-analysis rather than as part of the optimization cost breakdown. If you need the credit as a reported line item, compute it yourself in post-processing from the v_state last-timestep values and the storage_state_reference_price.

Having multiple storage methods can create infeasible problems. This is why some of the combinations shouldn't (and cannot) be used at the same time. If multiple methods are used, some of them might be ignored by the method hierarchy. More information can be found from Model Parameters: Using nodes as storages.

Battery also needs charging and discharging capabilities. These could be presented either with a connection or by having a charging unit and a discharging unit. In here, we are using a connection called battery_inverter. Please note that the efficiency parameter of the connection applies to both directions, so the round-trip efficiency will be efficiency squared.

The transfer_method can be used by all types of connections, but in this case it is best to choose regular, which tries to avoid simultaneous charging and discharing, but can still do it when the model needs to dissipate energy. exact method would prevent that, but it would require integer variables and make the storage computationally much more expensive. Model leakage will be reported in the results (forthcoming).

The connection needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The required paremeters of the connection are:

  • existing: The capacity of energy transsmission [MW]
  • transfer_method: (see above)

Additional parameters:

  • efficiency: by default 1

Finally connection_node_node is needed between inverter, the battery and the demand node (west).

docs.title: How to create a hydro reservoir
docs.text: hydro_reservoir.sq

docs.title: Simple hydro reseroir
docs.text:
(scenario: hydro)

The objective is to create a hydro power plant with a reservoir and connect it to a demand node.

Hydro reservoir power plant requires three components:

  • Reservoir node
  • Hydro unit
  • Output node

It can be useful to create a new alternative for these components to be able to include and exclude them from the scenarios.

The reservoir is made with a node as only nodes can have storage in FlexTool. The incoming water can be represented by the inflow parameter. It can be a constant or a time variant.

There are two ways to handle the water to electricity coefficient. In this example we store the water as volume and convert it to electricity in the unit. This option is better when modelling river systems with multiple reservoirs. Note that in the results, the state of the reservoir is then as volume. For the other option of converting the volume to potential energy in the reservoir, look at the start of the 'How to create a hydro pump storage'.

In this implementation of reservoir hydro power, there is an option to spill water from the storage so that it does not run through the plant. The simplest way of allowing spilling is setting the downward penalty of the node to 0. This way the energy can disappear from the storage without a cost. The quantity of spilled water can be seen from the results as the 'downward slack' of the node.

Add the reservoir node to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The required parameters of the reservoir node are (node_c and node_t sheets if using Excel input data):

  • node_type: storage
  • inflow: Mapping of the incoming water as volume [m^3/h]
  • existing: The maximum size of the reservoir [m^3]
  • penalty_up: a larger number than with the demand node to not allow creating extra water if not enough electricity is being created
  • penalty_down: 0 or a large number (spilling or not)
  • a storage_method to set the behaviour on how the storage levels should be managed - for short duration storages bind_within_timeblock may be best and for seasonal storages it could be best to use bind_within_solve. If historical storage level time series are available, it can be beneficial to use fix_start in the storage_start_end_method together with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value, which will pick the storage level at the end of each solve from the time series provided as a reference (storage_state_reference_value). See flextool/schemas/spinedb_schema.json for the full enumeration of storage_binding_method values and the silent-degrade behaviour of the *_blended_weights variants; DB migration v55 renamed several legacy names (e.g. bind_within_timeset → bind_within_timeblock).

The unit is connected to the reservoir node and the output node demand_node (unit_c and unit_node_c in excel):

  • Add the unit to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.
  • The efficiency of the plant is the coefficient of transfering an unit of volume to an unit of electricity (using piecewise linear efficiency is naturally possible), here we use 0.57.
  • Set existing capacity [MW]
  • Create entities unit__inputNode: hydro_plant|reservoir and unit__outputNode: hydro_plant|demand_node.

docs.title: River system with multiple reservoirs
docs.text:
(scenario: hydro_with_downriver_spill_unit) (scenario: river_system)

In this example, we create a hydro system with multiple reseroirs and downriver water demand. Here the the reservoir content is represented as volume of water (m3) and the conversion factor to electricity (MWh) is expressed in the hydro power plant parameters. This could also be done the other way around where the reservoir content is expressed as energy (MWh). Especially in a cascading river system it is better to use the first approach.

The reservoir and demand node are the same as above. The penalty_down of the reservoir now needs to be the other than 0 as the spilled water needs to flow to the downriver node

Let's start with the downriver demand.

The downriver node represents the requirement to pass a minimum amount of water through the plant to not dry out the river. The downriver node needs:

  • To be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.
  • node_type: balance
  • inflow: Minimum requirement of water flow as the potential power (Map or constant)[m^3/h]
  • penalty_up: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere
  • penalty_down: 0, this makes the requirement to be at least the amount of water as the demand, not the equal to it

The hydro plant unit now also needs the relation unit_outputNode: hydro_plant|downriver .

The hydro plant now needs to both pass the water to downriver and the electricity to the demand node. Also, it needs to handle the water to electricity transformation as the reservoir now has volume not energy. The user needs to get the water to electricity coefficient ie. how much energy does one unit of volume create when passing the unit in this example the coefficient is 0.57. As the unit creates both the water and the electricity, the efficiency now is the sum of the two.

  • efficiency: 1 + coefficient

Now the unit creates enough stuff to output, but the model can still choose how it will distribute it between the two output nodes. We still need to fix the ratio of output flows. This is done with an user constraint. Here we call this constraint hydro_split. First, it needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The constraint needs parameters:

  • sense: equal
  • constant: 0

As we are fixing the output flows, the we need to add the flows with their coefficients to this constraint. This is done with the unit_outputNode parameter constraint_flow_coeff:

  • unit_outputNode(hydro_plant|downriver): constraint_flow_coeff: Map (hydro_split| 0.57)
  • unit_outputNode(hydro_plant|demand_node): constraint_flow_coeff: Map (hydro_split| -1)

These create the constraint: 

-flow_to_demand_node + 0.57 flow_to_downriver = 0

The capacity of an unit is the sum of outputs. With the electrical capacity of 500MW and water to elecricity coefficient of 0.57 the water flow capacity is 878 (m^3). Making the total unit capacity 1378 (m^3 / MW). Now at full power, 878 units of water flow to downriver and 500MW of electricity flow to the demand node.

To add a spill option to the reservoir we need to create another unit. This is because just making extra water disappear with the penalty_down: 0, will not transfer this water to the downriver node to fulfil its needs. This spill unit has to be in entities:

  • unit_inputNode (spill_unit|reservoir)
  • unit_outputNode (spill_unit|downriver)

It needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

And parameters:

  • efficiency: 1
  • existing: A large enough number to not be a limit

The database also includes an example of a river system with two additional reservoirs and plants. Both of them flow to the reservoir already made in this how to. These two are created the exact same way as above, but with just different values and the relation unit_outputNode: (hydro_plant_2| reservoir) and unit_outputNode: (hydro_plant_3| reservoir).

In principle you can create as large river systems as you want, but each reservoir adds extra computational burden. Think about the possibility to combine the reservoirs and plants in the system and what information you lose with this approximation.

docs.title: How to create a hydro pump storage
docs.text:
(hydro_with_pump.sqlite)

For a hydro pump storage one needs the following components:

  • Demand node
  • hydro_plant unit with
  • storage node,
  • hydro_pump unit with
  • pump storage node
  • a source for external energy (pumped storage plant will lose energy due to charging losses). Wind power plant will be used as a source for external energy.

There are two ways to handle the water to electricity coefficient. Here, we convert the reservoir capacity and inflow to potential energy. The inflow should be the energy that can be created from the incoming water of each time step at maximum efficiency [MWh] per time step (on hourly steps, the potential power in MW). In the same way, the existing storage capacity should be the maximum amount of stored energy that the reservoir can hold [MWh]. In this implementation of reservoir hydro power, there is an option to spill water (energy) from the storage so that it does not run through the plant. The simplest way of allowing spilling is setting the downward penalty of the node to 0. This way the energy can disappear from the storage without a cost. The quantity of spilled energy can be seen from the results as the 'downward slack' of the node.

The reservoir node needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The required parameters of the reservoir node are (node_c and node_t sheets if using Excel input data):

  • node_type: storage
  • inflow: Mapping of the incoming water as the potential energy [MWh] per time step (on hourly steps, the potential power in MW)
  • existing: The maximum size of the reservoir as the potential energy [MWh]
  • penalty_up: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere
  • penalty_down: 0 or a large number (spilling or not)
  • a storage_method to set the behaviour on how the storage levels should be managed - for short duration storages bind_within_timeblock may be best and for seasonal storages it could be best to use bind_within_solve. If historical storage level time series are available, it can be beneficial to use fix_start in the storage_start_end_method together with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value, which will pick the storage level at the end of each solve from the time series provided as a reference (storage_state_reference_value). See flextool/schemas/spinedb_schema.json for the full enumeration of storage_binding_method values and the silent-degrade behaviour of the *_blended_weights variants; DB migration v55 renamed several legacy names (e.g. bind_within_timeset → bind_within_timeblock).

The unit is connected to the reservoir node and the output node nodeA (unit_c and unit_node_c in excel):

  • It needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.
  • The efficiency of the unit can be set to 1 as the inflow time series are directly expressed in MWh (using piecewise linear efficiency is naturally possible).
  • Set existing capacity [MW]
  • Create entities unit__inputNode: hydro_plant|reservoir and unit__outputNode: hydro_plant|nodeA.

Next create the pump_storage. This is the downstream storage from the hydro plant. Again it should be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet and have same the parameters as the reservoir:

  • node_type: storage
  • existing: The maximum size of the storage [MWh]. Note that this really represents the mass of the water and it should be converted as the potential of the energy of the reservoir-plant system. So that 1 liter of water has the same energy in both storages.
  • penalty_up: a large number to avoid creating energy from nowhere
  • penalty_down: 0

In this example database, we have both a closed system and a river system. The difference is that in the closed system the inflow is zero in both reservoir and pump_storage. In river system we have the incoming water for the reservoir as in the reservoir example. In the downstream pump storage, we implement an outflow as the negative inflow representing the minimum amount of water that has to flow out of the system at each timestep to not dry out the river. The penalty_down is set as 0 to allow it let more water go when it needs to, otherwise the storages will keep filling up if the incoming water is larger than the minimum outgoing water.

The storage level fixes should be the same in both storages (reservoir and pump storage). Here:

  • fix_start_end_method: fix_start
  • storage_state_start: 0.5
  • bind_storage_method: bind_with_timeset

This sets the starting storage levels to be 50%. The binding will also constrain the state of the storage at the end of of each timeset to be the same as in the beginning of the timeset.

Then create the pump unit and add it to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

It only needs three parameters:

  • efficiency = 1, The real efficiency of the pump is set elsewhere, so use 1.0 here.
  • existing: The wanted capacity

Set the entities as follows:

  • unit_outputNode for (hydro_plant | nodeA), (hydro_plant | pump_storage ), (hydro_pump | reservoir)
  • unit_inputNode for (hydro_plant | reservoir), (hydro_pump | pump_storage), (hydro_pump | nodeA)

Your system should look something like:

Next comes the tricky part of preserving the water and energy as both are represented as generic energy in the model. This is done by setting extra coefficents and constraints to the flows. First the hydro_plant needs to both create the energy for the demand node and pass the mass to the pump_storage. This is done by doubling the efficiency in this example to 2 and setting a extra constraint to force the output flows to both the demand node and the storage to be the same.

For the hydro plant:

  • Efficiency: 2

Create a new constraint (here plant_storage_nodeA_split), add it to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet and add the parameters:

  • sense: equal
  • constant: 0.0

And for the unit_outputNodes:

  • (hydro_plant | nodeA) constraint_flow_coeff Map: plant_storage_nodeA_split , 1
  • (hydro_plant | pump_storage) constraint_flow_coeff Map: plant_storage_nodeA_split , -1
  • Meaning: 
    flow to nodeA - flow to pump_storage = 0

As for the pump storage, we will have to make sure that the same amount of water leaves the pump_storage and enters the reservoir. Also it still should use electricity from the demand node without increasing the amount of water that is moving from storage to another. First to prevent the energy from the demand node from increasing the water flow, add a coefficient to the flow between the demand node and the pump.

unit_inputNode (hydro_pump|nodeA):

  • Coefficient: 0 (Default is 1)

This prevents the water amount from increasing as: 

unit_output_flow = coeff1 * unit_input_flow1 + coeff2 * unit_input_flow2.
We still have to make the unit to consume electricity even though it does not affect the unit output directly. This is done by setting a new constraint to tie the flows to the pump unit from pump storage and the nodeA. Add a constraint (here pump_storage_nodeA_fix), add it to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet , and add the parameters:

  • sense: equal
  • constant: 0.0

And setting parameters for unit_inputNode:

  • (hydro_pump | nodeA) constraint_flow_coeff Map: pump_storage_nodeA_fix , 2
  • (hydro_pump | pump_storage) constraint_flow_coeff Map: pump_storage_nodeA_fix , -1

2 * flow_from_nodeA - flow_from_pump_storage = 0
Note that here the (constraint_flow_coeff Map: plant_storage_nodeA_split , 2) actually sets the efficiency of the pump. This means that here only half of the electricity used by the pump can be recovered when that amount of water is used by the hydro_plant. (Two units of energy are used to move 1 unit of water_energy) The constraint_flow_coeff for pump_input should therefore be (1/efficiency)

docs.title: How to create combined heat and power (CHP)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: coal_chp) init - west - coal_chp - heat

First, a new heat node is added with the necessary parameters. The nodes can be used for energy form of energy or matter, so the heat demand node does not differ from the electricity demand node.

The heat node needs to be added to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet.

The required parameters are:

  • node_type: balance
  • inflow: Map for the heat demand (negative) [MW]
  • penalty_up: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere
  • penalty_down: a large number to prefer not creating energy from nowhere

The heating systems tend to have some level of storage capability, so one could also add storage parameters to the node as well, but here they are not used.

Then the coal_chp unit is made with a high efficiency parameter, since CHP units convert fuel energy to power and heat at high overall rates. In FlexTool, efficiency is a property of the unit - it demarcates at what rate the sum of inputs is converted to the sum of outputs. However, without any additional constraints, the unit is free to choose in what proportion to use inputs and in what proportion to use outputs. In units with only one input and output, this freedom does not exist, but in here, the coal_chp needs to be constrained as otherwise the unit could produce only electricity and no heat at 90% efficiency, which is not feasible.

This CHP plant is an another example where the user defined constraint (see the last equation in the previous example) is used to achieve the desired behaviour. In a backpressure CHP, heat and power outputs are fixed - increase one of them, and you must also increase the other. In an extraction CHP plant the relation is more complicated - there is an allowed operating area between heat and power. Both can be represented in FlexTool, but here a backpressure example is given. An extraction plant would require two or more greater_than and/or less_than constraints to define an operating area: the extraction CHP of How to model cogeneration with desalination is built this way. The shipped coal_chp_extraction alternative takes another way: it turns coal_chp_fix off (is_enabled no) and shapes the operating area with conversion_flow_coeff and capacity_max_coeff on the outputs, as the next paragraph explains.

For extraction CHP specifically, the unit__inputNode / unit__outputNode coefficients interact. conversion_flow_coeff multiplies into the edge's contribution in the conversion equation (conversion_indirect) — a higher coefficient means more input energy per unit of that edge's output, so a premium electricity output might use conversion_flow_coeff = 2 while a byproduct heat output uses 0.2. The unit capacity caps the sum of the outputs, and capacity_max_coeff on an output adds a per-output upper cap. With a minimum load (min_load plus a startup_method), the floor electricity + heat >= min_load × online capacity applies once, to the sum of the outputs, so both the pure-condensing mode (heat = 0) and the pure-heat mode (electricity = 0) remain available while online with the default coefficients. Only if an output must carry part of the minimum load on its own, set capacity_min_coeff on that output (e.g. 1 on electricity: electricity >= min_load × online capacity, which rules out the pure-heat mode). On the inputs, input_share_max limits the share of the full-load input a single input may supply (default 1: no effective limit) and input_share_min sets the smallest share of the current input an input must supply while the unit runs (default 0). Without the capacity-coefficient split, each output would be capped individually at conversion_flow_coeff × capacity, which prevents the model from using the full operating envelope.

Electricity and heat outputs are fixed by adding a new constraint coal_chp_fix where the heat and power co-efficients are fixed. You need to create the two entities unit__outputNode, for coal_chp--heat and coal_chp--west. As can be seen in the bottom part of the figure below, the constraint_flow_coeff parameter for the coal_chp--heat and coal_chp--west is set as a map value where the constraint name matches with the coal_chp_fix constraint entity name. The values are set so that the constraint equation forces the heat output to be twice as large as the electricity output.

Create constraint coal_chp_fix, add it to an alternative in the Entity Alternative sheet and add parameters:

  • sense: equal
  • constant: 0.0

Create unit_outputNode (coal_chp|heat):

  • constraint_flow_coeff : coal_chp_fix, -0.5

Create unit_outputNode (coal_chp|west):

  • constraint_flow_coeff : coal_chp_fix, 1

Again, the negative value can be turned positive by arranging it to the right side of the equality, creating this:

1 x *electricity* = 0.5 x *heat*, which is true only if *heat* is 2 x *electricity*

docs.title: How to model cogeneration with desalination
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenarios: desal_backpressure, desal_extraction, desal_ro_invest, desal_water_storage) init - west - coal - desal_system - (one desalination alternative)

Water is one more node. A desalination plant turns heat or electricity into fresh water. In FlexTool the water is a node like any other, and its unit of measure is your choice. Here the node water is in m³: its flows are in m³/h, its demand in m³/h and its storage in m³. Set unit_of_measure m3 on water (and, if you like, MWh_th on desal_heat) so that the results, plots and the AI assistant say m³/h, m³ and CUR/m³ instead of MW, MWh and CUR/MWh; FlexTool changes no number (see Units of measure). A thermal desalination unit (for example multi-effect distillation, MED) takes heat from a CHP plant. A reverse-osmosis (RO) unit takes electricity. The four examples show a backpressure CHP, an extraction CHP, an RO investment and a water storage.

The example system. The alternatives init, west and coal are the tutorial's system: the 48-hour solve y2020_2day_dispatch, the node west and the 500 MW coal_plant fed from coal_market. Coal costs 20 CUR/MWh of fuel; at efficiency 0.4 that is 50 CUR/MWh of electricity. The alternative desal_system adds:

Alternative Entity Parameter Value desal_system node west inflow −300 [MW] desal_system node desal_heat node_type, penalty_up, penalty_down balance, 1000, 1000 [CUR/MWh] desal_system node water node_type, inflow balance, −3000 [m³/h] desal_system node water penalty_up, penalty_down 50, 50 [CUR/m³] desal_system unit bp_chp conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 0.85, 600 [MW] desal_system constraint bp_chp_ratio sense, constant equal, 0 desal_system unit__outputNode (bp_chp, west) constraint_flow_coeff (bp_chp_ratio | 1) desal_system unit__outputNode (bp_chp, desal_heat) constraint_flow_coeff (bp_chp_ratio | −0.5) desal_system unit med_desal conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 12 [m³/MWh], 3000 [m³/h]

Entities. desal_system turns on the nodes desal_heat and water and the units bp_chp and med_desal (Entity Alternative). bp_chp has a unit__inputNode (bp_chp, coal_market) and two unit__outputNode entities, (bp_chp, west) and (bp_chp, desal_heat). med_desal has a unit__inputNode (med_desal, desal_heat) and a unit__outputNode (med_desal, water).

The results. The results per hour are the same in all 48 hours. The objective is the cost per hour × 8760 / 10⁶ (the 48 hours scaled to a year).

Scenario Water [m³/h] CHP [MW] coal_plant [MW] Cost per hour [CUR] Objective [M CUR] desal_backpressure MED 3000 bp_chp: heat 250, power 125, fuel 441.18 175 17 573.5 153.944 desal_extraction MED 3000 ext_chp: heat 250, power 300, fuel 750 0 15 000 131.400 desal_ro_invest MED 1000, RO 2000 bp_chp: heat 83.33, power 41.67 266.33 16 257.8 + the RO annuity 147.233 desal_water_storage MED 3000 (demand 2000 or 4000) bp_chp: heat 250, power 125 175 17 573.5 153.944

docs.title: Backpressure CHP and thermal desalination
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: desal_backpressure) init - west - coal - desal_system

What it does. med_desal makes 12 m³ of water per MWh of heat, so 3000 m³/h needs 250 MW of heat. bp_chp_ratio is power − 0.5 × heat = 0, so heat = 2 × power, as in the CHP example. The water demand therefore fixes the CHP: heat 250 MW, power 125 MW and fuel (125 + 250) / 0.85 = 441.18 MW. coal_plant makes the other 175 MW. This is the demand-driven must-run of option 5: nothing forces bp_chp to run except the water demand.

The water slack price. The penalty_up of water (50 CUR/m³) must be above the cost of the dearest real way to make a cubic metre, including the cost of the power the CHP is forced to make with it. Otherwise the model leaves water demand unserved instead. In a winter with low electricity demand, the power made with the water can exceed the demand; the model then weighs dumping that power at the penalty_down of west against unserved water. Check that node_slack_up of water is 0, and give the system flexibility through RO, water storage or heat storage rather than a low penalty.

Own electricity use. A real MED or MSF plant also draws about 1.5–4 kWh of electricity per m³ for its pumps; the example leaves this out. To include it, give med_desal a second unit__inputNode (med_desal, west) with conversion_flow_coeff 0, so it stays out of the conversion. Then tie it to the water output with an equal user constraint: electricity input − 0.0025 × water output = 0 for 2.5 kWh/m³.

One equality. A backpressure plant has one degree of freedom: the ratio fixes power and heat together. One equal user constraint is enough.

Efficiency above 1. efficiency is output / input in the units of the nodes, here m³ per MWh. A value above 1 is fine. The unit's capacity is on its output side, so existing 3000 is in m³/h. At full load its input capacity factor (unit_cf__inputNode) is therefore 1/efficiency.

Very large ratios. With a very large ratio the input coefficients can fall below the model parameter small_number_threshold and become 0, so the unit would make water for free; see efficiency in units. Rescale the unit of measure (for example 1000 m³) if that happens.

docs.title: Extraction CHP: an operating region
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: desal_extraction) init - west - coal - desal_system - desal_extraction

The data. desal_extraction turns bp_chp off (its Entity Alternative is false) and turns on the unit ext_chp, with the same input and outputs as bp_chp:

Entity Parameter Value unit ext_chp conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 0.45, 1000 [MW] unit__outputNode (ext_chp, west) conversion_flow_coeff 1 unit__outputNode (ext_chp, desal_heat) conversion_flow_coeff 0.15 constraint ext_chp_backpressure_line sense, constant greater_than, 0 constraint ext_chp_max_heat sense, constant less_than, 0 unit__outputNode (ext_chp, west) constraint_flow_coeff (ext_chp_backpressure_line | 1) unit__outputNode (ext_chp, desal_heat) constraint_flow_coeff (ext_chp_backpressure_line | −0.5), (ext_chp_max_heat | 1) unit ext_chp constraint_capacity_coeff (ext_chp_max_heat | −0.6)

What it does. The conversion is 0.45 × fuel = power + 0.15 × heat: each MWh of heat costs 0.15 MWh of power (the power-loss ratio). The two constraints draw the operating region. ext_chp_backpressure_line is power − 0.5 × heat ≥ 0: the plant cannot make more heat than on its backpressure line. ext_chp_max_heat is heat − 0.6 × capacity ≤ 0: a flow term and a capacity term in one row, written for every time step. Inside the region the model chooses power and heat freely.

What the capacity caps. The unit's capacity (existing 1000) caps power + heat, the sum of the outputs (see capacity_max_coeff in units), not the fuel. So the top edge of the region is power + heat ≤ 1000, not the iso-fuel line power + 0.15 × heat ≤ constant that is drawn for an extraction turbine. For an iso-fuel edge, add a less_than row with the flow coefficients power 1 and heat 0.15 and a constraint_capacity_coeff −c on the unit, with c the full-condensing power per unit of capacity. Size the capacity so that the sum cap does not cut that edge: power + heat is largest on the backpressure line, at 1.5 / 0.65 = 2.31 × the full-condensing power. A minimum condensing flow or a minimum power line is one more greater_than row of the same kind.

The results. Power from ext_chp costs 20 / 0.45 = 44.4 CUR/MWh, less than the 50 of coal_plant. So ext_chp makes all 300 MW of power and the 250 MW of heat, with fuel (300 + 0.15 × 250) / 0.45 = 750 MW. Power ≥ 0.5 × heat holds (300 ≥ 125) and the heat limit (600 MW) does not bind.

A constraint with nothing in it. bp_chp_ratio still exists here, but all its coefficients are on flows of bp_chp, which is off. Its row reads 0 = 0, so FlexTool leaves it out of the model and prints a warning that names it: in desal_extraction this warning is expected. To switch a constraint off on purpose, set its is_enabled to no, as the coal_chp_extraction alternative does.

docs.title: Reverse osmosis investment
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: desal_ro_invest) init - west - coal - desal_system - desal_ro_invest

The data. desal_ro_invest turns on the unit ro_desal, with a unit__inputNode (ro_desal, west) and a unit__outputNode (ro_desal, water), and sets invest_periods [p2020] on the solve y2020_2day_dispatch:

Entity Parameter Value unit ro_desal conversion_method, efficiency constant_efficiency, 250 [m³/MWh] unit ro_desal invest_method, invest_max_total invest_total, 2000 [m³/h] unit ro_desal invest_cost 30 (= 30 000 CUR per m³/h) unit ro_desal lifetime, discount_rate 20, 0.05

invest_cost is per kW of the unit's capacity unit. FlexTool reads every capacity as if it were in MW, and invest_cost is per kW, that is per 0.001 of the capacity unit (with unit_of_measure m3 on water the results label it CUR/(0.001 m³/h) and the annuity CUR/(m³/h)). For a capacity in m³/h, enter the cost per m³/h divided by 1000: 30 000 CUR per m³/h is invest_cost 30. The same holds for fixed_cost. The capacities themselves are entered in m³/h unchanged: existing, invest_max_total and invest_min_total of 2000 m³/h are 2000, not 2. An other_operational_cost on a water flow is per m³ directly (it is per MWh of flow, no ÷ 1000).

MED or RO. A cubic metre from MED costs 1/12 MWh of heat. The heat costs 1.5/0.85 MWh of fuel at 20 CUR/MWh, but the CHP also makes 0.5/12 MWh of power that coal_plant would otherwise make at 50 CUR/MWh: 2.941 − 2.083 = 0.858 CUR/m³. A cubic metre from RO costs 0.004 MWh of power at 50 CUR/MWh = 0.2 CUR/m³. The saving, 0.658 CUR/m³ × 8760 h = 5 764 CUR per m³/h and year, is more than twice the annuity (30 000 × 0.0802 = 2 407 CUR per m³/h and year at 5 % over 20 years).

The results. ro_desal is invested to its 2000 m³/h limit and uses 8 MW of power. MED makes the other 1000 m³/h, with 83.33 MW of heat, so bp_chp makes 41.67 MW of power and coal_plant 300 + 8 − 41.67 = 266.33 MW. The operation costs 16 257.8 CUR/h (142.419 M CUR a year) and the RO annuity is 2000 × 30 000 × 0.0802 = 4.815 M CUR: 147.233 M CUR. The investment is in unit_capacity__d and in the unit investment & retirement row of the costs.

docs.title: Water storage
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: desal_water_storage) init - west - coal - desal_system - desal_water_storage

The data. desal_water_storage makes water a storage and gives it a demand that changes during the day:

Entity Parameter Value node water node_type, existing storage, 15 000 [m³] node water storage_binding_method bind_within_timeblock node water storage_start_end_method, storage_state_start fix_start, 0 node water inflow a time series: in each day 12 h at −2000, then 12 h at −4000 [m³/h]

What it does. The mean demand is 3000 m³/h, the capacity of MED. Without the storage, MED could not cover the 4000 m³/h hours and the water slack would pay 50 CUR/m³. With it, MED runs flat at 3000 m³/h in every hour: the storage fills to 12 000 m³ in the 12 hours of low demand and empties in the 12 hours of high demand, twice. The cost is that of desal_backpressure. The case is tight by design (the MED capacity equals the mean demand), so the storage state is unique: see node_state__dt.

Storage in m³. A water storage is a storage node in the water's own unit. existing is in m³ here, and for a storage invest_cost enter the cost per m³ ÷ 1000 (as per kWh for an MWh storage), the same rule as for RO.

docs.title: How to add a reserve
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite: scenario network_coal_wind_reserve)

In FlexTool, reserves are defined for a group of nodes. If there is a need to have a reserve requirement for a single node, it needs its own group. Therefore, when creating a reserve, the first step is to add a new group (e.g. electricity) with all member nodes (e.g. west, east and north) using the group__node entity. Then, a new reserve categories can be added (e.g. primary) to the reserve entity. Finally, make sure there are up and down entities in the `UpDown' entity. These are hard-coded names in FlexTool and need to be used when creating reserves.

Next, the reserve requirement will be defined. An entity between the reserve__upDown__group class (e.g. primary--up--electricity) allows to define the reserve parameters reserve_method, reservation (i.e. the amount of reserve) and penalty_reserve (i.e. the penalty cost in case of lack of reserve). For example, a constant of 10 MW could be used. Even though the name of the reserve_method is timeseries_only, it can also accept a constant value - it's an exogenous reserve requirement whereas the other two reserve methods are endogenous. Dynamic reserve method calculates the reserve requirement from generation and loads according to user defined factors (increase_reserve_ratio). Largest failure method will force enough reserve to cope with a failure of the chosen unit and connection flows.

Parameters from the reserve__upDown__unit__node class should be used to define how different units can contribute to different reserves. Note that the entities in this class need to be added to the Entity Alternative sheet. Parameter max_share says how large a share of the unit's capacity at that node (its built capacity: existing + invested − retired; at a node the unit consumes from, its full-load input there) can be held for this reserve category (e.g. coal_plant may be limited by ramp constraint to provide only 1% of its capacity to an upward primary reserve.) Meanwhile, parameter reliability affects what portion of the reserved capacity actually contributes to the reserve (e.g. wind_plant may contribute only 80% of its generation to reserve due to uncertainty).

If the reserve is provided by a battery or other storage (a unit discharging from, or a connection/charger tied to, a storage node), set reserve_duration (hours) on the reserve__upDown__group entity so the storage actually holds enough energy to sustain the committed reserve power. For example, a 4-hour upward reserve from a battery uses reserve_duration = 4: the model then guarantees the battery's stored energy can back its reserve commitment for 4 hours (corrected by the round-trip efficiency). Without reserve_duration the reserve is instantaneous-power-only — the battery could commit reserve it has no energy to deliver. The coupling only applies to storage-backed providers; ordinary fuel-fed units are unaffected.

docs.title: How to add a minimum load, start-up and ramp
docs.text:
(ramp_and_start_up.sqlite)

Some plants cannot vary their output freely, but have some cost and limits associated with it. In this example we will add the minimum load behaviour to a coal_plant unit and add the cost and limits for starting up and ramping the plant respectively.

Minimum load requires that the unit must have an online variable in addition to flow variables and therefore a startup_method needs to be defined and an optional startup_cost can be given. The startup_cost is added to the total cost every time the unit is required to start-up. Here we use a value 1000 (Currency/MW started up).

The options for the startup_method are no_startup, linear and binary. binary would require an integer variable so linear is chosen. However, this means that the unit can startup partially. The minimum online will still apply, but it is the minimum of the online capacity in any given moment (sum of output flows >= min_load x capacity x online), where 0 <= online <= 1. The minimum load applies once per unit, to the sum of its outputs; a unit with several inputs can run on any mix of them.

The units online in a time step are linked to the units online in the previous step along the timeline, in the same way as ramp limits: also from the last step of a period into a period whose time steps continue it on the same timeline, and into the first step of a forecast branch. A step without a previous step — the first step of a solve, the first step of a period that does not continue the previous one (e.g. a period that reuses the same timeset), the first step after a gap in the timeline and the first step of a representative period — is linked to the last step of its own stretch of the timeline (the steps up to the next gap or the end of the period): the commitment cycles within that stretch and never across a gap, a representative-period start or into another period. So a stretch that ends offline starts up (and pays startup_cost) at its first step when it needs the unit there. Only the start of a stretch wraps: the step before a gap has no next step, so no pre-shutdown output limit applies there. In a rolling solve the units online that the previous roll realized are carried to the steps of the next roll that continue its last realized step on the timeline (also when the next solve has longer time steps: it continues the finer step that ends where its previous step ends); a roll that starts after a gap, at a new year that reuses the timeset or at a representative-period start takes no carry and cycles within its stretch.

The online variable also allows to change the efficiency of the plant between the minimum and full loads. A unit with a part-load efficiency will obey the following equation:

  + sum_i[ input(i) * input_coefficient(i) ]
  =
  + sum_o[ output(o) * output_coefficient(o) ] * slope
  + online * section

where   slope = 1 / efficiency - section
  and section = 1 / efficiency 
                - ( 1 / efficiency - min_load / efficiency_at_min_load) / ( 1 - min_load )

By default, input_coefficient and output_coefficient are 1, but if there is a need to tweak their relative contributions, these coefficients allow to do so (e.g. a coal plant might have lower efficiency when using lignite than when using brown coal).

The input is required at different ouput levels is shown in the figure below, when Capacity = 100, Efficiency = 0.8, Minimum load = 0.6 and Efficiency at minimum load = 0.5.

Next we will add ramp limits. With the ramping limits, the user can force the change of a flow from a unit to be below a certain value each timestep. The ramping is an attribute of the flow. Therefore it does not require the minimum load behaviour and its parameters are added to the unit_outputNode entity:

  • ramp_method: ramp_limit, ramp_cost or both. ramp_limit uses the speeds below, ramp_cost the cost below, both uses both.
  • ramp_speed_up: Limit on how fast the plant can ramp up. (fraction of unit / min) ie. Value 0.01 allows the change of 60% of capacity per hour; with 2-hour time steps, 120% (i.e. no limit). The change between two time steps of different length uses their average length.
  • ramp_speed_down: Limit on how fast the plant can ramp down. (fraction of unit / min) ie. Value 0.01 allows the change of 60% of capacity per hour.

The first time step of a solve, the first step after a gap in the timeline and the first step of a representative period have no ramp limit (there is no previous step to ramp from). A rolling window ramps from the flow of the previous window where it continues the previous window's last realized step on the timeline; a solve with longer time steps continues the finer step that ends where its own previous step ends (by position in time). Unlike the online status, the ramp has no cyclic link from the first step of a stretch to its last step.

  • ramp_cost: The cost of changing the flow [CUR/MW]: every MW of change from the previous time step costs this much, up and down alike, whatever the length of the steps (a change is an event, like a start-up). It uses the same previous step as the ramp limit above, so there is no cost at the first step of a solve, after a gap or at the start of a representative period, and a rolling window is charged once for the change from the previous window's realized flow. A start-up from zero pays both the startup cost and the ramp cost. The cost is reported in the cost category ramps. With a ramp cost, the price at a node where a ramp-costed unit sets the price and its flow does not change is not unique: it can lie up to 2 × ramp_cost / step duration [CUR/MWh] above or below that unit's marginal cost.

docs.title: How to give a unit a start-up fuel or start-up heat
docs.text:
A start-up can use energy that the running unit does not: a coal unit is started on oil, a gas turbine burns gas to warm up, a CSP turbine takes steam from its tank before it delivers power. The input arc of the unit (unit__inputNode) says what it supplies, with startup_input_method:

  • just_input (default) - the normal input flow;
  • startup_and_input - the normal input flow, and each start-up also takes startup_energy × MW started from the node;
  • startup_only - only the start-up energy: the arc has no flow, and it takes no part in the unit's conversion, capacity, input shares or ramps.

startup_energy is in MWh per MW started (constant or period). The unit needs online variables: startup_method linear or binary (or a minimum_time_method). With linear start-ups a start-up of 0.6 units of a 100 MW unit is 60 MW started; the model stays an LP.

Coal started on oil. A coal unit coal_plant with its fuel input (coal_plant, coal_market) gets a second input arc (coal_plant, oil_market) with startup_input_method startup_only and startup_energy 2. A start-up of 60 MW then takes 120 MWh of oil from oil_market in the step it starts in, priced as the oil commodity and with the oil's co2_content. The oil arc is not a flow, so the unit stays a one-input, one-output unit (no extra flow variable, no conversion row), and the oil cannot be used to run the unit.

CSP turbine started on tank heat. A turbine whose start-up heat comes from the tank uses its normal input: on (csp_turbine, csp_heat) set startup_input_method startup_and_input and startup_energy (for example 0.5 MWh_th per MW_e started). A start-up of 20 MW takes 10 MWh_th from the tank on top of the heat the turbine converts.

Results. unit_startup_energy__dt [MWh in the step] and unit_startup_energy__d [MWh/a] show the start-up input per unit and node. The unit's input from the node (unit__inputNode__dt / __d), the commodity costs, the CO2 emissions and costs and the node balance include it.

Caveats. The start-up input is not part of user constraints (constraint_flow_coeff), flow groups or the capacity margin. A solve whose reduce_unit_detail_method leaves out the online variables (online, online_ramps) also leaves out the start-up input, as it leaves out the start-up cost: an investment solve at that level under-counts both. See the startup_input_method / startup_energy entries in Units.

docs.title: How to add minimum uptime and downtime
docs.text:
Some power plants cannot be started and stopped freely due to thermal stress, safety requirements, or operational constraints. Minimum uptime forces a unit to stay online for a specified duration after starting up. Minimum downtime forces a unit to stay offline for a specified duration after shutting down.

To add minimum uptime and/or downtime constraints to a unit:

  1. Set the minimum_time_method parameter on the unit:

    • min_uptime - only enforce minimum uptime
    • min_downtime - only enforce minimum downtime
    • both - enforce both constraints
    • none - no minimum time constraints (default)

  2. Set the duration parameters (in hours):

    • min_uptime - e.g. 8 for an 8-hour minimum online time
    • min_downtime - e.g. 4 for a 4-hour minimum offline time

Setting minimum_time_method to anything other than none will automatically activate online variables for the unit (at least linear startup), even if startup_method is not explicitly defined. This means you do not need to separately set startup_method to linear or binary, although you can if you also want startup costs or binary commitment.

The minimum time constraints work with variable timestep durations. The constraint checks that the cumulative duration of consecutive online (or offline) timesteps meets the minimum requirement, rather than simply counting timesteps.

The look-back follows the timeline in the same way as ramp limits: it continues into a period whose time steps continue the previous period's on the same timeline and into the steps before a forecast branch starts, and stops at a gap in the timeline (the minimum time restarts after the gap), at the start of a representative period, at a period that reuses the same timeset as the previous one and at the first step of a solve. In rolling window solves, the start-ups and shut-downs that the previous roll realized count for the time steps of the next roll that continue its last realized step on the timeline, in the same way as the ramp continues: the same period, a period that continues it and every forecast branch that starts there (not a period that reuses the same timeset, a step after a gap or a representative-period start). So the solve horizon overlap does not need to cover the minimum times. A solve with longer time steps (for example a 6-hour storage roll after an hourly dispatch) continues the realized hourly step that ends where its own previous step ends, by position in time. A warning is printed only when a solve continues the timeline of an earlier solve but its first step neither follows nor ends at the earlier solve's last realized step (a hole or an overlap between the two), since no realized on-line history reaches it then.

If the unit also has ramp limits (ramp_method with ramp_speed_up, ramp_speed_down), the model additionally tightens the maximum output in the startup and pre-shutdown timesteps based on how fast the unit can ramp within one timestep. A unit that starts in a timestep reaches on average at most min_load + ½ × ramp_speed_up × 60 × timestep duration of the started capacity in that step (it synchronises at minimum load and then ramps up: half a step's ramp on average), and in the step before it shuts down at most min_load + ½ × ramp_speed_down × 60 × timestep duration (both capped at full output and by availability). A unit online for a single step gets the smaller of the two. On an input with a ramp limit of a unit with several inputs or outputs, the limit is on the input it draws (at minimum load it needs the input of its minimum-load output). Without ramp limits, the unit can reach full output immediately after starting.

Startups and shutdowns count exactly the units coming online and going offline. A unit with online variables ramps on its online capacity: the units online in both steps change by at most the ramp; a unit starting in a step reaches at most the startup-step output above, and a unit shutting down drops from at least its minimum load (and, in the step before, at most the pre-shutdown output). Starting and stopping units in the same step therefore gives no extra ramp room on a unit's output. On an input, or on one output of a unit with several outputs, a start/stop pair can still gain up to the minimum-load share of that flow, which the startup cost pays for.

docs.title: How to make a unit run all the time (must-run)
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenarios: must_run_none, must_run_profile, must_run_constraint_one, must_run_fleet_output_floor, must_run_flowgroup, must_run_heat_demand, must_run_fleet_two_online, must_run_min_load_only) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - (one must-run alternative)

No single switch. FlexTool has no must-run parameter. A unit runs when the optimisation wants it to, so a must-run is a floor that you put on its flow or on its units online. The table lists the ways to do it. The examples are the same small system with a different floor each.

Option Where it is set LP or MIP What it forces When to use it 1. Profile lower limit unit__node__profile, profile_method lower_limit LP flow ≥ profile × availability × capacity A share of the capacity that follows investments or changes in time 2. User constraint on one flow constraint + constraint_flow_coeff on unit__outputNode LP flow ≥ constant [MW] A fixed MW floor on one unit, constant or per period 3. User constraint on a fleet's output the same, with a coefficient on each unit LP sum of the flows ≥ constant [MW] A floor on a group of units; the model picks the cheapest ones 4. flowGroup minimum flow flowGroup + flowGroup__unit__node, min_instant_flow LP sum of the member flows ≥ min_instant_flow [MW] As option 3, also with a floor that changes in time 5. Demand-driven the unit's other output has a demand (heat, steam, water) LP nothing directly: the unit runs because its other product is needed CHP and other plants that run for a heat or process demand 6. User constraint on the units online constraint + constraint_online_coeff on unit MIP with binary startup (LP with linear) at least N units online, each at least at min_load A requirement for N machines on line, for example for system strength

The example system. The alternatives init, west, coal and wind are the tutorial's system: the 48-hour solve y2020_2day_dispatch, the node west, the 500 MW coal_plant fed from coal_market and the 1000 MW wind_plant. Coal costs 20 CUR/MWh of fuel at efficiency 0.4, i.e. 50 CUR/MWh of electricity. The other alternatives add:

Alternative Entity Parameter Value must_run_system node west inflow −300 [MW] must_run_system unit__outputNode (wind_plant, west) other_operational_cost 1 [CUR/MWh] must_run_fleet unit steam_1, steam_2, steam_3 entity alternative on must_run_fleet unit steam_k conversion_method, efficiency, existing constant_efficiency, 0.4, 100 [MW] must_run_fleet unit__outputNode (steam_k, west) other_operational_cost 0, 1 and 2 [CUR/MWh]

Entities of the fleet. Each steam_k also needs a unit__inputNode (steam_k, coal_market) and a unit__outputNode (steam_k, west). The other_operational_cost is on the output flow, not on the unit. The costs of 0, 1 and 2 CUR/MWh make the model always prefer the units in that order.

The results. Wind can cover the demand in every hour, so without a floor no coal runs. The results per hour are the same in all 48 hours:

Scenario Dispatch [MW] Cost per hour [CUR] Objective [M CUR] must_run_none wind 300 300 2.628 must_run_profile baseload_plant 200, wind 100 10 100 88.476 must_run_constraint_one coal_plant 150, wind 150 7 650 67.014 must_run_fleet_output_floor steam_1 100, wind 200 5 200 45.552 must_run_flowgroup steam_1 100, wind 200 5 200 45.552 must_run_heat_demand coal_chp 150 (and 300 heat), wind 150 10 150 88.914 must_run_fleet_two_online steam_1 50, steam_2 50, wind 200 5 250 45.990 must_run_min_load_only wind 300 300 2.628

Floors are hard. None of these floors has a slack of its own. If a floor forces more output than the node can use, the extra energy goes to the node's downward slack, which costs penalty_down (with penalty_method off on the node, the model is infeasible instead). If the unit's capacity or another floor cannot meet a floor, the model is infeasible.

Set the sense. Without sense, a constraint is equal: always set greater_than for a floor.

docs.title: Option 1: profile lower limit
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_profile) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_profile

The data. Create a profile (here must_run_share) with profile 0.4 and connect it to the flow with a unit__node__profile entity (baseload_plant, west, must_run_share) with profile_method lower_limit. baseload_plant is a coal unit like coal_plant: unit__inputNode (baseload_plant, coal_market), unit__outputNode (baseload_plant, west), conversion_method constant_efficiency, efficiency 0.4 and existing 500 [MW]. The alternative must_run_profile holds all of these values and turns baseload_plant on.

What it does. In every time step the flow is at least profile × availability × capacity, here 0.4 × 500 = 200 MW. The capacity includes invested capacity, so the floor grows with investments. The profile can be a constant, a period, a time series or both (see units constrained by profiles), so the floor can change from hour to hour.

Give the profile a value

A unit__node__profile entity whose profile has no value in the scenario would hold the flow at 0: profile_method defaults to upper_limit, and a missing profile value is 0. FlexTool stops with an error that names the link. Entities are the same in every scenario, so fix it with one of these:

  • give the profile a value in an alternative that every scenario uses;
  • set profile_method lower_limit in such an alternative (a missing value is then a floor of 0, which does nothing);
  • put the profile on a unit that is on only where the profile is used, as the example does with baseload_plant.

docs.title: Option 2: user constraint on one flow
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_constraint_one) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_constraint_one

The data. Create a constraint coal_plant_floor with sense greater_than and constant 150. On unit__outputNode (coal_plant, west) set constraint_flow_coeff to the map (coal_plant_floor | 1).

What it does. In every time step, the flow from coal_plant to west is at least 150 MW. The constant is in MW (the unit of the flow times its coefficient). It can be a constant or a period map, not a time series. The floor does not follow investments; use a constraint_capacity_coeff term on the unit (see user constraints) if it should.

docs.title: Option 3: user constraint on a fleet's output
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_fleet_output_floor) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_fleet - must_run_fleet_output_floor

The data. Create a constraint steam_fleet_output_floor with sense greater_than and constant 100, and set constraint_flow_coeff (steam_fleet_output_floor | 1) on the output flow of each of steam_1, steam_2 and steam_3.

What it does. The sum of the three flows is at least 100 MW in every time step. The model chooses how to share it: here steam_1, the cheapest, runs at 100 MW and the other two stay off. Use this when the requirement is on the fleet, not on each unit.

docs.title: Option 4: flowGroup minimum flow
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_flowgroup) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_fleet - must_run_flowgroup

The data. Create a flowGroup steam_fleet, add the flows with flowGroup__unit__node entities (steam_fleet, steam_k, west) and set min_instant_flow to 100.

What it does. The same as option 3: the sum of the member flows is at least 100 MW (output flows count positive, input flows negative). min_instant_flow can also be a time series or a period+time map, so the floor can change in time (see flow groups). A user constraint is the better choice when the flows need different weights.

docs.title: Option 5: demand-driven running
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_heat_demand) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - coal_chp - heat

The data. The alternatives coal_chp and heat of the CHP example add a node heat with inflow −300 [MW] and the unit coal_chp, with input coal_market, outputs west and heat and efficiency 0.9. The constraint coal_chp_fix (sense equal) has the coefficient 1 on the west output and −0.5 on the heat output.

What it does. Many plants that run all the time do so because their other product is needed. Here coal_chp must make 300 MW of heat for the heat node, and coal_chp_fix ties its electricity to half of the heat. So it makes 150 MW of electricity in every hour, although wind could cover the whole electricity demand. Model the demand that makes the plant run instead of forcing its output, when you know that demand. The heat demand, not an artificial floor, is then what makes the plant run, and the heat node's price shows what it costs. A water demand works the same way: see How to model cogeneration with desalination.

docs.title: Option 6: user constraint on the units online
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_fleet_two_online) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_fleet - must_run_fleet_two_online

The data. On each of steam_1, steam_2 and steam_3 set startup_method binary, min_load 0.5 and constraint_online_coeff (steam_fleet_two_online | 1). Create a constraint steam_fleet_two_online with sense greater_than and constant 2. The example also sets solver_mip_gap 0 on the solve, so the solver proves the best integer solution.

What it does. In every time step at least two of the three units are online, and each online unit makes at least its minimum load: steam_1 and steam_2 are online at 50 MW each. The count is in units of virtual_unitsize; without it, of the unit's existing capacity (here 100 MW, so each unit is one), else of 1000 MW. Set virtual_unitsize on a unit that is invested. A constraint_online_coeff on a unit without online variables is an error. See the two of three units online example.

Output floor or count. The output floor of option 3 and this count cost almost the same here (5 200 against 5 250 CUR/h), but they force different things. The floor asks for 100 MW from any units; the count asks for two machines on line, whatever their output. Use the count only when the requirement really is about machines (for example inertia or short-circuit power from several units); it needs integer online variables, which makes the solve slower.

Binary or linear. With binary startup the count is a whole number, so ≥ 1.5 needs two units online. With linear startup the count is continuous: ≥ 1.5 keeps 1.5 units' worth of capacity online (150 MW here), with the minimum load applying to that capacity, not two whole machines. Linear is an LP and solves fast; binary gives the exact count.

An exact count. To fix the number of units online, use the same data with sense equal and constant N. The constant can be a constant or a period map, not a time series. There is no parameter that fixes a unit's online status directly; only a stochastic realization solve fixes it internally.

docs.title: min_load is not a must-run
docs.text:
(examples.sqlite scenario: must_run_min_load_only) init - west - coal - wind - must_run_system - must_run_fleet - must_run_min_load_only

What it does. The steam units have startup_method binary and min_load 0.5, but no floor. The minimum load applies only while a unit is online, and the model is free to keep it offline, so all three stay off and wind covers the demand (the same result as must_run_none). min_load limits how low an online unit can go; it does not make the unit run.

docs.title: Avoid a negative cost as a must-run bonus
docs.text:
Why not. A large negative other_operational_cost makes the unit run, but it pays the unit for every MWh it makes. The bonus is then in the node prices, the cost results and the objective, so none of them is the system's real cost.

Dumped energy. Once the bonus, less the unit's own costs, is larger than the node's penalty_down, the unit runs above the demand and the extra energy is dumped through the downward slack. Use one of the floors above instead: they force exactly the output you want and show it as a constraint.

docs.title: Model parameters
docs.text:
These pages list the entity classes of a FlexTool model and the parameters you can give them, one page per topic.

  • Entities and time structure — the main entities, the timeline, periods, timesets, solves and the units of measure.
  • Nodes — balance and storage nodes: inflow, penalties, storage and investment parameters.
  • Units — conversion units, their inputs and outputs, investment, retirement and profile limits.
  • Connections — transfers between nodes, their transfer methods and investment parameters.
  • Commodities — fuels and other commodities bought or sold at a price.
  • Groups — capacity, investment and emission limits, stochastics, decomposition and outputs for a set of entities.
  • Flow groups — cumulative and instant limits on summed flows.
  • Reserves — reserve requirements and the units and connections that provide them.
  • User constraints — linear constraints you write yourself over flows, states and capacities.
  • Parameter groups and conventions — the parameter group labels, the behaviour-change notices of upgraded databases and the input checks a run makes before it starts.
  • Parameter catalogue (web docs) — every parameter in one table per entity class: unit, allowed shapes, default, allowed values and group, generated from the schema of this FlexTool version. python -m flextool.docs_build --xlsx catalogue.xlsx writes it as an Excel data dictionary (see How to make a data dictionary for your model).

docs.title: Commodities
docs.text:
Some nodes can act as a source or a sink of commodities instead of forcing a balance between inputs and outputs. To make that happen, commodities must have a price and be connected to those nodes that serve (or buy) that particular commodity at the given price. In other words, commodity is separate from node so that the user can use the same commodity properties for multiple nodes. Commodities can also have a co2_content. The commodity and its nodes are connected by establishing a new entity between the commodity and each of its nodes (e.g. coal--coal_market).

  • price - [CUR/MWh or other unit] Price of the commodity. Constant, period or time.
  • co2_content - [tCO2/MWh] Constant.
  • price_method - How the commodity price enters the LP. price (default) treats price as the marginal cost of every traded MWh. price_ladder_annual / price_ladder_cumulative activate a stepped supply curve authored via the parameters below; the engine then represents commodity trade as a sum of tier variables, one per ladder step.
  • price_ladder_annual - Stepped supply curve for price_method = price_ladder_annual. 2d map of (tier, period) → price/volume entries. Each tier's quantity is a per-year amount; a solve covering less than a full year (a short solve, or one roll of a rolling solve) is only allowed its own share of that year's quantity, in proportion to the hours it covers. In a stochastic solve the forecast branches of a period use that period's ladder.
  • price_ladder_cumulative - Stepped supply curve for price_method = price_ladder_cumulative. 2d map with rolling cumulative breakpoints.
  • Ladder tiers (both ladders): a tier label is a name, kept as written (1, 01 and a are three different tiers); the model buys the tiers by price, whatever their labels or order. Every tier needs a price (a tier without one is an error). A tier without a quantity is unlimited.
  • unitsize - [MWh] Numeric scaling for the v_trade variable (analogous to virtual_unitsize on units). Used with the price-ladder methods to keep tier-step variables well scaled; default 1.0.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: Connections can transfer energy between two nodes. Parameters for the connection are defined in the connection entity, but the two nodes it connects are defined by establishing an entity between connection--leftNode--rightNode.

docs.title: Defining how the connection functions
docs.text:
• transfer_method to define the way the connection transfers energy between the nodes
  • startup_method gives the connection online capacity. linear: the online capacity is anything between 0 and the built capacity; binary: whole units of the connection (of virtual_unitsize, else the whole connection), computationally more demanding. The connection's flow in each direction is limited by its online capacity × availability, its reserve by its online capacity, and startup_cost is paid per MW brought online. Connections have no minimum load or minimum up/down times. Not available for connections in a dc_power_flow_with_angles group, other than is_DC connections (an error: switching a DC power-flow line off would need line-switching constraints).
  • invest_method to define investment and retirement limits: either not_allowed or then a combination of
    • invest and/or retire
    • investment limits for each period and/or for all periods (total) or no_limit
    • cumulative_limits considers investments, retirements and existing together, requires cumulative_max_capacity and/or cumulative_min_capacity
    • any method other than not_allowed offers investment (retirement) in every investment period, also without invest_cost (salvage_value) or where it is 0: that capacity has no annuity, its fixed_cost still counts. To forbid investment in a period, use a period method (invest_period, invest_period_total and their invest_retire_ forms) and set invest_max_period 0 for it: the other methods do not use invest_max_period. A 0 in an invest_cost map does not forbid it.
  • lifetime_method to choose how the investments behave after unit runs out of lifetime. Automatic reinvestment (reinvest_automatic - default) causes the model to keep the capacity until the end of model horizon and applies the annualized investment cost until the end of model horizon without further choice by the model. Choice of reinvestment (reinvest_choice) removes the capacity at the end of the lifetime and the model needs to decide how much new capacity is to be built. One-shot investment (no_investment) allows the model to invest freely within the first-period lifetime window (subject to the usual invest_method / invest_max_period caps) but pins v_invest to zero for any period after that window — the asset retires once and cannot be rebuilt. Use for physical one-off additions such as plant refurbishments that cannot be repeated at the same cost. If there is a need to remove the possibility to invest after lifetime, then the investment limits can be used.

docs.title: Main data items for connections
docs.text:
• existing - [MW or count] Existing capacity or number of units. If virtual_unitsize is given, then existing is the number of units (capacity = existing × virtual_unitsize). Otherwise existing is the existing capacity of a single unit (typically in MW). Constant or period.
  • efficiency - [factor, typically between 0-1] Efficiency of a connection. Constant, period, time or period+time.
  • delay - [hours] Not yet applied to connections (planned). A connection delay is ignored: the connection is modelled exactly as if no delay were set (the flow arrives in the same time step) and the model prints a warning naming the connection. To model a delayed flow between two nodes, use a unit with delay instead.
  • startup_cost - [CUR/MW] Cost of starting up one MW of capacity (used when startup_method activates online variables on the connection). Constant or period.
  • reactance - [p.u.] Per-unit reactance of the transmission line. Used for DC power flow when the enclosing group__node has transfer_method = dc_power_flow_with_angles.
  • constraint_invested_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) putting the capacity that comes online in each period on the left side of the user-defined constraint. Without a construction lead time, this is the capacity invested in that period. Coefficient per MW. Renamed from constraint_capacity_coefficient; the old expression summed v_invest once per active investment period, giving incorrect results in multi-period models. See User constraints.
  • constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity in service at the start of each period on the left side of the user constraint. This is existing capacity plus capacity that came online in earlier periods, minus earlier retirements. Capacity coming online in the period itself is in the invested term. Enables learning-effect and period-over-period growth limits (pair with constraint_invested_capacity_coeff on the same constraint). Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the connection's capacity in service in each period on the left side of the user constraint (existing plus investments still in service minus retirements). Coefficient per MW. Capacity in construction is not included. See User constraints.
  • constraint_retired_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity retired in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity in construction in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Capacity is in construction from the period of the investment decision until it comes online. It is zero without a construction lead time. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_online_coeff - [unit of the constraint per unit online] A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient).
