Puts the number of units of the connection online in each time step (both directions together) on the left side of the user constraint. One unit is virtual_unitsize; without it, the largest existing capacity, else 1000 MW — set virtual_unitsize on a connection that is invested in. Needs startup_method linear or binary; a coefficient on a connection without it is an error. With linear startup the number is continuous. For MW online, use the unit size as the coefficient. See User constraints.
  • other_operational_cost - [CUR/MWh] Other operational variable cost for trasferring over the connection. Constant, period, time or period+time.
  • fixed_cost - [CUR/kW/a] Annual fixed cost. New capacity pays it only while it operates. Constant or period.
  • invest_cost - [CUR/kW] Overnight investment cost of new capacity. It is paid as an annuity over the years the capacity operates. Construction time costs with their interest must be included here. Constant or period: the value of the period when the capacity is built (comes online) is used.
  • discount_rate - [e.g. 0.05 equals 5%] Discount rate for investments (WACC). Reflects the financing cost and risk for this technology. Should be nominal when model inflation_rate > 0, real when inflation_rate = 0. Constant or period.
  • lifetime - [years] Operating lifetime. It starts when the capacity starts to operate: with a construction lead time, after the construction. Used with the discount rate to calculate the annuity. What happens at the end of the lifetime depends on lifetime_method: reinvest_automatic keeps the capacity to the end of the model horizon, reinvest_choice retires it, no_investment retires it once. The existing capacity ends at the first year of the model run plus the lifetime of the first period (in every solve of a chain of solves). Constant or period.
  • construction_lead_time - [years] Time from the investment decision until the capacity starts to operate. The start is rounded to the start of a period (see construction_lead_time_method). Investments whose rounded start is after the end of the solve or the model horizon are not offered, with a warning. Constant or period. Default 0. See construction lead time.
  • construction_lead_time_method - How the start of operation (decision year plus construction_lead_time) is rounded to the start of a period: immediate (no lead time, the capacity operates from the decision period), closest_seam (the nearest period start; a tie goes to the later one), previous_seam (the period start before), next_seam (the period start after). Without a value: immediate when there is no lead time, else closest_seam.
  • other investment parameters: invest_max_total, invest_max_period, invest_min_total, invest_min_period, salvage_value (only existing capacity can be retired, see retirements)
  • is_DC - A flag whether the connection is DC: its flow into a node of a group with a non_synchronous_limit counts as non-synchronous (both directions; between two nodes of the same group it does not count). Default false. An is_DC connection inside a dc_power_flow_with_angles group is not a DC power-flow line: it keeps its own transfer_method and needs no reactance.
  • virtual_unitsize - [MW] Size of one unit of the connection. With it, existing is the number of units. Binary startups commit whole units of this size. Investments and retirements are continuous; their limits are in MW. No value: the existing capacity, or 1000 MW without it.
  • availability - [e.g. 0.9 means 90%] Fraction of capacity available for connection flows. Constant, period, time or period+time.

docs.title: connection__profile
docs.text: • profile_method - limits the connection's flow with a profile (upper_limit, lower_limit, fixed; the profile is a share of the capacity). The default is none: the profile is not applied, and FlexTool warns about a link without a profile_method. An upper_limit or fixed link to a profile without a value in the scenario stops the run with an error (it would hold the flow at 0). See units constrained by profiles.

docs.title: Investment parameters for connections
docs.text: These are the same as for units, see here

docs.title: connection__node (per-endpoint properties)
docs.text:
On the membership entity between a connection and one of its endpoint nodes:

  • constraint_flow_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) placing this connection-to-node flow variable on the left side of a user-defined constraint. Applied per timestep. See User constraints.

docs.title: Main entities to define a power/energy system
docs.text:
Elemental entities (one dimensional):

  • node: maintain a balance between generation, consumption, transfers and storage state changes (nodes can also represent storages)
  • unit: power plants or other conversion devices that take one or more inputs and turn them into one or more outputs
  • connection: transmission lines or other transfer connections between nodes
  • commodity: fuels or other commodities that are either purchased or sold at a price outside of the model scope
  • profile: timeseries that can be used to constraint the behaviour of units, connections or storages
  • reserve: reserve categories to withhold capacity to cope with issues outside of model scope

Entities with two or more dimensions:

  • unit__inputNode and unit__outputNode: defines the inputs, outputs and their properties for the conversion units
  • connection__node__node: defines which nodes a connection will connect
  • unit__node__profile and connection__profile: defines a profile limit (upper, lower or fixed) for an energy flow
  • node__profile: defines a profile limit (upper, lower, or fixed) for the storage state of the node
  • commodity__node: defines if a node is a source or sink for a commodity
  • reserve__upDown__unit__node and reserve__upDown__connection__node: reserve capacity from a source to the target node

See the other pages of this section for more detailed explanations.

docs.title: How to define the temporal properties of the model
Timesteps and periods
docs.text:
FlexTool has two different kinds of time varying parameters. The first one represents a regular timeline based on timesteps. The duration of each timestep can be defined by the user. There can be multiple timelines in the database - the user needs to define which timeline to use (and what parts of the timeline should be used, as will be explained later). The timestep names in the timeline are defined by the user - they can be abstract like 't0001' or follow a datetime format of choice. However, the timestep names between different timelines must remain unique (usually there should be only one timeline in a database and therefore no issues).

The second time varying dimension is period, which is typically used to depict assumptions about the future. One model can include multiple solves that the model will solve in sequence (to allow multi-stage modelling). Each solve can include multiple periods (so that the user can change parameter values for different parts of the future).

A parameter of particular type can be either constant/time-varying or constant/period-based. For example inflow is either a constant or time-varying, but it cannot be period-based (a period-keyed inflow is rejected; use annual_flow for demand that varies by period).

The time steps of a time series must be time steps of a timeline (the names are case sensitive). A time series may be longer than what the model uses (a full year with a timeset that picks two weeks is fine), but a value whose time step is not a step of any timeline of the scenario is not used: FlexTool prints a warning that names the parameter, the entities and the first such steps (for example hourly data on a 3-hour timeline, or the stamps of another year). A time series with none of its steps on a timeline is an error. The branch names of a stochastic time series and the periods of a period+time map are not time steps and are not checked; neither is a map keyed by the periods of another scenario (that entity gets no value in this scenario). Date-time stamps are compared as dates, so 2050-01-01 00:00 matches the step 2050-01-01T00:00:00. A time series whose steps are all on a timeline of another scenario (its timestep_duration is in an alternative this scenario does not include) gets a warning, not an error.

The keys of a period map must be periods named somewhere in the database: in the period_timeset, the period lists or years_represented of some solve (of any scenario), the first level of stochastic_branches, a stochastic branch period (the period, an underscore and the branch name, such as p2035_high), or model.periods_available. A key that is none of these (a typing mistake such as y2020 for p2020, or 2020) stops the run with an error that names the entity, the parameter, the key and the closest period. When the data covers more years than the solves use (a 2020-2050 trajectory for a model that solves 2030), list the extra periods in model.periods_available.

Recommendation — name the Map index for parameters that accept both period and time. A few parameters accept either a period map or a time series (for example the flowGroup min_instant_flow / max_instant_flow limits, which accept "Constant, period, time or period+time"). Period and time Maps look structurally identical in Spine Toolbox — both are 1-dimensional Maps — so FlexTool tells them apart from the Map's index_name. Set it explicitly to period or time when authoring such a Map. If you leave the default (Spine stores it as x), FlexTool falls back to inspecting the Map's index values and matching them against the model's period and timestep names to guess the intended axis; this works when the keys clearly belong to one set, but is ambiguous if they don't. The guess is made per entity: a map whose keys are periods of another solve only (not of this one) gives that entity no value in that solve (the same as if nothing had been authored for it, so the parameter's own default applies) — it never affects any other entity's value. A map whose keys are periods of no solve in the database and no timesteps stops the run: keys that look like timesteps (t0099, T0001, a date-time stamp) with the time-series error, other keys (p2050) with the period-key error. Keys that match both a period and a timestep name are an error. Setting index_name removes the guesswork. (Parameters that accept only one of the two — e.g. inflow is time-only — are never ambiguous and need no index_name.)

docs.title: Timesets
docs.text: Timesets pick one or more sections from the timeline to form a timeset. Each timeset defines a start and a duration. The aim of timesets is to allow the modeller to create models with representative periods often used in the investment planning.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• model: model defines the sequence of solves to be performed (e.g. first an investment solve and then a dispatch solve)

  • solves: sequence of solves in the model represented with an array of solve names.

  • inflation_rate: [e.g. 0.02 for 2%] Model-wide inflation rate applied to all future costs. When inputs are in real (constant-price) terms, set to 0 (default). When inputs are in nominal terms, set to expected inflation.
  • inflation_offset_investment: [years] Offset from the period (often year) start to the first payment of the investment cost annuity.
  • inflation_offset_operations: [years] Offset from the period (often year) start to the payment of operational costs.
  • periods_available: (Optional) Array of periods available for the model. Use this for periods that are in the data, but are not in period_timeset.
  • max_flow_for_unconstrained_variables: [MW] Upper bound for capacities and flows that have no other limit: how much capacity an entity with invest_method invest_no_limit or invest_retire_no_limit (or cumulative_limits without cumulative_max_capacity) can add on top of its existing capacity, and the flow on a unit's input or output whose conversion_flow_coeff is 0. The value is used as given; with several model entities the largest value is used. Keep it large enough not to limit the real solution and small enough to avoid numerical problems (see dev/scaling.md). Default 1,000,000.
  • debug: Instruction set for performing model debugging and testing.

  • version: Database schema version. Written by the migration chain — do not edit manually.

  • solve: each solve is built from an array of periods (e.g. one period for 2025 and another for 2030). Periods use timesets to connect with a timeline. Parameters are split into two parameter-group tags in the master template — solve_basics (knobs a typical user touches) and solve_advanced (rolling/nested/stochastic structures, solver options, cross-solve handoff). The split is purely cosmetic in the Spine DB editor; behaviour is identical.

  • period_timeset: map of periods with associated timesets that will be included in the solve. Index: period name, value: timeset name.

  • new_stepduration: [hours] Creates a new timeline for this solve, with time steps of this length. See also the group-level new_stepduration for flex-temporal decomposition.

    How the data is combined. Each time series gets one value per new time step, combined over the time steps of the timeline that form it by a rule that depends on what the value is:

    • Summed: inflow and energy_margin_adder (energy per time step). A constant counts once per time step it combines.
    • Averaged, weighted by the durations of the time steps: commodity price, co2_price, other_operational_cost, availability of units, connections and nodes, min_load, penalty_up / penalty_down, reservation, self_discharge_loss, inertia_limit, non_synchronous_limit, max_instant_flow / min_instant_flow (the limit applies to the step-average flow), timeset_weights and profile. self_discharge_loss compounds per hour, so its mean is a close approximation (0.01 and 0.03 give 0.02; the exact rate would be 0.019951).
    • Harmonic mean: efficiency and efficiency_at_min_load take the mean of 1/efficiency (the fuel per output), so the fuel use of a flow that is constant over the step is exact: 0.4 and 0.5 give 1/efficiency 2.25, not 1/0.45. With a min_load that varies within a new time step, the min_load_efficiency curve of that step is an approximation (a warning names the units).
    • Last: storage_state_reference_value takes the value of the new time step's last time step (the state at its end).

    Stochastic (branch) time series are combined the same way, each branch on its own. A time series with values for only some time steps of a new time step uses the time steps it has (a warning names the parameter); the default value of the other time steps is not part of it. A new time step whose values are all equal keeps that value exactly, so a constant and an equivalent time map give the same model.

    Values of time steps that are not on the original timeline are not part of a new time step (a warning names them, see Timesteps and periods).

    How the steps are formed. Steps are aggregated from the start of each timeset_duration block. A block that is not a multiple of the step ends with a shorter step. A gap between blocks stays a gap. When several timesets share the timeline, each period keeps its own time steps.

    Rules and errors. The new_stepduration must be a whole multiple of the timeline's time steps. On a timeline with time steps of different lengths, every new time step must end where a time step of the timeline ends. FlexTool stops with an error otherwise. All timesets used by the solve must resolve to the same underlying timeline. A timeset used by this solve cannot be used by a solve without new_stepduration or with a different one.

  • realized_periods: these are the periods the model will 'realize' - i.e., what periods will be reported in the results from this solve

  • realized_invest_periods Array of the periods that will realize the investment decisions. If this is not defined when the invest_periods exist, the realized_periods that are also invest_periods are used to realize the invests as well. Every realized investment period must be one of the solve's invest_periods: FlexTool stops with an error naming the solve and the periods otherwise (also for a solve that has realized_invest_periods but no invest_periods). When invest_periods is a 2D map, realized_invest_periods must be a 2D map with the same solve names.
  • invest_periods: array of periods in which investments can be decided in this solve (applies only to entities that can be invested in). With a construction lead time, the capacity comes online later.
  • years_represented: Map to indicate how many years the period represents before the next period in the solve. Used for discounting. Can be below one (multiple periods in one year). Index: period, value: years.
  • solver: choice of a solver. HiGHS is the default and only fully supported backend (called via the highspy Python bindings). Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress and COPT can be used by licensed users, with their own options in solver_arguments; see Solvers.
  • solver_arguments: Map of solver option name → value, forwarded verbatim to the active solver. This is where the former highs_* shortcuts now live. For HiGHS, set solver to choose the method ('simplex' or 'ipm' which is interior point method; use 'choose' for MIP models, since 'simplex' and 'ipm' will not work), parallel ('on' or 'off') to control parallelisation of single solves (it can be better to turn it off when executing multiple scenarios in parallel), and presolve ('on' or 'off') to toggle presolve (which can have a large impact on solution time when solves are large). These only affect speed, not results.
  • solve_mode: a single solve or a set of rolling optimisation windows solved in a sequence
  • timeline_hole_multiplier: [-] default 1.0. Multiplier applied to the inverse-step-duration term in the nodeBalance_eq for variable-step timelines. Tunes how strongly an unrepresented gap between two timesteps is amortised into the storage state equation. Leave at the default unless investigating large-step / sparse-timeline numerical issues.

  • Rolling window parameters:

    • rolling_solve_jump: Hours, (Required if rolling_window solve). Interval between the start points of the rolls. Also the output interval. This should be smaller than the horizon
    • rolling_solve_horizon: Hours, (Required if rolling_window solve). The length of the horizon of the roll. How long into the future the roll sees. For an individual roll, horizon is the solve length and jump is the output length.
    • rolling_duration: Hours, (Optional). Duration of rolling, if not stated, assumed to be the whole timeline of the solve

  • Nested solve sequence parameters:

    • contains_solves: Array of solves that are run with after this solve using the realized data of this solve. Read 'How to use Nested Rolling window solves (investments and long term storage)'
    • fix_storage_periods: Array of periods where this solve produces a storage-state handoff for the contained solve at the end of each listed period. The handoff carries any subset of three metrics — fix_storage_quantity, fix_storage_price, fix_storage_usage — selected per node by the node parameter storage_nested_fix_method.

  • Stochastic parameters:

    • stochastic_branches: 4D-map defining the solve's forecast branches — the probability-weighted possible futures. Index columns: period, branch, analysis_time (the branch's start timestep), realized (yes/no), and the value is the branch's probability weight. The weights are normalized to sum to one across the forecast branches at each start time. The realized flag is an optional designation (at most one branch per start time) marking which branch's data are treated as the actuals for the committed / realized-dispatch results; a realized-flagged branch is not a weighted member of the forecast fan. A period-indexed value (a map keyed by period, e.g. efficiency, startup cost, commodity price, availability, variable cost or a per-period limit) also applies to that period's forecast branches; a value authored for a branch period itself takes precedence. See 'How to use stochastics' for more information.
    • stochastic_invest_method: none (default) or recourse. none makes a single shared here-and-now investment plan across all forecast branches (operations still fan per branch). recourse gives per-branch (wait-and-see) investment: each forecast branch invests on its own data at and after the branching period, with probability-weighted investment costs and per-branch investment limits, and reports EVPI/VSS-style stochastic value. Forecast-branch (unrealized) investments are not in the normal outputs, only in the raw dump of model.output_horizon (a debug flag). Incompatible with Benders decomposition. See 'How to use stochastics' for the interpretation caveats.

  • Detail reduction parameters (see Leaving out detail in a solve):

    • reduce_unit_detail_method: choice. Detail of units and connections this solve leaves out: integer units online, ramps, min limits or the online variables. Default none.
    • reduce_system_detail_method: choice. System detail this solve leaves out: reserves, inertia limits, non-synchronous limits or the angles of DC power flow. Default none.

  • For commercial solvers:

    • solver_precommand is not used: FlexTool never runs commands stored in a database (FlexTool 3 ran it in front of CPLEX). It is kept only so that older databases still read, and a value gives a warning; to hold a floating licence, use the solver's own licence server setup.
    • solver_arguments Map of the solver's own parameters (name → value), see Solvers. From the database, a parameter that names a file or folder takes only a plain file name (written in the solve's work folder), and Gurobi server, cloud and licence parameters are refused; set those in the solver option file instead.

  • timeset: timesets are sets of time with a start (from timeline) and a duration (number of time steps)

  • timeset_duration a map with index timestep_name that starts the timeset and value that defines the duration of the timeset (how many timesteps). A block must start at a time step of the timeset's timeline; otherwise the run stops with an error that names the timeset and the block. A block length that is not a whole number gets a warning (the whole part is used). A block longer than the rest of the timeline is cut at the end of the timeline, with a warning that says how many time steps are not used (for a timeset with representative_period_weights this is an error: a representative period cannot be cut). Only the timesets that the solves of the model use are checked. The stochastic forecast branches of a period use the period's timeset, its representative periods included (every branch has the same selection and weights).

  • timeline The name of the timeline that the timeset uses. (String)

  • timeset_weights: Optional per-timestep weight map (index: timestep name, index_name time or left empty; value: float) applied to cost and slack terms in the objective. Use for non-RP models where timesteps represent unequal fractions of the year — e.g. a coarse OSeMOSYS-style timeslice structure where wet-season steps cover more year-hours than dry-season ones. Weights are normalized per period to sum to 1 and then scaled by the number of active timesteps, so uniform input reproduces weight = 1 per step (the default). Must not be combined with representative_period_weights on the same timeset — the runner errors out if both are set. The stochastic forecast branches of a period use the weights of the period's timeset. Any other shape (a scalar, a map indexed by period) is an error.

  • timeline: continuous timeline with a user-defined duration for each timestep. Timelines are used by time series data. A time series value whose time step is not a step of any timeline is not used (a warning names the parameter and the first such steps); a time series with none of its steps on a timeline is an error.

  • timestep_duration: a map with timestep_name as an index and duration as a value (hours, above 0). Only the timelines a solve uses (through the timesets of its period_timeset, or the timeset a solve without period_timeset takes by default) need durations; a spare timeline without them is ignored.

  • timeline_duration_in_years Total duration of the timeline in years. Used to relate operational part of the model with the annualized part of the model.

docs.title: Leaving out detail in a solve
docs.text:
Two solve parameters make one solve faster by leaving out detail: reduce_unit_detail_method for units and connections, reduce_system_detail_method for the system. The typical use is an investment solve that leaves out unit commitment and reserves, followed by a dispatch solve with all the detail (see LP investment and a detailed dispatch check).

Only reduces. Both default to none, which keeps everything: the solve is then the same as without the parameters. A level only leaves out or relaxes detail that the data gives. It never adds any, and an entity without the feature is untouched. A level that finds nothing to leave out says so in the run log.

reduce_unit_detail_method. Each value leaves out the parts marked:

value integer online, exact ramps min limits online variables none (default) integers continuous those without a use left out integers_ramps continuous left out those without a use left out integers_min_limits continuous left out those without a use left out integers_ramps_min_limits continuous left out left out those without a use left out online — left out left out online_ramps — left out left out left out

What each value removes:

  • none removes nothing.
  • integers removes: whole units online (they become continuous) and the exact connection method (those connections become regular).
  • integers_ramps removes: what integers removes, and the ramp limits and ramp costs.
  • integers_min_limits removes: what integers removes, and min load, the capacity_min_coeff floors and the minimum up and down times.
  • integers_ramps_min_limits removes: what integers removes, the ramp limits and ramp costs, and the min limits.
  • online removes: what integers_min_limits removes, and the online variables: units online, start-ups, shut-downs, start-up costs, the user constraints with a constraint_online_coeff term and the part-load curve of min_load_efficiency units. Ramp limits stay and apply to the capacity.
  • online_ramps removes: what online removes, and the ramp limits and ramp costs.

Each integers* level also removes the online variables that nothing in the solve uses any more (see Online variables without a use below).

The parts in detail:

  • Integer units online. Units and connections with startup_method binary get continuous units online.

    The rows stay the same, so units online, start-ups and shut-downs can be fractional. A connection with transfer_method exact behaves as regular: both directions keep their own flow and losses, only the binary that blocks simultaneous flow in both directions goes. Without other integer variables the solve is an LP: node and reserve prices are LP duals, and solver_mip_gap no longer applies.

  • Ramps. Ramp limits (ramp_method ramp_limit or both with ramp_speed_up / ramp_speed_down) and ramp costs (ramp_method ramp_cost or both).

    The start-up and shut-down allowance of the ramp limits goes with them. The ramps cost category is 0 for the solve.

  • Min limits. min_load, the capacity_min_coeff floors and the minimum up and down times (min_uptime, min_downtime).

    A unit with min_load_efficiency keeps its part-load curve. Without the min load floor its units online can follow its output (units online ≈ output / capacity), so its fuel becomes close to linear in output.

  • Online variables. The units online of every unit and connection with a startup_method, and with them start-ups, shut-downs, start-up costs and the min limits.

    A unit with conversion_method min_load_efficiency uses its full-load efficiency at every output: the same fuel at full load and less at part load. A user constraint with a constraint_online_coeff term is left out of the solve whole, with a warning that names it. Ramp limits that are kept apply to the capacity, so a unit that starts from zero ramps up at its ramp speed (there is no start-up allowance). online contains every effect of integers, so the solve is an LP.

  • Online variables without a use (integers* only). After its own removals, an integers* level also leaves out the online variables of each unit or connection that nothing in the solve still uses, as if its startup_method were no_startup.

    The online variables are used by: a start-up cost (startup_cost), min_load and the capacity_min_coeff floors, the minimum up and down times, the part-load curve of a min_load_efficiency unit, a constraint_online_coeff term in a user constraint of the solve, a reserve that the unit or connection holds, inertia (an inertia_constant at a node of a group with has_inertia), ramp limits (their start-up and shut-down allowance) and, in a realization solve, the units online it takes from its parent solve. A reserve or an inertia limit that reduce_system_detail_method leaves out is no use. The ties that make the forecast branches of a stochastic solve have the same units online are no use either. For example, under integers_min_limits a unit with only a min_load loses its online variables, a unit with a start-up cost or a reserve keeps them; under integers the unit with the min_load keeps them.

    Without a use, the online rows only repeat the capacity limit, so the solution is the same and the solve is smaller. The solve's info line in the run log names these units and connections ("online variables left out (nothing in this solve uses them)"), and their units online and start-up cells of the solve are empty in the outputs. online and online_ramps leave out every online variable anyway; none keeps them all.

reduce_system_detail_method. Each value leaves out the parts in its name:

value reserves inertia non-synchronous DC power flow none (default) reserves left out inertia left out non_synchronous left out inertia_non_synchronous left out left out reserves_inertia_non_synchronous left out left out left out dc_power_flow lossless transport reserves_inertia_non_synchronous_dc_power_flow left out left out left out lossless transport

What each value removes:

  • none removes nothing.
  • reserves removes: the reserve requirements, the reserves that units and connections hold and the reserve shortfall penalty.
  • inertia removes: the inertia limits and the inertia shortfall penalty.
  • non_synchronous removes: the non-synchronous share limits and their shortfall penalty.
  • inertia_non_synchronous removes: what inertia and non_synchronous remove.
  • reserves_inertia_non_synchronous removes: what reserves, inertia and non_synchronous remove.
  • dc_power_flow removes: the voltage angles of dc_power_flow_with_angles groups; their lines become lossless transport limited by capacity.
  • reserves_inertia_non_synchronous_dc_power_flow removes: all of the above.

The parts in detail:

  • Reserves. Every reserve requirement (reserve__upDown__group) and the reserve that units and connections hold, with its limits and shortfall penalty.

    In a stochastic solve the ties that make the forecast branches hold the same reserve go too. An investment solve without reserves invests less in flexible capacity.

  • Inertia. The inertia limits of groups with has_inertia and their shortfall penalty.

  • Non-synchronous. The non-synchronous share limits of groups with has_non_synchronous and their shortfall penalty.

  • DC power flow. The angles of dc_power_flow_with_angles groups: the lines become lossless transport connections limited by their capacity.

    Loop flows disappear, so a meshed network can carry more than its physics allows, and an investment solve invests less in lines. Links with is_DC = yes keep their own method.

The capacity margin (capacity_margin_method) is never left out.

Interactions. When the unit level leaves out something that the system detail the solve keeps relies on, the run log says so in the solve's info line:

  • online* with reserves kept: the reserves come from built capacity, not from the capacity online.
  • online* with inertia kept: inertia is counted from the flows (flow × inertia_constant), not from the units online.
  • *min_limits or online* with downward reserves kept: the downward reserve can reach down to zero flow, not only to min load.
  • integers* with a constraint_online_coeff term: the user constraint counts fractional units online.

An approximation, never tighter. Every part only removes constraints or integer restrictions, except the full-load efficiency of min_load_efficiency units under online*, which uses less fuel than the part-load curve. CO2 limits read that fuel, so they relax as well. The reduced solve is therefore never more constrained than the full one.

Across solves. Every roll of a rolling solve uses the solve's levels. A nested solve uses its own levels, not its parent's. A Benders decomposition can split connections whose reserves, online variables or exact method the solve leaves out.

Realization and continuing solves. A realization solve (the dispatch of a stochastic solve's realized branch) uses its parent solve's levels, whatever is set on it, since it takes the parent's units online and reserves. A warning names a different value set on a declared realization solve. A solve that continues the ramp of a solve without online variables starts its commitment and ramps cold, with an info line.

Run log and run status. A solve with a level other than none writes one info line to the run log at its first roll: what each level left out, for how many units, connections and groups, and the interactions above. The line names the entities when there are five or fewer, otherwise it gives their count. The entry of each roll in _run_status.json records reduced: the two levels, and on the solve's first roll that line too.

Which cells. The result cells of a feature that a solve left out are empty, not 0, in the time steps that solve realized: units online and start-ups, reserves, reserve prices and reserve shortfall, the inertia of groups, their largest flow and inertia shortfall, the non-synchronous shortfall, and the DC angles. "Not modelled" is not "zero". The tables of other solves that kept the feature are complete. When no solve keeps a feature, its tables have no entity columns.

Per-period values and costs. A per-period cell is empty when every solve that realized the period left the feature out. A period shared with a solve that kept the feature keeps its per-period value, in which the time steps of the solve that left it out count as 0. Its row is labelled with the last solve that realized the period, which may be the one that left the feature out. The costs stay: a left-out feature costs nothing in the solve. The fuel of a min_load_efficiency unit under online* is its output divided by its full-load efficiency.

docs.title: Time structure assumptions
docs.text:
The tool includes some assumptions about the time structure, in case something parts are missing. These will work if there is only one option for the model to choose. The assuptions are the following:

  • If timeset: timeline is not set and only one timeline is defined, it is used
  • If no timeset is exist and only one timeline is defined, create a full timeline timeset
  • If period_timeset is defined, but no realized_periods or invest_periods exists, all periods are realized
  • If period_timeset does not exist and only one timeset exists, create timesets for all realized_periods and invest_periods
  • If model: solves does not exist, and only one solve exists, that it is used
  • If a solve in model: solves does not exist, create a solve where all periods_available are realized

For example in the case above, it would have been possible to not fill the timeset: timeline as there is only one timeline to choose. Leaving out the period_timeset would result in an error as there are multiple timesets to choose.

docs.title: Units of measure
docs.text:
FlexTool does not check or convert units. It combines the numbers you enter as they are, so any set of units works as long as it is consistent. The parameter descriptions, the defaults and the result labels use a default convention because it reads well for most energy models:

  • power and flows: MW; energy and storage: MWh
  • money: CUR, the currency of your model (results show costs in millions, M CUR)
  • emissions: tonnes of CO2
  • time: hours for time steps, years for lifetimes and years represented — these are fixed, not a convention.

A node in another unit. A node can hold something else than electricity: water in m3, hydrogen in t, heat that you want to label MWh_th. Set the node's unit_of_measure to the unit of its amounts (default MWh), and the result labels of that node follow it. Time steps are hours, so the node's rate is the amount per hour:

What MWh node (default) unit_of_measure m3 unit_of_measure MWh_th flows into and out of the node, unit and connection capacities on its side MW m3/h MW_th storage state and capacity, inflow per time step MWh m3 MWh_th flows summed over a period (annualized) MWh/a m3/a MWh_th/a prices, penalty_up / penalty_down, commodity price CUR/MWh CUR/m3 CUR/MWh_th invest_cost, fixed_cost, salvage_value of a unit whose capacity is on the node CUR/kW CUR per 0.001 m3/h CUR/kW_th the same of a storage node CUR/kWh CUR per 0.001 m3 CUR/kWh_th

The rule: a unit ending in Wh drops the h for the rate (MWh → MW, MWh_th → MW_th, kWh → kW), any other unit gets /h (m3 → m3/h, t → t/h). The value is case-sensitive (mwh gives mwh/h). It is a label only: FlexTool changes no number. Set the amount unit, not the rate: m3, not m3/h (FlexTool warns about a value that looks like a rate).

Costs per kW and kWh. invest_cost, fixed_cost and salvage_value (and the group penalty_capacity_margin) are entered per kW or kWh, and FlexTool multiplies them by 1000. For a node in another unit they are per 0.001 of the rate or the amount. A desalination unit that costs 500 CUR per m3/h of capacity has invest_cost 0.5 (500 × 0.001); a water tank that costs 20 CUR per m3 has invest_cost 0.02. The capacities themselves are entered unchanged (2000 m3/h is 2000).

Efficiencies are output units per input unit: a desalination unit that makes 12 m3 of water per MWh of heat has efficiency 12 [m3/MWh].

Penalties (penalty_up 10 000 CUR/MWh by default) are sized for MWh. Set them yourself for a node in another unit, above the cost of the dearest real way to serve it.

Which node a result follows. A result of a node, or of a flow into or out of it, takes that node's unit. A unit's capacity follows its output nodes (its input nodes when it has no output). When the outputs are in different units, the label shows how the capacity is used: MW + MW_th when the outputs share the capacity (a unit with several outputs or inputs, which FlexTool models with a sum of its outputs), MW; MW_th when each output is only capped on its own. A connection's flow to each of its nodes takes that node's unit (connection__leftward / __rightward). A storage node's annuity and investment cost are per its amount unit (CUR/MWh, CUR/m3): its capacity is an amount, how much it holds. A unit's or connection's are per its rate unit (CUR/MW, CUR/(m3/h)): its capacity is a rate.

Mixed units of measure! One quantity summed over nodes whose units differ has no unit, and its label is Mixed units of measure!: a nodeGroup's flows over an electricity and a water node, a connection's net flow and losses between them, a plot that stacks or sums such columns. FlexTool warns about such sets when it reads the input data (a connection, a commodity, a nodeGroup or flowGroup, and a group capacity limit over different units). Reserves, inertia, the non-synchronous share and the capacity margin are power features: they stay in MW, and FlexTool warns about a member node of such a group that is not MWh (or MWh with a suffix, such as MWh_el).

You can also use other units without setting unit_of_measure. Then every value connected to those nodes has to use them (prices in CUR/kg, capacities in kg/h, efficiencies between the units), and the results of those nodes are in your units even where the label says MW or MWh.

The units written with the results (the Units sheet and unit of measure header row of the Excel workbook, units.csv of the CSV output, the parquet metadata, the plot labels) follow these rules; see Units in the files.

docs.title: Flow groups (flowGroup)
docs.text: A flowGroup aggregates a set of flows — where each flow is a (process, node) arc. Members are declared through the 3-dim membership classes flowGroup__unit__node and flowGroup__connection__node. A flowGroup carries the flow-limit parameters and the flow_aggregator method; it does not carry any of the node-group / system-constraint / investment parameters (those stay on group).

docs.title: Cumulative and instant flow limits
docs.text:
• max_cumulative_flow - [MW] Maximum average flow, which limits the cumulative flow for a group of connection_nodes and/or unit_nodes. The average value is multiplied by the model duration to get the cumulative limit (e.g. by 8760 if a single year is modelled). Applied for each solve. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error). An explicit 0 is a limit of 0 (the net flow into the group can be negative).
  • min_cumulative_flow - [MW] Minimum average flow, which limits the cumulative flow for a group of connection_nodes and/or unit_nodes. The average value is multiplied by the model duration to get the cumulative limit (e.g. by 8760 if a single year is modelled). Applied for each solve. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error). An explicit 0 is a limit of 0 (the net flow into the group can be negative).
  • max_instant_flow - [MW] Maximum instantenous flow for the aggregated flow of all group members. Constant, period, time or period+time. A period map, or the period level of a period+time map, must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error). An explicit 0, also at a single time step, is a limit of 0.
  • min_instant_flow - [MW] Minimum instantenous flow for the aggregated flow of all group members. Constant, period, time or period+time. A period map, or the period level of a period+time map, must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error). An explicit 0, also at a single time step, is a limit of 0.

When authoring min_instant_flow / max_instant_flow as a Map, set the Map's index_name to period or time so the period-vs-time axis is unambiguous — see the note on naming the Map index above. A map without that name whose keys are none of the solve's periods is read as giving no value for the solve, so a missing period is not caught there.

docs.title: Flow aggregation method
docs.text:
• flow_aggregator — choice of flow-aggregation method for this flowGroup (default none). Values:
    • none (default) — no aggregated output; the flowGroup exists only for flow limits / investment.
    • dispatch_plots_only — member flows are shown as aggregated bands inside a node group's dispatch table (the table produced by print_dispatch on a group). Produces no output file of its own.
    • standalone_aggregator_only — emits the flowGroup's own outputs: the per-period cumulative_flow (MWh/a, scaled to a full year) and average_flow (MW), plus a signed net-flow timewise series (see Results). Does not feed any node-group dispatch table.
    • both — both of the above.

Double-counting guard. If a flow arc belongs to two flowGroups that are both dispatch-bound (dispatch_plots_only or both), the arc is double-counted in the node-group dispatch balance; the model emits a loud validation warning in this case. For overlapping thematic aggregates, use standalone_aggregator_only — overlap is harmless there.

Some of the outputs are optional. They can be removed to speed up the post-processing of results. The user can enable/disable them by changing parameters of the the model entity:

  • output_node_balance_t: Default: yes. Produces detailed inflows and outflows for all the nodes for all timesteps. Mainly useful to diagnose what is wrong with the model.
  • output_connection__node__node_flow_t: Default: yes. The flows between the nodes for each timestep.
  • output_unit__node_flow_t: Default, yes. The flows from units to the nodes for each timestep.
  • output_ramp_envelope: Default, no. Includes seven parameters that form the ramp room envelope. How much there is additional ramping capability in a given node. (Parameter node_ramp_t)
  • output_connection_flow_separate: Default, no. Produces the connection flows separately for both directions.
  • output_unit__node_ramp_t: Default, no. Produces the ramps of individual units for all timesteps.

Additionally a model level option to exclude all node, connection and unit level outputs and only leave group and model level results. This will significantly increase the speed of importing data to the result database.

  • model: exclude_entity_outputs: Default, no. Excludes results on node, unit and connection level, but preserves group level results

A further debug option writes everything the LP holds over the model horizon to a separate raw dump: the look-ahead of each roll after rolling_solve_jump and the forecast branches of stochastic solves. The normal outputs keep only the realized results, with or without it.

  • model: output_horizon: Default, no. Writes one raw parquet per LP variable and constraint, with every row of every solve and a realized column, to output_parquet/<scenario>/horizon/ (see Results). The normal outputs are unchanged.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Groups are used to make constraints that apply to a group of nodes, units and/or connections. A group is defined by creating a group entity and then creating an entity between the group and its members. The membership entity classes are group__node, group__unit, group__connection and reserve__upDown__group. The choice of group members depends on what the group is trying to achieve. For instance a group that limits investments could have a set of units included in the group.

Flow aggregation (flow limits and aggregated flow outputs) lives on a separate flowGroup class with its own 3-dim membership classes flowGroup__unit__node and flowGroup__connection__node; see that section below.

docs.title: Capacity limits for nodes, units and connections
docs.text:
• invest_method - How the group limits investment and retirement of its members (a value list of its own, group_invest_methods). not_active (default): the group sets no limits. invest / retire / invest_retire: which decisions the limits apply to; _period uses the …_period limits, _total the …_total limits, _period_total both; no_limit: no limits even if values are set; cumulative_limits uses the cumulative capacity limits. Before database version 77 not_active was called not_allowed; the upgrade renames stored values, and a database that still holds not_allowed for a group stops the run with an error.
  • invest_max_total / invest_min_total - [MW or MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required total investment of the group over all solves, summed over its units and connections (MW) and storage nodes (MWh). Every investment decision counts; retirements do not reduce it. Constant.
  • invest_max_period / invest_min_period - [MW or MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required capacity coming online in each period, summed over the group's members. With a construction lead time, the investment is decided earlier. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period in which capacity of the solve comes online: its investment periods, or with a construction lead time the periods the investments start to operate in (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_max_period / retire_min_period - [MW or MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required retirement in each period, summed over the group's members. Needs a retire …_period option in the group's invest_method. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_max_total / retire_min_total - [MW or MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required total retirement of the group over all solves. Needs a retire …_total option in the group's invest_method. Constant.
  • cumulative_max_capacity - [MW or MWh] Maximum cumulative capacity for a group of entities (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error). Only applies when invest_method is cumulative_limits.
  • cumulative_min_capacity - [MW or MWh] Minimum cumulative capacity for a group of entities (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error). Only applies when invest_method is cumulative_limits.

docs.title: Transfer method override for connections in a group
docs.text:
• transfer_method - Overrides the transfer_method chosen on each individual connection whose both endpoints belong to this group (group__node). Options: use_connection_transfer_methods (default, no override), no_losses_no_variable_cost, regular, exact, variable_cost_only, unidirectional, dc_power_flow_with_angles. The connection-level options work exactly as in the connection reference; dc_power_flow_with_angles activates B-theta DC power flow on the subnet and requires each member connection to have reactance; is_DC connections are not overridden and need no reactance. A connection with both endpoints in several groups that set different overrides is an error.
  • base_MVA - [MVA] Base power for the per-unit system used in DC power flow. Default 100. Only relevant when this group's transfer_method = dc_power_flow_with_angles.
  • reference_node - Name of the reference bus node (angle fixed to zero) for DC power flow. Optional; if not set the engine picks one deterministically.
  • candidate_precapacity_to_avoid_big_m - [MW] Small pre-existing capacity assigned to investment-candidate connections in DC power-flow subnets to avoid big-M angle constraints. Tuning parameter for numerical stability of the angle formulation.

docs.title: Limits for nodes
docs.text:
• has_inertia - A flag whether the group of nodes has an inertia constraint active. Default no. Without yes the group has no inertia constraint, even if inertia_limit is given.
  • inertia_limit - [MWs] Minimum for synchronous inertia in the group of nodes. Used only when has_inertia is yes; no value (or 0) means no requirement. Constant, period, time or period+time. A time map (or the time level of a period+time map) of a group with has_inertia yes must give a value for every time step of the solve, look-ahead included (a missing time step is an error, reported before the first solve; give 0 for an hour without a requirement). A solve whose reduce_system_detail_method leaves inertia out is not checked. A period map (or the period level of a period+time map) must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error).
  • penalty_inertia - [CUR/MWs per hour] Penalty for violating the inertia constraint. The cost scales with the duration of the violation. Default 5000, applied to every group without a value of its own (and to the periods a map leaves out); 0 makes the violation free. Constant or period.
  • has_non_synchronous - A flag whether the group of nodes has the non-synchronous share constraint active. Default no. Without yes the group has no non-synchronous constraint, even if non_synchronous_limit is given.
  • non_synchronous_limit - [share, e.g. 0.8 means 80%] The maximum share of non-synchronous generation in the node group, of the group's supply measured with the real demand (without an energy margin). Flows between the group's nodes are excluded. Used only when has_non_synchronous is yes; with the flag and no value (or 0), no non-synchronous infeed is allowed (violations are penalised). Constant, period, time or period+time. A time map (or the time level of a period+time map) of a group with has_non_synchronous yes must give a value for every time step of the solve, look-ahead included (a missing time step is an error, reported before the first solve; an authored 0 is a limit of 0, give 1 for an hour without a limit). A solve whose reduce_system_detail_method leaves the non-synchronous limit out is not checked. A period map (or the period level of a period+time map) must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error).
  • penalty_non_synchronous - [CUR/MWh] Penalty for violating the non synchronous constraint. Default 5000, applied to every group without a value of its own (and to the periods a map leaves out); 0 makes the violation free. Constant or period.
  • capacity_margin_method - Whether the group of nodes has a capacity margin in investment solves, and how the margin is given. Options: none (default, no margin), manual (the margin is capacity_margin MW) and share_of_peak (the margin is capacity_margin_share times the group's peak demand). The margin applies in the investment periods of each solve (and their stochastic branch periods); a solve without invest_periods (dispatch, rolling dispatch) has none. See The capacity margin below for what counts and how.
  • capacity_margin - [MW] The margin of a group with capacity_margin_method manual: the capacity the group needs above its demand at every time step of an investment period. Without that method the value is ignored (a warning says so). No value (or 0) means the capacity must still cover the demand. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • capacity_margin_share - [share, e.g. 0.15 means 15%] The margin of a group with capacity_margin_method share_of_peak, as a share of the group's peak demand in the period. Without that method the value is ignored (a warning says so). No value (or 0) means no margin. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve.
  • penalty_capacity_margin - [CUR/kW/a] Penalty for violating the capacity margin constraint. Uses operational discounting (not annualized over lifetime like investment costs), so a penalty of e.g. 1000 CUR/kW is not comparable to an investment cost of 1000 CUR/kW which would be annualized to a much lower annual cost. Default 5000, applied to every group without a value of its own (and to the periods a map leaves out); 0 makes the violation free. In a stochastic fan each forecast branch period has its own shortfall, and its penalty is weighted by the forecast's probability. Constant or period.
  • share_loss_of_load - Force the upward slack of the nodes in this group to be equal or inflow (demand) weighted

docs.title: The capacity margin
docs.text:
At every time step of an investment period, the capacity margin row of a group asks:

firm capacity + VRE potential + what the group's other entities deliver or take at that step ≥ the group's demand + the margin.

The demand is the real demand of the group's nodes (the negative inflow, without an energy margin). Storage nodes have no demand in the row: a storage node of the group with demand gets a warning (model that demand on a balance node of the group), a group of storage nodes only is an error, and so is a balance_within_period node in the group (its balance is per period, the margin per time step). The entities count as follows:

Entity Counts as Firm unit: a unit with an output into the group that is not one of the kinds below. Units fed from fuel or commodity nodes, from balance nodes outside the group, and units without inputs (e.g. demand response) its capacity × availability × capacity_max_coeff of the output. A unit with several outputs into the group (a CHP) counts its capacity once: capacity × availability × min(1, the sum of capacity_max_coeff of those outputs), the limit the sum of its outputs has VRE unit: a unit whose output into the group has an upper_limit or fixed profile its capacity × min(profile, capacity_max_coeff) × availability Storage-backed unit: a unit with an input from a storage node, unless its other inputs can run it at full output alone (their input_share_max adds up to at least 1; the default is 1) its actual flow, minus the energy the storage node's balance slack makes in the period (see below) Unit inside the group with efficiency ≥ 1: a unit with an input from one of the group's nodes (a heat pump in an electricity + heat group, an inverter fed from a DC bus of the group) its actual flow, and its input as consumption Lossy unit inside the group: a unit whose inputs all come from the group's nodes and whose outputs all go to them, with an efficiency (at full load) below 1 at some step (an electric boiler, an electrolyser into a hydrogen node of the group) left out: the demand it serves counts one to one Connection inside the group: both ends in the group left out: the demand at its far end counts one to one, without its losses Other connection (imports, exports, a battery behind an inverter connection) its actual flow, into the group positive, out of it negative Consumption by the units fed from the group's nodes that are not inside the group (electrolysers into a node outside the group, pumps, chargers) its actual flow, negative

Inputs and outputs with conversion_flow_coeff 0 carry no energy limit: such an output counts by its flow, and such an input is left out of the storage and inside-the-group rules.

What this means in practice:

  • Only firm and VRE capacity can hold the margin. Imports, storage and the group's own consumption help only by what they deliver at that step, which lets the firm units run less. A group fed only by imports cannot hold any margin. Energy dumped through the node's downward slack does not count.
  • Fuel is assumed to last. A unit fed from a fuel or commodity node, or from a balance node, counts at its capacity, even if the fuel is limited (a fuel node with a storage state makes its units storage-backed). To have a fuel-limited unit count by its flow, model the fuel as a storage node.
  • Storage counts by what it delivers. A battery, a hydro reservoir or a CSP heat tank counts with its discharge at that step, which is conservative when the storage is full. Pumped hydro: the turbine counts by its flow, the pump as consumption. Run-of-river counts at capacity when the river node (a balance node with inflow, no storage state) is outside the group; with the river node in the group, the turbine is a unit inside the group and counts by its flow, and the river's inflow lowers the group's demand.
  • Slack energy is not storage delivery. Energy that a storage node's upward balance slack makes could be stored and sent into the group at the binding step. For a storage node that feeds the group through a storage-backed unit or a connection, the row takes back all slack energy the node makes in the period, divided by the step's length. A storage node with penalty_method off has no slack. The same can happen through a node outside the group whose slack makes the energy it exports into the group; that is not taken back, so give such nodes a high penalty_up (or penalty_method off).
  • Exports add to the requirement. A connection out of the group counts negative, so the capacity behind an export cannot also hold the margin.
  • Losses inside the group are not part of the requirement. Connections with both ends in the group and lossy units inside the group are left out of the row: their far end's demand counts one to one. If the losses at the peak matter, add an estimate of them to the margin. (Had the row kept them, it would require the losses of the dispatch at each step, and shedding the load behind a lossy line would lower that requirement by more than the unserved energy raises the shortfall: a margin MW is priced for the whole year, a shed MWh only for its hour, so the model would shed load to hold the margin.) A heat pump (efficiency ≥ 1) stays in the row by its flow: its input is the power the heat demand needs.
  • Unserved energy is priced once. Load the group does not serve leaves the row unchanged where firm capacity would have served it, and is priced by penalty_up only.
  • The energy margin does not change the capacity margin. The row uses the real demand. Storage and imports count with the power they deliver at the step, also when it serves the energy margin's added demand: that power is real capability at that step. Firm output that serves the added demand leaves the row unchanged.

The margin of a share_of_peak group is capacity_margin_share × the group's peak demand: the largest sum of the demand of the group's nodes over the period's full time series, on the period's original timeline (before representative periods and new_stepduration, and the same in every roll of a solve). If the representative periods leave the peak out, the margin still uses the real peak. When several investment periods of a solve use different parts of one timeline (a multi-year timeline, one block per period), each period's peak is over its own part: the time steps of its timeset blocks, or, with representative periods, of the base periods they stand for. A stochastic branch period has its own peak, from its own branch data.

Reading the result. After each investment solve that leaves a shortfall, the run log prints capacity margin shortfall: solve …, group …, period …: … MW at … (penalty … M CUR). The table capacity_margin__d has, per solve, group and investment period, the binding time step, the requirement, what each class above counts there and the shortfall; capacity_margin_entity__d has what each unit, connection and node counts, which shows which rule applies to it. slack__capacity_margin__d and the capacity margin penalty of the costs are those of the solve that decided the investments.

With representative periods, the row holds at the sampled time steps only, and the storage that counts is the storage of the sampled days: force-include the peak days. Over a coarse time step (new_stepduration) the row may be averaged (see below).

Under spatial Benders decomposition (decomposition_method benders_regional), a capacity margin group (and an inertia or non-synchronous group) with nodes in more than one region is an error: each region would have to hold the whole margin. Use one group per region.

docs.title: CO2 costs and limits
docs.text:
• co2_method - Choice of the CO2 method or a combination of methods: no_method, price, period, total, price_period, price_total, period_total, price_period_total. A method with period in it needs co2_max_period and a method with total in it needs co2_max_total; a group without that value is an error.
  • co2_price [CUR/tCO2] CO2 price for a group of nodes. Constant or period. A period-indexed Map may cover more periods than the current solve realises — extra entries are silently ignored, so the same shared CO2-price dataset can drive solves with different period subsets. If the active solve activates co2_price topology (a priced commodity is wired up) but no co2_price or co2_content value is supplied for a needed period, the engine logs a warning and skips the CO2 cost term for that period rather than raising an error.
  • co2_max_period [tCO2/a] Annualized maximum limit for emitted CO2 in each period (tonnes per year of the period). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period of the solve, look-ahead periods included (a missing period is an error). In a rolling solve each roll applies the limit to its own window (realized part and look-ahead): its emissions are annualised over the window's hours of each period. The limit is carried across the rolls: each roll may emit the share of the period's limit reached by the end of its horizon, minus the emissions earlier rolls already realized in the period, so the realized emissions of a period stay within the limit. In a rolling solve the reported CO2 price of a period is the shadow price of the last roll that covers the period.
  • co2_max_total [tCO2] Cumulative limit for emitted CO2 over the whole solve horizon: each period's annualized emissions times the years it represents (years_represented), summed over the periods, so the model chooses when to emit. In a rolling solve or a chain of solves the limit is carried: each roll or solve may emit the part of the limit allotted to the periods it reaches (in a rolling solve, the years_represented-weighted share of the solve's periods reached by the end of the roll's horizon; a solve of a chain reaches all of its own periods) minus what earlier rolls and solves already realized, counted the same way (annualized and times years_represented). The realized emissions of the whole chain therefore stay within the limit, but an early solve of a chain may use up what later solves would have needed. In a stochastic solve each forecast path gets the whole remaining limit.

The emissions that the CO2 price and the limits apply to are the fuel drawn from the group's nodes times the commodity's co2_content, including the extra fuel that min_load_efficiency units burn at part load.

docs.title: Stochastics
docs.text: • include_stochastics Flag to choose if stochastic timeseries are to be used for the units/nodes/connections of this group

docs.title: Decomposition (spatial Benders)
docs.text:
• decomposition_method (on group) - Decomposition strategy to apply to this group. Currently supported: none (no decomposition; default) and benders_regional (the group becomes a spatial region when a solve sets decomposition = benders — the _region suffix emphasises that this is the geographic flavour, distinct from any future temporal variant). See dev/decomposition.md for the algorithm, gap tolerances, and the membership classes the decomposer expects.
  • decomposition (on solve) - Whether this solve decomposes. none (default) solves monolithically; benders routes the solve through the spatial Benders coordinator (master trade flows + trade invest + per-region recourse, optimality cuts) over the benders_regional groups. Chosen per solve, so one chain can mix schemes. The optional knobs benders_max_iter (default 50) and benders_tolerance (default 1e-3) cap the cut loop and set the relative optimality-gap threshold.

docs.title: Flex-temporal decomposition (per-group step duration)
docs.text:
• new_stepduration - Hours. Balances the nodes of this group once per coarse step of this length, while the rest of the model keeps the solve's time step.

    What it does. The balance and storage nodes of this group are balanced once per coarse step when the step is longer than the solve's time step. An example is hourly electricity nodes next to daily hydrogen nodes. The energy over each coarse step balances, so the node may shift energy freely within the step. A storage node's state is constant within the step.

    Which units and connections go coarse. A unit or connection with a node outside the coarse groups keeps the solve's time step. A coarse node sums its flows over the step, so an arc between an hourly and a daily node conserves energy at both ends. A unit or connection whose balance nodes are all coarse uses the coarse step: it has one flow per coarse step, a rate that stays the same over the step. If its nodes have different coarse steps, it takes the shortest one when that step divides the others; otherwise it keeps the solve's step. Listing a unit or connection in the group has no effect (a warning names those that touch a node outside the group).

    Nodes without a balance. Commodity and price nodes and balance_within_period nodes do not count. A unit that also buys fuel can therefore be coarse; it pays the average price of the step.

    Averaged limits. The capacity, availability, profile, efficiency and input-share limits of a coarse unit or connection apply to the average over each coarse step. This gives the same result as hourly flows when each arc has at most one limit that varies within the step, and its cost, efficiency and prices do not vary within the step. Otherwise the result can differ. With a cost or efficiency that varies, hourly flows could use the cheapest or most efficient hours. With two or more varying limits, the averaged limits are looser.

    Ramps. Ramp limits apply between consecutive coarse steps, with the average duration of the two steps (see ramp_speed_up). Inside a coarse step the flow does not change.

    Online units. A unit or connection with online variables uses the coarse step too. Its units online, start-ups and shut-downs are decided once per coarse step; it starts or stops at the start of the step. Its minimum load and online capacity apply to the average over the step. A minimum up or down time counts whole coarse steps: a start-up counts while the steps since its start last less than min_uptime. On daily steps a min_uptime of at most 24 h adds nothing.

    Online units with ramp limits. The start-up and shut-down capacity reduction uses the coarse step. While the ramp does not reach full output within the step, a unit started at the start of a step reaches on average min_load + ½ × ramp_speed_up × 60 × step duration of its capacity over the step. When the ramp does reach full output (full output for the rest of the step), the average is 1 − (1 − min_load)² / (2 × ramp_speed_up × 60 × step duration). The same holds with ramp_speed_down before a shut-down. Its units online ramp between coarse steps.

    Reserves. A unit or connection whose balance nodes are all coarse and that provides reserves holds one reserve per coarse step. Its reserve limits apply to the average over the step, with the average availability or profile. These limits are the reserve share of its capacity, a connection's net position, the floor of its flow, and the storage energy for the reserve duration when the storage node and every provider are coarse. The room its ramp limit leaves for reserve is the smallest of the step's time steps, each with its own capacity factor. The reserve requirement is still checked at every time step of the solve, and nodes of a coarse group may belong to reserve groups.

    Exact connections and DC power flow. An exact connection whose nodes are all coarse chooses its direction once per coarse step; its direction limits apply to the average over the step. A DC power-flow line whose nodes are all coarse has one flow per coarse step. When every line of a DC network uses the coarse step (all its nodes with the same coarse step), its nodes have one voltage angle per coarse step. In a DC network with a line at the solve's step, every angle stays at the solve's step, so that line keeps its per-step physics.

    Rows that combine several entities. These rows follow one rule: the capacity-margin, inertia and non-synchronous rows of a group, the instant flow limits of a flow group, a user constraint with flow, storage or online terms (constraint_flow_coeff, constraint_state_coeff, constraint_online_coeff), the DC power-flow row of a line, and the stochastic storage-use tie of a node. Such a row becomes one row per coarse step, the average of the row over the step, when every unit and connection in it uses the coarse step. In a user constraint, every storage node in it must also be coarse. In a capacity-margin row only the entities counted by their flow (storage-backed units, units inside the group, connections, consumption) are in it: firm and VRE units count by their capacity, and the units and connections left out are not in the row.

    Averaged rows. An averaged row uses the step mean of the demand, inflow, profile, limit or constant in it. An averaged capacity margin therefore covers the mean net demand of the step, not its peak hour. A row given on only part of a coarse step (e.g. a max_instant_flow map without values for some hours) stays at the time steps it covers. An inertia_limit or non_synchronous_limit time map must give a value for every original time step (hour) of a coarse step; its row uses the step mean. The inertia and non-synchronous shortfalls are then one value per coarse step.

    Mixed rows. A row that mixes units or connections on the coarse step with others on the solve's step is checked at every time step of the solve. It sees the coarse flows as constant through their step. A coarse DC line in a DC network with a line at the solve's step keeps the angle difference across it constant through the coarse step, while the angles stay per time step.

    Exceptions. Units and connections with a delay keep the solve's time step. In a Benders decomposition, flows that cross regions and every flow in the master keep the solve's step. In a stochastic solve, a unit or connection at a stochastic node, with online variables or providing reserves, keeps the solve's step when the forecasts are tied over only part of one of its coarse steps. In a realization solve, the same applies to one whose committed units online or reserve change within a coarse step or are pinned on only part of it.

    Messages. An info line lists the units and connections that use a coarse step, and those that keep the solve's step with the reason. A database upgraded from an earlier FlexTool version prints a notice naming the coarse units and connections whose results can differ from flows at the solve's step, and why.

    Outputs. Flows, units online, reserves, voltage angles and the shortfalls of averaged rows are written at every time step of the solve, with the same value through each coarse step. Start-ups and shut-downs are written whole at the first time step of their coarse step and as 0 at the others. A coarse node's price is the dual of its coarse-step balance, the same at every time step of the step.

    Rules for the step. The group step must be a multiple of the solve's time step; a shorter group step is ignored with a warning. Coarse steps start from the start of each timeset block. They restart after a gap in the timeline, at each representative period and at the end of the realized part of a roll. A block that is not a multiple of the step ends with a shorter step; with representative periods the step must divide the representative period.

    Storage. Storage binding methods, fix_start, storage_solve_horizon_method, nested fix methods and the roll carry apply to coarse nodes as to others. bind_intraperiod_blocks cannot be combined with a coarse group.

docs.title: Controlling outputs
docs.text:
Two group-level flags drive the extra outputs computed from a node group, and the flow_aggregator method (on the flowGroup class) drives the flow-aggregation outputs. Each has a specific intent and requires a matching membership class; setting it without the right members yields an empty result (the runner will log a warning).

You want … Set this on … Must contain Summary metrics (loss of load, VRE share, curtailment, excess load, annualised inflow) for a collection of nodes print_indicators: yes on group group__node rows A per-timestep in/out decomposition (group_flow_t) of a node collection, one column per contributing process/connection print_dispatch: yes on group group__node rows Member flows shown as aggregated bands inside a node group's dispatch table flow_aggregator: dispatch_plots_only on flowGroup flowGroup__unit__node or flowGroup__connection__node rows The flowGroup's own aggregated outputs (per-period cumulative_flow in MWh/a and average_flow in MW, plus a signed net-flow timewise series) flow_aggregator: standalone_aggregator_only on flowGroup flowGroup__unit__node or flowGroup__connection__node rows Both of the above flow_aggregator: both on flowGroup flowGroup__unit__node or flowGroup__connection__node rows
  • print_indicators (on group) — emits aggregate indicator metrics (loss-of-load share, VRE share, curtailment share, excess-load share and annualised inflow) over the node members. Acts as a summary of the node group. Requires group__node members.
  • print_dispatch (on group) — emits the per-timestep in/out decomposition of the node group, with one column per contributing process or connection (units feeding the group, connections crossing its boundary, storage, slacks). Requires group__node members. If any of those contributing flows belong to a flowGroup whose flow_aggregator is dispatch_plots_only or both, their columns are replaced by a single aggregated band named after the flowGroup.

See Flow groups (flowGroup) for the flow_aggregator method values and the flow-limit parameters.

docs.title: Defining how the node functions
docs.text:
These parameters will define how the node will behave and use the data it is given (available choices are marked in italics):

  • name - unique name identifier (case sensitive)
  • node_type - role of the node in the LP (default balance):
    • commodity - price-exposed source/sink with no balance constraint (fuel imports, no storage)
    • balance - energy balance maintained every timestep
    • storage - balance plus a state variable (battery, reservoir)
    • balance_within_period - balance aggregated over the whole period (e.g. an annual gas budget)
  • invest_method - Choice of investment method: either not_allowed or then a combination of
    • invest and/or retire
    • investment limits for each period and/or for all periods (total) or no_limit
    • cumulative_limits considers investments, retirements and existing together, requires cumulative_max_capacity and/or cumulative_min_capacity
    • any method other than not_allowed offers storage investment (retirement) in every investment period, also without invest_cost (salvage_value) or where it is 0: that capacity has no annuity, its fixed_cost still counts. To forbid investment in a period, use a period method (invest_period, invest_period_total and their invest_retire_ forms) and set invest_max_period 0 for it: the other methods do not use invest_max_period. A 0 in an invest_cost map does not forbid it.
  • inflow_method - choice how to treat inflow time series
    • use_original - does not scale the original time series (no value defaults here)
    • no_inflow - ignores any inserted inflow time series
    • scale_to_annual_flow - will scale the time series to match the annual_flow so that the sum of inflow is multiplied by 8760/hours_in_solve
    • scale_in_proprotion - calculates a scaling factor by dividing annual_flow with the sum of time series inflow (after it has been annualized using timeline_duration_in_years)
    • scale_to_annual_and_peak_flow - scales the time series to match the 'annual_flow' target while transforming the time series to match the highest load with the 'peak_inflow'
  • unit_of_measure - [text] The unit of the node's amounts, for example m3, t or MWh_th (default MWh). A label only: FlexTool converts nothing.
