The node's results and the inputs about it are labelled in it: flows and the capacity of a unit on its side per hour (m3 → m3/h), storage and inflow per time step in the unit (m3), annual results per year (m3/a), prices and penalties per the unit (CUR/m3). See Unit of measure.

docs.title: Unit of measure
docs.text:
unit_of_measure names what the node holds: MWh (the default) for electricity, m3 for water, t for hydrogen, MWh_th to tell heat from electricity. FlexTool uses it only for the labels of the results, the plots and the AI assistant; it changes no number. The node's rate is its unit per hour: m3 gives m3/h for its flows and for the capacity of a unit that delivers to it, MWh_th gives MW_th. The full rule and the table of labels are in Units of measure.

The inputs about the node are then in its units too:

  • inflow, existing, invest_max_total and the other capacities: in the node's unit (m3, or m3/h for a unit's capacity on the node), entered as they are.
  • penalty_up, penalty_down, the price of a commodity on the node, other_operational_cost of a flow into or out of it: per the node's unit (CUR/m3). Size the penalties for the unit: the default 10 000 is per MWh.
  • invest_cost, fixed_cost, salvage_value: per kW or kWh in an MWh model, so per 0.001 of the rate or the amount here. A water tank that costs 20 CUR per m3 of storage has invest_cost 0.02 (20 × 0.001); a desalination unit that costs 500 CUR per m3/h of capacity has invest_cost 0.5. Its annuity in the results is per m3 for the tank (a storage capacity is an amount) and per m3/h for the unit (a capacity is a rate).
  • efficiency of a unit between nodes of different units: output units per input unit (12 m3/MWh).

FlexTool warns when a connection, a commodity, a nodeGroup or flowGroup, or a group capacity limit spans nodes of different units (their sums are labelled Mixed units of measure!), when a reserve, inertia, non-synchronous or capacity-margin group has a member node that is not MWh, and when the value looks like a rate (m3/h instead of m3).

docs.title: Data for nodes
docs.text:
Input data is set with the following parameters:

  • inflow - [MWh] per time step. Energy flowing into the node in each time step (negative is outflow, e.g. demand). The value is the energy of the whole step, not a rate: on 1 h steps it equals the average MW, and on 3 h steps it is 3 × the average MW. When the step length of your data changes, rescale the values yourself, e.g. sum hourly values to get 3 h steps, or halve MW values for 0.5 h steps. FlexTool does not convert them, and time-series values whose time names are not on the timeline are ignored. FlexTool sums the values for you only when a solve's new_stepduration coarsens the timeline, and when a group's new_stepduration balances the node per coarse step. A constant value is used as the same energy in every step. Constant or time series.
  • annual_flow - [MWh/a] Annual flow in energy units (always positive, the sign of inflow defines in/out). Constant or period.
  • peak_inflow - [MWh] per time step. The highest inflow of a time step that the scaled inflow should reach. Used only with inflow_method = scale_to_annual_and_peak_flow, which then needs annual_flow and an inflow profile for every period. Use the same scale and sign as inflow (negative for a demand); if you change the step length, rescale it as you rescale inflow. Each period reaches its own peak_inflow; with a solve's new_stepduration, peak_inflow is matched per original time step.
  • energy_margin_method - How the node's investment-stage energy margin is applied. Options: none (default, off, no scaling), inflow_multiplier (multiply this node's inflow by energy_margin_multiplier in the investment solve only) and inflow_adder (add energy_margin_adder MWh of extra demand to each time step of the investment solve only). See How to add an energy margin for investment adequacy.
  • energy_margin_multiplier - [factor] Multiplier applied to the node's inflow in the investment solve only, when energy_margin_method = inflow_multiplier. Default 1 (no effect). A value of 1.1 makes the investment stage build for ~10% more demand, so the built capacity meets the true demand under the true (lower) annual VRE availability. Dispatch solves always see the true, un-margined inflow. The margin does not enter the reserve requirement (a group increase_reserve_ratio), the non-synchronous limit or the capacity margin, which follow the real demand (set capacity_margin for a capacity surplus). Constant.
  • energy_margin_adder - [MWh] per time step of the timeline. Extra demand (negative inflow) added to every time step of the investment solve, when energy_margin_method = inflow_adder. The value is not a total that is divided over the steps: each time step gets the full value. On a timeline of 24 h time steps, a margin of 10 MW needs a value of 240. When the investment solve uses new_stepduration, a solve step gets the sum of the values of the time steps it combines (a constant or period value counts once per time step: on 4 h solve steps of an hourly timeline, 10 adds 40 MWh per solve step). Default 0 (no effect). Adds a fixed amount of demand rather than scaling existing demand, so it also works on a node with no native inflow (e.g. a zero-inflow slack node) where the multiplier is a no-op. Dispatch solves always see the true, un-margined inflow. Like the multiplier, the added demand does not enter the reserve requirement, the non-synchronous limit or the capacity margin. Constant, period or period+time.
  • existing - [MWh or count] Existing storage capacity or number of storage units (requires node_type=storage). If virtual_unitsize is given, then existing is the number of units (capacity = existing × virtual_unitsize). Otherwise existing is the existing capacity of a single unit (typically in MWh). Constant or period.
  • invest_cost - [CUR/kWh] Overnight investment cost of new storage capacity. It is paid as an annuity over the years the storage capacity operates. Construction time costs with their interest must be included here. Constant or period: the value of the period when the storage capacity is built (comes online) is used.
  • salvage_value - [CUR/kWh] Salvage value of the storage. A retirement earns it as an annuity over lifetime (see retirements). Constant or period.
  • lifetime - [years] Operating lifetime of the storage capacity. It starts when the storage capacity starts to operate: with a construction lead time, after the construction. Used with the discount rate to calculate the annuity. What happens at the end of the lifetime depends on lifetime_method: reinvest_automatic keeps the storage capacity to the end of the model horizon, reinvest_choice retires it, no_investment retires it once. The existing storage ends at the first year of the model run plus the lifetime of the first period (in every solve of a chain of solves). Constant or period.
  • construction_lead_time - [years] Time from the investment decision until the storage capacity starts to operate. The start is rounded to the start of a period (see construction_lead_time_method). Investments whose rounded start is after the end of the solve or the model horizon are not offered, with a warning. Constant or period. Default 0. See construction lead time.
  • construction_lead_time_method - How the start of operation (decision year plus construction_lead_time) is rounded to the start of a period: immediate (no lead time, the storage capacity operates from the decision period), closest_seam (the nearest period start; a tie goes to the later one), previous_seam (the period start before), next_seam (the period start after). Without a value: immediate when there is no lead time, else closest_seam.
  • discount_rate - [e.g. 0.05 equals 5%] Discount rate for investments (WACC). Reflects the financing cost and risk for this technology. Should be nominal when model inflation_rate > 0, real when inflation_rate = 0. Constant or period.
  • invest_max_total - [MWh] Largest allowed total storage investment over all solves. Every investment decision counts, also reinvestments and investments that are no longer in service; retirements and existing capacity do not reduce it (to limit the capacity in service, use cumulative_max_capacity). Constant.
  • invest_max_period - [MWh] Largest allowed storage capacity coming online in each period. Existing capacity and retirements do not change it. With a construction lead time, the investment is decided earlier. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period in which capacity of the solve comes online: its investment periods, or with a construction lead time the periods the investments start to operate in (a missing period is an error).
  • invest_min_total - [MWh] Smallest required total storage investment over all solves, counted as for invest_max_total. Constant.
  • invest_min_period - [MWh] Smallest required storage capacity coming online in each period, counted as for invest_max_period. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period in which capacity of the solve comes online: its investment periods, or with a construction lead time the periods the investments start to operate in (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_max_period / retire_min_period - [MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required retirement of storage capacity in each period. Counts only what is retired in that period. Only existing storage can be retired (see retirements). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_max_total / retire_min_total - [MWh] Largest allowed / smallest required total retirement over all solves. Investments and existing capacity do not change it. Constant.
  • cumulative_max_capacity - [MWh] Maximum cumulative capacity (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • cumulative_min_capacity - [MWh] Minimum cumulative capacity (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • fixed_cost - [CUR/kWh/a] Annual fixed cost for storage. New storage capacity pays it only while it operates. Constant or period.
  • penalty_up - [CUR/MWh] Penalty cost for energy not served (decreasing consumption) in the node. The cost scales with both the magnitude (MW) and the duration (hours) of the violation. Default value is 10 000. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time. The default applies to every node without a value of its own, and to the periods and timesteps that a map leaves out.
  • penalty_down - [CUR/MWh] Penalty cost for excess energy (increasing consumption) in the node. The cost scales with both the magnitude (MW) and the duration (hours) of the violation. Default value is 10 000. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time. The default applies to every node without a value of its own, and to the periods and timesteps that a map leaves out.
  • virtual_unitsize - [MWh] Size of one unit. With it, existing is the number of units. Investments and retirements are continuous; their limits are in MWh. No value: the existing capacity, or 1000 MWh without it.
  • self_discharge_loss - [-] e.g. 0.01 means the content shrinks by the factor 1/1.01 every hour. Loss of stored energy over time: the content decays continuously at ln(1 + loss) per hour, for every modelled time step whatever its length; energy charged or discharged within a step is treated as spread evenly over the step. Constant, period, time or period+time (a time-varying loss decays each step at its own rate; a coarse step or timeset block decays by the sum of its hours' losses; this is exact for stored energy, while energy charged within such a step is weighted as if the loss were constant over the step, which overstates what is kept when the loss changes a lot inside the step).
  • availability - [e.g. 0.9 means 90%] Fraction of capacity available for storage. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time.
  • invest_forced - [MWh] Forces exactly this much new storage capacity to come online in the period, overriding the investment optimisation (as setting invest_min_period and invest_max_period equal). Constant or period.
  • constraint_state_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) placing the storage state variable on the left side of a user-defined constraint. See User constraints.
  • constraint_invested_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) putting the storage capacity that comes online in each period on the left side of a user-defined constraint. Without a construction lead time, this is the storage capacity invested in that period. Coefficient per MWh. See User constraints.
  • constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the storage capacity in service at the start of each period on the left side of the user constraint. This is existing capacity plus capacity that came online in earlier periods, minus earlier retirements. Capacity coming online in the period itself is in the invested term. Coefficient per MWh. See User constraints.
  • constraint_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the node's storage capacity in service in each period on the left side of the user constraint (existing plus investments still in service minus retirements). Coefficient per MWh. Capacity in construction is not included. See User constraints.
  • constraint_retired_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the storage capacity retired in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Coefficient per MWh. See User constraints.
  • constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the storage capacity in construction in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Capacity is in construction from the period of the investment decision until it comes online. It is zero without a construction lead time. Coefficient per MWh. See User constraints.
  • node__profile with profile_method - limits the storage state with a profile (upper_limit, lower_limit, fixed; the profile is a share of the storage capacity). The default is none: the profile is not applied, and FlexTool warns about a link without a profile_method. An upper_limit or fixed link to a profile without a value in the scenario stops the run with an error (it would hold the storage state at 0). See units constrained by profiles.

docs.title: Using nodes as storages
docs.text:
FlexTool manages storages through nodes. A regular node maintains an energy/material balance between all inputs and outputs (node_type=balance). A storage node includes an additional state variable, which means that the node can also use charging and discharging of the storage while maintaining the energy balance. A storage node is created by setting node_type=storage and by adding storage capacity using the existing parameter and/or by letting the model invest in storage capacity (invest_method, invest_cost, invest_max_period and invest_max_total parameters).

Since FlexTool allows different temporal structures (multi-periods, rolling optimization, etc.) there needs to be ways to define how the storages behave when the model timeline is not fully consequtive. By default, storages are forced to match start level to the end level within timesets. This is an acceptable setting for small storages that do not carry meaningful amounts of energy between longer time periods in the model.

There are three methods associated with storage start and end values: storage_binding_method, storage_start_end_method and storage_solve_horizon_method.

  • The most simple one of these is the storage_start_end_method and it overrides the other methods, since it forces the start and/or the end state of the storage to a predefined value based on the proportional parameters storage_state_start and storage_state_end (proportional means that the parameter needs to be set between 0-1 and will be scaled by the storage capacity in the model). The default is fix_nothing (the start and the end are not fixed). fix_start needs storage_state_start on the node and fix_end needs storage_state_end; fix_start_end needs both. A node that fixes a start or an end without its value stops the run with an error naming every such node, the method and the missing parameter (set the value, or a method that does not fix that end). In older databases the default was fix_start, and a fix without its value was not applied, or pinned the node at 0 when another node had a value; the upgrade rewrites such stored methods to what they did (fix_nothing, or a value of 0) where every scenario of the database used them the same way, and lists them (results unchanged). A node that used the old default with its own storage_state_start gets fix_start written in that value's alternative (results unchanged). Where scenarios differ, the method is left and the error names the scenarios. Storage nodes that relied on the old default now start free; in a model where another node had a storage_state_start they started at 0 (or at their own value) before, and runs of an upgraded database name them (see "Behaviour-change notices" below). These two parameters affect only the first and the last timesteps of the entire model (even when the model has more than one solve). A later solve or roll starts from the storage state realised before it: the end of the realised part of the previous roll or solve at the same nesting level or below (so a storage or investment solve continues from the dispatch solved below it). In nested solves the start applies to the first step of each nested level where the level first appears; a cyclic binding method (bind_within_timeblock, bind_within_period, bind_within_solve, a looping bind_intraperiod_blocks) cycles within each later solve without the start value, and a representative-period node (_blended_weights) starts each block from its own free start state. The end value (fix_end, fix_start_end) applies to the last timestep of the entire model, in every solve whose horizon contains that timestep: e.g. both an investment solve and the last dispatch solve (or roll) when both reach the end of the model, the solve of each nested level that contains it, and a roll whose look-ahead reaches it; a solve whose horizon ends earlier is not pinned. In a stochastic solve each terminal branch ends at it. Where an upper-level solve fixes the storage at that step with storage_nested_fix_method fix_quantity or fix_usage, the upper solve's value takes precedence; fix_price only values that end, so the end value still applies. storage_start_end_method is meant for simple models: in a model with several solves or rolls storage_state_reference_value with storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value is usually the better choice, since it guides the storage at the end of every solve horizon (from a time series when one is available), not only at the end of the model.
  • storage_binding_method chooses the cycle-closure scope for the storage state over discontinuities in the model timeline. There are seven cycle-scope methods plus one orthogonal aggregation method. See the parameter description in flextool/schemas/spinedb_schema.json for the canonical enumeration; in short:
    • bind_within_timeblock — state cycles within each timeblock (block start = block end + flows); in a rolling solve within the timeblock's part in the roll. With fix_start the start state is pinned at the last step of the first timeblock (in a rolling solve, of its part in the roll), the state the first step starts from.
    • bind_within_period — state cycles within each FlexTool period; blocks chain inside the period; in a rolling solve within the period's part in the roll.
    • bind_within_solve — state cycles across the whole solve horizon; in a rolling solve across each roll. With fix_start the start state is pinned at the last step of the solve, the state the first step starts from (bind_within_period: at the last step of the first period). In a stochastic solve the cycle closes once per path: the last step of every forecast branch ends at the level the solve's first step starts from; when the forecasts open in the solve's first period, each forecast's first step continues from the last step of its own path, so they all start from the same level. With storage_start_end_method fix_start (or fix_start_end) the start of each forecast is pinned to the given share (storage_state_start) of that forecast's own storage capacity, so where the capacity differs by forecast (investment or divestment per forecast) the starting energy differs although the share is the same; without a fixed start all the forecasts start from the same level.
    • With these three methods the storage level is not carried from one roll of a rolling solve to the next.
    • bind_forward_only (default) — state chains forward across the solve; no end-to-start closure. In a stochastic solve whose forecasts open in the solve's first period, all the forecasts start from the same level (the carried state, or without one a single free level). The exception is fix_start (or fix_start_end): each forecast's start is the storage_state_start share of its own storage capacity, so the starting energy differs between forecasts whose capacity differs (investment or divestment per forecast).
    • bind_within_solve_blended_weights, bind_within_period_blended_weights, bind_forward_only_blended_weights — representative-period variants of the three above. They apply RP weighting on top of the same cycle scope. With several periods each period uses its own representative periods and base periods (also when periods share a timeset); bind_within_solve_blended_weights and bind_forward_only_blended_weights chain the periods in solve order like bind_within_solve / bind_forward_only. With a blended variant every period of the solve needs a timeset with representative_period_weights. In a stochastic solve each forecast branch period uses the representative periods of the period it branches from, and each branch is independent: its first period continues from the last base period of the trunk period (the shared period before the split), a later period from the previous period of the same branch. bind_within_solve_blended_weights closes once per path: every branch's last period ends at the level the trunk period starts from. bind_within_period_blended_weights closes every branch period on itself. When the forecasts open in the solve's first period, all of them start from the same level (bind_within_solve_blended_weights through its closure, bind_forward_only_blended_weights through an equal chain start, also with fix_start, which pins the state in the first block). Inside the non-anticipativity window of a node in an include_stochastics group the start levels of the representative blocks are the same in every forecast. In a rolling solve (solve_mode rolling_window) the blended variants are not applied: those nodes bind forward only (bind_forward_only) and the storage state is passed directly from roll to roll; a warning names them once per solve (so a rolling solve that mixes periods with and without representative periods does not stop for them either).
    • bind_intraperiod_blocks — orthogonal aggregation method: state is held constant within each block and the energy balance of the node is summed over each block (every flow stays at the solve's time step); the blocks of a period form a loop, and the state of a block is its state at the end of the block. With fix_start the start state is pinned at the end of the first period's last block, the state the first block starts from. In a rolling solve (solve_mode rolling_window) the blocks of each roll also end at the end of the roll's realized part. A period that the roll holds whole loops as above (so a single roll over the whole timeline gives the same result as a solve that is not rolling). In a period that the roll holds only in part, the blocks chain forward: the first block of the period continues from the previous step of the roll, and the storage level is carried from roll to roll, as for bind_forward_only. When the roll's first period is held in part, the roll starts from fix_start (first roll) or from the level carried from the previous roll. With neither (fix_nothing), the first block has no state change, so its flows must balance on their own. Without a loop, storage_solve_horizon_method sets the end of the roll; it also sets the end of a period held in part when the next period of the roll is held whole (that period loops, so nothing continues from the end of the part). A rolling_solve_jump that is a whole number of periods keeps every realized period looping; otherwise a warning is given.
  • Silent-degrade behaviour: any *_blended_weights method on a node in a solve whose active timeset has no representative_period_weights is automatically downgraded to the corresponding non-RP variant for that solve. The same storage entity can therefore drive an RP investment solve and a chronological dispatch solve back-to-back without changing the parameter value.
  • Older databases: the parameter used to take an array of methods, and three methods had other names (bind_within_timeset → bind_within_timeblock, bind_using_blended_weights → bind_within_solve_blended_weights, bind_within_model → bind_within_solve). Migration reduces an array to one method, by priority, and renames the old methods.
  • storage_solve_horizon_method is meant for models that roll forward between solves and have an overlapping temporal window between those solves (e.g. a model with 36 hour horizon rolls forward 24 hours at each solve - those 12 last hours will be overwritten by the next solve). In these cases, the end state of the storage will be replaced by the next solve, but it can be valuable to have some guidance for the end level of storage, since it will affect storage behaviour. There are three methods: free is the default and will simply let the model choose where the storage state ends (usually the storage will be emptied, since it would have no monetary value). use_reference_value will use the value set by storage_state_reference_value (a share of the storage capacity in the period, invested storage included) to force the end state in each solve (the last step of its last period and of each stochastic branch of it) to match the reference value (not for a node whose storage_binding_method ties its end to its start: bind_within_timeblock, bind_within_period, bind_within_solve and bind_intraperiod_blocks (in a rolling solve only when the roll holds its last period whole: otherwise its blocks chain forward and the pin applies, also at the end of a period held in part that a period held whole follows), including a _blended_weights node in a solve without representative periods, which uses the method without _blended_weights). In a solve with representative periods the _blended_weights nodes keep the end pin: it applies to the state at the end of the last representative block, which their base-period chain does not tie to the start. use_reference_price assigns a monetary value (in CUR per energy unit, consistent with other commodity prices) to the storage content at the end of the solve horizon — only at the last (d, t) of the solve's last period (and of each stochastic branch of it), not at every roll boundary or at the end of an earlier period of a multi-period solve, also when the periods share a timeset — using the storage_state_reference_price parameter; the model is then free to choose how much it stores at the end of horizon based on this monetary value. In a nested lower-level solve, where the upper-level solve fixes the storage at the end of the horizon (storage_nested_fix_method fix_quantity, fix_usage or fix_price), the upper solve's value overrides the use_reference_value end value at that step. The objective term is negative (−Σ storage_state_reference_price × v_state_end × unitsize × weight_factors), so a higher terminal state reduces the objective, offsetting the operational cost of leaving energy in storage.

Note: reference-price credit is in the solver objective but not in the calculated cost totals. The credit above influences the solver's optimization but is omitted from the costs_discounted_d_p / costs_discounted_p_ parquet files and the summary_solve.csv totals — it is an artificial endogenous valuation, not a real-world cost. End-of-horizon storage valuation has several valid interpretations and is typically computed as post-analysis rather than as part of the reported cost breakdown. If needed, compute the credit from last-timestep v_state values and the storage_state_reference_price parameter yourself.

-Method hierarchy:

  1. storage_start_end_method
  2. storage_binding_method
  3. storage_solve_horizon_method

-Meaning:

  • The storage_binding_method is ignored (exeption bind_forward_only), if storage_start_end_method has the value fix_start_end: such a node chains forward like bind_forward_only (a _blended_weights method like bind_forward_only_blended_weights), so that the start and the end can take different values. A bind_intraperiod_blocks node keeps its timeset blocks, which then chain forward from period to period instead of looping within each period,
  • The storage_solve_horizon_method use_reference_value is ignored, if other storage state methods are used. Only exeptions are fix_start or bind_forward_only

-Nested Parameters:

  • storage_nested_fix_method: Sets this storage as a long-term storage whose end state at the period boundary is passed to the contained lower-level solve as a constraint. Available choices:
    • fix_nothing (or no) — no handoff for this node (default).
    • fix_quantity — pins the lower solve's storage state at the boundary to the parent-solved level (v_state equality at the last (d, t) of each fix_storage_periods entry, via node_balance_fix_quantity_eq_lower).
    • fix_price — gives the lower solve a per-MWh price tier p_fix_storage_price (taken from the parent solve's node price price_t at the fix step, or from storage_state_reference_price); the lower solve then chooses its own boundary state, paying this price for the energy it holds. Uses the same storage_state_reference_price-driven objective term described in the use_reference_price paragraph.
    • fix_usage — passes the change in storage between the solve start and the boundary (i.e. net energy charged or discharged across the dispatch window) as a less-than-or-equal cap p_fix_storage_usage, enforced by node_storage_usage_fix_le. Useful when the parent solve cares about total throughput rather than the absolute level. A parent solve may set any subset of the three metrics per node — the carriers are independent and each travels as its own handoff/fix_storage_* Provider key.

docs.title: Parameter groups (metadata)
docs.text:
Spine's parameter_definition table carries an optional parameter_group_name field — a lightweight category label that the Spine DB editor uses to group related parameters visually. FlexTool historically left this field blank. Schema v43 introduced the mechanism with a narrow Outputs foothold, and schema v44 populates it fully: every parameter_definition row in the master template is now tagged with one of 15 groups.

The scheme has no semantic meaning to the solver — it is purely metadata consumed by the Spine DB editor and anything else that walks parameter_group_name. Names are lowercase snake_case (FlexTool convention). Priorities are sparse by design so future groups can slot in without renumbering.

The groups are organised in three informal tiers — asset physics (what the thing is and how it runs), decision overlays (investment, retirement, storage state, advanced dynamics, reserves, emissions, network, flow caps, user-defined constraints), and model plumbing (model-wide settings, solve configuration, timeline definitions, output toggles).

Group Priority Colour Purpose basics 10 b3cde3 What the thing is and how it runs at steady state — default home for any parameter not clearly in a decision overlay. investment 20 fdbf6f Capacity expansion: invest costs, methods, cumulative bounds, lifetime, discount rate, annualised fixed costs, capacity margin. retirement 25 ffb870 Retirement/divestment bounds and salvage value. storage 30 cab2d6 Storage state variable, cross-solve and horizon-edge behaviour, reference price/value. tech_advanced 35 b2df8a Unit commitment (startup, min times), ramp rates, time delays — advanced operational dynamics. reserve 40 fb9a99 Spinning / standing / N-1 reserve provision parameters. emission 45 ccebc5 CO2 accounting: fuel content, group caps, prices. network 50 80b1d3 DC power flow, inertia, non-synchronous share — network-aware modelling. flow_limit 55 fccde5 Group-level aggregated flow caps / floors and loss-of-load share control. constraint 70 bc80bd User-authored linear constraints plus the coefficient parameters on other entities that couple into them. model 80 d9d9d9 Whole-model scope, horizons, numeric framing (version, periods, inflation). solve_basics 85 bebada Per-solve knobs a typical user touches (solver, mode, periods, years). solve_advanced 87 9f94c6 Per-solve internals: solver options, rolling/nested/stochastic structures, cross-solve storage handoff. timeline 90 ffed6f Time-structure definitions consumed by solves (timestep duration, timeset metadata). output 95 a6cee3 Toggles that shape what the run writes to outputs.

docs.title: Convention for new parameters
docs.text:
When you add a new parameter definition, also assign it a parameter_group_name. Use the table above to pick the group — err on the side of matching why the user sets the parameter, not where it is mathematically consumed (e.g. constraint_state_coeff on node belongs to constraint, because the user writes it to participate in a user-defined constraint, not to configure storage).

Both the group definition and the tag are set inside the same db_migration step:

db.add_update_item("parameter_group", name="my_group",
                   color="a6cee3", priority=60)
db.add_update_item("parameter_definition",
                   entity_class_name="unit",
                   name="my_param",
                   parameter_group_name="my_group")

The colour is a 6-digit hex string with no leading #. Priority controls display order in the Spine DB editor — pick a value that fits the tiered scheme above (asset physics 10–15, decision overlays 20–55, constraints 70, plumbing 80–95).

After editing the migration, run python -m flextool.update_flextool.sync_master_json_template to regenerate schemas/spinedb_schema.json — the group assignment is exported as the 6th slot of the parameter-definition tuple. The coverage pytest (tests/test_parameter_groups_coverage.py) fails loudly if any parameter is left ungrouped.

docs.title: Behaviour-change notices
docs.text:
When a FlexTool release changes what an existing model does, the database upgrade marks the upgraded database with a metadata item flextool_behaviour_change:<change> (visible in the database editor's Metadata tab). While the marker is present, every run prints a notice for each affected entity, once per run: which FlexTool version changed the behaviour (and when it was published), what changed, the entities whose results change, and how to keep the old behaviour or silence the notice. Deleting the marker stops the notice. New databases carry no markers. The markers travel with the database: copies, the Spine Toolbox editor and the Excel export / import keep them.

The markers:

  • storage_default_fix_nothing — the default storage_start_end_method became fix_nothing. The notice names the storage nodes without their own storage_start_end_method in models where some node has a storage_state_start (before: fixed at the start; now: free). Setting storage_start_end_method on those nodes silences it.
  • storage_fix_method_rewritten — the upgrade rewrote storage_start_end_method values that had no value to fix at, and wrote fix_start on the nodes that used the old default with their own storage_state_start (results unchanged); the notice lists node, alternative, old method and what was written. Its value also lists the stored methods the upgrade left because scenarios used them differently.
  • user_constraint_prebuilt_nets_retirements — constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff now subtracts the retirements of earlier periods, also those decided in the same solve (before: only those of earlier solves of a chain). The notice names the user constraints whose pre-built entity can retire; results change only if the model retires capacity. Deleting the marker silences it.

docs.title: Input checks
docs.text:
Before it reads the parameters, FlexTool checks the data of the scenario for values it cannot use sensibly. An error stops the run; one message lists every offending value of the period-key, profile-link and value checks (class, entity, parameter, value, alternative and, for a map, the first key that is wrong) with what to do, so one rerun fixes them all. A warning is printed once per scenario read in the run log; the run goes on.

Errors

  • An upper_limit or fixed unit__node__profile, node__profile or connection__profile link whose profile has no value in the scenario (it would hold the flow or the storage state at 0). The message names the link and the profile, and the alternatives that hold the profile's value when the scenario does not include them. A lower_limit link without a value is allowed (a floor of 0).
  • efficiency of a unit or a connection at or below 0.
  • Unit min_load outside [0, 1]; availability below 0 (unit, connection, node).
  • capacity_max_coeff below 0.
  • A minimum above its maximum, when the invest_method uses that pair: invest_min_period / invest_max_period, retire_min_period / retire_max_period, cumulative_min_capacity / cumulative_max_capacity (compared per period; a constant applies to every period), invest_min_total / invest_max_total, retire_min_total / retire_max_total (unit, connection, node, group). No capacity could meet both.
  • lifetime at or below 0 on an entity that can invest or retire (the investment would be charged for no years).
  • A map key of a period parameter (existing, invest_cost, startup_cost, co2_max_period, lifetime, and every other parameter that takes a period map) that is not a period: the readers would drop the value without a word (y2020 for p2020 gave no capacity). Periods are the keys of every period_timeset, the solve period lists, years_represented, the first level of stochastic_branches, the stochastic branch periods (p2035_high: the period, an underscore and the branch name) and model.periods_available, over the whole database, so a key that is a period of another scenario is fine. The message suggests the closest period (p2030x → p2030). When the data covers more years than any solve names (a 2020–2050 trajectory for a 2030 model), add the extra periods to model.periods_available. A map without an index name of a parameter that can also vary over time (availability, self_discharge_loss, ...) whose keys are neither periods nor time steps is read as a period map, unless its keys look like time steps (t0099, T0001, a date-time stamp: then the time-series check reports them). Maps keyed by something else (constraint_flow_coeff by constraint, delay by hours) are not period maps and are not checked.
  • A time-step key, a time level or a time series on a period parameter that cannot vary over time (existing, startup_cost, invest_cost, lifetime, ...; use a constant or a period map), and numeric map keys (2020) on any period parameter (periods are names such as p2020). A name that is both a period and a time step is read as a period.
  • A timeline used by a solve (through a timeset named in a period_timeset, or the timeset a solve without period_timeset takes by default) without timestep_duration, or with a step of 0 hours or less (or not a number). Only the timelines a solve uses need durations: a spare timeline in the database is ignored.

Warnings

  • A node__profile or connection__profile link without a profile_method (the default none does not apply the profile).
  • availability above 1.5, and a profile above 1.5 on an upper_limit / fixed unit link: values above 1.5 look like percentages (95 for 0.95). A capacity factor slightly above 1 (rounding, measured data) is not reported. The profile check runs right after the data is read.
  • Connection efficiency above 1 (creates energy).
  • virtual_unitsize at or below 0 (ignored: existing is then the capacity itself and the entity is one unit of it).
  • A negative existing (unit, connection or node). It is allowed: a unit with a negative capacity is an "anti-energy" unit whose flows run the other way, a node gets a negative storage capacity and a connection a negative transfer capacity. It is more often a typing mistake, and combined with a profile, min_load, storage limits or invest / retire limits it can make the problem infeasible.
  • A map of a period parameter that can also vary over time (availability, other_operational_cost, ...) without an index name whose keys are neither periods nor time steps but look like time steps, on a parameter the time-series check does not cover (the value is not used).
  • A unit flow with conversion_flow_coeff 0 that no user constraint, flowGroup maximum or upper_limit / fixed profile ties: only max_flow_for_unconstrained_variables bounds it. Such an input is a free dump load on its node, such an output a free source. Tie it with a user constraint (constraint_flow_coeff), or give it a non-zero conversion_flow_coeff. A unit with an input whose outputs all have coefficient 0 gets one warning (it uses no input). capacity_max_coeff / capacity_min_coeff on such an output has no effect.
  • A node (not commodity) without any unit (unit__inputNode, unit__outputNode) or connection (connection__node__node) in the scenario: with an inflow only the penalty slack (penalty_up / penalty_down) can meet it; without one the node does nothing. Also a balance or balance_within_period node whose units and connections only take energy out, without a positive inflow (a supply), or only bring energy in, without a negative inflow (a demand) or an energy_margin_method inflow_adder: those flows stay at 0, or only the penalty slack can balance them. A node that only has demand (negative inflow) and units or connections that only take energy out is warned about too. A connection with transfer_method unidirectional (its own, or the transfer_method of a group that holds both its nodes) only takes from its first node and brings to its second; other connections count both ways. A unit with a negative existing (an anti-energy unit) counts on both sides of its nodes. storage nodes are not checked for this (the storage state takes the rest). An inflow of 0 and inflow_method no_inflow count as no inflow. The check stays silent when in doubt.

Other checks (time series keys, timesets, input shares, minimum-load curves, ladders, group limits) are described with their parameters.

docs.title: Reserves
docs.text:
The user defines reserve categories through reserve entity. Reserves are reservations of capacity (either upward or downward) and that capacity will not therefore be available for other use (flowing energy or commodities). There are three different ways how a reserve requirement can be calculated: timeseries, large_failure and dynamic.

  • Timeseries requires that the user provides a pre-defined time series for the amount of reserve to be procured in each time step.
  • Large_failure requires that the user defines the energy flows that could be the largest failure in the system. The highest possible failure (flow multiplied by large_failure_ratio) in each timestep will then set the reserve requirement for that timestep. Each failing unit or connection is checked separately, and the reserve it holds itself does not count towards covering its own failure. For upward reserve the failure is the loss of the flow into the group's nodes; for downward reserve it is the loss of a large consumption (flow out of the group's nodes). Every unit or connection given a large_failure_ratio adds one small reserve constraint per reserve group and time step (its failure against the group's total reserve minus its own reserve), so the model grows with the number of such units plus the number of reserve providers. Still give the ratio only to the units and connections whose failure can be the largest, since each one adds constraints.
  • Dynamic means that there is a requirement based on user chosen energy flows - each participating flow is multipled by increase_reserve_ratio and then summed to form the reserve requirement, for upward and downward reserve alike (the ratio stands for the variability of the flow, which can go either way). This can be useful for covering variability within timesteps. Also demand variability can be included through increase_reserve_ratio parameter in reserve__upDown__group entity: the requirement then also grows with the demand of the group's nodes (see below).

When the same reserve category (e.g. primary upward) has more than one of these (timeseries, large_failure and dynamic) in use, then the largest requirement will apply for that timestep. If they are separated into different reserves, then they need to be fulfilled separately.

Reserve requirement is defined for groups of nodes. This means that multiple nodes can have a common reserve requirement (but it is also possible to make a group with only one node). One node can be in multiple groups and therefore subject to multiple overlapping reserve requirements. Only units can generate reserve, but connections can move reserve from one node to another (therefore, there is no impact if the nodes are in the same reserve group, but it can be useful to import reserve from outside the group).

docs.title: Reserve groups
docs.text:
For reserve__upDown__group entities:

  • reserve_method - Choice of reserve method (no_reserve, timeseries_only, dynamic_only, large_failure_only or their combinations). A dynamic or large_failure requirement needs no reservation: it applies once a unit or connection at a node of the group has an increase_reserve_ratio (dynamic; or the group has one) or a large_failure_ratio (large_failure) for this reserve.
  • reservation - [MW] Amount of reserve required. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time.
  • penalty_reserve - [CUR/MW per hour] Penalty cost for not fulfilling the reserve requirement, per MW of shortfall and hour. Constant. Default 5000 (applied to every reserve group without a value of its own, so a reserve requirement is never free to leave unmet). The unmet part (reserve shortfall) can cover the whole requirement of every method and is always priced with this penalty: for a timeseries requirement the shortfall is at most reservation; for a dynamic requirement at most the sum of the participating flows' capacities × increase_reserve_ratio (at a node a unit consumes from, its full-load input), plus the group's demand term; for a large_failure requirement at most the largest failing unit's or connection's capacity × large_failure_ratio (summed over its flows into the group, or the full-load input it draws from the group for downward reserve) (capacity = existing plus the most that can be invested by that period; with unlimited investment max_flow_for_unconstrained_variables is used). A group combining methods adds these up.
  • increase_reserve_ratio - [factor] For a group with a dynamic reserve_method: in each time step the requirement increases by this ratio times the demand of the group's nodes in that step (the negative part of each node's inflow, in MW: the step's inflow divided by the step duration; a node with positive inflow does not count and does not offset another node's demand). The extra demand of an energy_margin does not count: the requirement follows the real demand. Ignored (with a warning) for other methods. Constant.
  • reserve_duration - [hours] Time span over which committed reserve power must be sustainable from storage. Constant. Absent or 0 means the reserve is instantaneous-power-only (legacy behaviour); no storage-energy coupling is added.

docs.title: Storage-backed reserve energy adequacy (reserve_duration)
docs.text:
By default a reserve reservation only withholds power (MW of headroom) from the provider. reserve_duration additionally requires the provider to hold enough energy to actually sustain that committed power for the given number of hours, when the provider draws on (upward reserve) or charges into (downward reserve) a storage node. This is a single-scalar simplification of Backbone's duty-cycle formulation (self-discharge over the window is ignored in this first version).

For each committed reserve MW the required energy is reservation_MW × reserve_duration, corrected by the provider's efficiency:

  • Upward / discharge — the storage node is the provider's source, so the energy drawn is divided by the efficiency (÷ η): a lossy discharge must draw more stored energy to deliver the same MW. The stored energy floor is v_state · unitsize ≥ Σ reservation_MW · reserve_duration / η.
  • Downward / charge — the storage node is the provider's sink, so the energy stored is multiplied by the efficiency (× η): a lossy charge stores less per MW of charging. The free-headroom bound is v_state · unitsize + Σ reservation_MW · reserve_duration · η ≤ capacity (with the same invest/divest capacity replication as the storage state bound).

The coupling is storage-only: reserve provided by non-storage units (e.g. a gas turbine drawing on a fuel commodity) is unaffected. The obligation uses the provider's full committed MW — the trust derating (reliability) is deliberately excluded, since the physical energy required is independent of how much of the reservation is counted towards the requirement.

Limitation under representative periods: the constraints reference the intra-representative-period storage state (v_state) only. Under the representative-period blended-weights storage modes the seasonal inter-period state is bounded separately and is not aligned to the reserve's time index, so reserve_duration couples reserve to intra-period state only — matching FlexTool's own intra-period capacity approximation.

docs.title: Reserve provision by units
docs.text:
For reserve__upDown__unit__node entities:

  • max_share - [factor] Maximum share of the unit's capacity at this node that can be held as this reserve: max_share × built capacity (existing + invested − retired), also for units with online variables (their online capacity limits the reserve separately, see below). At a node the unit consumes from, the capacity is the unit's full-load input there (for a unit with one input and one output: capacity / efficiency; for a unit with several inputs: input_share_max × full-load input). Without a value the unit offers no reserve. Constant.
  • reliability - [factor] The share of the reservation that is counted to reserves (sometimes reserve sources are not fully trusted). Constant.
  • increase_reserve_ratio - [factor] The reserve requirement is increased by the flow between the unit and the node multiplied by this ratio, for upward and downward reserve alike. At a node the unit consumes from, the flow is what the unit draws there (output / efficiency, as in the node balance). Constant.
  • large_failure_ratio - [factor] Each unit using the N-1 failure method will have a separate constraint to require sufficient reserve to cover a failure of the unit generation (multiplied by this ratio); for downward reserve, the loss of the consumption the unit draws from the group's nodes (output / efficiency). The failing unit's own reserve does not count towards covering its own failure. With virtual_unitsize, the failure is the whole unit (all its units of virtual_unitsize), not one of them. Constant.

A unit can only offer reserve that reduces its flow as far as its flow allows: downward reserve at a node the unit feeds, and upward reserve at a node the unit consumes from (a consumption cut), cannot exceed the flow, and for an online unit cannot take the sum of its outputs below min_load × online capacity, nor an output with capacity_min_coeff below its own floor. The effective limit is the smaller of this and max_share × capacity. An upward reserve at the input node of a unit with one input and one output is converted to output flow by the unit's efficiency. A unit with several outputs or inputs that offers upward reserve at an input node is only kept from cutting that input below zero; together with downward reserve on its outputs it can then end up below min_load.

Reserve that raises a unit's flow needs headroom: upward reserve at a node the unit feeds and downward reserve at a node it consumes from (consuming more) cannot exceed the free capacity of that flow (built capacity; online capacity for a unit with online variables), so a unit at full consumption offers no downward reserve at its input, and an offline unit none. A downward reserve at the input node of a unit with one input and one output is converted to output flow by the unit's efficiency; such a unit with several outputs needs the headroom on each output. A unit with several inputs is only kept within that input's capacity, and its upward reserve at an output and downward reserve at an input (both "burn more") are each checked against the unit's capacity separately, not together. The effective limit is the smaller of these and max_share × capacity. A connection's reserve at a node is limited by its net position there: upward reserve by its free capacity towards the node plus the flow it sends away from the node (which it can stop), downward reserve by the flow it brings to the node plus its free capacity away from it (power at the node, after losses). A one-way connection can therefore offer upward reserve at its sending node only up to what it draws there. For a connection with online variables the online capacity counts; for an exact connection, the capacity of the direction it is set to.

A unit with online variables (startup_method linear or binary, or a minimum_time_method other than none) holds upward reserve only from its online capacity: at a node the unit feeds, its output plus the upward reserve it holds there cannot exceed online capacity × availability (× capacity_max_coeff), and for a unit with several outputs the sum of its outputs plus the upward reserve held at them cannot exceed online capacity × availability. An offline unit therefore offers no upward reserve, and an upward reserve requirement can make it worth committing a unit. This is a simplification: offline units are assumed unable to start within the reserve's activation time (reserve activation time versus unit start-up time is not modelled yet). Units without online variables are limited by their built capacity.

A unit with ramp limits (ramp_method ramp_limit or both) can hold upward reserve only within its upward ramp room of the time step after the change of its flow from the previous step, and downward reserve within its downward ramp room: the flow plus the upward reserve may rise from the previous step's flow by at most ramp_speed_up × 60 × (average duration of the two steps) × capacity, and the flow minus the downward reserve may fall by at most the same with ramp_speed_down (so a unit ramping down in a step can hold more upward reserve in it). "Consume more" downward reserve at a node the unit consumes from uses the ramp room of that input (an upward input ramp), converted by the efficiency on a unit with one input and one output; upward reserve there (consume less) uses the downward room. In the first step of a solve, and after a gap in the timeline, the reserve alone is limited to one step's room, using the online capacity for a unit with online variables. For units with online variables the reserve uses the ramp room of the unit's online capacity: a unit starting or stopping in a step is limited by its startup / shutdown output there instead (see the how-to on start-ups), not by any extra room from declaring the start or stop itself. The ramp room is per model step; the reserve's activation time is not considered.

docs.title: Reserve transfer by connections
docs.text:
For reserve__upDown__connection__node entities:

  • max_share - [factor] Maximum share of the connection's built capacity (existing + invested − retired) that can be held as this reserve at this node. Constant.
  • reliability - [factor] The share of the reservation that is counted to reserves (sometimes reserve sources are not fully trusted). Constant.
  • increase_reserve_ratio - [factor] The reserve requirement is increased by the flow between the connection and the node, in either direction, multiplied by this ratio, for upward and downward reserve alike (at the node the connection takes from: the flow it draws there, including its losses; a no_losses_no_variable_cost or DC power-flow connection's reverse flow counts too). Constant.
  • large_failure_ratio - [factor] Each connection using the N-1 failure method will have a separate constraint to require sufficient reserve to cover a failure of the connection (multiplied by this ratio): for upward reserve the loss of its flow into the group's nodes, for downward reserve the loss of the flow it draws from them, in either direction (a no_losses_no_variable_cost or DC power-flow connection's reverse flow counts too). The failing connection's own reserve does not count towards covering its own failure. With virtual_unitsize, the failure is the whole connection (all its units of virtual_unitsize), not one of them. Constant.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Units convert energy (or matter) from one form to another (e.g. open cycle gas turbine), but the can also have multiple inputs and/or outputs (e.g. combined heat and power plant). The input nodes are defined with the entity unit--inputNode while the output nodes are defined through the entity unit--outputNode.

docs.title: Defining how the unit functions
docs.text:
• 'conversion_method' to define the way unit converts inputs to outputs
  • startup_method - Choice of startup method. 'Linear' startup means that the unit can start partially (anything between 0 and full capacity) but will face startup cost as well as minimum load limit based on the capacity started up. 'Binary' startup means that the unit is committed in whole-unit steps — the online status is a general-integer variable in [0, capacity / unit_size], so the solver must branch on integer commitment. The time penalty relative to linear is not from "binary vs integer" — FlexTool uses one general-integer variable per process per timestep in both binary and the virtual-unitsize cluster form, never N independent 0/1 plants. The penalty comes from the granularity of the decision: if unit_size equals the full plant (say 1000 MW), every on/off flip moves 1000 MW of dispatch, the LP relaxation rounds badly, and primal heuristics struggle. Setting virtual_unitsize to a smaller value (e.g. 50–200 MW) keeps the whole-unit semantics but represents the fleet as finer commitment decisions; this is the clustered-UC form and is normally essential to solve a UC model in reasonable time. See also the How to make the Flextool run faster note.
  • minimum_time_method - Choice between minimum up- and downtimes: none (default, no constraints), min_uptime, min_downtime, both. When set to anything other than none, online variables are automatically activated (at least linear startup) even if startup_method is not explicitly set. This enables the unit commitment tracking needed for minimum time constraints.
  • Online status along the timeline: the units online in a step are linked to the previous step as ramp limits link flows (within a period, into a period that continues the previous one on the same timeline, into a forecast branch's first step). A step with no previous step (the first step of a solve or of a period that does not continue the previous one, the step after a gap in the timeline, a representative-period start) is linked to the last step of its own stretch of the period (up to the next gap or the period end): the commitment cycles within the stretch and never across a gap, a representative-period start or into another period. In a rolling solve the units online that the previous roll realized carry over to the next roll's steps that continue its last realized step on the timeline, by position in time (so also into a solve with longer time steps); a roll starting after a gap, at a new year that reuses the timeset or at a representative-period start takes no carry. The same applies to connections with startup_method.

docs.title: Main data items for units
docs.text:
• Capacity: existing - [MW or count] Existing capacity or number of units. If virtual_unitsize is given, then existing is the number of units (capacity = existing × virtual_unitsize) — see virtual_unitsize below. Otherwise existing is the existing capacity of a single unit (typically in MW). Constant or period.

  • Technical: efficiency, min_load, efficiency_at_min_load, min_uptime, min_downtime

    • efficiency - [-] Output / input of the unit at full load (each flow weighted by its conversion_flow_coeff). It may be above 1: a heat pump with COP 3 has efficiency 3, and a desalination unit with an electricity input and a water node output in m³ has the m³ per MWh ratio (e.g. 250). The unit's capacity is on its output side (m³/h for the desalination unit), so its input capacity factor (unit_cf__inputNode) is 1/efficiency when the unit runs at full load (1/3 for the heat pump). With a very large ratio (above about 10 000 × the unit size: virtual_unitsize, else existing, else 1000; lower with sub-hour time steps or a non_synchronous_limit), the input coefficients fall below the model parameter small_number_threshold (default 0.0001) and become 0, so the unit draws no input and its output is free. Lower small_number_threshold or rescale the output unit of measure. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time.
    • min_uptime - [hours] Minimum time the unit must stay online after starting up. Requires minimum_time_method set to min_uptime or both. The constraint looks back over the time steps before each step and adds up their durations, so it accounts for variable timestep durations. The look-back follows the timeline as ramp limits do: it continues into a period whose time steps continue the previous period's on the same timeline and, in a stochastic solve, into the steps before a forecast branch starts; it stops at a gap in the timeline (the minimum time restarts after the gap), at the start of a representative period, at a period that reuses the same timeset as the previous one and at the first step of a solve (no cyclic wrap). In a rolling solve the start-ups that the previous roll realized count for the steps of the next roll that continue its last realized step on the timeline (as the ramp continues: also into a continuing period and every forecast branch that starts there); a solve with longer time steps continues the realized step that ends where its own previous step ends (by position in time). A warning is printed only when a solve continues the timeline of an earlier solve with a hole or an overlap between its first step and the earlier solve's last realized step, since no realized on-line history reaches it. Constant.
    • min_downtime - [hours] Minimum time the unit must stay offline after shutting down. Requires minimum_time_method set to min_downtime or both. The look-back works as for min_uptime, with shut-downs. Constant.

    • min_load - [0-1] Minimum load of the unit. Applies only if the unit has an online variable. With linear startups, it is the share of capacity started up. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time. Applied once per unit, for all timesteps:

    • the sum of the unit's output flows >= min_load * online capacity

    The output flows are the ones that define the unit's capacity: all outputs with a non-zero conversion_flow_coeff (for a unit with one input and one output, its single flow; for a unit without outputs, its input). Inputs never have their own minimum: a unit with several inputs can run on any mix of them (use input_share_min to require a share of an input). The floor is not scaled by availability, so a unit whose availability falls below min_load cannot be online. capacity_min_coeff on an output does not lower this floor; to lower or switch off the minimum load, lower min_load (0 switches it off; no value means 0, so a unit with an online variable does not need a min_load). Downward reserve (and upward reserve at an input node, i.e. reduced consumption) offered by the unit cannot take its outputs below this floor (see Reserves).

    • efficiency_at_min_load - [-] Output / input at minimum load, like efficiency (e.g. 0.4; may be above 1). Efficiency of a min_load_efficiency unit at its minimum load; the fuel use is linear between minimum load at this efficiency and full load at efficiency. Matters only for a unit with a min_load above 0 (with min_load 0 the unit uses efficiency). Without a value (or for the periods or timesteps a map leaves out) the unit uses efficiency at minimum load too, i.e. a flat curve as with constant_efficiency, while its minimum load still applies; a warning names such units. Constant, period, time or period+time.

  • availability - [e.g. 0.9 means 90%] Fraction of capacity available for flows from/to the unit. For online units, the online variable is multiplied by the availability. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time.

  • Economic: startup_cost ([CUR/MW] cost of starting up one MW of capacity; constant or period), fixed_cost (fuel cost comes through the use of fuel commodities and other variable costs are defined for flows between unit and node, see below)

docs.title: Investment parameters for capacity expansion
docs.text:
With virtual_unitsize, investment and retirement limits stay in MW; the amounts are not whole units.

  • invest_method - Choice of investment method: either not_allowed or then a combination of
    • invest and/or retire
    • investment limits for each period and/or for all periods (total) or no_limit
    • cumulative_limits considers investments, retirements and existing together, requires cumulative_max_capacity and/or cumulative_min_capacity
    • any method other than not_allowed offers investment (retirement) in every investment period, also without invest_cost (salvage_value) or where it is 0: that capacity has no annuity, its fixed_cost still counts. To forbid investment in a period, use a period method (invest_period, invest_period_total and their invest_retire_ forms) and set invest_max_period 0 for it: the other methods do not use invest_max_period. A 0 in an invest_cost map does not forbid it.
  • lifetime_method to choose how the investments behave after unit runs out of lifetime. Automatic reinvestment (reinvest_automatic - default) causes the model to keep the capacity until the end of model horizon and applies the annualized investment cost until the end of model horizon without further choice by the model. Choice of reinvestment (reinvest_choice) removes the capacity at the end of the lifetime and the model needs to decide how much new capacity is to be built. One-shot investment (no_investment) allows the model to invest freely within the first-period lifetime window (subject to the usual invest_method / invest_max_period caps) but pins v_invest to zero for any period after that window — the asset retires once and cannot be rebuilt. Use for physical one-off additions such as plant refurbishments that cannot be repeated at the same cost. If there is a need to remove the possibility to invest after lifetime, then the investment limits can be used.
  • invest_cost - [CUR/kW] Overnight investment cost of new capacity. It is paid as an annuity over the years the capacity operates. Construction time costs with their interest must be included here. Constant or period: the value of the period when the capacity is built (comes online) is used.
  • salvage_value - [CUR/kW] Salvage value of the unit capacity. A retirement earns it as an annuity over lifetime (see retirements). Constant or period.
  • lifetime - [years] Operating lifetime. It starts when the capacity starts to operate: with a construction lead time, after the construction. Used with the discount rate to calculate the annuity. What happens at the end of the lifetime depends on lifetime_method: reinvest_automatic keeps the capacity to the end of the model horizon, reinvest_choice retires it, no_investment retires it once. The existing capacity ends at the first year of the model run plus the lifetime of the first period (in every solve of a chain of solves). Constant or period.
  • construction_lead_time - [years] Time from the investment decision until the capacity starts to operate. The start is rounded to the start of a period (see construction_lead_time_method). Investments whose rounded start is after the end of the solve or the model horizon are not offered, with a warning. Constant or period. Default 0. See construction lead time.
  • construction_lead_time_method - How the start of operation (decision year plus construction_lead_time) is rounded to the start of a period: immediate (no lead time, the capacity operates from the decision period), closest_seam (the nearest period start; a tie goes to the later one), previous_seam (the period start before), next_seam (the period start after). Without a value: immediate when there is no lead time, else closest_seam.
  • discount_rate - [e.g. 0.05 equals 5%] Discount rate for investments (WACC). Reflects the financing cost and risk for this technology. Should be nominal when model inflation_rate > 0, real when inflation_rate = 0. Constant or period.
  • invest_max_total - [MW] Largest allowed total investment over all solves. Every investment decision counts, also reinvestments and investments that are no longer in service; retirements and existing capacity do not reduce it (to limit the capacity in service, use cumulative_max_capacity). Constant.
  • invest_max_period - [MW] Largest allowed capacity coming online in each period. Existing capacity and retirements do not change it. With a construction lead time, the investment is decided earlier. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period in which capacity of the solve comes online: its investment periods, or with a construction lead time the periods the investments start to operate in (a missing period is an error).
  • invest_min_total - [MW] Smallest required total investment over all solves, counted as for invest_max_total. Constant.
  • invest_min_period - [MW] Smallest required capacity coming online in each period, counted as for invest_max_period. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every period in which capacity of the solve comes online: its investment periods, or with a construction lead time the periods the investments start to operate in (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_cost - [CUR/kW] Retirement cost for new capacity. Constant or period.
  • retire_max_total - [MW] Largest allowed total retirement over all solves. Investments and existing capacity do not change it. Constant.
  • retire_max_period - [MW] Largest allowed retirement in each period. Counts only what is retired in that period; existing capacity and investments do not change it. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • retire_min_total - [MW] Smallest required total retirement over all solves. Constant.
  • retire_min_period - [MW] Smallest required retirement in each period. Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • Only existing capacity (the capacity before the model run) can be retired, until its end of life; a required retirement (retire_min_period, retire_min_total) that the existing capacity cannot supply stops the run with an error naming the entity and the period. See retirements.
  • cumulative_max_capacity - [MW] Maximum cumulative capacity (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • cumulative_min_capacity - [MW] Minimum cumulative capacity (considers existing, invested and retired capacity). Constant or period. A period map must give a value for every investment period of the solve (a missing period is an error).
  • fixed_cost - [CUR/kW/a] Annual fixed cost for capacity. New capacity pays it only while it operates. Constant or period.
  • delay - [hours] A time delay between the input nodes and the output nodes of the unit. Either a constant (the delay in hours) or a map of delays (index: delay in hours, value: weight, the share of the input flow arriving after that delay; the weights should sum to 1). Requires that the time resolutions in the model are always integer multiples of these delays. Used when modelling process delays (e.g. heat-storage charge cycles or production lag).
  • constraint_invested_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) putting the unit's capacity that comes online in each period on the left side of a user-defined constraint. Without a construction lead time, this is the capacity invested in that period. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity in service at the start of each period on the left side of the user constraint. This is existing capacity plus capacity that came online in earlier periods, minus earlier retirements. Capacity coming online in the period itself is in the invested term. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the unit's capacity in service in each period on the left side of the user constraint (existing plus investments still in service minus retirements). Coefficient per MW. Capacity in construction is not included. See User constraints.
  • constraint_retired_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity retired in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the capacity in construction in each period on the left side of the user constraint. Capacity is in construction from the period of the investment decision until it comes online. It is zero without a construction lead time. Coefficient per MW. See User constraints.
  • constraint_online_coeff - [unit of the constraint per unit online] A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient). Puts the number of units online in each time step on the left side of the user constraint. One unit is virtual_unitsize; without it, the largest existing capacity, else 1000 MW — set virtual_unitsize on a unit that is invested in. Needs online variables (startup_method linear or binary, or a minimum_time_method); a coefficient on a unit without them is an error. With binary startup the number is a whole number, with linear startup it is continuous (the online capacity in units' worth). For MW online, use the unit size (MW per unit) as the coefficient. See User constraints.
  • virtual_unitsize - [MW] Size of one unit. With it, existing is the number of units. Binary startups commit whole units of this size. Investments and retirements are continuous; their limits are in MW. No value: the existing capacity, or 1000 MW without it. Also used, in conjunction with startup_method = binary, for unit commitment granularity: there, an unset virtual_unitsize falls back to the unit's whole built capacity, so every commitment decision moves the full plant — correct only when the modeled entity is inherently a single indivisible unit. Set this to the actual physical sub-unit size (e.g. the size of one boiler, turbine, string or module inside the modeled entity) for finer commitment decisions.
    • FlexTool represents unit commitment with a single general-integer variable per process per timestep, counting how many sub-units are online. Its upper bound is existing (plus any invested/retired units) when virtual_unitsize is set and used as the commitment granularity. So existing = 5 and virtual_unitsize = 200 MW describe a 1000 MW plant built from five physical 200 MW units (commitment variable ∈ [0, 5]) — the same MIP as if the plant were entered directly as five separate 200 MW units.
    • virtual_unitsize is not a free tuning knob. Picking a value smaller than the real sub-unit size (e.g. 50 MW for a plant whose boilers are actually 200 MW) lets the solver commit fractions that don't physically exist, mis-representing minimum load, startup fuel use and minimum-uptime/downtime behavior. Pick the value that reflects reality. If reality genuinely is a single 1 GW boiler, accept the slower MIP or use startup_method = linear; see How to make the Flextool run faster for the trade-offs.

docs.title: Discount calculations
docs.text:
Each asset that can be invested in should have invest_cost, lifetime and discount_rate parameters set and could have an optional fixed_cost. These are used to calculate the annuity of the investment. Annuity is used to annualize the investment cost, since FlexTool scales all costs (operational, investment and fixed) to annual level in order to make them comparable. Annuity is calculated as follows:

invest_cost * discount_rate / { 1 - [ 1 / ( 1 + discount_rate ) ] ^ lifetime } + fixed_cost

A discount_rate of 0 gives the straight-line annuity invest_cost / lifetime + fixed_cost. Without a value the discount_rate is 0.05; a negative value is an input error. lifetime is required when the asset invests or retires with a cost, and when its lifetime_method is reinvest_choice or no_investment. An asset whose invest_method allows investing is offered investment also without invest_cost (then it has no annuity, only its fixed_cost).

The next step is to consider inflation adjustment - future costs are adjusted to a common price base. There is a model-wide assumption for the inflation_rate. By default it is 0 (i.e. no inflation, real inputs), but it can be changed through the inflation_rate parameter set for the flexTool model entity. The inflation adjustment factor for every period in the model is calculated from the inflation_rate using the years_represented parameter of each solve, which defines how many years the period represents. Values for years_represented are used to calculate how many years_from_solve_start each year is. The formula is:

[ 1 / ( 1 + inflation_rate ) ] ^ years_from_solve_start
