Operational costs are also adjusted for inflation using the same inflation_rate. However, with operational costs it is assumed that they take place on average at the middle of the year whereas investment costs are assumed to take place at the beginning of the year (they are available for the whole year). These can be tweaked with the inflation_offset_investment and inflation_offset_operations parameters (given in years). Please note that given this formulation, invest_cost should be the overnight built cost, also with a construction_lead_time: the financing costs of the construction period need to be included in your cost assumptions. The annuity and the fixed cost of new capacity are paid only over the years it operates (from the period it comes online), and the invest_cost (and lifetime, discount_rate) of the period it comes online is used.

The model has a model horizon based on the years_represented parameters. The model will not include investment annuities after the model horizon (in other words, the investments are 'returned' at the end of the model horizon). Naturally also operational costs are included only until the end of the model horizon.

Finally, the retirements work similar to investments using the same inflation_rate and discount_rate parameters but with salvage_value as the benefit from retiring the unit.

docs.title: Retirements
docs.text:
• Only capacity that existed before the model run (existing) can be retired; investments of the model are not. A period where the entity has no existing capacity (none given, or past its end of life) has no retirement option. An entity with a retire option in invest_method but no existing capacity gets a warning; its retired-capacity terms of user constraints are 0.
  • A retirement removes the capacity from its period until the end of life of the existing capacity: for reinvest_choice and no_investment the first year of the model run plus the lifetime (counted from the start of the run also in a chain of solves), for reinvest_automatic the end of the model horizon. From the end of life on, the existing capacity is gone anyway.
  • The capacity retired and still in effect in a period cannot exceed the existing capacity of that period (also with an existing that declines over the periods).
  • The retirement saves the fixed cost the retired capacity would have paid in each of those periods (each period's fixed_cost, discounted as the fixed cost of existing capacity), and earns the salvage_value as an annuity over lifetime, in the periods from the retirement until lifetime later that are inside the model horizon (as the annuity of an investment, so retiring existing capacity and building identical new capacity gains nothing).
  • A required retirement (retire_min_period, retire_min_total, also of a group) that the existing capacity cannot supply stops the run with an error naming the entity (or group) and the period.

docs.title: Entities between units and nodes
docs.text:
• If the unit’s outputs are flowing into the node, the node acts as output for the unit.
  • If the unit’s inputs are flowing out of the node (into the unit), the node acts as input for the unit.
  • Not all units necessary have both an input and an output node. E.g. VRE generators have only output nodes and their generation is driven by profiles

docs.title: Properties of unit--inputNode and unit--outputNode entities
docs.text:
• is_non_synchronous - Chooses whether the unit is synchronously connected to this node.

  • conversion_flow_coeff - [factor, default 1] How much input energy one unit of this flow stands for. Constant.

    What it does. The coefficient goes into the unit's efficiency (conversion) equation: the slope and section of its fuel-use curve. It is not a separate multiplier in the node balance. The node always gets or gives the flow v_flow itself. A higher coefficient means more fuel per unit of flow on this edge.

    The equations. A direct-method unit (one input, one output) uses input·source_flow_coef = output·sink_flow_coef·slope⁰ + section⁰·online (nodeBalance_eq). An indirect-method unit (several flows) sums the same terms over its arcs: Σ v_flow_source × source_flow_coef = Σ v_flow_sink × sink_flow_coef × slope + section × online (conversion_indirect).

    Typical uses. Scale fuels of different energy content (fuel₂ = 2 MWh per flow unit → conversion_flow_coeff = 2). Weight the outputs of a CHP unit: a premium electricity output that costs more fuel per unit can have a higher coefficient than a byproduct heat output. Convert units of measurement.

    With a minimum-load section. When the unit has a min_load_efficiency section and an output coefficient other than 1, efficiency and efficiency_at_min_load are no longer the unit's energy efficiencies. The section is per unit of native output capacity and is not weighted by the output coefficient. The full-load energy efficiency is then sink_flow_coef / (sink_flow_coef·slope⁰ + section⁰).

    A zero coefficient. conversion_flow_coeff = 0 takes the edge out of every per-edge capacity, ramp and min-load constraint. This is the hydro pass-through pattern. The edge stays uncapped: a zero coefficient is not folded into the slope and section, which would divide by zero or make the input free. Only max_flow_for_unconstrained_variables (model, default 1 000 000) bounds such a flow, so tie it to another flow with a user constraint (constraint_flow_coeff), a flowGroup max_instant_flow / max_cumulative_flow or an upper_limit / fixed profile. FlexTool warns about a zero-coefficient flow with none of these (a flowGroup minimum does not tie it: it bounds only from below), about a unit with an input whose outputs all have coefficient 0 (it uses no input, its outputs are free), and about capacity_max_coeff / capacity_min_coeff on a zero-coefficient output (no effect).

  • capacity_max_coeff (unit--outputNode) - [factor, default 1] The share of the unit's capacity that this output may use. Constant.

    What it does. The capacity is existing + invested − retired. The unit capacity caps the sum of the outputs of a multi-output (indirect) unit. capacity_max_coeff adds a cap on each output. A value of 0 is a zero cap. To take an edge out of the capacity constraints, use conversion_flow_coeff = 0 instead.

    Where it applies. In maxFlow, in maxToSource (reverse direction of a 2-way unit), in minToSink_1var (reverse-direction cap of a 2-way unit with one flow variable), in the online flow cap and in the ramp constraints, up and down. The ramp limit always scales with the capacity ceiling.

  • capacity_min_coeff (unit--outputNode) - [factor 0..1, default 0] Optional extra floor on this output of a unit with several outputs. Constant.

    While the unit is online, output >= capacity_min_coeff × min_load × online capacity. The unit's own min_load applies once to the sum of its outputs and is not scaled by this coefficient. The default 0 means no separate floor on this output. The coefficient has no effect on a unit with one output. Downward reserve on this output cannot take it below the floor.

  • input_share_max (unit--inputNode) - [factor, default 1] The largest share of the unit's full-load input energy that this input may supply. Input energy is the flow × conversion_flow_coeff. Constant.

    The limit. The input flow is limited to input_share_max × availability × capacity × L. L is the input flow that runs the unit at full output from this input alone: L = (slope × W + section) / conversion_flow_coeff_input. W is the largest output-side input energy per unit of capacity that the outputs can demand. To find it, fill the outputs in descending conversion_flow_coeff order, each up to its capacity_max_coeff, until their sum reaches the capacity. Then W = Σ conversion_flow_coeff × fill.

    Choosing a value. The default 1 lets this input alone run the unit at full output, so there is no real limit. Values above 1 act like 1. With two inputs at 0.6 each, neither can run the unit at full output alone, but together they can. An input with lower energy content needs no smaller share: its conversion_flow_coeff already raises its flow limit.

    How it enters the model. When the unit has no investment or retirement in the solve, the limit is a bound on the flow variable. Otherwise it scales with the invested and retired capacity in maxFlow. The source-side ramp limits scale with the same input limit. Inputs with conversion_flow_coeff = 0 are not limited.

    Units with one input and one output, or no output. On a direct-conversion unit an input_share_max you set caps the flow at input_share_max × capacity. If the output has a capacity_max_coeff, the smaller of the two applies. On a unit without outputs, it is the share of the unit's capacity available to the input.

    Older databases. This parameter used to be capacity_max_coeff on unit--inputNode. Migration renames it.

  • input_share_min (unit--inputNode) - [factor 0..1, default 0] While the unit runs, the smallest share of its current input energy that this input must supply. Constant.

    The requirement. conversion_flow_coeff_s × input_s >= input_share_min_s × Σ conversion_flow_coeff × input. The sum is over the unit's inputs with a non-zero conversion_flow_coeff. The default 0 means no minimum. It applies with or without online variables. When the unit has no input, the requirement is met trivially.

    Minimum versus maximum. input_share_max is a share of the full-load input, input_share_min a share of the current input. Setting input_share_min on every input, with shares summing to 1, fixes the blend. A required share makes the unit unable to run whenever that input cannot supply.

    Errors and warnings. These are errors: a share above the same input's input_share_max, a share outside 0..1, shares of a unit's inputs that sum above 1, and a share on a unit that has an input with a negative conversion_flow_coeff. The share has no effect on an input with conversion_flow_coeff = 0 or on a unit with a single input; FlexTool gives a warning.

    Older databases. Migration renamed the old capacity_min_coeff on unit--inputNode to input_share_min. It deleted the stored values, because they had a different meaning. Set the share again if you used the old parameter.

  • other_operational_cost - [CUR/MWh] Other operational variable costs for energy flows. Constant, period, time, period+time or stochastic time.

  • inertia_constant - [MWs/MW] Inertia constant for a synchronously connected unit to this node. Constant.
  • ramp_method - [choice] Choice of ramp method. ramp_limit limits the ramp speed (ramp_speed_up, ramp_speed_down). ramp_cost charges every change in the flow between consecutive time steps (ramp_cost). both adds the limit as well.

  • ramp_cost - [CUR/MW] Cost per MW of change in the step-average flow, up or down, between a time step and the step before it. Charged per change, independent of step length. Needs ramp_method ramp_cost or both. Constant.

    What is charged. Every change of the flow from the previous step costs ramp_cost per MW, up and down alike. A change is an event, like a start-up, so the step length does not enter: ramping 0 → X → 0 costs 2 × ramp_cost × X however long the steps are. Finer time steps can show more variation of the flow, and the cost charges it. The cost is reported in the cost category ramps.

    Which flow. The cost is on the flow of the side it is set on: an output of the unit on unit__outputNode, an input on unit__inputNode. A constant_efficiency unit with one input and one output has one flow, its output: an input-side ramp cost then prices the change of that output flow, as the input-side ramp limit limits it. Costs on both sides of such a unit add up. A unit with several inputs or outputs has a flow per input and per output: each is charged by the ramp cost of its own side, so switching fuels at a constant output is charged only by input-side ramp costs.

    Where the cost applies. The cost uses the same previous step as the ramp limit (see ramp_speed_up): no cost at the first step of a solve, across a gap in the timeline, at the start of a representative period or between periods that reuse the same timeset. A rolling window is charged for the change from the flow the previous window realized, once. A unit between coarse nodes is charged between its coarse steps. A stochastic solve charges each forecast branch with its weight.

    Interactions. A start-up from zero pays both startup_cost and the ramp cost of the flow it adds. A conversion_flow_coeff of 0 removes the ramp limit of the flow but not its ramp cost. Reserves are not charged. With a ramp cost, the price at a node where a ramp-costed unit sets the price and its flow does not change is not unique: it can lie up to 2 × ramp_cost / step duration [CUR/MWh] above or below that unit's marginal cost. A negative ramp_cost is an error. - ramp_speed_up - [share of capacity per minute] Maximum ramp up speed, as a share of capacity per minute. Constant.

    The limit. Between two consecutive time steps the flow may rise by at most ramp_speed_up × 60 × (average duration of the two steps in hours) × capacity. The capacity is that of the side: capacity_max_coeff × capacity on an output, the input limit of input_share_max on an input. A speed of 1/60 or more on hourly steps never binds within a period.

    Coarse time steps. Time steps aggregated with a solve's new_stepduration ramp from each other as consecutive steps. A unit or connection between coarse nodes (a group's new_stepduration) ramps between its coarse steps, with their durations. With 24-h steps, a speed of 1/1440 or more never binds within a period.

    Where the ramp starts. No limit applies across a gap in the timeline, at the start of a representative period or at the first step of a solve. A period whose time steps continue the previous period's on the same timeline ramps from the previous period's last step. Examples are consecutive parts of one timeline, or a forecast branch that continues the timeline in a stochastic solve. Periods that reuse the same timeset (the usual multi-year setup) do not ramp from each other. A rolling window continues from the flow of the previous window where it continues the previous window's last realized step on the timeline, by position in time. A solve with longer time steps continues the finer step that ends where its own previous step ends.

    Units with online variables. The ramp applies to the capacity online in both steps. Units starting or stopping in the step are limited by the start-up and shutdown limit instead, not by the online capacity's own ramp. That limit caps the output in the step the unit starts in to min_load + ½ × ramp_speed_up × 60 × step duration of the started capacity (and uses ramp_speed_down in the step before a shutdown). See How to add a minimum load, start-up and ramp.

    Infeasible combinations. An online unit with a ramp limit can be held online by something else: the online status that a stochastic realization solve fixes, a user constraint on its units online (constraint_online_coeff), a minimum-uptime carry, a fixed profile, or a min_load time series that jumps more than the step's ramp room. If its reachable flow then moves faster than the ramp allows, the model is infeasible. Units without online variables behave the same way.

  • ramp_speed_down - [share of capacity per minute] Maximum ramp down speed, as ramp_speed_up for decreases. Constant.

  • constraint_flow_coeff - A map of coefficients (Index: constraint name, value: coefficient) placing this flow variable on the left side of a user-defined constraint. Applied per timestep to the directional flow between the unit and the node. See User constraints.
  • startup_input_method (unit--inputNode) - [choice, default just_input] What the input arc supplies. just_input: the normal input flow. startup_and_input: the normal input flow, and each start-up of the unit also takes startup_energy × MW started from this node. startup_only: only the start-up energy; the arc has no flow.

  • startup_energy (unit--inputNode) - [MWh per MW started] Energy taken from the input node per MW of capacity started up (start-ups × unit size). Used with startup_input_method startup_and_input or startup_only. Constant or period.

    What it is for. A start-up uses energy that the running unit does not: a coal unit is started on oil, a gas turbine burns gas to warm up, a CSP turbine takes steam from the tank before it delivers power. The start-up input can be fuel, heat (for example from the tank of a CSP plant) or electricity. With startup_only the node is used only for start-ups (oil for a coal unit); with startup_and_input the unit's normal input also supplies its start-ups (the tank of a CSP turbine). See How to give a unit a start-up fuel or start-up heat.

    The term. Each step, the node balance takes v_startup × startup_energy × unit size [MWh]: an event, so the step length does not enter, as for startup_cost. Linear start-ups take a share of it, binary start-ups whole units' worth; a linear unit stays an LP. A unit with coarse time steps (new_stepduration) starts at the first time step of its coarse step. The start-up input is priced as the node's commodity (also on a price ladder), counts in the CO2 price and the CO2 caps of the node's groups (also when it is the group's only emitter) and in the rolling carry of the CO2 caps.

    A startup_only arc. It is not an arc of the model: it has no flow and no part in the unit's conversion, capacity, input shares, ramps, reserves, profiles or minimum load, and it does not count as an input for the unit's method (a coal unit with one fuel input and an oil start-up arc stays a one-input unit). A unit whose every input is startup_only is modelled like a unit without inputs; FlexTool warns when it has no profile. conversion_flow_coeff, input_share_*, ramp parameters, other_operational_cost, inertia_constant and is_non_synchronous on such an arc have no effect (a warning).

    Not included. The start-up input is not part of constraint_flow_coeff (a startup_only arc with it is an error; a startup_and_input arc gets a warning), of flow groups (max_instant_flow, max_cumulative_flow, …; a startup_only arc in a flowGroup is an error), of input shares or of the capacity margin. A reduce_unit_detail_method that leaves out the online variables (online, online_ramps) also leaves out the start-up input, as the start-up cost: an investment solve at that level under-counts both. Under the integers levels a start-up input is a use of the online variables, so the unit keeps them.

    Checks. Errors: startup_energy on a just_input arc, a negative startup_energy, a start-up role on a unit without online variables (startup_method no_startup and no minimum_time_method), constraint_flow_coeff on a startup_only arc and a unit__node__profile, flowGroup__unit__node or reserve__upDown__unit__node entity on a startup_only arc. Warnings: a start-up role without startup_energy, flow parameters on a startup_only arc, a start-up node of type commodity that is no commodity's node (the energy is taken from nowhere), a unit whose every input is startup_only and that has no profile, and the constraints and flow groups that leave out the start-up input of a startup_and_input arc.

    Results. unit_startup_energy__dt [MWh in the step] and unit_startup_energy__d [MWh/a] per unit and start-up node (unit__node startup_energy_t / startup_energy_annualized in the results database). The unit's input from the node (unit__inputNode__dt / __d), the commodity cost, the CO2 emissions and costs and the node balance (To units) include the start-up input; a startup_only arc has a column of its own in the unit input tables. The capacity factors count the flow only.

docs.title: Choosing the coefficients: typical patterns
docs.text:
case conversion_flow_coeff capacity_max_coeff / input_share_max capacity_min_coeff / input_share_min standard unit, 1 source + 1 sink 1 (default) 1 (default) 0 (default; the unit's min_load applies to its output) hydro pass-through (water sink on hydro plant) 0 (tie the flow with a user constraint) any (skipped) any (skipped) extraction CHP, electricity output (premium, costs more input energy per unit) 2 (say) 1 0 (default) — or 1 if electricity alone must reach min_load while online (this rules out the pure-heat mode) extraction CHP, heat output (byproduct, cheap per unit of input energy) 0.2 (say) 1 (allow full-heat mode) 0 (default; allows the zero-heat pure-condensing mode) input with lower energy content (e.g. 1.5 flow units per MWh of input energy) 1.5 input_share_max 1 (it can still run the unit alone) – two inputs, each limited to 60 % of the full-load input 1 input_share_max 0.6 on each input – an input must supply at least 30 % of the unit's input while it runs 1 1 (default) input_share_min 0.3 on that input

Output coefficients do not change the caps

On a unit--outputNode, conversion_flow_coeff acts only in the efficiency (conversion) equation. The node balance gets the flow itself. The capacity caps come from capacity_max_coeff. The floors come from the unit's min_load (on the sum of its outputs) and the optional capacity_min_coeff of each output.

docs.title: Units constrained by profiles
docs.text:
Some generators (e.g. VRE) are not converting energy from one node to the other. Instead, their generation is determined (or limited) by a specific generation profile set by a profile entity with a profile_method, thats state whether the profile forces an upper_limit, lower_limit or equality. Finally profile entity is given a profile value: constant, period (applies to all timesteps of that period), time, period+time or stochastic time. A 1-D map without index_name is read as a period map when its keys are periods and as a time series when they are time steps; keys of both kinds stop the run with an error (set index_name to period or time). A period+time map (two levels) whose outer level has no index_name is read as period+time when its outer keys are periods; outer keys that are time steps, of both kinds or no period stop the run with an error. Its inner level is read as the time steps whether or not it has index_name time (also under an outer level named period); inner keys without index_name that are periods stop the run with an error. A period map that leaves out a period of the solves gives the profile 0 in that period, with a warning. One needs to use node__profile, unit__node__profile or connection__profile to apply the profile to specific energy flow (or storage state in the case of node__profile).

profile_method defaults to upper_limit on unit__node__profile and to none (the profile is not applied) on node__profile and connection__profile. A profile without a value in the scenario is 0, so an upper_limit or fixed link to it would hold the flow (or the storage state) at 0: FlexTool stops with an error that names the link and the profile, and the alternatives that hold the profile's value when the scenario does not include them. Give the profile a value in an alternative of the scenario, set profile_method lower_limit (a floor of 0 does nothing) or none, or remove the link. A node__profile or connection__profile link with no profile_method gets a warning (an explicit none does not). A profile above 1.5 on an upper_limit / fixed unit link gets a warning (values above 1.5 look like percentages: the profile is a share of the capacity, 0.35, not 35). Capacity factors slightly above 1 are not reported.

docs.title: User constraints
docs.text: A user constraint is a linear row that you write yourself. It ties flows, storage states, units online and capacities of nodes, units and connections together, for example a fixed ratio between two capacities or a minimum share of a flow.

docs.title: The constraint entity
docs.text:
• constraint: a user-defined linear constraint between flow, state, units-online and capacity variables on nodes, units and connections. The left-hand side is assembled by tagging the relevant entities with the matching coefficient parameter (constraint_flow_coeff on unit__inputNode / unit__outputNode / connection__node, constraint_state_coeff on node, constraint_online_coeff on unit / connection, constraint_invested_capacity_coeff / constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff / constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff / constraint_capacity_coeff / constraint_retired_capacity_coeff on node / unit / connection); the constraint entity itself carries:

    • sense - The sense of the constraint: greater_than, less_than, or equal.
    • constant - Right-hand side of the user constraint (default 0). A period map gives each period its own value; it must cover every period of the solve (a missing period is an error). Constant or period.
    • constraint_period_method - per_timestep (default) or period_total: whether the constraint holds in each time step or once for the total of each period (see Rows per period or per time step).

Capacity terms, all in MW (MWh for storage nodes) and multiplied by the coefficient: invested (constraint_invested_capacity_coeff) is the capacity that comes online in the period, in construction (constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff) the capacity decided but not yet operating, retired (constraint_retired_capacity_coeff) what is retired in it, pre-built (constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff) the capacity in service at the start of the period and capacity (constraint_capacity_coeff) the capacity in service in the period — the same capacity that limits the flows. Capacity = pre-built + invested − retired holds with or without a construction lead time; capacity in construction is not in capacity.

Online (constraint_online_coeff) is the number of units online in each time step (of virtual_unitsize; without it, the largest existing capacity, else 1000 MW).

A constraint with only capacity terms is written once per period, otherwise once per time step (rows process_constraint_{equal,less_than,greater_than}_period with dimensions (constraint, period) in the output_horizon raw dump, instead of (constraint, period, time)). With constraint_period_method period_total, the constraint is written once per period over the period's total (rows process_constraint_{equal,less_than,greater_than}_period_total, dimensions (constraint, period)). For plain sums of capacity with a period trajectory, the group parameters (invest_max_period, retire_max_period, cumulative_max_capacity and their minimum counterparts) are simpler: user constraints are for weighted, cross-class and ratio forms.

docs.title: The coefficient parameters
docs.text:
Map parameters. Every coefficient is a map: the index is the name of a constraint, the value is the coefficient. One entity can take part in several constraints with different coefficients. An entity takes part in a constraint only if it has a coefficient for it.

The row. The model multiplies each variable by its coefficient and adds the terms up on the left-hand side. The sense compares that sum with the constant. The unit of the row is your choice: the coefficients carry it (for example, a coefficient of 1 on a flow keeps the row in MW).

Parameter Set on Term it puts in the row Unit of the variable constraint_flow_coeff unit__inputNode, unit__outputNode, connection__node The flow between the unit or connection and the node, in each time step. MW constraint_state_coeff node (storage) The storage state of the node, in each time step. MWh constraint_online_coeff unit, connection (with online variables) The number of units online, in each time step. One unit is virtual_unitsize; without it, the largest existing capacity, else 1000 MW. Whole numbers with binary startup, continuous with linear. count of units constraint_invested_capacity_coeff node, unit, connection The capacity that comes online in the period. Without a construction lead time, this is the capacity invested in that period. MW (MWh for a storage node) constraint_in_construction_capacity_coeff node, unit, connection The capacity in construction in the period: decided, but not yet online. It is zero without a construction lead time. MW (MWh for a storage node) constraint_retired_capacity_coeff node, unit, connection The capacity retired in the period. MW (MWh for a storage node) constraint_cumulative_pre_built_capacity_coeff node, unit, connection The capacity in service at the start of the period: existing capacity plus capacity that came online in earlier periods, minus earlier retirements. MW (MWh for a storage node) constraint_capacity_coeff node, unit, connection The capacity in service in the period: existing plus investments still in service minus retirements. Capacity in construction is not included. MW (MWh for a storage node)

The full descriptions are with each entity: nodes, units, unit flows and connections.

docs.title: Rows per period or per time step
docs.text:
Capacity terms only. A constraint that has only capacity terms is the same in every time step of a period. The model writes it once per period, and a period map in constant gives each period its own right-hand side.

Flow, state or online terms. A constraint with at least one constraint_flow_coeff, constraint_state_coeff or constraint_online_coeff is written once per time step. Any capacity terms in it take the value of their period in each of those time steps.

Period total. With constraint_period_method period_total, the constraint is written once per period, over the sum of all the time steps of the period. Use it for limits on energy over a period, such as "gas covers at most 15 % of the CSP output over the year" or "a unit runs at most 30 % of the year at full capacity". The max_cumulative_flow parameters of a group are a simpler choice for a limit on the flow of a group alone; they take the limit as an average MW.

docs.title: Period total: units and weighting
docs.text:
Annual equivalent. A period_total row is per year, like co2_max_period. Each time step's terms are multiplied by its duration (hours) and its timestep weight, summed over the period, and divided by the period's share of a year. So a flow term is in MWh per year, and the constant is per year too (for example MWh/yr). For a solve that covers a whole year, this is the plain total of the period. For representative periods, the timestep weights scale each modelled step to the time it stands for, so the row counts the whole year. A share constraint (constant 0) is the same whatever the scaling.

Units online. An online term counts unit-hours per year (units online × hours), for example "at least 4000 online hours per year". With linear startup the units online are continuous, so the row counts unit-hours of fractional units.

Capacity terms. Every capacity term (invested, in construction, retired, pre-built, capacity), with its existing capacity, is multiplied by the hours of the year that the period's steps stand for (8760 for a whole year; the model computes it from the step durations and weights). Each term is then its per-step quantity summed over the period, so the coefficients keep their per-step meaning: a flow − 0.3 × capacity ≤ 0 row caps the annual capacity factor of the unit at 30 %. A period_total constraint with only capacity terms is the per_timestep per-period row × H (the hours above), so its constant is in MWh per year.

State terms are not allowed. A storage state summed over the time steps of a period is not an energy. A period_total constraint with a constraint_state_coeff stops the run with an error naming the constraint and the node; use per_timestep for constraints on storage states.

Rolling solves. A row needs the whole period. In a rolling solve, the row is written in a roll that realizes the whole period (its rolling_solve_jump is a multiple of the period length and starts at a period start); a period that a roll holds only in its look-ahead in part gets no row in that roll. So the look-ahead tail of a roll is free of the constraint (unlike a per_timestep constraint, which holds in the look-ahead steps too): for example, gas limited by a yearly share is not limited in the look-ahead, which can change how the roll uses storage at the end of its realized part. When the rolls of a rolling solve do not each realize whole periods, that solve leaves the period_total constraints out and the run log warns, naming the constraints, the solve and the period. A typical case is an investment solve on representative periods followed by a rolling dispatch solve with daily rolls: the investment solve enforces the constraint, the dispatch does not. When no solve of the run enforces the constraint, the run stops with an error.

Chains of solves. Each solve writes the rows of its own whole periods, so an investment solve and a later dispatch solve both enforce the constraint, each on its own time steps. Because the row is annualised, the two are comparable. A greater_than row in a dispatch solve has no slack: if the investment solve built too little for it, the dispatch solve is infeasible (as with a per_timestep row).

Stochastic solves. Each forecast branch period has its own row: every forecast meets the limit on its own, without a probability weight.

Dual. The dual of a period_total row (in the output_horizon raw dump) is in objective units per unit of the constant per year.

docs.title: Example: storage size tied to turbine capacity
docs.text:
Goal. A pumped-hydro reservoir must hold 6 hours of its turbine capacity: storage capacity (MWh) = 6 × turbine capacity (MW). Both can be invested in.

Data.

  • constraint reservoir_6h: sense equal, constant 0
  • node reservoir: constraint_capacity_coeff Map (reservoir_6h | 1)
  • unit turbine: constraint_capacity_coeff Map (reservoir_6h | -6)

The row. In each period: 1 × reservoir capacity (MWh) − 6 × turbine capacity (MW) = 0. The row has only capacity terms, so it is written once per period. It counts existing capacity, investments and retirements, so it holds for the whole capacity in service, not only for the new build. To tie only the new build, use constraint_invested_capacity_coeff instead.

docs.title: Example: minimum share of a flow
docs.text:
Goal. In every time step, at least 40 % of the electricity flowing into node elec comes from unit wind. The only other unit that feeds elec is coal_plant.

The algebra. wind ≥ 0.4 × (wind + coal) is the same as 0.6 × wind − 0.4 × coal ≥ 0.

Data.

  • constraint wind_share: sense greater_than, constant 0
  • unit__outputNode (wind | elec): constraint_flow_coeff Map (wind_share | 0.6)
  • unit__outputNode (coal_plant | elec): constraint_flow_coeff Map (wind_share | -0.4)

The row. The row has flow terms, so it is written once per time step: the share must hold in each time step, not only on average. Every unit that feeds the node has to be in the constraint, or its flow is left out of the total.

docs.title: Example: a 15 % share over the year
docs.text:
Goal. Over each year, the gas backup gas_backup of a CSP plant produces at most 15 % of the CSP output. In a single time step it may produce more, as long as the yearly total stays within the share.

The algebra. gas ≤ 0.15 × csp over the year is the same as gas − 0.15 × csp ≤ 0, summed over the time steps.

Data.

  • constraint gas_share: sense less_than, constant 0, constraint_period_method period_total
  • unit__outputNode (gas_backup | elec): constraint_flow_coeff Map (gas_share | 1)
  • unit__outputNode (csp | elec): constraint_flow_coeff Map (gas_share | -0.15)

The row. Once per period: Σ_t (gas − 0.15 × csp) × duration × weight / period share ≤ 0. For four 1-hour steps with CSP output 100, 100, 50 and 0 MW (250 MWh), gas may produce 0.15 × 250 = 37.5 MWh in total, in any of the steps (the row is annualised, so for a share the period length does not matter: both sides are × 2190 here). With per_timestep, gas could produce only 7.5 MW in the third step (15 % of 50 MW) and nothing when the CSP plant is off.

docs.title: Example: two of three units online
docs.text:
Goal. In every time step, at least two of the three units g1, g2, g3 are online (for example, to keep spinning capacity), whatever the demand.

Data.

  • constraint two_online: sense greater_than, constant 2
  • unit g1, g2, g3: startup_method binary, constraint_online_coeff Map (two_online | 1)

The row. In each time step: online(g1) + online(g2) + online(g3) ≥ 2. The row counts units, so it is the same for one entity of three units: existing 3, virtual_unitsize 100 and constraint_online_coeff Map (two_online | 1). With linear startup, the count is continuous: ≥ 2 then means at least two units' worth of online capacity, with the minimum load applying to it, not two whole machines. A coefficient on a unit without online variables (startup_method unset and no minimum_time_method) stops the run with an error naming the unit and the constraint.

docs.title: Solver selection in FlexTool
docs.text: FlexTool can dispatch each solve in a scenario tree to a different LP / MIP solver. The default — and what every existing scenario continues to use without any extra configuration — is HiGHS, the open-source solver that ships with FlexTool. Commercial solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, COPT) are opt-in: install the vendor's Python wrapper, obtain a licence, then set solver = "<name>" on the affected solve entity in the Spine database. Solver choice is per-solve, not global, so a scenario can mix (for example) a large dispatch LP on Gurobi with a small validation solve on HiGHS.

docs.title: Supported solvers
docs.text:
Solver License HiGHS Free, open source Gurobi Commercial / academic free / WLS CPLEX Commercial / academic free / subscription Xpress Commercial / community (5000 var/row cap) COPT Commercial / academic free

Per-solver installation, licensing, and verification:

  • HiGHS — bundled, no setup
  • Gurobi
  • CPLEX
  • Xpress
  • COPT

PLEASE NOTE: The instructions can be out-of-date. Let us know if this is the case by opening an issue.

docs.title: How to switch solvers
docs.text:
Solver selection lives on the solve entity in the Spine database, in the solve_advanced parameter group. Each parameter is optional and falls back to a documented default if omitted, so existing scenarios behave exactly as they did before this feature was added.

The DB-level solver parameters are, with their per-solver defaults:

Parameter Default One-line description solver "highs" Solver name from [highs, gurobi, cplex, xpress, copt] solver_arguments empty Map Raw option name → value pairs forwarded verbatim to the solver solver_mip_gap unset Relative MIP gap; normalised across solvers solver_precommand unset Not used: FlexTool never runs it (kept so older databases still read); a value gives a warning, see Solver precommand

A handful of options that used to be DB parameters are now controlled by CLI flags on flextool (they apply to the whole run rather than per solve):

CLI flag Former DB param (removed in v56; a stored value was dropped) Values / notes --solver-time-limit solver_time_limit Seconds per solve, on every solver (HiGHS time_limit, Gurobi TimeLimit, CPLEX timelimit, Xpress MAXTIME, COPT TimeLimit); unset means no limit. See Time limit. --solver-mip-gap Relative MIP gap of every solve, on every solver (HiGHS mip_rel_gap, Gurobi MIPGap, CPLEX mip tolerances mipgap, Xpress MIPRELSTOP, COPT RelGap); wins over the solve's solver_mip_gap --solver-config-dir The folder of the solver option files; see Where the option files come from --highs-threads solver_threads HiGHS only: integer thread count (default 1); >1 enables HiGHS parallel mode --solver-log-level solver_log_level silent hides the log of every solver; normal (default) shows it; verbose is HiGHS only

--presolve, --highs-threads, --user-bound-scale and --solver-log-level verbose are HiGHS options. When one of them is given and a solve runs on a commercial solver, the run warns once: set the solver's own parameter in the solve's solver_arguments or in its option file instead. Commercial solvers take their thread count from their option file (for example Threads in gurobi.opt); --threads does not change it.

The environment variables FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_TIME_LIMIT and FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_MIP_GAP are the twins of the two flags (the flag wins). The older names FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_TIME_LIMIT and FLEXTOOL_HIGHS_MIP_GAP still work, for HiGHS only. See Environment variables.

Example — set Gurobi on a single solve, with a 60-second time limit on each solve of the run:

solve entity:  yearly_dispatch
  solve_advanced.solver = "gurobi"

flextool <input_db_url> --solver-time-limit 60

Set the DB parameter in Spine Toolbox by selecting the solve entity, opening its parameter editor, finding the solve_advanced group, and entering the values above. Unspecified parameters take their defaults.

docs.title: Solver precommand is not run
docs.text:
FlexTool 3 ran the solve's solver_precommand in front of the CPLEX call, for example to reserve a floating licence for the solve. FlexTool 4 never runs it: a command stored in a database would run on the computer of anyone who opens that database and presses Run, so a database from someone else could run any program. A database that still has a value loads and solves as before, with a warning once per solve and run that the command is not run.

To hold a floating licence, use your solver's own licence server setup (for example a Gurobi token server set in gurobi.lic, or the licence server in the licence file of CPLEX, Xpress or COPT); the solver then checks a licence out and back in for the solve by itself. A solver wrapper set on this computer (never in a database) is planned for a later release.

docs.title: The parameters in detail
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description solver str "highs" Solver name. Must be one of highs, gurobi, cplex, xpress, copt. solver_arguments map empty Map of option name → value passed verbatim to the underlying solver. Use this for any solver-native option that is not one of the convenience knobs below. Raw options always override the convenience knobs on key collision. solver_mip_gap float unset Relative MIP optimality gap (e.g. 0.01 for 1 %). Translated to each solver's native parameter (MIPGap / mip tolerances mipgap / MIPRELSTOP / RelGap / mip_rel_gap). --solver-mip-gap wins over it. solver_precommand str unset Not used: FlexTool never runs this command (FlexTool 3 ran it in front of CPLEX). The parameter is kept only so that older databases still read; a value gives a warning once per solve. See Solver precommand.

The corresponding CLI flags (--solver-time-limit, --solver-mip-gap, --highs-threads, --solver-log-level) are documented in the table above.

docs.title: Authoring solver_arguments in Spine
docs.text:
solver_arguments is a Spine Map of string keys to string-or-float values. Keys are the solver's own parameter names (e.g. Presolve for Gurobi or presolve for HiGHS), values are whatever that solver expects.

Example (Gurobi, in Spine Toolbox's map editor):

solver_arguments:
  Presolve   = 2
  Method     = 2
  Heuristics = 0.1

These are passed through untouched, within the limits of What the database may set. Parameter names match the way the solver reads them: without regard to case (mipgap and MIPGap are one parameter); Gurobi also ignores _ (MIP_Gap is MIPGap) and Xpress an XPRS_ prefix; for CPLEX a dotted name such as mip.tolerances.mipgap is the same as mip tolerances mipgap. Write CPLEX names in full: an abbreviation is not matched to its full name when the layers are merged (the file and folder parameters below excepted: they are recognised abbreviated too). What a solver does with a misspelt name is the solver's own: Gurobi ignores it with a message, and FlexTool repeats that message as a warning naming where the name was set.

FlexTool's results are not affected by a solver's file parameters (they are in output_parquet/<scenario>/ and the outputs you chose). Gurobi's ResultFile is FlexTool's own: FlexTool names the result file and reads the solution from it, so a ResultFile set anywhere is ignored with a warning. A commercial solver's log is saved as <work folder>/solve_data/subprocess/<solve>.log (see below). HiGHS' log is part of the run's console output, which flextool-run and the FlexTool window save in the run's log, output_parquet/<scenario>/_run.log.

docs.title: What the database may set
docs.text:
An input database can come from someone else, so FlexTool trusts solver_arguments and solver_mip_gap less than the files and the command line of your own computer. The solver option files (solver_config/<solver>.opt), the flags and the environment variables keep full paths and server parameters; from the database:

  • Ordinary parameters (gaps, tolerances, methods, thread counts, switches) are taken as they are.
  • A parameter that names a file or folder takes only a plain file name: ASCII letters, digits and _ . + -, starting with a letter, digit or _, with no /, \, : or ... The file is written in the solve's work folder, <work folder>/solve_data/subprocess/. A full path is refused. These are the parameters whose name contains file, dir or path, and also:
Solver File and folder parameters HiGHS log_file, solution_file, read_solution_file, read_basis_file, write_basis_file, write_model_file, write_presolved_model_file, write_iis_model_file, mip_improving_solution_file Gurobi ResultFile, LogFile, SolFiles, NodefileDir, InputFile, ConcurrentSettings, MultiObjSettings, TuneBaseSettings, TuneIgnoreSettings, TuneParams, Record CPLEX logfile, workdir, output intsolfileprefix (also abbreviated, as the Interactive Optimizer accepts) and names starting with read or write Xpress TUNERMETHODFILE, TUNEROUTPUTPATH, TUNERSESSIONNAME COPT LogFile

Names are matched as the solver reads them (above), so Log_File for Gurobi or XPRS_TUNEROUTPUTPATH for Xpress is the same parameter. A number or a switch in such a parameter (Gurobi NodefileStart 0.5) passes. - Gurobi server, cloud and licence parameters are refused: ComputeServer, ServerPassword, ServerTimeout, the CS... Cluster Manager parameters (CSManager, CSAPIAccessID, CSAPISecret, CSGroup, CSPriority, CSRouter, ...), the Cloud... Instant Cloud parameters, the WLS... Web License Service parameters, TokenServer, TSPort, LicenseID, UserName, WorkerPool and WorkerPassword.

The error names the parameter, its value and the solve. Put a file path or a server parameter in the solver's option file, solver_config/<solver>.opt (or that file in a folder given with --solver-config-dir), which keeps them. The checks against extra commands (no line breaks, spaces, quotes, ;, #, = or a backslash at the end) apply to every source.

docs.title: Per-solver baseline .opt files
docs.text:
Every solver gets a baseline parameter file in a solver_config/ folder (which folder: see Where the option files come from). These are user-local files, not committed to the repo: each ships in the wheel as a solver_config/<solver>.opt.template, and flextool-update and the GUI seed the workspace's solver_config/<solver>.opt from its template (and re-seed any that are missing). The runtime files are gitignored, so you can edit them — or delete one to reset it to the bundled default — with zero git-committed change. The FlexTool window (at start) and flextool-update replace a workspace solver_config/<solver>.opt that is an unedited copy of an earlier FlexTool default with the current one; an edited file is never touched. The option values are the same, so no solve changes.

Solver Baseline file Native format HiGHS solver_config/highs.opt key=value per line, # comments Gurobi solver_config/gurobi.opt ParamName value per line, # comments CPLEX solver_config/cplex.opt name value per line; name uses interactive set syntax (e.g. mip tolerances mipgap) Xpress solver_config/xpress.opt CONTROL value per line COPT solver_config/copt.opt ParamName value per line

FlexTool reads results from the solver directly and needs no HiGHS solution file, so write_solution_to_file, solution_file and write_solution_style are ignored in highs.opt (older templates set them; projects created then still have the lines). To have HiGHS write a solution file anyway, set these options in the solve's solver_arguments (solution_file takes a plain file name there; the file is written in <work folder>/solve_data/subprocess/).

FlexTool reads each solver's baseline once at the start of the run, overlays the solve's solver_mip_gap, its solver_arguments Map and the run's flags parameter by parameter (one value per parameter, the highest layer wins), writes the merged result next to the MPS file (the record of what the solver received) and feeds it to the solver via the per-solver mechanism:

Solver How FlexTool feeds the merged file to the CLI HiGHS --options=<file> argv flag on the flextool.cli.cmd_solve_mps subprocess Gurobi gurobi_cl <Name>=<value> ... ResultFile=<sol> <mps>: one Name=value argument per line of the file CPLEX Each line emitted as set <name> <value> on the interactive optimizer's stdin before read Xpress Each line emitted as setControl <NAME> <value> on the optimizer console's stdin before readprob COPT Each line emitted as set <ParamName> <value> on copt_cmd's stdin before read

Override precedence (highest wins), the same for every solver:

  1. The run's flags: --solver-time-limit and --solver-mip-gap (or FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_TIME_LIMIT / FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_MIP_GAP; the GUI's time limit is sent as the flag). HiGHS also takes --highs-threads, --presolve, --solver-log-level and --threads here (a commercial solver's log is hidden by --solver-log-level silent too, but that is not one of its parameters).
  2. Raw solver_arguments entries on the solve.
  3. Translated convenience knobs (solver_mip_gap).
  4. The baseline file <solver>.opt.

For HiGHS every solve receives this one layered set: warm and cold solves, --save-memory and the subprocess solve of warm=False alike. FlexTool's own determinism defaults sit below the baseline file.

Before each solve the run prints what the solver receives: Solver args: for HiGHS (the options set above FlexTool's defaults), and for a commercial solver Solver args (<solver>): with every parameter under its native name, for example Solver args (gurobi): Threads=1, MIPGap=0.001, TimeLimit=1800.

A commercial solver's program runs in <work folder>/solve_data/subprocess/. FlexTool writes there the model (<solve>.mps), the parameters passed (<solve>.opt) and, for CPLEX, Xpress and COPT, the command script it pipes to the program (<solve>.script). To replay a solve by hand, run the program in that folder with the script as its input, for example cd solve_data/subprocess && cplex < y2020_dispatch.script. The solver's result file and its own log file (gurobi.log, cplex.log) are written there too.

The solver's log is shown as the solver writes it, in the terminal, the FlexTool window (greyed, like HiGHS' log) and the run log, after a line Running <solver> (<program>), and it is saved as <solve>.log in the same folder. Like the other files there, <solve>.log holds the last roll of a rolling solve. A failed solve's message points to the log instead of repeating it. With --solver-log-level silent the log is not shown (nor the Running line), but FlexTool still reads it to know how the solve ended, saves it, and a failure message then carries its last 20 lines. If FlexTool stops the solver (the time-limit watchdog, Ctrl-C, a failure), it also stops the processes the solver started.

docs.title: Where the option files come from
docs.text:
A run takes all its <solver>.opt files from one solver_config folder, the first of:

  1. --solver-config-dir PATH (the GUI always sends it: the workspace's solver_config, or the folder of FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR when that variable is set for the GUI);
  2. the FLEXTOOL_SOLVER_CONFIG_DIR environment variable;
  3. solver_config/ next to the input database, then, for a database in a GUI project (<workspace>/projects/<project>/input_sources/), the workspace's solver_config/. The search goes no further up, so a solver_config folder somewhere above an unrelated database is never picked up;
  4. for a Spine Toolbox run with --project-folder-file, the solver_config/ of that Toolbox project;
  5. solver_config/ in the current folder;
  6. none found: FlexTool's defaults (the shipped templates), with a warning that lists the folders tried.

Tiers 3 to 5 count a folder only when it holds at least one <solver>.opt. They skip solver_config/ in the current folder when every .opt in it is an unedited FlexTool template (of this or an earlier version) and the current folder is not a FlexTool folder: FlexTool 4.3 and older left such a copy in the folder a run was started from. The run then takes the next tier and warns, naming the skipped folder; to use your own option files, pass --solver-config-dir <the folder with your files>, and delete the skipped folder to stop the warning. The FlexTool folder itself (the workspace, which holds templates/project_folder.txt) is never skipped: its solver_config/ is the folder the FlexTool window uses, and a run from there uses it without a warning, edited or not. In the chosen folder, a solver whose file is missing uses its shipped default. A Spine Toolbox run (whose Data Store is the workspace's input_data.sqlite) therefore uses the workspace's solver_config, even though Toolbox runs the tool in a temporary folder.

The run header and the log say which folder was used and why, for example:

Solver config:  /home/me/flextool/solver_config (next to the input database)

The run reads the files once at its start: every roll and solve of the run uses them as they were then, and an edit during the run reaches only the next run. The files the run used are copied to <work folder>/solve_data/solver_config/ as its record; the copy is written afresh every run and never read back. Up to FlexTool 4.3 runs read a copy in <work folder>/solver_config/; such a folder is no longer read as the work folder's copy (the run warns and names it when it differs from the files the run uses). When the work folder is also the current folder, the folder is tier 5: it is used when you have edited a file in it (or it is the FlexTool folder), and skipped, with a warning, while it holds only the templates 4.3 copied there. To run with the files of a particular folder, pass --solver-config-dir <folder>.

docs.title: Time limit
docs.text:
--solver-time-limit (and the GUI's time limit) applies to each solve separately: each roll of a rolling solve, and each master and region solve of a Benders decomposition, gets the full limit. The solver enforces it. When a solve stops at its time limit:

  • a MIP with a solution found keeps that solution, with a warning naming the solve and, when the solver reports it, the gap reached; the run goes on;
  • an LP, or a MIP without a solution, stops the run with an error;
  • in a Benders decomposition, a master or region solve stopped by its limit stops the run with an error, MIP or not: the decomposition needs each of its solves to be optimal.

Another limit or an interrupt (a node, iteration, solution or memory limit, or an aborted solve) is not a time limit: it stops the run, naming the solver's status, even with a solution. So does a solution the solver does not certify as optimal, such as CPLEX's "optimal with unscaled infeasibilities" or "optimal face unbounded".

FlexTool reads how a solve ended from the solver's result file (HiGHS, Gurobi's JSON result, CPLEX) or from its console log (COPT, Xpress; Gurobi when it writes a text result file). With COPT's log turned off (Logging 0 or LogToConsole 0), or a text Gurobi result with LogToConsole 0, a finished solve cannot be told from one stopped by a limit, so the run stops and says so: keep the log on (the shipped option files do). Xpress: FlexTool knows only its time limit and an unfinished solve, from the console and the print solution; another Xpress limit with a solution is not told apart.

FlexTool also stops a solver that has not finished well after its limit (after twice the limit plus 10 minutes), which only guards against a solver that hangs: reading the model and writing the result are not counted in the solver's own limit.

docs.title: Warm-start caveat
docs.text: The cross-solver dispatch always builds a fresh solver instance per call. HiGHS retains its existing warm-start fast path because FlexTool uses HiGHS directly (not via the cross-solver solve() entry point) when no solver parameter is set. Picking any non-HiGHS solver disables the in-process warm path for that solve: each sub-solve is built and solved through the cross-solver dispatch. Rolls of a rolling-horizon scenario are built anew on every solver (HiGHS reuses a built model only for an identical sub-solve), so the solver choice itself does not change how often the LP is built.

docs.title: Benders-decomposition caveat
docs.text:
decomposition_method = benders_regional is currently HiGHS-only. Setting a non-HiGHS solver on a Benders-decomposed scenario raises a FlexToolUserError at startup. The error names both the offending solve and the two remedies (either set solver = highs for that solve, or remove the Benders decomposition from the group).

This is an upstream constraint in polar-high: the Benders master is a persistent WarmProblem, and warm-LP machinery is HiGHS-only by design. Lifting the restriction is tracked separately; in the meantime FlexTool fails loudly rather than silently running on HiGHS.

The layered options above also reach the Benders master and every region subproblem. Benders' own settings stay on top of them: the region subproblems always run crossover (or the interior-point settings of the experimental interior-dual mode), and the per-solve HiGHS log is silenced. While the regions are solved in parallel (more than one worker), threads and parallel (--highs-threads) apply to the master only; the regions stay single-threaded so that the result does not depend on the worker count. HiGHS has one thread scheduler per process, so the master re-initialises it before each of its solves (polar-high 3.10.0 or later; with an older polar-high the thread count is not used while the regions run in parallel). A time limit (--solver-time-limit, or time_limit in solver_arguments) applies to each master and region solve separately, not to the whole decomposition. A master or region solve that stops at its limit stops the run (see "Time limit" above).

docs.title: Verifying which solvers are installed
docs.text:
To see which solver Python wrappers polar-high has detected on this system, run:

python -c "from polar_high.solvers import available_solvers; print(available_solvers)"

Example output on a developer machine with all five wrappers installed:

['gurobi', 'cplex', 'xpress', 'copt', 'highs']

A solver appears in available_solvers if its Python wrapper is importable. That is not the same as "the solver is usable" — license checks happen later, when FlexTool actually dispatches a solve. The most common failure mode is available_solvers lists (say) gurobi but the first solve raises a FlexToolUserError about a missing licence file; see the relevant per-solver page for the licence setup.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Setting solver without installing the wrapper. Run the verification command above before authoring solver = "gurobi" (or similar) on a solve. If the solver name is missing from available_solvers, the per-solver page has the pip install line you need.
  • Setting solver without a valid licence. The wrapper installs without one; the licence check only fires at solve time. FlexTool's error will point you at the licensing section of the solver page.
  • Mixing solvers without checking. A scenario tree can route each solve to a different solver, but every solve needs its own solver parameter if you want anything other than HiGHS. Unset solves stay on HiGHS.
  • Commercial solvers on very large models. A non-HiGHS solver is always given the model as an MPS file and run in its own process. The trade-off is bounded peak RSS (the Problem.write_mps writer caps ~2-3 GB on the largest LPs) at the cost of file I/O plus a fresh solver process per sub-solve.
  • Setting the same parameter in several places. One value reaches the solver, from the highest layer of the precedence list above. If you pass --solver-time-limit 60 and also set solver_arguments = {TimeLimit: 30} on a Gurobi solve, Gurobi sees TimeLimit = 60; without the flag it sees 30. A solver_arguments entry wins over solver_mip_gap and over the option file.
  • Xpress and integer variables. FlexTool's Xpress driver solves linear problems only; a solve with integer variables (integer investments, unit online variables) stops with a message. Use another solver for such solves.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
COPT (Cardinal Optimizer) from Cardinal Operations is a newer commercial linear, mixed-integer, second-order cone, and semidefinite programming solver. FlexTool writes each solve's model to an MPS file and runs COPT's command-line solver copt_cmd (found on PATH or in ~/copt/bin) on it in a separate process, giving every parameter as a set <ParamName> <value> command. FlexTool never imports coptpy directly.

Official site: https://www.copt.de/ (Cardinal Operations product portal). Also https://www.shanshu.ai/ offers licensing options.

docs.title: License options
docs.text:
• Commercial. Cardinal Operations sells perpetual and floating-server licences directly and through resellers.
  • Academic. Free for academic users. Request through the Cardinal Operations academic programme on the official site.
  • Cloud / WLS-style token licences. Cardinal supports floating-licence servers and token discovery, similar to Gurobi's WLS model.
  • Trial / community. A free trial is typically offered; specifics change with release. Check the vendor site.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the Python wrapper:

pip install coptpy

For licensing:

  1. Obtain copt.lic (node-locked) or floating-licence credentials from Cardinal Operations.
  2. Place copt.lic at the path indicated by the vendor installer, or set COPT_LICENSE_DIR to the directory containing it. Refer to the vendor's installation guide for the precise discovery order [FIXME: confirm URL].
  3. Floating-licence users configure the licence server endpoint per the COPT documentation; polar-high accepts a pre-built coptpy.Envr via the env= pass-through.

docs.title: HiGHS / COPT process-coexistence warning
docs.text:
COPT 8.x ships native code (coptpy.coptcore) that conflicts with highspy when both are loaded into the same Python interpreter: highspy.Highs.run() can segfault once coptpy has been imported.

polar-high auto-detects this situation and transparently routes COPT solves through the MPS-file fallback (HiGHS writes an MPS, the copt_cmd CLI is invoked as a subprocess) so the in-process load does not happen. This requires the standalone copt_cmd binary on PATH. If it is missing, FlexTool surfaces a clear "binary not found" error. The binary ships with the COPT distribution.

In a FlexTool scenario that uses only COPT (no HiGHS solves anywhere in the run), the in-process direct path is used.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
After installing coptpy, run:

python -c "from polar_high.solvers import available_solvers; print(available_solvers)"

Expected: 'copt' appears in the list.

['gurobi', 'cplex', 'xpress', 'copt', 'highs']

To verify the licence works:

python -c "import coptpy as cp; cp.Envr().createModel('test')"

A clean exit (no CoptError) means the licence is found.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
The error messages below are what FlexTool surfaces as FlexToolUserError. polar-high's COPT adapter classifies licence errors by both numeric errno and message keywords (because the published errno table is not as cleanly documented as Gurobi's).

  • No licence file found. CoptError with errno in the provisional licence range (2, 7, 8, 9) or a message containing "license", "licence", "token", or "expired". FlexTool shows: "Solver 'copt' is installed but its license check failed. Details: ...". Fix by placing copt.lic or setting COPT_LICENSE_DIR.
  • Licence expired. Same FlexTool message family with the vendor's expiry text. Renew through the Cardinal Operations licence portal.
  • Time limit reached. A MIP stopped at its time limit with a solution is kept with a warning; an LP, or a MIP without a solution, stops the run. See Time limit.
  • copt_cmd not on PATH (HiGHS-coexistence fallback). FlexTool shows: "Solver 'copt' returned an error: ..." with the cause naming the missing binary. Add the COPT distribution's bin directory to PATH, or run COPT solves from a process that does not also use HiGHS.

docs.title: How to set it in FlexTool
docs.text:
On the solve entity:

solve_advanced.solver         = "copt"
solve_advanced.solver_mip_gap = 0.005
solve_advanced.solver_arguments:
  Presolve   = 1
  LpMethod   = 2

flextool <input_db_url> --solver-time-limit 60 --solver-mip-gap 0.001

--solver-time-limit and --solver-mip-gap reach COPT as TimeLimit 60 and RelGap 0.001, over the solve's solver_mip_gap, its solver_arguments and copt.opt (precedence in Solver selection). Parameter names match without regard to case. The thread count comes from Threads in copt.opt; --threads and --highs-threads do not change it. The run prints what COPT receives in a Solver args (copt): line before each solve.

Verified install on: [empty]

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
IBM ILOG CPLEX is a long-established commercial linear, mixed-integer, and quadratic programming solver. FlexTool writes each solve's model to an MPS file and runs the CPLEX interactive optimizer (cplex, found on PATH or in ~/cplex/bin) on it in a separate process, giving every parameter as a set <name> <value> command. FlexTool itself never imports cplex directly.

Official site: https://www.ibm.com/products/ilog-cplex-optimization-studio

docs.title: License options
docs.text:
• Commercial. Perpetual or subscription licences via IBM and IBM partners.
  • Academic. Free for students, faculty, and staff at recognised institutions through the IBM Academic Initiative.
  • Subscription / cloud. IBM offers a subscription model with bundled cloud entitlements; details and SKU naming change over time — refer to the IBM product page for the current options.
  • Community Edition. A size-limited free version exists (limits change by release; check IBM's documentation). Not recommended for FlexTool models above toy size.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the Python wrapper:

pip install cplex

The PyPI cplex wheel embeds the runtime needed for typical single-machine use. If you have a system-wide CPLEX Studio installation (commercial or academic), use the setup.py shipped in <CPLEX_STUDIO_DIR>/cplex/python/<py-version>/<platform>/ instead:

cd <CPLEX_STUDIO_DIR>/cplex/python/<py-version>/<platform>
python setup.py install

The system-wide install path is the right one when you need licence features (FlexNet, ILM) that the wheel does not include.

Licence files are discovered automatically by the CPLEX runtime. For FlexNet licences, set ILOG_LICENSE_FILE to the licence file or @server syntax for a floating licence. Academic users typically install via the IBM Academic Initiative installer, which writes a licence as part of the install.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
After installing the wrapper, run:

python -c "from polar_high.solvers import available_solvers; print(available_solvers)"

Expected: 'cplex' appears in the list.

['gurobi', 'cplex', 'xpress', 'copt', 'highs']

To verify the licence is found:

python -c "import cplex; cplex.Cplex().solve()"

A clean exit (no CplexSolverError / CplexError) means the licence is discoverable.

docs.title: Authoring solver_arguments for CPLEX
docs.text:
Write the parameter names of the interactive optimizer's set command, in full and with spaces (mip tolerances mipgap). A dotted name (mip.tolerances.mipgap, the Python-API spelling) is read as the spaced one; an abbreviation (mip tol mipg) is passed as written and does not replace the full name from another layer.

solver_arguments:
  timelimit                = 60
  mip tolerances mipgap    = 0.01
  threads                  = 8

--solver-time-limit (CPLEX timelimit) and --solver-mip-gap (mip tolerances mipgap) win over these; solver_mip_gap is below them.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
The error messages below are what FlexTool surfaces as FlexToolUserError.

  • No licence found. CplexSolverError with code 1016 (CPXERR_NO_LICENSE). FlexTool shows: "Solver 'cplex' is installed but its license check failed. Details: ..." with the vendor's message about a missing or unreadable licence. Fix by installing the licence file or setting ILOG_LICENSE_FILE.
  • ILM / subscription failure. Code 32024 (and other 32000-range codes). Same FlexTool licence-error message family. Re-authenticate your IBM Cloud subscription or refresh the ILM token.
  • Unknown CPLEX parameter. A set command CPLEX does not know is reported in the solver output; FlexTool does not check CPLEX's names. The names are in the IBM CPLEX parameters reference (https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/icos/22.1.0?topic=cplex-list-parameters).
  • Time limit reached. A MIP stopped at its time limit with a solution is kept with a warning; an LP, or a MIP without a solution, stops the run. See Time limit.

docs.title: How to set it in FlexTool
docs.text:
On the solve entity:

solve_advanced.solver         = "cplex"
solve_advanced.solver_mip_gap = 0.01
solve_advanced.solver_arguments:
  lpmethod   = 4
  preind     = 1

flextool <input_db_url> --solver-time-limit 60 --solver-mip-gap 0.001

--solver-time-limit and --solver-mip-gap reach CPLEX as timelimit 60 and mip tolerances mipgap 0.001, over the solve's solver_mip_gap, its solver_arguments and cplex.opt (precedence in Solver selection). Parameter names match without regard to case (and a dot is read as a space). The thread count comes from threads in cplex.opt; --threads and --highs-threads do not change it. The run prints what CPLEX receives in a Solver args (cplex): line before each solve.
